ox: Incorrect. Alanine's α-carbon carries four different groups: H, a CH₃ side chain, the amino group and the carboxyl group. Four different substituents make a stereocenter, so alanine exists as two mirror-image forms (L and D, or S and R). Natural L-alanine is S. A methyl group is small, but small is not the same as identical to H.

Incorrect. Proline's side chain loops back and bonds to its own α-nitrogen, forming a five-membered ring. Even so, the α-carbon still has four different neighbors: H, the ring CH₂, the ring nitrogen and the carboxyl carbon. The ring makes proline rigid, not symmetric, so its α-carbon is a stereocenter (S in L-proline).

Correct. A stereocenter (chiral center) is a carbon bonded to four different groups. Glycine's side chain is just a hydrogen atom, so its α-carbon carries two identical H atoms plus the amino and carboxyl groups. With two identical groups, glycine is superimposable on its mirror image, so it has no L or D form and no R or S label. It is the only achiral standard amino acid.

Incorrect. Cysteine is chiral: its α-carbon carries H, CH₂SH, the amino group and the carboxyl group. It is memorable because natural L-cysteine is labelled R instead of S, but that is only a naming consequence of sulfur's high priority in the CIP rules. Having an unusual R/S label does not mean it lacks a stereocenter.

p: A carbon is a stereocenter (chiral center) when its four substituents are all different. Then the molecule and its mirror image cannot be superimposed, like left and right hands, and the two forms are called enantiomers. Every standard amino acid has an α-carbon bonded to H, an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain (R group).

Glycine is the one exception: its R group is H, so two of the four groups are identical and the α-carbon is not a stereocenter. All 19 other standard amino acids are chiral, and proteins use only the L form. Threonine and isoleucine go further, with a second stereocenter in the side chain.

Do not confuse two separate questions: is a center chiral (four different groups?) and what is its label (L/D from the Fischer projection, R/S from CIP priorities)? Cysteine is chiral and L but is R; proline's ring does not remove chirality.

x1A_001.trap: Look for two identical groups on the carbon. Only glycine (H, H) lacks a stereocenter; an odd R/S label is not achirality.

fig.cap: The four answer choices with the α-carbon shaded and its four groups listed. Only glycine's α-carbon carries two identical groups (two H atoms).
fig.alt: Structures of alanine, proline, glycine and cysteine. Alanine is chiral S, proline chiral S, glycine achiral with groups H, H, NH3+ and COO-, cysteine chiral R.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES, CIP labels computed with RDKit.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Correct. Ribosomes build human proteins only from L-amino acids. The aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that load amino acids onto tRNAs, and the ribosome's peptidyl transferase center, are themselves chiral and select the L enantiomer. In a Fischer projection with the carboxyl at the top and the side chain at the bottom, an L-amino acid has its α-amino group on the left.

Incorrect. D-amino acids are the mirror images of the L forms. They do occur in nature, for example D-alanine and D-glutamate in bacterial peptidoglycan cell walls and in some antibiotics, but those are made by enzymes outside the ribosome. Translation itself does not incorporate D-amino acids into human proteins.

Incorrect. A racemic mixture is a 50 : 50 mix of both enantiomers, which is what a non-chiral laboratory synthesis gives. Biology is stereospecific: chiral enzymes and the tRNA-charging step pick one enantiomer, so protein synthesis is not a random mix. A racemic protein would not fold into one defined structure.

Incorrect. R and S are CIP labels, a different naming system from D and L. For most L-amino acids the α-carbon is S, not R; only L-cysteine (and selenocysteine) is R, because sulfur or selenium raises the side chain's priority. So 'R in every case' is wrong twice: it mixes up the two systems and gets most amino acids backwards.

p: L and D describe the absolute arrangement around the α-carbon by comparison with glyceraldehyde. Draw a Fischer projection with the COO⁻ at the top and the side chain at the bottom: if the NH₃⁺ is on the left the amino acid is L, if on the right it is D. In a Fischer projection the horizontal bonds point toward you and the vertical bonds point away.

Ribosomal protein synthesis uses only L-amino acids. D-amino acids appear in bacterial cell walls, some peptide antibiotics, and as signaling molecules such as D-serine in the brain, but they are not put into proteins by ribosomes.
R/S is a separate system based on CIP priorities, not on geometry relative to glyceraldehyde. Most L-amino acids are S; L-cysteine is R. Glycine is neither L nor D because it is not chiral.

x1A_002.trap: D/L (Fischer, compared with glyceraldehyde) and R/S (CIP priorities) are different systems; L-amino acids are mostly S, not R.

fig.cap: Fischer projections of L- and D-alanine. With COO⁻ on top and the side chain at the bottom, the amino group is on the left in the L form used by ribosomes.
fig.alt: Two Fischer projections. L-alanine has NH3+ on the left and H on the right and is labelled S and used by ribosomes. D-alanine has H on the left and NH3+ on the right and is labelled R and found in bacterial cell walls.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn from coordinates.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Incorrect. In L-serine the four groups on the α-carbon rank NH₃⁺ (N) first, then COO⁻, then CH₂OH, then H. The COO⁻ carbon carries (O, O, O) after duplicating the C=O, while the CH₂OH carbon carries only (O, H, H), so the carboxyl wins at the first point of difference. That is the usual order, so L-serine is S like most amino acids.

Incorrect. Methionine does contain sulfur, but it is two carbons away from the α-carbon. The first side-chain atom is a CH₂ whose substituents are (C, H, H), which ranks below the carboxyl carbon's (O, O, O). The usual priority order holds, so L-methionine is S. Sulfur only flips the label when it is directly attached to the first side-chain carbon.

Incorrect. Glycine has two hydrogen atoms on its α-carbon, so it is not a stereocenter and receives neither an R nor an S label (nor L or D). A molecule with no stereocenter cannot be the exception to an R/S rule.

Correct. In L-cysteine the side chain is CH₂SH. The atoms directly on the α-carbon are N, C, C and H, so N ranks first. To break the tie between the two carbons, compare their substituents: CH₂SH has (S, H, H) and COO⁻ has (O, O, O). Comparing highest first, S (atomic number 16) beats O (8), so CH₂SH ranks second and COO⁻ third. The 3D shape is the same as other L-amino acids, but swapping priorities 2 and 3 turns the label from S to R.

concept.t: Assigning R and S to amino acids
p: The Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) rules rank the four groups on a stereocenter by atomic number of the directly attached atoms. If two attached atoms tie, list the atoms attached to each (counting a double bond as two bonds to the same element) and compare them highest first; the first difference decides. With the lowest priority group (H) pointing away, 1 → 2 → 3 clockwise is R and counterclockwise is S.
For a typical L-amino acid the order is NH₃⁺ > COO⁻ > side chain > H, which gives S. The side-chain carbon loses to COO⁻ because the carboxyl carbon carries three oxygens.

Cysteine breaks the pattern because its side-chain carbon bears a sulfur, and S outranks O. The geometry is still L; only the label changes to R. This is why L and S are not synonyms: L/D describes geometry relative to glyceraldehyde, R/S depends on priorities.

x1A_003.trap: Compare substituent atoms at the first point of difference: one S on CH₂SH beats three O on COO⁻. The sulfur must be on the first side-chain carbon, which is why methionine stays S.

fig.cap: L-serine, L-methionine and L-cysteine have the same 3D arrangement, but only in cysteine does the side chain outrank the carboxyl, so only cysteine is R.
fig.alt: Structures of L-serine (S), L-methionine (S) and L-cysteine (R) with side chains shaded and the CIP priority list for each: for cysteine, NH3+, CH2SH, COO-, H.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES, CIP labels computed with RDKit.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 5.5 Sequence Rules for Specifying Configuration

ox: Incorrect. Asparagine and glutamine are the amide versions of aspartate and glutamate: the side-chain –COOH is replaced by –CONH₂. Amides are not meaningfully acidic or basic in water (the N–H pKa is about 15 to 17, and the nitrogen lone pair is tied up in resonance with the C=O), so these side chains stay neutral at pH 7.4. They are polar and hydrogen-bond well, which is why they are tempting, but polar does not mean charged.

Correct. Aspartate and glutamate both end in a side-chain carboxylic acid with pKa ≈ 3.9 to 4.2. At pH 7.4 the pH is more than 3 units above the pKa, so by Henderson–Hasselbalch the ratio [COO⁻]/[COOH] is about 10³ or more: essentially every side chain is deprotonated and carries a −1 charge. That is why they are called the acidic amino acids and why they often sit on protein surfaces and bind cations such as Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.

Incorrect. Lysine (side-chain amine, pKa ≈ 10.5) and arginine (guanidinium, pKa ≈ 12.5) are the basic amino acids. At pH 7.4 the pH is well below their pKa values, so their side chains stay protonated and carry a +1 charge. This choice has the right idea (charged at physiological pH) but the opposite sign.

Incorrect. Serine and threonine have side-chain hydroxyl groups. Their pKa is about 13 or higher, so at pH 7.4 they are fully protonated and neutral. They are polar (and are the residues that kinases phosphorylate), but they carry no charge unless they are phosphorylated.

p: Whether a group is charged depends on its pKa compared with the pH. If pH > pKa, the group is mostly deprotonated; if pH < pKa, it is mostly protonated. For an acid (–COOH) deprotonation gives a negative charge; for a base (–NH₃⁺) protonation gives a positive charge.

At pH 7.4 this gives five charged side chains to memorize: aspartate and glutamate (−1, pKa ≈ 4), lysine and arginine (+1, pKa ≈ 10.5 and 12.5), and histidine, whose pKa ≈ 6 means only about 4% is protonated at 7.4, so it is mostly neutral but can shuttle protons in active sites.

The polar uncharged group (serine, threonine, asparagine, glutamine, plus tyrosine and cysteine, whose pKa values are about 10 and 8) hydrogen-bond with water but carry no net charge at 7.4. A classic MCAT trap is to confuse Asp/Glu with their amides Asn/Gln.

x1A_004.trap: Asn and Gln look like Asp and Glu but are amides: polar, never charged.

fig.cap: Each answer pair drawn as it exists at pH 7.4, side chains shaded. Only aspartate and glutamate carry a negative side chain.
fig.alt: Structures of aspartate, glutamate, asparagine, glutamine, lysine, arginine, serine and threonine at pH 7.4 with side-chain charges -1, -1, 0, 0, +1, +1, 0, 0.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Incorrect. Lysine's side-chain amine has pKa ≈ 10.5. At pH 7, which is 3.5 units below the pKa, the ratio of protonated to deprotonated forms is about 10³·⁵ ≈ 3000 : 1, so lysine is almost always –NH₃⁺. It can donate a proton, but almost no –NH₂ is present to accept one back. Lysine is a good catalytic base only when its pKa is shifted by its environment.

Correct. A residue that both donates and accepts protons near pH 7 needs a pKa near 7, so that useful amounts of both the protonated and deprotonated forms are present. Histidine's imidazole side chain has pKa ≈ 6, the closest of any standard side chain to physiological pH. At pH 7 about 9% is protonated (imidazolium) and 91% neutral, and in an active site its pKa is often tuned even closer to 7. That is why histidine is the classic general acid–base catalyst, as in the serine protease catalytic triad.

Incorrect. Arginine's guanidinium group has pKa ≈ 12.5, so at pH 7 it is protonated about 10⁵·⁵ : 1. Its positive charge is spread over three nitrogens by resonance, which makes it very stable. Arginine is excellent for binding anions such as phosphate, but it essentially never deprotonates at pH 7 and so cannot shuttle protons back and forth.

Incorrect. Aspartate's side-chain carboxyl has pKa ≈ 3.9, so at pH 7 it is about 99.9% deprotonated (–COO⁻). It can accept a proton in principle, but the protonated form is so rare that it cannot also donate one. Aspartate often helps catalysis indirectly, for example by orienting and stabilizing histidine in the catalytic triad.

concept.t: Choosing an acid–base catalyst by pKa
p: A group is a good general acid–base catalyst at a given pH when its pKa is close to that pH. By Henderson–Hasselbalch, pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]); within about one pH unit of the pKa, both forms exist in meaningful amounts (between about 10 : 1 and 1 : 10), so the group can donate a proton and then take one back.

Side-chain pKa values to know: Asp 3.9, Glu 4.2, His 6.0, Cys 8.3, Tyr 10.1, Lys 10.5, Arg 12.5. Only histidine sits near 7, so it is the residue most often found shuttling protons in active sites (serine proteases, carbonic anhydrase, RNase A).

Remember that pKa values inside proteins can shift by several units because of nearby charges and the low-polarity interior. On the MCAT, though, use the free amino acid values unless the question says otherwise.

x1A_005.trap: A charged residue is not automatically a good catalyst: what matters is having both protonation states present, which needs pKa ≈ pH.

fig.cap: Percent protonated against pH for each answer choice. At pH 7 only histidine has substantial amounts of both forms; Lys and Arg are stuck protonated and Asp is stuck deprotonated.
fig.alt: Four sigmoid curves of percent protonated versus pH with midpoints at pH 3.9 (Asp), 6.0 (His), 10.5 (Lys) and 12.5 (Arg). A dashed line at pH 7 crosses His at about 9 percent, Lys and Arg at about 100 percent and Asp near 0 percent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKa values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. A net charge of −1 would require both amino groups to be neutral (–NH₂) while the carboxyl is –COO⁻. That happens only well above pH 10.5 (about pH 12 and higher), where both amines have lost their protons; at pH 10.5 itself the side chain is still half protonated. At pH 7 the pH is 2 units below the α-amino pKa (9.0) and 3.5 units below the side-chain pKa (10.5), so both amines are still protonated.

Incorrect. A net charge of 0 counts the α-carboxylate (−1) and the α-amino group (+1) but forgets the side-chain amine. That would be right for a neutral amino acid like alanine, whose pI is near 6, but lysine has a third ionizable group. Lysine is net zero only near its pI, (9.0 + 10.5)/2 ≈ 9.75.

Correct. Compare pH 7 with each pKa. The α-COOH (pKa 2.2) is below the pH, so it is deprotonated: −1. The α-NH₃⁺ (pKa 9.0) and side-chain NH₃⁺ (pKa 10.5) are above the pH, so both stay protonated: +1 each. The sum is −1 + 1 + 1 = +1 (computed exactly, about +0.99). That is why lysine counts as a basic, positively charged amino acid at physiological pH.

Incorrect. +2 would mean the carboxyl group is still –COOH (0) while both amines are –NH₃⁺. That is the fully protonated form, which dominates only below about pH 2.2. At pH 7, nearly five units above the carboxyl pKa, the ratio COO⁻ : COOH is about 10⁴·⁸ : 1, so the carboxyl is essentially always ionized.

p: To find the charge of an amino acid at a given pH, go group by group. If pH < pKa the group keeps its proton; if pH > pKa it loses it. A protonated carboxyl (–COOH) is 0 and a deprotonated one (–COO⁻) is −1. A protonated amine (–NH₃⁺) is +1 and a deprotonated one (–NH₂) is 0. Add up the charges.

When the pH is two or more units away from a pKa, the group is more than 99% in one form, so whole-number charges are a good estimate. Exactly at a pKa, that group is half protonated and contributes ±0.5.

Lysine has three ionizable groups: α-COOH (≈ 2.2), α-NH₃⁺ (≈ 9.0) and the ε-amino side chain (≈ 10.5). At pH 7 its net charge is +1, and it stays positive up to its pI near 9.75, which is why it binds negatively charged DNA in histones.

x1A_006.trap: Acids are 0 or −1, bases are +1 or 0. Below pKa means protonated for both, but protonation means different charges for the two kinds of group.

fig.cap: Lysine's average net charge across the pH scale. At pH 7 the curve sits on the +1 plateau; +2, 0 and −1 occur only well below pH 2.2, near pH 9.75 and well above pH 10.5.
fig.alt: Net charge of lysine versus pH, falling from +2 at low pH to +1 between pH 3 and 8, to 0 near 9.75, and to −1 above 12. At pH 7 the value is about +0.99.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKa values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

x1A_006.eli: Count each group's charge at pH 7: a group is on (has its proton) if pH is BELOW its pKa.
mem: Group is protonated if pH < pKa.
COOH pKa 2.2 → COO⁻ (−1) at pH 7; α-NH₃⁺ pKa 9.0 → +1; side chain pKa 10.5 → +1.
Lysine is basic: net +1 at pH 7.

fm.f: Net charge = sum of the charges of all groups, where a group is protonated (acid form) when pH < its pKa
fm.v: pH = 7.0; groups: COOH 2.2, α-NH₃⁺ 9.0, side chain 10.5
fm.why: We compare pH with each pKa because that tells us whether each group is holding its proton.

x1A_006.sc: Below 7 → deprotonated (acid gave its proton: −1). Above 7 → still protonated (+1 each). −1 + 1 + 1 = +1.
x1A_006.mn: HKR = basic: Histidine, Lysine, Arginine all can carry a plus.

ox: Correct. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH where the average net charge is zero. Fully protonated glycine (⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH) is +1. Losing the carboxyl proton (pKa 2.3) gives the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, net 0; losing the amino proton (pKa 9.7) gives the anion, net −1. The neutral form lies between the two pKa values, so pI = (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 12.0/2 = 6.0.

Incorrect. pH 7.0 is neutral for water (where [H⁺] = [OH⁻]), but that has nothing to do with whether an amino acid carries net charge. The pI depends only on the molecule's own pKa values. For glycine it is 6.0; for aspartate it is near 2.8 and for arginine near 10.8, far from 7.

Incorrect. 9.7 is the pKa of the α-amino group, where half of the amino groups are –NH₃⁺ and half are –NH₂. At that pH half the molecules are zwitterions (0) and half are anions (−1), so the average charge is −0.5, not zero. At any pKa the solution is buffering, whereas the pI sits at the steep equivalence point between the pKa values.

Incorrect. 12.0 is the sum of the two pKa values, 2.3 + 9.7, without dividing by 2. At pH 12 glycine is more than 99% in the anionic form H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻, with net charge −1. A quick check: the pI must lie between the two pKa values, and 12.0 is outside that range.

concept.t: Isoelectric point of a neutral amino acid
p: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which a molecule's average net charge is zero, so it does not migrate in an electric field. For amino acids without an ionizable side chain (glycine, alanine, valine, leucine and others), the only charged groups are the α-carboxyl (pKa ≈ 2) and the α-amino group (pKa ≈ 9 to 10).

Below the first pKa the molecule is mostly cationic (+1); between the two pKa values it is mostly the zwitterion (net 0); above the second it is mostly anionic (−1). The pI is the midpoint of the two pKa values that bracket the zwitterion, so pI = (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2, which is about 6 for these amino acids.
On a titration curve, the pI is the steep equivalence point at one equivalent of base, not a flat buffering region. Students often confuse it with neutral pH (7) or with one of the pKa values.

fx.w: pKa₁ is the α-carboxyl pKa and pKa₂ the α-amino pKa. This simple form applies to amino acids with no ionizable side chain; with an ionizable side chain, average the two pKa values that bracket the net-zero form.

steps: Past pKa₁ = 2.3 the carboxyl loses its proton: –COO⁻ (−1) and –NH₃⁺ (+1), net 0. This is the zwitterion.
Past pKa₂ = 9.7 the amine loses its proton: –COO⁻ (−1) and –NH₂ (0), net −1.
The zwitterion is bracketed by 2.3 and 9.7, so pI = (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 12.0/2 = 6.0.
x1A_007.trap: The pI always lies between two pKa values: average them, do not add them, and do not assume it is 7.

fig.cap: Glycine's titration curve computed from pKa 2.3 and 9.7. The pI of 6.0 sits at one equivalent of base; 7.0, 9.7 and 12.0 fall where glycine is not net neutral or is buffering.
fig.alt: Titration curve of glycine, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide from 0 to 2, with buffering plateaus at pH 2.3 and 9.7 and a steep rise at 1 equivalent where pH 6.0 is marked as the isoelectric point. Wrong values 7.0, 9.7 and 12.0 are marked.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the two pKa values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Correct. The pI is the pH at which the average net charge is zero. Start fully protonated (net +1: α-COOH, side-chain COOH and α-NH₃⁺) and remove protons in order of pKa. After the α-COOH (2.2) loses its proton, the molecule is net 0; after the side-chain COOH (4.2) loses one, it is net −1. The neutral form is bracketed by pKa 2.2 and 4.2, so pI = (2.2 + 4.2)/2 = 3.2.

Incorrect. 5.4 is the mean of all three pKa values, (2.2 + 4.2 + 9.7)/3 ≈ 5.4. The pI is never an average of every pKa; it is the average of the two that sit on either side of the neutral species. At pH 5.4 both carboxyls are deprotonated and the amine is protonated, so glutamate is net −1, not neutral.

Incorrect. 6.0 comes from averaging only the α-carboxyl and α-amino pKa values, (2.2 + 9.7)/2 ≈ 6.0. That rule works for amino acids with a non-ionizable side chain, such as glycine or alanine, but glutamate has an extra acidic group that must be counted. Ignoring it overestimates the pI by almost 3 units.

Incorrect. 7.0 averages the side-chain and α-amino pKa values, (4.2 + 9.7)/2 ≈ 7.0. That is the pattern for a basic amino acid such as lysine, where the neutral form lies between the two highest pKa values. For an acidic amino acid the neutral form lies between the two lowest pKa values.

p: The isoelectric point is the pH at which a molecule has no net charge, so it does not move in an electric field. To find it, list the pKa values in increasing order, start from the fully protonated form, and track the net charge as each proton comes off. The pI is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the net-zero form.

For neutral amino acids (no ionizable side chain) that means the α-COOH and α-NH₃⁺ pKa values, giving a pI near 6. For acidic amino acids (Asp, Glu) it is the two lowest pKa values, giving a pI near 3. For basic amino acids (Lys, Arg, His) it is the two highest, giving a pI near 7.6 to 10.8.

On a titration curve the pI sits at the equivalence point between the two flanking pKa plateaus. The MCAT uses pI with electrophoresis: at a pH below its pI a molecule is positive and moves to the cathode; above its pI it is negative and moves to the anode.

fx.f: pI = (pKa below neutral form + pKa above neutral form) / 2
fx.w: Use the two pKa values that bracket the species with net charge 0. For glutamate these are 2.2 (α-COOH) and 4.2 (side-chain COOH).

steps: Lose the proton at 2.2: (−1) + 0 + (+1) = 0. This is the neutral form.
The neutral form lies between pKa 2.2 and 4.2, so pI = (2.2 + 4.2)/2 = 6.4/2 = 3.2.
x1A_008.trap: Find the neutral form first, then average the two pKa values around it. Never average all three.

fig.cap: Glutamate's titration curve. The pI (3.2) sits between the first two pKa plateaus. The three wrong values all fall where glutamate is already net −1.
fig.alt: Titration curve of glutamate, pH against equivalents of hydroxide, with plateaus at pH 2.2, 4.2 and 9.7; the isoelectric point 3.2 is marked at one equivalent; wrong values 5.4, 6.0 and 7.0 are marked on the steep jump near two equivalents.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKa values in the question.

ox: Incorrect. 5.6 is the average of the α-carboxyl and α-amino pKa values, (2.2 + 9.0)/2 = 5.6. That shortcut works for amino acids with a non-ionizable side chain, but arginine's guanidinium side chain carries an extra +1 charge until pH 12.5. At pH 5.6 arginine is net +1 (COO⁻ −1, α-NH₃⁺ +1, side chain +1), not neutral.

Incorrect. 7.9 is the mean of all three pKa values, (2.2 + 9.0 + 12.5)/3 ≈ 7.9. Averaging every pKa has no chemical meaning: the pI is set only by the two pKa values on either side of the net-zero species. At pH 7.9 both amino groups are still protonated, so arginine is net +1.

Correct. Start fully protonated: –COOH (0), α-NH₃⁺ (+1) and side-chain guanidinium (+1), net +2. Losing the carboxyl proton (pKa 2.2) gives net +1. Losing the α-amino proton (pKa 9.0) gives net 0. Losing the side-chain proton (pKa 12.5) gives net −1. The net-zero form is bracketed by 9.0 and 12.5, so pI = (9.0 + 12.5)/2 = 21.5/2 = 10.75. This is the 'average the two highest' rule for basic amino acids.

Incorrect. 12.5 is the side-chain pKa. At that pH half of the side chains are protonated and half are not, so the average charge is −0.5 (between the neutral form and the −1 form). A pI never equals a single pKa; it is the midpoint between two of them.

concept.t: Isoelectric point of a basic amino acid
p: To find any pI, list the pKa values in order, start from the fully protonated form, and track the net charge as each proton is removed. The pI is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the species with net charge 0.

Basic amino acids (lysine, arginine, histidine) start at +2 because both the α-amino group and the side chain are protonated. The first proton lost (α-COOH) gives +1, so the neutral form appears only after the second proton is lost. The pI is therefore the average of the two highest pKa values: about 10.8 for arginine, 9.7 for lysine and 7.6 for histidine.
For acidic amino acids (Asp, Glu) the rule mirrors this: average the two lowest pKa values. A high pI tells you the molecule stays positively charged over most of the pH range.

fx.f: pI = (pKa below neutral form + pKa above neutral form) / 2
fx.w: For a basic amino acid these are the two highest pKa values. For arginine: (9.0 + 12.5)/2.

steps: Order the pKa values: 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺), 12.5 (guanidinium side chain).
After pKa 9.0: (−1) + 0 + (+1) = 0. This is the neutral form.
The neutral form lies between 9.0 and 12.5, so pI = (9.0 + 12.5)/2 = 10.75.
x1A_009.trap: For a basic amino acid the neutral form lies between the two highest pKa values; averaging the α-groups or all three pKa values gives a pH where it is still +1.

fig.cap: Arginine's titration curve computed from pKa 2.2, 9.0 and 12.5. The pI (10.75) is at two equivalents of base, between the two highest pKa plateaus; 5.6 and 7.9 fall where arginine is still +1.
fig.alt: Titration curve of arginine, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide from 0 to 3, with plateaus at 2.2, 9.0 and 12.5. The isoelectric point 10.75 is marked at 2 equivalents; wrong values 5.6 and 7.9 are marked on the steep rise at 1 equivalent and 12.5 at the last plateau.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKa values in the question (water autoionization ignored).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. 1% protonated corresponds to a base : acid ratio of about 100 : 1, which by Henderson–Hasselbalch needs pH − pKa = 2, that is pH 8.0. At pH 7.0 the pH is only one unit above the pKa, so the ratio is 10 : 1 and about ten times more side chains are protonated than this choice says.

Correct. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]). Here 7.0 = 6.0 + log(ratio), so [base]/[acid] = 10¹ = 10. For every 10 neutral imidazoles there is 1 protonated imidazolium, so the protonated fraction is 1/(10 + 1) = 1/11 ≈ 0.09, about 9%. Note the denominator is 11, not 10: the total includes both forms.

Incorrect. 50% protonation means [acid] = [base], which happens only when pH = pKa, here pH 6.0. At pH 7.0 the solution is one unit more basic than that, which shifts the balance tenfold toward the deprotonated form.

Incorrect. 91% (10/11) is the deprotonated fraction at pH 7.0, not the protonated one. This is the classic flipped ratio: when the pH is above the pKa, the deprotonated (base) form dominates. 91% protonated would be the answer at pH 5.0, one unit below the pKa.

p: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), links pH, pKa and the ratio of deprotonated to protonated forms. Each pH unit away from the pKa changes the ratio tenfold: pH = pKa gives 1 : 1, pKa + 1 gives 10 : 1, pKa + 2 gives 100 : 1.

To turn a ratio into a percentage, divide by the total. A 10 : 1 base : acid ratio means 1 part acid out of 11 parts, about 9% protonated and 91% deprotonated. Fraction protonated = 1/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)).

Histidine's imidazole (pKa ≈ 6) is the only side chain with a pKa near physiological pH, so small pH changes shift its charge noticeably. That makes it a key proton shuttle in enzymes and part of the buffering by hemoglobin. Remember: pH above pKa favors the deprotonated form.

fx.w: [A⁻] is the deprotonated (base) form, [HA] the protonated (acid) form. For histidine's side chain, HA is the positively charged imidazolium and A⁻ is the neutral imidazole.
Gives the share of molecules carrying the proton at a given pH; equals 0.5 at pH = pKa.

steps: [base]/[acid] = 10¹ = 10, so there are 10 neutral side chains for every 1 protonated side chain.
x1A_010.trap: Convert the ratio to a fraction with the total in the denominator (1/11, not 1/10), and remember pH above pKa favors the deprotonated form.

fig.cap: Percent of histidine side chains protonated against pH for pKa 6.0. At pH 7 the curve gives 9%; the wrong answers correspond to pH 8 (1%), pH 6 (50%) and pH 5 (91%).
fig.alt: Falling sigmoid curve of percent protonated versus pH from 2 to 10, midpoint at pH 6. Points mark 91 percent at pH 5, 50 percent at pH 6, 9 percent at pH 7 (correct) and 1 percent at pH 8.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKa in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

x1A_010.eli: Think of histidine as a light switch whose 'halfway' point is pH 6.0. At pH 7.0 the switch is one notch toward OFF (deprotonated), so only 1 in 11 still holds its proton.
mem: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Each 1 unit of pH away from pKa = 10 : 1 ratio.
Histidine side chain pKa ≈ 6.0; it is the only side chain near physiological pH.

fm.f: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), where pH = how acidic the solution is (7.0), pKa = pH at which half is protonated (6.0), [A⁻] = deprotonated form, [HA] = protonated form
fm.why: We use Henderson–Hasselbalch because it turns a pH and a pKa into a ratio of the two forms.

x1A_010.sc: pH − pKa = 1 means a ratio of 10 : 1. No log button needed. Fraction of the minority form = 1/11 ≈ 9%.
x1A_010.mn: Above the pKa, the base wins: 'pH over pKa, deprotonated Pops up'. (pH > pKa → A⁻ favored.)

ox: Incorrect. Glutamate does have three ionizable groups, so its curve also shows three buffering regions, but they sit near 2.2 (α-COOH), 4.2 (side-chain COOH) and 9.7 (α-NH₃⁺). Its extra region is in the acidic range because the side chain is a carboxylic acid. Nothing in the unknown's curve buffers near pH 4.

Incorrect. Histidine's three buffering regions are near 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2. The imidazole side chain is the one that buffers near neutral pH, at about 6.0. The unknown has no plateau between pH 3 and 8, so its side chain cannot be histidine's.

Incorrect. Alanine's side chain is a methyl group, which cannot gain or lose a proton. Its titration curve therefore has only two buffering regions (about 2.3 and 9.7) and needs only two equivalents of base to deprotonate fully. A third plateau rules out any amino acid with a non-ionizable side chain.

Correct. Each buffering region (flat part of the curve) is centered at one pKa, so the unknown has three ionizable groups with pKa 2.2, 9.0 and 10.5. Every amino acid has the α-COOH (about 2) and α-NH₃⁺ (about 9 to 10), so the extra pKa of 10.5 belongs to the side chain. A side-chain pKa near 10.5 is the ε-amino group of lysine, a basic side chain that stays protonated until well above physiological pH.

p: When a fully protonated amino acid is titrated with a strong base, each ionizable group gives one buffering region: a flat stretch where pH changes slowly because the group is half protonated. The midpoint of each flat stretch is that group's pKa, reached at 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 equivalents of base and so on. Between them are steep jumps (equivalence points), where one group has finished losing its protons.

Count the flat regions to count the ionizable groups: two for amino acids with non-ionizable side chains, three for Asp, Glu, His, Cys, Tyr, Lys and Arg. Then match the extra pKa to the side chain: about 3.9 to 4.2 (Asp, Glu), 6.0 (His), 8.3 (Cys), 10.1 (Tyr), 10.5 (Lys), 12.5 (Arg).
When two pKa values lie close together, as lysine's 9.0 and 10.5 do, their buffering regions merge into one long, gently sloping stretch, but it still takes one equivalent of base per group.

x1A_011.trap: Count plateaus to count ionizable groups, then identify the amino acid by the pKa that is not α-COOH or α-NH₃⁺.

fig.cap: Titration curve computed for pKa 2.2, 9.0 and 10.5. The third buffering region at 10.5 is lysine's ε-amino group; glutamate or histidine would buffer at 4.2 or 6.0, and alanine would stop after two equivalents.
fig.alt: Titration curve with a plateau at pH 2.2, a steep jump at 1 equivalent, and a long gently sloping region containing pKa 9.0 and 10.5, ending at 3 equivalents. Dotted lines at pH 4.2 and 6.0 show where glutamate and histidine would buffer instead.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKa values in the question (water autoionization ignored).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Correct. Glycine's pI (about 6.0) is reached after exactly one equivalent of base, when every carboxyl has lost its proton and no amino group has started to. That is an equivalence point: the carboxyls are already fully deprotonated and almost no –NH₂ has formed yet, so neither group is present as a buffering acid–base pair. Each small addition of OH⁻ therefore shifts the tiny [–NH₂]/[–NH₃⁺] ratio by a large factor, and the pH jumps. On the curve the pI is the steepest point between the two flat pKa regions.

Incorrect. pH resists change most strongly (maximum buffering) at a pKa, where a group is half protonated and half deprotonated, so it can absorb added acid or base. For glycine that is at pH 2.3 (0.5 equivalents) and 9.7 (1.5 equivalents). The pI sits halfway between them, where buffering is weakest.

Incorrect. pH equals the amino group's pKa (about 9.7) at 1.5 equivalents of base, when half of the –NH₃⁺ groups have been deprotonated. At that point the average charge is −0.5, not 0. The pI is the average of the two pKa values, (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0, not either pKa alone.

Incorrect. A net charge of +1 (⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH) describes glycine at the very start of the titration, below pH 2.3. At the pI the dominant species is the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, whose +1 and −1 cancel to give net 0. That is the definition of the isoelectric point.

p: A titration curve alternates between flat and steep regions. Flat regions are centered on each pKa: there, the group exists as a near 1 : 1 mix of acid and conjugate base, so added base is absorbed with little pH change. That is where the amino acid buffers best.

Steep regions are equivalence points, where one group has been fully deprotonated and the next has not yet started. With no buffer pair present, a little base causes a large pH jump. For an amino acid with two ionizable groups the first equivalence point is the pI, where the zwitterion dominates and the net charge is 0.

MCAT shortcuts: at 0.5 equivalents pH = pKa₁; at 1 equivalent pH = pI; at 1.5 equivalents pH = pKa₂; at 2 equivalents the molecule is fully deprotonated (net −1). The most common error is thinking the pI is where buffering is strongest.

x1A_012.trap: Flat parts of a titration curve are pKa values (best buffering); the pI is a steep equivalence point (worst buffering).

fig.cap: Glycine titration with each answer choice located on the curve. The pI at one equivalent is the steepest point; the flat buffer zones are at the two pKa values.
fig.alt: Glycine titration curve, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide. Shaded buffer zones around 0.5 and 1.5 equivalents mark pH 2.3 and 9.7. The pI at 1.0 equivalent, pH 6.0, is on the steep jump and labelled net charge 0; the starting point is labelled net +1 and the end point net −1.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from glycine's pKa values (2.3 and 9.7).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. After 0.5 equivalents of OH⁻, only half of the carboxyl groups have been deprotonated. The pH equals pKa₁ (about 2.3), and the solution is a 1 : 1 mix of the cation (+1) and the zwitterion (0), so the average charge is +0.5. This is the middle of the first buffering region, not the pI.

Correct. Fully protonated glycine, ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COOH, has net charge +1 and two removable protons. The more acidic proton (carboxyl, pKa ≈ 2.3) comes off first. One equivalent of OH⁻ removes exactly one proton per molecule, converting every molecule to the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻, net 0. By definition that is the isoelectric point, at pH (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0.

Incorrect. At 1.5 equivalents, the carboxyl is fully deprotonated and half of the amino groups have lost their proton. The pH equals pKa₂ (about 9.7) and the solution is a 1 : 1 mix of zwitterion (0) and anion (−1), average charge −0.5. This is the second buffering region.

Incorrect. Two equivalents remove both protons, giving the anion H₂N–CH₂–COO⁻ with net charge −1. This is the second equivalence point, the end of the titration. The molecule has gone past neutral, not reached it.

concept.t: Equivalents of base along a titration
p: One equivalent of base is the amount that removes one proton from every molecule. Titrating a fully protonated amino acid therefore steps the net charge down by 1 for each equivalent added. Glycine starts at +1 (–COOH, –NH₃⁺), reaches 0 after one equivalent, and −1 after two.

Half-equivalence points (0.5, 1.5 equivalents) are where pH = pKa, because a group is exactly half deprotonated. Whole-number equivalence points (1, 2) are steep jumps. The pI of an amino acid with two ionizable groups is the first equivalence point.

For amino acids with an ionizable side chain, count how many protons must be removed to reach net 0 from the fully protonated form: one for acidic amino acids (start +1), two for basic amino acids (start +2).

fx.f: net charge = (starting charge) − (equivalents of OH⁻ added)
fx.w: Holds for whole equivalents when the protons come off one group at a time. Glycine starts at +1, so net charge 0 needs 1 equivalent.

steps: To reach net 0, remove one proton per molecule.
The carboxyl proton (pKa 2.3) leaves first, giving the zwitterion after 1.0 equivalent of OH⁻.
x1A_013.trap: Half-equivalents give pH = pKa (half-charged states); the pI of glycine needs a whole equivalent.

fig.cap: Each answer choice located on glycine's titration curve. Only 1.0 equivalent gives the zwitterion with net charge 0; 0.5 and 1.5 equivalents are the pKa points and 2.0 is fully −1.
fig.alt: Glycine titration curve, pH versus equivalents of hydroxide. Points at 0.5 equivalents (pH 2.3, net +0.5), 1.0 equivalent (pH 6.0, pI, net 0, correct), 1.5 equivalents (pH 9.7, net −0.5) and 2.0 equivalents (fully −1).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from glycine's pKa values (2.3 and 9.7).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. Hydrolysis is the reverse reaction: water is added across the C–N amide bond to split a peptide into a free carboxylate and a free amine. It is how proteases and stomach acid break proteins down, not how they are built. Remember hydro-lysis means splitting with water.

Incorrect. Oxidizing two cysteine thiols (–SH) joins them into a disulfide bond (–S–S–), a covalent cross-link that stabilizes tertiary and quaternary structure, especially in secreted proteins. It connects side chains, not the backbone, and it is not how amino acids are linked in sequence.

Correct. A peptide bond is an amide. The carboxyl carbon of one amino acid bonds to the amino nitrogen of the next, and the –OH from the carboxyl plus an H from the amine leave as H₂O. That makes it a condensation (dehydration) reaction. In cells the ribosome drives it using an activated aminoacyl-tRNA, because the uncatalyzed reaction is unfavorable in water.

Incorrect. An ester forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol (an O-linked C–O–C=O bond), as in triglycerides and phospholipids. Peptide bonds link carbon to nitrogen, not to oxygen, and two hydroxyl groups joining would make an ether or anhydride, not an ester.

p: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, which are amide bonds between the α-carboxyl group of one residue and the α-amino group of the next. Forming each bond releases one water molecule (condensation, also called dehydration synthesis), and breaking it consumes one (hydrolysis). A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds.

The peptide bond has partial double-bond character because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the C=O (resonance). As a result the six atoms around it lie in one plane, rotation about C–N is restricted, and the bond is almost always trans. Backbone flexibility comes only from rotation about the bonds to the α-carbon (the φ and ψ angles).

Hydrolysis of a peptide bond is thermodynamically favorable (ΔG < 0) but kinetically very slow without a catalyst, which is why proteins persist in water. Do not confuse peptide bonds with disulfide bonds (side-chain cross-links) or glycosidic and ester bonds (carbohydrates and lipids).

x1A_014.trap: Building polymers releases water (condensation); breaking them uses water (hydrolysis).

fig.cap: Glycine and alanine condense into the dipeptide Gly-Ala. The atoms that leave as water and the new peptide bond are shaded.
fig.alt: Glycine plus alanine gives glycylalanine and water; the carboxyl OH of glycine and the amino group of alanine are highlighted, and the new amide bond is highlighted in the product.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Incorrect. Side chains are attached to the α-carbons, not to the peptide C–N bond itself, and the restriction is present even between two glycines, which have no side chains at all. Bulky side chains do limit which φ and ψ angles are comfortable, but that is a separate, steric effect on different bonds.

Incorrect. If the peptide bond were a full C=N double bond, its length would be about 1.27 Å and the C=O would become a single bond. Measured peptide C–N bonds are about 1.33 Å, between a single C–N (≈ 1.47 Å) and a double C=N. The true structure is a resonance hybrid with partial double-bond character, not a full double bond.

Incorrect. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to the C=O and N–H, but these interactions are weak and constantly breaking and re-forming. Peptide groups buried in the water-free core of a protein, and amides in the gas phase, are still planar. The rigidity is built into the electronic structure of the amide, not imposed by the solvent.

Correct. The nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl π system, so the amide is a resonance hybrid of C(=O)–N and C(–O⁻)=N⁺. The C–N bond therefore has partial double-bond character (roughly 40%). Rotating it would break the p-orbital overlap that creates this π bonding, which costs a lot of energy, so the six atoms Cα, C, O, N, H and the next Cα stay in one plane.

concept.t: Resonance and planarity of the peptide bond
p: In an amide, the nitrogen lone pair is conjugated with the C=O. Two resonance structures contribute: one with C=O and C–N, the other with C–O⁻ and C=N⁺. The real bond is in between, so the C–N is shorter (about 1.33 Å) than a normal single bond and has partial double-bond character.

Because of this π overlap, rotation about the C–N bond is restricted and the peptide group is planar: the α-carbon, carbonyl C and O, amide N and H, and the next α-carbon lie in one plane. The same resonance makes the nitrogen non-basic (its lone pair is busy) and the amide unreactive.
Backbone flexibility therefore comes only from the bonds on either side of each α-carbon (the φ and ψ angles). On the MCAT, link 'resonance' to 'planar, rigid, mostly trans'.

x1A_015.trap: Partial double bond, not full: the peptide bond is a resonance hybrid, shorter than single but longer than double.

fig.cap: The two resonance contributors of a peptide group (modelled by N-methylacetamide). The real bond is a hybrid with partial double-bond character, which locks the group flat.
fig.alt: Two structures linked by a double-headed resonance arrow: on the left C=O and C–N single; on the right C–O minus and C=N plus double. A box states the real C–N bond is about 1.33 angstroms, between single and double, so rotation is restricted.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES; bond lengths are standard textbook values.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.4 Peptides and Proteins

ox: Incorrect. The peptide bond is planar, but cis is the rare arrangement. In cis, the two α-carbons sit on the same side of the C–N bond and their substituents bump into each other. Cis bonds make up well under 1% of ordinary peptide bonds; they are found mainly before proline (about 5% of X–Pro bonds), where cis and trans clash about equally.

Incorrect. Trans is right, but 'freely rotating' is not. Resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, so rotating it costs about 80 kJ/mol, far more than thermal energy at body temperature. The bond is locked in place; cis–trans switching, mostly at prolines, is slow enough that cells use enzymes (peptidyl-prolyl isomerases) to speed it up.

Correct. Two facts combine. First, resonance makes the C–N bond partially double, so the peptide group is planar. Second, of the two planar arrangements, trans puts the two α-carbons on opposite sides of the C–N bond, which keeps their side chains and backbone atoms apart. Cis puts them on the same side and causes steric clash, so more than 99.9% of non-proline peptide bonds are trans.

Incorrect. A tetrahedral (sp³) nitrogen would hold its lone pair in an sp³ orbital, unable to overlap with the carbonyl π system. In amides the nitrogen is sp² and trigonal planar so that its lone pair, in a p orbital, can delocalize into the C=O. That planarity is exactly what resonance requires.

p: Because of resonance, the peptide C–N bond has partial double-bond character. Like a C=C double bond, it cannot rotate freely, and the atoms attached to it lie in a single plane. The peptide group can therefore exist as two planar isomers, cis and trans.

In the trans form the α-carbons on either side of the bond point in opposite directions; in the cis form they point the same way and collide. Trans is strongly favored, so nearly every peptide bond in a protein is trans. The exception is the bond before proline, whose ring makes both forms similarly crowded, so a few percent of X–Pro bonds are cis.
Do not mix up the rigid peptide bond (ω, fixed near 180°) with the flexible bonds to the α-carbon (φ and ψ), which rotate and give the chain its shape.

x1A_016.trap: Planar and trans: free rotation and a tetrahedral nitrogen both contradict the resonance that defines the peptide bond.

fig.cap: Planar peptide units in the trans and cis forms. In trans the two α-carbons are on opposite sides; in cis they are on the same side and clash.
fig.alt: Two planar peptide units drawn with 120 degree angles inside dashed rectangles. Trans: O and the second C-alpha point up, the first C-alpha and H point down. Cis: both C-alpha atoms point down with a red dashed line showing their clash.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn from coordinates.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.4 Peptides and Proteins

ox: Incorrect. The peptide C–N bond has partial double-bond character and stays planar; its torsion angle is called ω and is fixed near 180° (trans). The C=O is a true double bond and does not rotate at all. These are exactly the bonds that do not contribute to backbone flexibility, so they cannot be what φ and ψ describe.

Correct. Each residue's backbone runs N–Cα–C. The bonds on either side of the α-carbon are ordinary single bonds that can rotate: φ (phi) is the torsion angle about the N–Cα bond, and ψ (psi) is about the Cα–C(carbonyl) bond. Because the peptide bond itself is rigid, the backbone's three-dimensional path is set by the sequence of φ and ψ pairs. Ramachandran plots show which pairs are allowed.

Incorrect. Rotations about side-chain bonds are described by χ (chi) angles: χ₁ about Cα–Cβ, χ₂ about Cβ–Cγ and so on. These set where a side chain points, not the path of the backbone. φ and ψ are reserved for the two backbone bonds that flank the α-carbon.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds link the side chains of two cysteines and can join distant parts of a chain or different chains. They are not part of the backbone and have their own torsion angle (about ±90°). They stabilize a fold but are not the bonds φ and ψ describe.

p: The polypeptide backbone repeats N–Cα–C units. Three bonds per residue are possible rotation axes: N–Cα (angle φ), Cα–C (angle ψ) and the peptide C–N (angle ω). Because the peptide bond is planar and almost always trans, ω is essentially fixed at 180°, so the backbone can be pictured as a chain of rigid flat plates hinged at each α-carbon.

The φ and ψ angles are therefore the backbone's only real degrees of freedom. Steric clashes between backbone atoms and side chains rule out many combinations. A Ramachandran plot maps the allowed regions: α-helices and β-sheets each occupy a characteristic φ/ψ region.

Glycine, with only H as a side chain, can reach the widest range of φ/ψ values; proline, whose ring includes the N–Cα bond, has φ fixed near −60°. Side-chain rotations are χ angles, which are a separate set.

x1A_017.trap: φ and ψ are the two single bonds touching Cα; the peptide bond itself (ω) does not rotate.

fig.cap: A stretch of backbone with each bond labelled. φ (N–Cα) and ψ (Cα–C) rotate; ω (the peptide bond) is fixed; χ angles belong to side chains.
fig.alt: Zigzag backbone N, C-alpha, C, N, C-alpha, C with carbonyl oxygens and side chains R. N to C-alpha bonds labelled phi and C-alpha to C bonds labelled psi in green; the C to N peptide bond labelled omega in red; side-chain bonds labelled chi in purple.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn from coordinates.

ox: Correct. By universal convention, peptide and protein sequences are written from the N-terminus (the residue with a free α-amino group) on the left to the C-terminus (the residue with a free α-carboxyl group) on the right. In Met-Gly-Ser, Met's amino group is free, Gly sits in the middle with both its groups in peptide bonds, and Ser's carboxyl is free. This matches the direction of translation, which starts with Met and adds residues to the growing C-terminus.

Incorrect. This is the reverse of the convention. Ser-Gly-Met would be a different peptide (with Ser at the N-terminus), because the peptide bonds point in one direction: each links the carboxyl of the residue on the left to the amino group of the residue on the right. Reading the sequence backward changes which groups are free.

Incorrect. Peptide bonds are backbone amides between α-carboxyl and α-amino groups, never side-chain bonds in normal proteins. Glycine's 'side chain' is only a hydrogen atom and cannot form any bond. Gly in the middle uses its α-amino group for one peptide bond and its α-carboxyl for the other.

Incorrect. Order matters: the sequence of residues is the protein's primary structure, specified by the gene and fixed by peptide bonds. Met-Gly-Ser, Ser-Gly-Met and Gly-Met-Ser are different molecules with different free termini and properties, just as rearranging letters changes a word.

p: A polypeptide has direction. One end has a free α-amino group (N-terminus) and the other a free α-carboxyl group (C-terminus). Sequences are always written and read N → C, using three-letter (Met-Gly-Ser) or one-letter (MGS) codes.

This matches biology: ribosomes read mRNA 5′ → 3′ and build proteins N → C, adding each new amino acid to the free carboxyl end of the growing chain. That is why almost every newly made protein starts with methionine at its N-terminus.

The order of residues is the primary structure. Two peptides with the same amino acids in a different order are different molecules: a tripeptide of three different amino acids has 3! = 6 possible sequences.

x1A_018.trap: Always N-terminus on the left, C-terminus on the right; reversing the order gives a different peptide.

fig.cap: Met-Gly-Ser drawn left to right: Met carries the free amino group (N-terminus) and Ser carries the free carboxyl (C-terminus).
fig.alt: Structure of the tripeptide Met-Gly-Ser with a free NH2 on methionine at the left, glycine in the middle, and serine with a free COOH at the right; an arrow beneath shows the N to C direction.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structure drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.4 Peptides and Proteins

ox: Incorrect. One water molecule hydrolyzes one peptide bond. A tripeptide has two, so one water gives one free amino acid plus a dipeptide, not three free amino acids. Complete hydrolysis needs every peptide bond broken.

Correct. Three amino acids are joined by n − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2 peptide bonds (residue 1 to 2 and residue 2 to 3). Each bond formed by condensation released one H₂O, so breaking each one by hydrolysis consumes one H₂O, adding –OH to the carbonyl carbon and –H to the nitrogen. Two bonds need two waters to release three free amino acids.

Incorrect. Three is the number of residues, not the number of bonds between them. A chain of three links has only two joints. This error assumes each amino acid needs a water, but the end residues have one free terminus already.
Incorrect. Four waters would be needed for a pentapeptide (5 − 1 = 4 bonds). Each peptide bond uses exactly one water; there is no extra water for the termini or side chains in a simple hydrolysis.

p: Forming a peptide bond is a condensation (dehydration) reaction that releases one H₂O. Hydrolysis is the reverse and consumes one H₂O per bond. A linear chain of n residues has n − 1 peptide bonds, so its synthesis releases n − 1 waters and its complete hydrolysis uses n − 1 waters.

The same counting appears with other polymers: a polysaccharide of n glucose units has n − 1 glycosidic bonds; a triglyceride has three ester bonds (three waters). The mass of a peptide is therefore the sum of its free amino acid masses minus 18 Da for each peptide bond.
Watch for cyclic peptides: in a ring of n residues there are n peptide bonds, so hydrolysis takes n waters.

fx.w: n is the number of residues in a linear peptide; each bond needs one H₂O to hydrolyze. For a cyclic peptide, bonds = n.

steps: One H₂O per bond, so complete hydrolysis uses 2 H₂O.
x1A_019.trap: Count the bonds between residues (n − 1), not the residues themselves.

fig.cap: Ala-Gly-Ser has two peptide bonds (shaded); breaking both with two water molecules releases alanine, glycine and serine.
fig.alt: Structure of the tripeptide Ala-Gly-Ser with its two amide groups shaded, plus 2 H2O, and an arrow to free alanine, glycine and serine.
