ox: Incorrect. An endergonic reaction has ΔG > 0, but the stem says hydrolysis has ΔG < 0, which makes it exergonic (thermodynamically favorable) at neutral pH. It is peptide bond formation that is endergonic, which is why the ribosome uses aminoacyl-tRNAs charged with energy from ATP.

Incorrect. Most backbone peptide bonds on a protein's surface, and all of them in an unfolded protein or a short peptide, are fully exposed to water. Short peptides in water also last for years without enzymes, so lack of water access cannot explain stability.

Correct. ΔG only tells you whether a reaction can proceed; the rate depends on the activation energy (Ea). Uncatalyzed peptide hydrolysis must pass through a high-energy tetrahedral intermediate, and the resonance-stabilized amide resists attack by water. With such a high barrier, the half-life of a peptide bond in neutral water is on the order of years. Proteases lower the barrier and make the same reaction occur in milliseconds.

Incorrect. Re-formation in water is the unfavorable direction (ΔG > 0), so peptide bonds do not re-form spontaneously at a rate that could balance breakdown. The equilibrium lies far toward hydrolysis; proteins persist only because the system takes so long to get there.

p: Thermodynamics (ΔG) says whether a reaction is favorable: ΔG < 0 means the products are lower in free energy and the reaction is spontaneous. Kinetics says how fast it happens, which depends on the activation energy (Ea), the height of the barrier between reactants and products. ΔG and Ea are independent: a very favorable reaction can be extremely slow.

Peptide hydrolysis is the textbook example. The products are lower in energy, but uncatalyzed hydrolysis at neutral pH has a large barrier, so peptide bonds last for years. Enzymes (proteases) speed reactions by lowering Ea; they never change ΔG or the equilibrium position.
Other MCAT examples of the same idea: diamond turning into graphite, and ATP, which is thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable in water until an enzyme acts on it.

x1A_020.trap: Spontaneous (ΔG < 0) does not mean fast; the rate depends on the activation energy.

fig.cap: Schematic free-energy profile for peptide hydrolysis. Products lie below reactants (ΔG < 0), but the uncatalyzed barrier is high; a protease lowers the barrier without changing ΔG.
fig.alt: Reaction coordinate diagram: reactants peptide plus water on the left, products two amino acids lower on the right. A tall red barrier is labelled very high activation energy, half-life of years; a lower green dashed barrier is labelled with a protease. ΔG less than 0 is marked.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic; curve drawn from a smooth function with illustrative relative heights, not measured values.

ox: Correct. Proline's three-carbon side chain curls back and bonds to its own α-amino nitrogen, closing a five-membered pyrrolidine ring. That makes its α-nitrogen a secondary amine (bonded to two carbons), which is why proline is sometimes called an imino acid. The ring locks the φ angle near −60° and, once proline is in a chain, leaves its nitrogen with no H to donate, so proline breaks α-helices and is common in turns.

Incorrect. Lysine's side chain is a straight chain of four CH₂ groups ending in a free ε-amino group (–NH₃⁺ at physiological pH). That amine is far from the backbone and is not bonded to the α-nitrogen; it is a primary amine that stays free to form salt bridges, accept ubiquitin or acetyl groups, or bind DNA.

Incorrect. Histidine's side chain is an imidazole ring attached to the β-carbon through a single CH₂. The ring contains two nitrogens, but neither is the backbone α-nitrogen. Having a ring in the side chain is not the same as having the side chain bonded to the backbone.

Incorrect. Tryptophan's side chain is an indole (fused benzene and pyrrole rings) attached through a CH₂ at the β-carbon. Its ring nitrogen is part of the indole, not the α-amino group. Tryptophan is bulky and aromatic, but its backbone nitrogen is an ordinary primary amine like that of most amino acids.

p: In 19 of the 20 standard amino acids, the side chain hangs off the α-carbon and the α-amino group is a primary amine. Proline is unique: its side chain (–CH₂CH₂CH₂–) bonds to the α-nitrogen, forming a five-membered ring that includes the backbone N and Cα.

This has three structural consequences. The ring fixes the φ angle, so proline is rigid. In a peptide, proline's nitrogen has no H, so it cannot donate the backbone hydrogen bond that stabilizes α-helices; proline therefore acts as a helix breaker and is common in turns and loops. And the bond before proline is cis more often (about 5%) than other peptide bonds.

Proline is also abundant in collagen, where it is hydroxylated to hydroxyproline by a vitamin C–dependent enzyme. Do not confuse proline's ring with the aromatic rings of His, Phe, Tyr and Trp, which are side-chain rings that do not touch the backbone.

x1A_021.trap: Having a ring in the side chain is not the same as being cyclized onto the backbone; only proline's ring includes the α-nitrogen.

fig.cap: The four choices at pH 7.4 with side chains shaded. Only proline's shaded ring includes the backbone α-nitrogen; the other rings and amines hang free.
fig.alt: Structures of proline, lysine, histidine and tryptophan. Proline's pyrrolidine ring including the NH2+ is shaded and marked correct; lysine's free terminal NH3+ and the imidazole and indole rings attached at the beta carbon are marked wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Incorrect. Serine's side chain is –CH₂OH. The hydroxyl group has a polar O–H bond that hydrogen-bonds with water as both donor and acceptor, so serine is a polar uncharged amino acid. It is often found on protein surfaces and in active sites, not in hydrophobic cores.

Incorrect. Glutamine's side chain ends in an amide (–CONH₂), which has a strong C=O dipole and N–H bonds. It hydrogen-bonds well with water, so glutamine is polar, though uncharged at physiological pH. It is the amide of glutamate, not a hydrophobic residue.

Incorrect. Aspartate's side-chain carboxyl (pKa ≈ 3.9) is deprotonated at physiological pH, giving a negative charge. Charged groups are strongly hydrated by water, which makes aspartate one of the most hydrophilic residues, the opposite of hydrophobic.

Correct. Leucine's side chain is an isobutyl group, –CH₂CH(CH₃)₂, made only of carbon and hydrogen. C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar, so the side chain cannot hydrogen-bond or form ionic interactions with water. Water molecules around it lose freedom (an entropy cost), so leucine side chains cluster together in the protein core. Leucine is one of the most hydrophobic standard amino acids.

p: Side chains are grouped by how they interact with water. Nonpolar (hydrophobic) side chains contain mostly C and H: glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan and proline. Polar uncharged side chains contain O–H, N–H or amide groups that hydrogen-bond: serine, threonine, cysteine, asparagine, glutamine and tyrosine. Charged side chains are acidic (Asp, Glu) or basic (Lys, Arg, His).

The hydrophobic effect drives protein folding: burying nonpolar side chains releases ordered water molecules, increasing the entropy of the water. That is why nonpolar residues end up in the core of soluble proteins and in the lipid-facing parts of membrane proteins.

On the MCAT, recognize hydrophobicity by structure: long or branched alkyl chains (Leu, Ile, Val) and plain aromatic rings (Phe) are hydrophobic; any –OH, amide or charged group makes a side chain polar.

x1A_022.trap: Glutamine is not glutamate: it is uncharged but still polar because of its amide.

fig.cap: The four choices at pH 7.4 with side chains shaded. Only leucine's side chain is pure hydrocarbon.
fig.alt: Structures of serine with a hydroxyl, glutamine with an amide, aspartate with a carboxylate and leucine with an isobutyl group; leucine is marked nonpolar and correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

x1A_022.eli: Leucine's side chain is a greasy hydrocarbon chain, like oil in water. Oil fears water, so leucine hides in the protein's core.
mem: Nonpolar (9): G, A, V, L, I, M, P, F, W (GAV LIMP FW).
Leucine, isoleucine, valine and phenylalanine are the classic hydrophobic core residues.
Polar uncharged (6): S, T, C, N, Q, Y; acidic (2): D, E; basic (3): H, K, R.
x1A_022.sc: Longest purely carbon-and-hydrogen side chain = most hydrophobic.
x1A_022.mn: GAV LIMP FW: G=Glycine, A=Alanine, V=Valine, L=Leucine, I=Isoleucine, M=Methionine, P=Proline, F=Phenylalanine, W=Tryptophan. Sentence: Grandma Always Visits London; Irene Makes Perfect Fresh Waffles.

ox: Incorrect. Alanine's side chain is a single methyl group (–CH₃). It has no oxygen and no hydroxyl, so there is no nucleophilic oxygen to attack ATP's γ-phosphate. Alanine is a small nonpolar residue that cannot be phosphorylated.

Correct. Protein kinases transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP to a side-chain hydroxyl, forming a phosphate ester. The three standard residues with hydroxyl side chains are serine, threonine and tyrosine; threonine's is a secondary alcohol, –CH(OH)CH₃. Adding the phosphate puts about two negative charges on the side chain at pH 7.4, which can switch a protein's shape, activity or binding partners. Phosphatases remove it again.

Incorrect. Phenylalanine is tyrosine without the para-hydroxyl: its benzyl side chain is pure hydrocarbon. Tyrosine kinases need that –OH, so phenylalanine cannot be phosphorylated. Researchers use Tyr → Phe mutations precisely to block phosphorylation at a site.
Incorrect. Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group, –CH(CH₃)₂, entirely carbon and hydrogen. With no hydroxyl it cannot accept a phosphate. Valine is a branched, hydrophobic residue.

concept.t: Phosphorylation of Ser, Thr and Tyr
p: Phosphorylation is the most common reversible post-translational modification. A kinase uses ATP to attach a phosphate group to the oxygen of a side-chain hydroxyl, making a phosphate ester; a phosphatase hydrolyzes it off. In eukaryotes the targets are serine, threonine and tyrosine.

Kinases are grouped by target: serine/threonine kinases (such as PKA and PKC) and tyrosine kinases (such as receptor tyrosine kinases like the insulin receptor). The added phosphate carries about −2 charge at physiological pH, so it can create new salt bridges, cause a conformational change, or form a docking site for other proteins.

A hydroxyl group is required. Residues that look similar but lack the –OH (Ala, Val, Phe) cannot be phosphorylated. Histidine and aspartate phosphorylation occurs in bacterial two-component systems but is rarely tested.

x1A_023.trap: Phosphorylation needs a side-chain –OH: Ser, Thr, Tyr. Phe is Tyr minus the OH and cannot be phosphorylated.

fig.cap: Top: the four choices; only threonine has a side-chain hydroxyl. Bottom: a kinase transfers a phosphate from ATP to that hydroxyl, making phosphothreonine.
fig.alt: Structures of alanine, threonine, phenylalanine and valine with side chains shaded; threonine's OH is marked correct. Below, threonine reacts with ATP via a kinase to give phosphothreonine with a doubly negative phosphate ester and ADP.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES, stereochemistry checked with RDKit CIP labels.

ox: Incorrect. Serine's side chain is a hydroxyl, so a sugar attached to it is bonded through oxygen. That is O-linked glycosylation, which occurs mainly in the Golgi apparatus and also targets threonine. It is real and common, but it is not the N-linked type described in the stem.

Correct. 'N-linked' means the sugar is bonded to a nitrogen, and the acceptor is the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine. In the lumen of the rough ER, the enzyme oligosaccharyltransferase moves a preassembled 14-sugar oligosaccharide from the lipid carrier dolichol phosphate onto Asn, but only when it sits in the sequence Asn-X-Ser/Thr (X any residue except Pro). The first sugar, N-acetylglucosamine, is joined by a β-N-glycosidic bond, and the glycan is then trimmed in the ER and Golgi.

Incorrect. Glutamate's side chain ends in a carboxylate (–COO⁻), which has no nitrogen. It cannot form an N-glycosidic bond. Glutamine, the amide of glutamate, does have a side-chain amide nitrogen, but it is not used for N-linked glycosylation either.

Incorrect. Lysine's side-chain ε-amino group is a nitrogen, which makes this tempting, but it is not the acceptor for enzymatic N-linked glycosylation. Lysine amines are modified in other ways (acetylation, methylation, ubiquitination), and sugars can stick to them nonenzymatically in glycation, as in HbA1c. In collagen, sugars attach to the oxygen of hydroxylysine, which is O-linked.

p: Glycosylation is the enzymatic addition of carbohydrates to proteins, mostly to secreted and membrane proteins as they pass through the secretory pathway. The name tells you the atom: N-linked glycans attach to the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine, O-linked glycans to the hydroxyl oxygen of serine or threonine.

N-linked glycosylation begins co-translationally in the rough ER, where a large preformed oligosaccharide is transferred from dolichol to Asn in the motif Asn-X-Ser/Thr. The glycans help folding (calnexin and calreticulin quality control) and are then trimmed and modified in the Golgi. O-linked glycosylation happens mainly in the Golgi, one sugar at a time.
Glycosylation affects protein folding, stability, targeting (for example mannose-6-phosphate sends enzymes to lysosomes) and cell recognition, including the ABO blood group antigens.

x1A_024.trap: N-linked = asparagine's amide nitrogen (ER); O-linked = serine or threonine hydroxyl (Golgi).

fig.cap: N-acetylglucosamine bonded to the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine, the first link of every N-linked glycan. Tags show why the other residues do not fit.
fig.alt: Structure of beta-N-acetylglucosamine attached through its anomeric carbon to the side-chain amide nitrogen of asparagine, with the N-glycosidic linkage shaded. Tags: asparagine amide N correct; serine OH is O-linked; glutamate carboxylate has no N; lysine is not the N-glycan acceptor.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structure drawn with RDKit from SMILES, stereochemistry checked with RDKit CIP labels.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.4 The Endomembrane System and Proteins

ox: Incorrect. Histidine's imidazole ring is aromatic, but it is small and absorbs mainly below about 220 nm. At 280 nm its absorbance is negligible, so it contributes almost nothing to the A280 signal. Being aromatic is not enough; the ring system must be large enough to absorb near 280 nm.

Incorrect. Leucine's side chain is a saturated hydrocarbon with only C–C and C–H σ bonds. Those electrons need far-UV light (below 200 nm) to be excited, so leucine is transparent at 280 nm. Aliphatic residues never contribute to protein absorbance at 280 nm.
Incorrect. Serine's –CH₂OH contains only single bonds and nonbonding oxygen electrons that absorb deep in the UV, well below 280 nm. With no conjugated π system it does not absorb at 280 nm.

Correct. UV absorbance at 280 nm comes from conjugated aromatic π systems. Tryptophan's indole (a benzene ring fused to a pyrrole) is the largest conjugated system among the side chains and has the highest molar absorption coefficient at 280 nm, about 5500 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ per residue, almost four times tyrosine's (about 1490). Phenylalanine absorbs only weakly, near 257 nm. Combined with the Beer–Lambert law, A = εlc, this lets you estimate protein concentration from A280.

p: Molecules absorb ultraviolet light when photons promote electrons in conjugated π systems to higher orbitals. The larger the conjugated system, the longer the wavelength it absorbs. Among amino acids, tryptophan (indole) and tyrosine (phenol) absorb strongly near 280 nm; phenylalanine absorbs weakly near 257 nm; disulfide bonds (cystine) add a little.

Because the peptide backbone and other side chains do not absorb at 280 nm, a protein's absorbance there depends mainly on its Trp and Tyr content. With the Beer–Lambert law (A = εlc), measuring A280 gives concentration if ε is known. Its ε can be estimated as about 5500 × (number of Trp) + 1490 × (number of Tyr) + 125 × (number of disulfides).
A protein with no Trp or Tyr has almost no A280 signal and must be measured another way, for example at 205 nm (peptide bonds) or with a dye-binding assay such as Bradford.

fx.w: Beer–Lambert law: A is absorbance (unitless), ε the molar absorption coefficient (M⁻¹cm⁻¹), l the path length (cm), c the concentration (M).

x1A_025.trap: A280 comes from Trp and Tyr (big aromatic rings); histidine is aromatic but absorbs far below 280 nm.

fig.cap: Molar absorption coefficients at 280 nm: tryptophan dominates, tyrosine is second, and histidine, leucine and serine contribute essentially nothing.
fig.alt: Bar chart of molar absorption coefficient at 280 nanometers: tryptophan 5500, tyrosine 1490, cystine 125, histidine, leucine and serine about zero.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph; values from Pace et al., Protein Science 1995.

ox: Correct. At pH 7, lysine's ε-amino group (pKa ≈ 10.5) is protonated, –NH₃⁺, and glutamate's side-chain carboxyl (pKa ≈ 4.2) is deprotonated, –COO⁻. Opposite charges a few ångströms apart attract by Coulomb's law, and the N–H groups can also hydrogen-bond to the carboxylate oxygens. This combined ionic interaction is called a salt bridge (ion pair), one of the noncovalent interactions that stabilize tertiary and quaternary structure.

Incorrect. A disulfide bond is a covalent S–S bond formed by oxidizing the thiol (–SH) groups of two cysteines. Neither lysine nor glutamate contains sulfur, so they cannot form a disulfide. Disulfides are also mostly found in extracellular proteins, because the cytosol is a reducing environment.

Incorrect. Hydrophobic interactions occur between nonpolar side chains such as leucine, valine and phenylalanine, driven by the release of ordered water. Lysine and glutamate end in charged groups that are strongly hydrated; their attraction is electrostatic, not hydrophobic.

Incorrect. A peptide bond is a covalent amide formed between the α-carboxyl of one amino acid and the α-amino group of the next, made by the ribosome during translation. It joins backbone groups, not side chains, and does not form spontaneously between folded side chains. (Rare side-chain amide cross-links, such as isopeptide bonds made by transglutaminase, need an enzyme.)

p: Tertiary structure (the overall 3D fold of one chain) is held together mostly by side-chain interactions. The noncovalent ones are the hydrophobic effect (nonpolar residues clustering away from water), hydrogen bonds (polar side chains), and salt bridges (ionic attraction between oppositely charged side chains such as Lys/Arg with Asp/Glu). The main covalent one is the disulfide bond between two cysteines.

Salt bridges depend on charge, so they depend on pH: lowering the pH below about 4 protonates Asp and Glu and breaks them, and raising it above 10 to 11 deprotonates Lys. That is one reason extreme pH denatures proteins. They are also weakened by high salt, which screens the charges.

Classify interactions by the groups involved: two charges → salt bridge; two –SH → disulfide; two nonpolar groups → hydrophobic; backbone α-COOH and α-NH₂ → peptide bond (primary structure, not tertiary).

x1A_026.trap: Match the interaction to the chemistry: oppositely charged side chains form salt bridges; only cysteines form disulfides.

fig.cap: Lysine's NH₃⁺ and glutamate's COO⁻ attract each other across a short distance: a salt bridge. The table shows what each other interaction would require.
fig.alt: Lysine side chain ending in NH3+ and glutamate side chain ending in COO- connected by a dashed line labelled ionic attraction. Below, salt bridge is marked correct; disulfide needs two cysteine thiols; hydrophobic interaction needs nonpolar side chains; peptide bond joins backbone groups.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

x1A_026.eli: A lysine (positive) and a glutamate (negative) are like opposite poles of two magnets: they snap together into a salt bridge.
mem: Acidic (negative at pH 7): D = Aspartate, E = Glutamate.
Basic (positive at pH 7): H = Histidine (partly), K = Lysine, R = Arginine.
Salt bridge = + next to −.
x1A_026.sc: Opposites attract: one + (K/R/H) and one − (D/E) means a salt bridge.
x1A_026.mn: DE = acidic (2 negatives); HKR = basic (3 positives): 'D and E are Down in charge, H K R are Rising'.

ox: Incorrect. Leucine is nonpolar and usually buried in the hydrophobic core; aspartate is negatively charged at physiological pH. Putting a charge where a nonpolar side chain was would force a charged group into the core, where it cannot be hydrated, or disrupt packing. This is a radical (nonconservative) substitution.

Incorrect. Glycine has only H as a side chain and allows unusual backbone angles; tryptophan has the largest side chain (an indole ring). Replacing glycine with tryptophan would both remove backbone flexibility, for example in a tight turn, and add a bulky group that may not fit. This is a drastic change in size and shape.

Correct. A conservative mutation replaces a residue with one of similar size, shape and chemistry, so the protein's structure is least likely to change. Leucine and isoleucine are structural isomers: both have C₄H₉ side chains, and both are branched, aliphatic and hydrophobic. They differ only in where the branch sits (γ-carbon in Leu, β-carbon in Ile), so isoleucine can usually fill leucine's place in a hydrophobic core.

Incorrect. Lysine is positively charged (+1) and glutamate is negatively charged (−1) at pH 7.4. Although both are charged and hydrophilic, reversing the charge breaks any salt bridge the lysine made and can create repulsion with neighboring negative groups. A conservative swap for lysine would be arginine (same charge).

p: A missense mutation changes one amino acid. Its effect depends on how different the new side chain is. A conservative substitution keeps the key properties: size, polarity and charge, for example Leu ↔ Ile ↔ Val, Asp ↔ Glu, Lys ↔ Arg, Ser ↔ Thr, Phe ↔ Tyr. These often have little effect on structure or function.

A nonconservative (radical) substitution changes the class: nonpolar to charged, charge reversal, small to bulky, or anything involving glycine or proline, which have special backbone roles. Sickle-cell disease (Glu → Val on the β-globin surface) shows that even one radical change can have major effects.

Evolutionary comparisons show the same pattern: positions that tolerate change across species tend to vary conservatively. On the MCAT, judge a substitution by asking whether size, polarity and charge are all preserved.

x1A_027.trap: Both residues being charged is not conservative if the charges are opposite; check size, polarity and sign of charge together.

fig.cap: Each answer as a before-and-after pair with side chains shaded. Only leucine to isoleucine keeps size, shape and polarity nearly unchanged.
fig.alt: Four panels of amino acid pairs: leucine to aspartate (nonpolar to charged), glycine to tryptophan (smallest to bulkiest), leucine to isoleucine (isomers, both nonpolar, correct), and lysine to glutamate (plus one to minus one charge).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Incorrect. Disulfide bonds form only between the thiol (–SH) groups of cysteines. Valine's side chain is an isopropyl group with no sulfur, so the mutation cannot create a disulfide. The HbS fibers are held together by noncovalent contacts, which is why they can dissolve again when the hemoglobin is reoxygenated.

Incorrect. Oxidizing heme iron from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ produces methemoglobin, which cannot bind O₂. That is caused by oxidizing agents or by mutations near the heme pocket (HbM variants), not by the β6 surface change in HbS. HbS iron is normally Fe²⁺ and binds oxygen.

Incorrect. HbS still assembles into normal α₂β₂ tetramers and binds and releases oxygen. The problem is not within one tetramer but between tetramers: deoxy HbS molecules stick to each other and polymerize. If assembly were blocked, there would be no tetramers to polymerize.

Correct. In sickle-cell disease a single nucleotide change replaces glutamate with valine at position 6 of β-globin, on the protein's surface. The charged Glu⁻ was well hydrated; the nonpolar Val creates a sticky hydrophobic patch. In the deoxy conformation, a complementary hydrophobic pocket (formed by β Phe85 and Leu88) is exposed on other HbS tetramers, so Val6 of one binds the pocket of the next. These contacts link tetramers into long fibers that distort red blood cells into the sickle shape.

concept.t: Sickle-cell hemoglobin and the hydrophobic effect
p: Sickle-cell disease is caused by a point mutation (GAG → GTG) that replaces Glu6 with Val6 in β-globin. Glutamate is charged and hydrophilic; valine is nonpolar. On the surface of the protein, this creates an exposed hydrophobic patch.

When HbS releases oxygen, the deoxy (T-state) conformation exposes a hydrophobic pocket on the β subunit. Val6 of one tetramer fits into this pocket on a neighbor, and repeated contacts build long, stiff polymers. Fibers form most readily when oxygen is low, the cell is dehydrated or the pH is low, conditions that favor deoxy-Hb. Sickled cells block capillaries and are destroyed early, causing pain crises and anemia.

The example shows how primary structure determines quaternary interactions, and why a charged-to-nonpolar change on a surface is a radical substitution. Heterozygotes (sickle-cell trait) are partly protected against malaria.

x1A_028.trap: HbS is not misfolded or unable to bind O₂; its deoxy form polymerizes through a new hydrophobic contact between tetramers.

fig.cap: Schematic: in HbA the charged Glu at β6 stays hydrated; in HbS the nonpolar Val at β6 docks into a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring deoxy tetramer, building fibers.
fig.alt: Cartoon of two pairs of hemoglobin circles. HbA has a red E on its surface that does not bind the neighbor's pocket. HbS has an orange V that fits a hydrophobic pocket on the neighbor, leading to long fibers and sickled cells. Tags mark the hydrophobic patch correct and disulfides, iron oxidation and blocked assembly wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic; content from standard biochemistry texts (Lehninger, Principles of Biochemistry).

ox: Incorrect. Glycine's pI is 6.0, the same as the buffer pH. At its pI a molecule has zero net charge (it exists mainly as the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH₂–COO⁻), so the electric field exerts no net force on it. Glycine stays near the origin rather than moving toward either electrode.

Incorrect. Lysine's pI is 9.7, above the buffer pH of 6.0. When pH < pI a molecule carries extra protons and a net positive charge (lysine is about +1 here). Positive species migrate toward the negative electrode, the cathode, which is the opposite direction from the anode.

Correct. The anode is the positive electrode, so only negatively charged species move toward it. Aspartate's pI is 2.8, and the buffer pH (6.0) is well above it. When pH > pI, a molecule has lost more protons than at its neutral point and carries a net negative charge: at pH 6 both carboxyls are deprotonated (−2) and the amino group is protonated (+1), net −1. Aspartate therefore migrates toward the anode.

Incorrect. All three amino acids contain a zwitterionic backbone, but being a zwitterion does not mean being net neutral. Aspartate has an extra negative side chain and lysine an extra positive one, so only glycine, whose pI equals the buffer pH, has zero net charge. Two of the three do move.

p: In electrophoresis charged molecules move in an electric field: cations toward the negative cathode, anions toward the positive anode. For amino acids and proteins the sign of the net charge depends on the pH relative to the pI.

If pH < pI, the molecule is protonated beyond its neutral form and is positive, moving toward the cathode. If pH > pI, it is deprotonated beyond neutral and is negative, moving toward the anode. If pH = pI, it has no net charge and does not move. The further the pH is from the pI, the larger the charge and the faster the migration (for molecules of similar size).

Remember the electrode names with 'An Ox, Red Cat' from electrochemistry and the fact that in electrophoresis the anode is +. Acidic amino acids (low pI) run to the anode at neutral pH; basic ones (high pI) run to the cathode.

x1A_029.trap: pH above pI → negative → anode (+); do not reverse the sign or treat 'zwitterion' as automatically neutral.

fig.cap: Electrophoresis at pH 6.0: aspartate (pI 2.8) is negative and runs to the anode, glycine (pI 6.0) stays at the origin, and lysine (pI 9.7) is positive and runs to the cathode.
fig.alt: Gel strip with the cathode (minus) on the left and anode (plus) on the right. Aspartate band moves right toward the anode, glycine stays at the origin, lysine moves left toward the cathode.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram using the pI values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. The stopping point (pH 5.5) is right, but the direction is wrong. At pH 8, which is above the pI of 5.5, the protein has a net negative charge. Negative molecules are repelled by the negative cathode and move toward the positive anode. A protein would move toward the cathode only if it were loaded at a pH below its pI.

Correct. In isoelectric focusing the gel has a stable pH gradient, low pH at the anode (+) and high pH at the cathode (−). Loaded at pH 8, above its pI, the protein is net negative and moves toward the anode, which is also toward lower pH. As it enters more acidic gel, its groups pick up protons and its net negative charge shrinks. At pH 5.5 its net charge is zero, so the field no longer pushes it and it stops in a sharp band. If it drifts past, it becomes positive and is pushed back.

Incorrect. Running to the end of the gel is what happens in ordinary electrophoresis at a single pH, where charge never changes. In IEF the pH changes along the gel, so the protein's charge falls as it travels. It stops once its charge reaches zero at pH 5.5, long before the end of the gel.
Incorrect. A protein stays put only where the local pH equals its pI. At pH 8 the protein's pI of 5.5 is 2.5 units lower, so it carries a substantial negative charge and migrates in the field.

p: Isoelectric focusing (IEF) separates proteins by pI. The gel contains a fixed pH gradient: acidic at the anode (+), basic at the cathode (−). A protein placed anywhere on the gel has a charge set by the local pH compared with its pI.

If local pH > pI the protein is negative and moves toward the anode, into lower pH; if local pH < pI it is positive and moves toward the cathode, into higher pH. Either way it moves toward the spot where pH = pI, loses its net charge and stops. Diffusion away is corrected because any drift gives it a charge that pushes it back, so bands are very sharp.

IEF is the first dimension of 2D gel electrophoresis; SDS-PAGE, which separates by mass, is the second. The key difference: in SDS-PAGE every protein is negative and runs toward the anode at a rate set by size, while in IEF proteins stop at their pI regardless of size.

x1A_030.trap: In IEF a protein does not run off the gel: its charge drops to zero at pH = pI and it stops there.

fig.cap: A pH 3 to 10 gradient with the anode at the acidic end. The protein loaded at pH 8 is negative, moves toward the anode, and stops at pH 5.5, its pI.
fig.alt: Horizontal gel with a pH gradient from 3 at the anode (plus, left) to 10 at the cathode (minus, right). A negatively charged protein loaded at pH 8 moves left and stops as a green band at pH 5.5.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; band position computed on a linear pH 3 to 10 gradient.

ox: Incorrect. −1 is what you get if you count the Lys (+1), Glu (−1) and C-terminal carboxylate (−1) but leave out the N-terminal α-amino group. In a peptide the first residue's α-NH₃⁺ is free (pKa about 8), so at pH 7 it is mostly protonated and adds about +1. Forgetting the termini is the most common error in peptide charge problems.

Correct. List every ionizable group and compare pH 7.0 with its pKa. N-terminal α-NH₃⁺ (pKa ≈ 8): pH below pKa, protonated, +1. Lys side chain (10.5): protonated, +1. Glu side chain (4.2): pH above pKa, deprotonated, −1. His side chain (6.0): pH above pKa, mostly neutral, about +0.09. C-terminal α-COO⁻ (pKa ≈ 3.5): deprotonated, −1. Sum: +1 + 1 − 1 + 0 − 1 = 0 (computed exactly, about 0.00). Internal α-groups are tied up in peptide bonds and do not ionize.

Incorrect. +1 results from counting histidine's side chain as fully protonated. Its pKa is 6.0, so at pH 7.0 the base : acid ratio is 10 : 1 and only about 9% of the imidazoles carry a proton. Histidine contributes roughly +0.09, not +1, and the total stays near 0.

Incorrect. +2 counts the two positive amines (N-terminus and Lys) but ignores both negative groups, the Glu side-chain carboxylate and the C-terminal carboxylate. At pH 7 both are far above their pKa values (4.2 and about 3.5), so each is deprotonated and contributes −1.

p: A peptide's charge comes from its free N-terminal α-amino group, its free C-terminal α-carboxyl group, and its ionizable side chains. The α-amino and α-carboxyl groups of internal residues are locked in peptide bonds (amides), which do not ionize at ordinary pH.

For each ionizable group, compare the pH with its pKa: below the pKa the group is protonated (amines +1, carboxyls 0), above it the group is deprotonated (amines 0, carboxyls −1). Groups whose pKa is within about one unit of the pH carry a fractional charge, which you can compute with Henderson–Hasselbalch when precision matters.
Typical values in peptides: N-terminal NH₃⁺ ≈ 8, C-terminal COOH ≈ 3 to 3.5, Asp 3.9, Glu 4.2, His 6.0, Cys 8.3, Tyr 10.1, Lys 10.5, Arg 12.5. Always remember the two termini.

steps: Groups: N-terminus (pKa ≈ 8), Lys (10.5), Glu (4.2), His (6.0), C-terminus (≈ 3.5). Terminal pKa values are typical peptide values, not given in the stem.
At pH 7.0: N-terminus +1 (≈ +0.91), Lys +1, Glu −1, His ≈ +0.09, C-terminus −1.
x1A_031.trap: Count the free termini and treat His as mostly neutral at pH 7.

fig.cap: Charge of each ionizable group of Lys-Glu-His at pH 7.0, computed from its pKa. The positive and negative contributions cancel to about zero.
fig.alt: Bar chart of charges at pH 7: N-terminal amino +0.91, Lys side chain +1.00, Glu side chain −1.00, His side chain +0.09, C-terminal carboxyl −1.00; the sum is about 0.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the side-chain pKa values in the question and typical terminal pKa values (8.0 and 3.5).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. 0 would require the negative charges to cancel the positive ones, but at pH 1 there are no negative charges. Both carboxyl groups (Asp side chain, pKa 3.9, and the C-terminus, pKa about 3) are well above pH 1, so they stay protonated as neutral –COOH. Zero net charge is closer to what this peptide shows near neutral pH.
Incorrect. +1 counts only one positive group, usually the N-terminus. Lysine's side-chain ε-amino group (pKa 10.5) is also protonated at pH 1, nearly 10 units below its pKa, so it adds a second +1.

Correct. At pH 1 the solution is far more acidic than every pKa in the peptide, so every group carries its proton. The N-terminal α-NH₃⁺ is +1 and the Lys side-chain –NH₃⁺ is +1. The Asp side chain and the C-terminus are –COOH, which is neutral (0). Net charge = +1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = +2. The internal α-groups are in peptide bonds and do not ionize.

Incorrect. +3 treats the protonated Asp side chain as positive. A carboxylic acid gains a proton to go from –COO⁻ (−1) to –COOH (0), never beyond. Only basic groups such as amines become positive when protonated. With two basic groups (N-terminus and Lys), the maximum charge is +2.

concept.t: Peptide charge at very low pH
p: At a pH well below every pKa, all ionizable groups are protonated. That makes every acidic group (carboxyl) neutral and every basic group (amine, guanidinium, imidazole) positive. The maximum positive charge of a peptide therefore equals the number of basic groups it has, including the free N-terminus.

For Gly-Lys-Asp the basic groups are the N-terminal amine and the Lys side chain (+2 total), and the acidic groups are the Asp side chain and the C-terminus (0 when protonated). As pH rises, the carboxyls lose their protons first (around pH 3 to 4), then the amines (around 8 to 10.5).
A quick rule: acids go from 0 to −1, bases go from +1 to 0. Neither type ever has a charge outside that range.

steps: List the ionizable groups: N-terminal NH₃⁺ (≈ 8), Lys side chain (10.5), Asp side chain (3.9), C-terminal COOH (≈ 3).
pH 1 is below every pKa, so every group is protonated.
x1A_032.trap: A protonated carboxyl is neutral, not positive; only basic groups add positive charge.

fig.cap: Gly-Lys-Asp as it exists at pH 1, with the two NH₃⁺ groups shaded blue and the two neutral COOH groups shaded gray. The tally gives +2.
fig.alt: Structure of the tripeptide Gly-Lys-Asp fully protonated: NH3+ at the N-terminus and on the lysine side chain, COOH on the aspartate side chain and C-terminus. A table sums the charges to +2.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structure drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Correct. A thioether is the sulfur analog of an ether: a sulfur atom bonded to two carbons (C–S–C). Methionine's side chain is –CH₂CH₂–S–CH₃, so its sulfur sits between a CH₂ and a methyl group. Because the sulfur has no hydrogen, methionine cannot form disulfide bonds and is fairly hydrophobic. Its sulfur can be oxidized to a sulfoxide, and in S-adenosylmethionine it carries the methyl group used in many methylation reactions.

Incorrect. Cysteine also contains sulfur, but its side chain is –CH₂–SH, a thiol (sulfhydryl): sulfur bonded to one carbon and one hydrogen. The S–H is what lets two cysteines be oxidized to a disulfide (–S–S–) bond and lets cysteine act as a nucleophile. A thiol is not a thioether.
Incorrect. Serine's side chain is –CH₂OH, a primary alcohol. It contains oxygen, not sulfur, so it cannot be a thioether. Serine is the oxygen analog of cysteine (–OH instead of –SH).
Incorrect. Threonine's side chain is –CH(OH)CH₃, a secondary alcohol, with no sulfur at all. It is polar and can be phosphorylated or O-glycosylated, but it has neither a thiol nor a thioether.

p: Two standard amino acids contain sulfur. Cysteine has a thiol (–SH, also called a sulfhydryl): sulfur bonded to carbon and hydrogen. Methionine has a thioether (C–S–C): sulfur bonded to two carbons, the sulfur version of an ether.

The difference matters chemically. Cysteine's S–H can lose its proton (pKa ≈ 8.3) to form a reactive thiolate, and two cysteines can be oxidized to a disulfide bond that cross-links proteins. Methionine's sulfur has no H, so it cannot form disulfides; it is relatively nonpolar and is often buried. Methionine is the start amino acid in translation (AUG).
Serine and threonine are the hydroxyl (–OH) amino acids; cysteine is the sulfur analog of serine. Do not confuse thiol (R–SH), thioether (R–S–R′) and disulfide (R–S–S–R′).

x1A_033.trap: Both Cys and Met have sulfur, but only Met has S between two carbons (thioether); Cys has –SH (thiol).

fig.cap: The four choices with side chains shaded. Methionine's sulfur sits between two carbons (thioether); cysteine's carries an H (thiol); serine and threonine have –OH and no sulfur.
fig.alt: Structures of methionine with CH2CH2-S-CH3 shaded, cysteine with CH2-SH shaded, serine with CH2-OH shaded and threonine with CH(OH)CH3 shaded; methionine is marked as the thioether.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Incorrect. Glutamate is polar, but it is charged: its side-chain carboxyl (pKa ≈ 4.2) is more than three units below pH 7.4, so it is deprotonated and carries −1. It belongs to the acidic (negatively charged) group, not the polar uncharged group.

Incorrect. Isoleucine's side chain, –CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, is made only of carbon and hydrogen. It is nonpolar (hydrophobic) and uncharged. It meets the 'uncharged' part of the description but not the 'polar' part.

Correct. Glutamine's side chain ends in an amide, –CH₂CH₂C(=O)NH₂. The C=O and N–H bonds are strongly polar, so glutamine hydrogen-bonds with water and other groups. But amides are neither acidic nor basic in water: the N–H pKa is about 15 to 17, and the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, so it does not pick up a proton. Glutamine therefore stays uncharged at physiological pH.
Incorrect. Lysine is polar, but its side-chain amine (pKa ≈ 10.5) is protonated at pH 7.4, giving a +1 charge. It belongs to the basic (positively charged) group.

concept.t: Classifying side chains at physiological pH
p: Amino acids are grouped by their side chains at pH 7.4. Nonpolar: Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Pro, Met, Phe, Trp. Polar uncharged: Ser, Thr, Asn, Gln, Cys, Tyr. Acidic (−1): Asp, Glu. Basic (+1): Lys, Arg, with His mostly neutral (pKa ≈ 6).

'Polar' means the side chain has bonds with significant dipoles (O–H, N–H, C=O) and can hydrogen-bond. 'Charged' means it carries a full ionic charge because an acid–base group has gained or lost a proton. Charged side chains are also polar, but polar side chains are not necessarily charged.

The amides asparagine and glutamine are the classic test: they look like Asp and Glu but are uncharged at any physiological pH. Under strong acid or heat they can be hydrolyzed (deamidated) to Asp and Glu.

x1A_034.trap: Polar does not mean charged: Gln and Asn are polar amides with no charge, unlike Glu and Asp.

fig.cap: The four choices as they exist at pH 7.4, side chains shaded. Glutamine's amide is polar but carries no charge.
fig.alt: Structures of glutamate (charged −1), isoleucine (nonpolar), glutamine (polar uncharged, correct) and lysine (charged +1) with side chains shaded.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Correct. Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). Rearranged, log([A⁻]/[HA]) = pH − pKa = 4.9 − 3.9 = 1, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10¹ = 10. There are ten deprotonated (–COO⁻) side chains for every protonated (–COOH) one. Because the pH is above the pKa, the deprotonated form is the majority, as expected.

Incorrect. 1 : 10 is the ratio flipped. It would be correct at pH 2.9 (one unit below the pKa), where the protonated form dominates. When pH > pKa, the group is mostly deprotonated, so the base form must be the larger number.

Incorrect. A 1 : 1 ratio means log(ratio) = 0, which happens only when pH = pKa, here pH 3.9. At pH 4.9 the solution is one unit more basic than that, so the balance has shifted tenfold toward the deprotonated form.
Incorrect. 100 : 1 means log(ratio) = 2, which needs pH − pKa = 2, that is pH 5.9. Each pH unit changes the ratio by a factor of 10, not 100, so one unit above the pKa gives only 10 : 1.

p: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), connects pH and pKa to the ratio of the deprotonated form (A⁻) to the protonated form (HA). Because it is logarithmic, each one-unit difference between pH and pKa changes the ratio tenfold.
Memorize the pattern: pH = pKa → 1 : 1; pKa + 1 → 10 : 1; pKa + 2 → 100 : 1; pKa − 1 → 1 : 10. Above the pKa the deprotonated form wins; below it the protonated form wins.

To convert a ratio to a percentage, divide by the total: 10 : 1 means 10/11 ≈ 91% deprotonated and 1/11 ≈ 9% protonated. The MCAT often asks for one of these forms, so read carefully which way the ratio is written.

fx.w: [A⁻] is the deprotonated form (–COO⁻ here) and [HA] the protonated form (–COOH). Valid for any weak acid–conjugate base pair.

x1A_035.trap: pH above pKa means the deprotonated form is the bigger number; one unit = tenfold, not a hundredfold.

fig.cap: The ratio [COO⁻] : [COOH] for aspartate's side chain on a log scale against pH. At pH 4.9 (one unit above pKa 3.9) the ratio is 10 : 1; the other choices belong to pH 3.9, 2.9 and 5.9.
fig.alt: Straight line of log ratio versus pH passing through 1 to 1 at pH 3.9. Points mark 10 to 1 at pH 4.9 (correct), 1 to 10 at pH 2.9, and 100 to 1 at pH 5.9.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKa in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. The fully uncharged form, with –NH₂ and –COOH, is how amino acids are often drawn, but it is a minor species in water at every pH. The carboxyl (pKa ≈ 2.3) is a much stronger acid than the ammonium (pKa ≈ 9.7) is, so the proton moves from carboxyl to amine. The zwitterion outnumbers the neutral form by roughly 10⁵ to 1.

Incorrect. ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COOH is the cation, with both groups protonated and net charge +1. It dominates only below pH 2.3, the pKa of the carboxyl group. At pH 7, almost five units above that pKa, the carboxyl has lost its proton.

Incorrect. H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻ is the anion, with both groups deprotonated and net charge −1. It dominates only above pH 9.7, the pKa of the amino group. At pH 7 the amino group is still more than 99% protonated.

Correct. Compare pH 7 with each pKa. The carboxyl (pKa ≈ 2.3) is below pH 7, so it is deprotonated: –COO⁻. The amino group (pKa ≈ 9.7) is above pH 7, so it keeps its proton: –NH₃⁺. The result is the zwitterion ⁺H₃N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻, with a positive and a negative charge and net charge 0. Calculated from the pKa values, about 99.8% of alanine is in this form at pH 7.

p: A zwitterion is a molecule that carries both a positive and a negative charge but has no net charge. Amino acids form zwitterions in water because the α-carboxyl (pKa ≈ 2) is far more acidic than the α-ammonium (pKa ≈ 9 to 10): between those pH values the carboxyl is deprotonated and the amine protonated.
The dominant form changes with pH: cation (+1) below pKa₁, zwitterion (0) between pKa₁ and pKa₂, anion (−1) above pKa₂. The zwitterion is most abundant at the pI, the midpoint of the two pKa values.

The zwitterionic nature explains why amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points and good water solubility, like salts. The neutral 'textbook' form with –NH₂ and –COOH is a drawing convention, not the real species in water.

x1A_036.trap: The uncharged H₂N–CHR–COOH drawing is a convention; in water at neutral pH the real form is the zwitterion.

fig.cap: Percentage of alanine present as cation, zwitterion and anion across the pH scale, computed from pKa 2.3 and 9.7. At pH 7 the zwitterion is about 99.8%.
fig.alt: Three species curves: the cation falls from 100 percent below pH 2.3, the zwitterion is near 100 percent from pH 4 to 8, and the anion rises above pH 9.7. A dashed line at pH 7 marks the zwitterion at 99.8 percent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from alanine's pKa values (2.3 and 9.7).

ox: Incorrect. Resonance stabilization of the carboxylate needs conjugation, an unbroken chain of p orbitals connecting the side chain to the COO⁻. The α-carbon is sp³ and breaks any such conjugation, and glycine, with no side chain, has the same low pKa (about 2.3). So resonance with the side chain cannot explain the effect.

Correct. Acid strength depends on how stable the conjugate base is. In an amino acid, the α-carbon carries a positively charged –NH₃⁺ right next to the carboxyl. It withdraws electron density through the σ bonds (inductive effect) and its positive charge electrostatically stabilizes the negative carboxylate that forms. A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid, so the α-COOH pKa drops from about 4.8 (acetic acid) to about 2.3, making it more than 100 times more acidic.

Incorrect. Solvation does affect pKa values, but differences in hydrogen bonding with water would not on their own produce a shift of more than two pKa units between two small carboxylic acids. The decisive difference between acetic acid and an amino acid is the charged ammonium group directly next to the carboxyl.

Incorrect. Delocalizing charge over a larger region can stabilize an anion, but simply adding more atoms does not do that unless they are conjugated or electronegative. Glycine is barely larger than acetic acid, yet it is over 100 times more acidic. The effect comes from the nearby positive NH₃⁺, not from size.

concept.t: Inductive and electrostatic effects on pKa
p: A Brønsted acid is stronger (lower pKa) when its conjugate base is more stable. Electron-withdrawing groups near the acidic site pull electron density away and spread out the negative charge of the conjugate base, which lowers the pKa. This inductive effect weakens rapidly with distance.

In amino acids the α-NH₃⁺ is both electron-withdrawing and positively charged, and it sits only one carbon from the carboxyl. Together these effects stabilize the carboxylate and lower the α-COOH pKa to about 2, compared with about 4.8 for acetic acid. Side-chain carboxyls (Asp 3.9, Glu 4.2), farther from the NH₃⁺, are less affected.

The same logic explains other trends: chloroacetic acid (pKa ≈ 2.9) is stronger than acetic acid, and the N-terminal amine of a peptide is more acidic than the free amino acid's because no carboxylate sits next to it.

x1A_037.trap: Ask what stabilizes the conjugate base: here it is the neighboring +NH₃ (inductive and electrostatic), not resonance or size.

fig.cap: Acetic acid (pKa ≈ 4.8) and glycine's α-COOH (pKa ≈ 2.3). The shaded –NH₃⁺ next to the carboxyl stabilizes the carboxylate and makes the acid more than 100 times stronger.
fig.alt: Acetic acid structure with the COOH shaded and pKa about 4.8 beside glycine in its cationic form with NH3+ shaded and pKa about 2.3. Tags mark NH3+ stabilization correct and resonance, hydration and size wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES; pKa values are standard textbook values.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 20.4 Substituent Effects on Acidity

ox: Incorrect. This would be true for a normal cysteine (pKa 8.3), which is about 89% protonated at pH 7.4. But the stem says the histidine lowers the pKa to 6.5. With pH 7.4 now above the pKa, the protonated –SH becomes the minority (about 11%). Lowering a pKa favors deprotonation.

Correct. With pKa 6.5 and pH 7.4, pH − pKa = 0.9, so [S⁻]/[SH] = 10⁰·⁹ ≈ 8, meaning about 89% of the cysteine is the thiolate anion. Thiolate is a much stronger nucleophile than the neutral thiol because it has a full negative charge and a reactive lone pair. The nearby histidine (protonated imidazolium) stabilizes the thiolate, as in cysteine proteases such as papain and caspases, where the Cys–His pair attacks peptide bonds.

Incorrect. A disulfide bond needs two thiols, one from each of two cysteines. Histidine's imidazole contains nitrogen, not sulfur, so it cannot form an S–S bond with cysteine. The His–Cys interaction is an ion pair and hydrogen bond, not a covalent link.

Incorrect. A thiol is an acid: losing its proton turns neutral –SH into negative –S⁻. Cysteine's side chain is never positively charged under physiological conditions. The positive charge in this pair sits on the histidine, which is what stabilizes the thiolate.

p: Side-chain pKa values in proteins can differ greatly from those of free amino acids because the surroundings stabilize one protonation state. A nearby positive charge stabilizes a negative conjugate base and lowers the pKa; a nearby negative charge or a nonpolar pocket can raise it.

Cysteine's thiol normally has pKa ≈ 8.3, so at pH 7.4 most is neutral –SH. Next to a histidine its pKa can fall to 6.5 or lower, making most of it thiolate (–S⁻), a far better nucleophile. This is how cysteine proteases and many redox enzymes activate their cysteines.
Use Henderson–Hasselbalch to see the effect: fraction deprotonated = 1/(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)). A 1.8-unit drop in pKa raises the thiolate fraction at pH 7.4 from about 11% to about 89%.

fx.w: Share of the group present as the conjugate base. For pKa 6.5 at pH 7.4: 1/(1 + 10^−0.9) ≈ 0.89.

steps: For comparison, with the normal pKa 8.3: 1/(1 + 10^0.9) ≈ 0.11, about 11%.
x1A_038.trap: Lower pKa means more deprotonated at a given pH; for a thiol, deprotonated means negative thiolate.

fig.cap: Percent of cysteine present as thiolate against pH for pKa 8.3 (normal) and 6.5 (next to His). At pH 7.4 the shifted cysteine is 89% thiolate versus 11% normally.
fig.alt: Two rising sigmoid curves of percent thiolate versus pH, centered at pH 6.5 (green) and 8.3 (red). At the dashed line pH 7.4, green is at 89 percent and red at 11 percent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with the pKa values in the question.

ox: Incorrect. Breaking peptide bonds requires hydrolysis, done by proteases or by strong acid with heat. β-mercaptoethanol (HS–CH₂CH₂–OH) is a small thiol reducing agent; it reacts only with disulfide bonds and leaves the backbone intact. Cutting peptide bonds would ruin the size measurement that SDS-PAGE is designed to make.

Incorrect. Giving every protein a uniform negative charge is the job of SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate), an anionic detergent that binds along the unfolded chain at about one SDS per two residues. That swamps the protein's own charge so migration depends on size. β-mercaptoethanol carries no charge that would do this.

Incorrect. SDS-PAGE samples are deliberately denatured (with SDS and heat), and β-mercaptoethanol helps by removing disulfide cross-links that would hold parts of the fold together. Native PAGE, which keeps proteins folded, leaves out both SDS and reducing agent.

Correct. Disulfide bonds (–S–S–) are covalent and survive SDS, which disrupts only noncovalent interactions. β-mercaptoethanol is a thiol that reduces each disulfide to two free –SH groups (it is oxidized itself, forming its own disulfide). This separates subunits held together by interchain disulfides and fully linearizes chains with intrachain disulfides, so each polypeptide runs at the position set by its own mass.

p: SDS-PAGE separates polypeptides by mass. SDS, an anionic detergent, unfolds proteins and coats them with negative charge roughly in proportion to their length, so all chains move toward the anode and smaller chains travel farther through the polyacrylamide mesh. Heating speeds the unfolding.

SDS breaks noncovalent interactions (hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges) but not covalent ones. Disulfide bonds can hold two chains together or keep a single chain partly looped. A reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol or dithiothreitol (DTT) converts each disulfide into two –SH groups.

Comparing gels run with and without reducing agent reveals disulfide-linked subunits: a band that splits only when reduced was held together by S–S bonds. Native PAGE, without SDS or reducing agent, keeps complexes intact.

x1A_039.trap: SDS breaks noncovalent bonds and gives the charge; β-mercaptoethanol breaks only disulfides.

fig.cap: SDS-PAGE sample preparation: β-mercaptoethanol reduces the disulfide between chains, while SDS (with heat) unfolds them and supplies the negative charge.
fig.alt: Schematic of a two-chain protein linked by an S-S bond turning into two separate unfolded chains coated with negative charges and ending in SH groups. A table lists β-mercaptoethanol reduces disulfides, SDS denatures and adds negative charge, heat speeds unfolding.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic diagram.

ox: Correct. SDS alone breaks all noncovalent contacts, so the 100 kDa species that survives without reducing agent must be held together covalently. Adding reducing agent converts it to a 50 kDa species, so the covalent links are disulfide bonds. A single 50 kDa band under reducing conditions means every released chain is the same size, so the best explanation is two identical (or at least equal-sized) 50 kDa subunits joined by interchain disulfides: 2 × 50 = 100 kDa.

Incorrect. A noncovalent dimer is separated by SDS alone, because SDS disrupts hydrophobic, ionic and hydrogen-bond contacts. It would therefore run at 50 kDa even without reducing agent. The observed 100 kDa band without reducing agent rules this out.

Incorrect. β-mercaptoethanol and other thiol reducing agents act only on disulfide bonds; they do not hydrolyze peptide bonds. A 100 kDa single chain with only intrachain disulfides would still run near 100 kDa after reduction (sometimes slightly slower, since it unfolds more fully), not at 50 kDa.

Incorrect. Two different subunits of 60 and 40 kDa linked by a disulfide would also run at 100 kDa without reducing agent, but after reduction they would separate into two bands, at 60 and 40 kDa. The observed single 50 kDa band shows both chains are the same size.

p: Running a protein on SDS-PAGE with and without a reducing agent tells you how its subunits are held together. SDS alone removes noncovalent associations; adding β-mercaptoethanol or DTT also breaks disulfide bonds.

Reading the result: if the size drops only when reducing agent is added, the pieces were linked by disulfides. If the size is already small without reducing agent, the subunits were held together noncovalently (or it is a monomer). The number of bands after reduction tells you how many different chain sizes there are; their masses should add up to the nonreduced mass.
Antibodies are the classic example: IgG runs near 150 kDa nonreduced and splits into heavy (≈ 50 kDa) and light (≈ 25 kDa) chain bands when reduced.

steps: Without reducing agent (SDS only): 100 kDa, so the subunits are joined covalently.
With reducing agent: 50 kDa, so the covalent links are disulfide bonds.
One band after reduction, so all chains are the same size: 100/50 = 2 chains of 50 kDa.
x1A_040.trap: SDS alone already separates noncovalent subunits; only disulfide-linked subunits need the reducing agent to come apart.

fig.cap: Gel lanes for the observed result (green) and what the two other models would show (red): a noncovalent dimer runs at 50 kDa in both lanes, and a 60 + 40 kDa disulfide dimer gives two bands when reduced.
fig.alt: Schematic SDS-PAGE gel with a molecular weight ladder from 150 to 20 kDa. Observed lanes: 100 kDa without beta-mercaptoethanol and 50 kDa with it. Noncovalent dimer lanes: 50 kDa in both. 60 plus 40 lanes: 100 kDa without and two bands at 60 and 40 kDa with reducing agent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; band positions computed as linear in log(molecular weight).

ox: Incorrect. Lysine's side chain ends in –NH₃⁺ at physiological pH. Burying a charge in the nonpolar core would strip away its shell of water molecules (a large desolvation penalty) without polar partners to replace them. Lysine is therefore almost always on the surface, where its long flexible chain lets the charged end reach the water.

Incorrect. Glutamate's side-chain carboxylate is negatively charged at pH 7.4 and strongly hydrated. Like other charged residues it prefers the water-exposed surface, where it can also form salt bridges or bind metal ions. Finding a buried glutamate usually signals a special functional role, such as in an active site.

Correct. Phenylalanine's benzyl side chain is a nonpolar aromatic hydrocarbon that cannot hydrogen-bond with water. When a soluble protein folds, burying nonpolar side chains in the core releases the ordered water molecules that surrounded them, increasing the entropy of the water. This hydrophobic effect is the main driving force of folding, so Phe, Leu, Ile, Val and Met are concentrated in the core.

Incorrect. Arginine's guanidinium group is positively charged at physiological pH (pKa ≈ 12.5) and forms many hydrogen bonds with water. Like lysine and glutamate, it is typically on the surface, often interacting with phosphate groups or negatively charged ligands.

concept.t: The hydrophobic effect and protein folding
p: Water-soluble globular proteins fold so that nonpolar side chains are buried in the interior and polar and charged side chains face the solvent. The driving force is the hydrophobic effect: water molecules form ordered cages around exposed nonpolar groups, and burying those groups frees the water, increasing entropy (ΔS > 0) and making folding favorable (ΔG < 0).

Charged residues (Lys, Arg, Asp, Glu) are rarely buried, because removing their water shell costs a lot of energy unless a partner charge is provided, as in a buried salt bridge. Polar residues are found both on the surface and inside, where they hydrogen-bond with each other or the backbone.

Membrane proteins invert part of this pattern: the surfaces that touch lipid tails are nonpolar. The MCAT often frames this as 'which residue is most likely in the core' or 'which mutation would destabilize the fold'.

x1A_041.trap: The hydrophobic effect is driven mainly by the entropy of water, not by attraction between nonpolar groups; charged residues go to the surface.

fig.cap: Schematic cross-section of a soluble globular protein: nonpolar side chains such as Phe pack in the core, while charged Lys, Arg, Glu and Asp line the water-facing surface.
fig.alt: A circle representing a protein surrounded by water. The inner core contains Phe, Leu, Ile and Val; the rim carries charged Lys+, Arg+, Glu- and Asp-. Tags mark phenylalanine in the core as correct and lysine, glutamate and arginine on the surface.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Aspartate, glutamate and lysine are charged at physiological pH. Moving a charge from water into the low-dielectric hydrocarbon core of a membrane costs a very large amount of energy, so charged residues are strongly excluded from the middle of transmembrane helices. They are typically found at the ends, near the phospholipid head groups and water.

Incorrect. Serine, asparagine and glutamine are polar and hydrogen-bond with water. Inside the bilayer there is no water to satisfy those hydrogen bonds, so a helix rich in these residues would prefer an aqueous environment. They are common in loops and on the surfaces of soluble proteins.

Incorrect. Proline lacks the backbone N–H needed for the helix's internal hydrogen bonds and its ring clashes with the preceding turn, so it breaks or kinks α-helices. Glycine is so flexible that it destabilizes them. A segment rich in these residues would not form one stable, continuous membrane-spanning helix.

Correct. The core of a lipid bilayer is made of fatty acid tails, about 30 Å thick and entirely nonpolar. An α-helix rises 1.5 Å per residue, so about 20 residues (20 × 1.5 = 30 Å) span it. Its side chains face the lipid tails, so they must be hydrophobic: leucine, isoleucine and valine are aliphatic, nonpolar and good helix formers. The helix's own backbone C=O and N–H groups are satisfied by internal hydrogen bonds, so the whole segment is compatible with the oily interior.

p: Most integral membrane proteins cross the bilayer with α-helices. A single-pass segment is typically about 20 consecutive hydrophobic residues, enough to span the roughly 30 Å hydrocarbon core because each residue adds 1.5 Å along the helix axis.

The helix solves two problems at once: its backbone polar groups hydrogen-bond to each other inside the helix, and its outward-facing side chains (Leu, Ile, Val, Phe, Ala) interact favorably with the lipid tails. Charged and polar residues are rare in the middle and cluster at the membrane edges; aromatic Trp and Tyr often sit at the interface.

Hydropathy plots, which average residue hydrophobicity along a sequence, find these segments by looking for stretches of about 20 hydrophobic residues. Pro and Gly are helix breakers and are uncommon in such segments (though Pro can create functional kinks).

fx.f: length of α-helix ≈ 1.5 Å × number of residues
fx.w: Rise per residue along the helix axis. 20 residues ≈ 30 Å, the thickness of the bilayer's hydrocarbon core.

x1A_042.trap: The middle of the bilayer is oil: transmembrane helices need nonpolar, helix-friendly residues, not charged ones or helix breakers.

fig.cap: A 20-residue α-helix of hydrophobic residues spanning the 30 Å hydrocarbon core of a phospholipid bilayer, drawn to scale.
fig.alt: Schematic phospholipid bilayer with head groups as circles and tails as lines. An orange helix containing letters L, I, V and F spans the core, with a bracket labelled about 30 angstroms, 20 residues times 1.5 angstroms. Tags mark leucine, isoleucine and valine correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram drawn to scale from a 1.5 Å rise per residue and a 30 Å hydrophobic core.

ox: Incorrect. Serine's α-carbon is a stereocenter, but its β-carbon (–CH₂OH) carries two identical hydrogen atoms plus OH and the α-carbon. With two identical groups, Cβ is not a stereocenter, so serine has only one.

Incorrect. Valine's β-carbon carries H, the α-carbon and two methyl groups. The two identical CH₃ groups mean Cβ is not a stereocenter, so valine has only its α-carbon stereocenter. Branching alone does not create a second one.

Correct. Threonine's α-carbon has four different groups (H, NH₃⁺, COO⁻ and the side chain). Its β-carbon, –CH(OH)CH₃, also has four different groups: H, OH, CH₃ and the α-carbon. So threonine has two stereocenters; natural L-threonine is (2S,3R). With two stereocenters there are 2² = 4 stereoisomers, which is why the diastereomer L-allothreonine exists.

Incorrect. Leucine's branch point is the γ-carbon, which carries H, the β-carbon and two identical methyl groups, so it is not a stereocenter. Only leucine's α-carbon is chiral. Its isomer isoleucine, which branches at the β-carbon (H, CH₃, CH₂CH₃, Cα), does have two stereocenters.

p: A stereocenter is a carbon with four different substituents. Every standard amino acid except glycine has one at Cα. Two, threonine and isoleucine, have a second stereocenter at Cβ because that carbon carries four different groups: in Thr, H, OH, CH₃ and Cα; in Ile, H, CH₃, CH₂CH₃ and Cα.

A molecule with n stereocenters can have up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers. Threonine therefore has four: L-threonine (2S,3R), its enantiomer D-threonine, and the two allothreonines, which are diastereomers of threonine (different at one center only). Only L-threonine is used in proteins.
To decide quickly, look for two identical groups on a side-chain carbon: the CH₂ of Ser, Cys, Asp and others, and the C(CH₃)₂ branch points of Val and Leu, are not stereocenters.

x1A_043.trap: Branching is not chirality: Val and Leu branch into two identical methyls; only Thr and Ile have a second stereocenter.

fig.cap: The four choices with the side-chain carbon in question shaded and its four groups listed. Only threonine's Cβ carries four different groups.
fig.alt: Structures of serine, valine, threonine and leucine with CIP labels. Serine's beta carbon has two H, valine's beta carbon two CH3, leucine's gamma carbon two CH3; threonine's beta carbon has H, CH3, OH and C-alpha and is labelled R, giving two stereocenters.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES, CIP labels computed with RDKit.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 5.5 Sequence Rules for Specifying Configuration

ox: Incorrect. Tryptophan's side chain is an indole, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring containing N–H. It is aromatic but has no hydroxyl and is structurally quite different from phenylalanine's single phenyl ring. It is the largest standard side chain.

Correct. Tyrosine is phenylalanine with an –OH on the ring carbon opposite (para to) the CH₂ attachment: 4-hydroxyphenylalanine. In the body this is exactly how it is made: phenylalanine hydroxylase adds the para-OH, using tetrahydrobiopterin. The hydroxyl makes tyrosine more polar than phenylalanine, gives it a weakly acidic side chain (pKa ≈ 10) and makes it a target for tyrosine kinases.

Incorrect. Histidine's side chain is an imidazole, a five-membered aromatic ring with two nitrogens, attached through a CH₂. It is basic (pKa ≈ 6), not a hydroxylated benzene ring, so it does not match phenylalanine plus one OH.
Incorrect. Serine does have a hydroxyl, but its side chain is just –CH₂OH with no aromatic ring. It is the smallest hydroxyl amino acid. Matching the OH but not the ring is a partial match.

p: The aromatic amino acids are phenylalanine (phenyl ring), tyrosine (phenol: phenyl plus para-OH) and tryptophan (indole). Histidine's imidazole is also aromatic but is usually grouped with the basic amino acids.

Tyrosine is synthesized from phenylalanine by phenylalanine hydroxylase. When this enzyme is deficient (phenylketonuria, PKU), phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine becomes essential in the diet. Tyrosine is the precursor of the catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine), thyroid hormones and melanin.

The para-OH makes tyrosine able to hydrogen-bond, be phosphorylated, and absorb more strongly at 280 nm than Phe. Phe, Trp and Tyr are commonly buried or found at membrane interfaces because their large rings are mostly nonpolar.

x1A_044.trap: Tyr = Phe + para-OH. Ser also has an OH but no ring; Trp and His have different rings.

fig.cap: Phenylalanine and tyrosine side by side: adding one para-OH to the ring converts Phe into Tyr. The other choices have different ring systems or no ring.
fig.alt: Structure of phenylalanine with its ring shaded and tyrosine with the hydroxylated ring shaded, labelled para-OH added. Below, tryptophan (indole, two rings), histidine (imidazole) and serine (OH, no ring) are marked wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Correct. In a free amino acid, the –COO⁻ on the same α-carbon is a nearby negative charge. It electrostatically stabilizes the positively charged –NH₃⁺, making the proton harder to remove and raising the pKa to about 9.6. In a peptide, the N-terminal residue's carboxyl has become a neutral amide, which is also mildly electron-withdrawing. Without the stabilizing negative neighbor, the ammonium gives up its proton more easily, so its pKa drops to about 8.

Incorrect. A lower pKa for an ammonium (R–NH₃⁺) means a stronger acid and therefore a weaker conjugate base (R–NH₂). This choice reverses the relationship. If the N-terminal amine were a stronger base, it would hold its proton more tightly and its pKa would be higher, not lower.

Incorrect. The N-terminal amino group is, by definition, the one amine not used in a peptide bond; it remains a free –NH₃⁺/–NH₂. Its own α-carboxyl is what forms the peptide bond to the next residue. If the nitrogen were in an amide, it would not be basic at all and would have no pKa near 8.

Incorrect. Electron-donating groups make a nitrogen richer in electrons, stabilizing the protonated form and raising an amine's pKa. That would push the value above 9.6, not lower it. The observed drop comes from losing the nearby carboxylate and gaining an electron-withdrawing amide.

concept.t: Terminal group pKa values in peptides
p: The α-groups of a free amino acid influence each other. The positive –NH₃⁺ makes the neighboring –COOH more acidic (pKa ≈ 2), and the negative –COO⁻ makes the neighboring –NH₃⁺ less acidic (pKa ≈ 9 to 10). Charges of opposite sign stabilize each other.

When residues are joined into a peptide, the internal α-groups disappear into amide bonds. Only the N-terminal amine and the C-terminal carboxyl remain ionizable, and each has lost its oppositely charged neighbor while gaining an electron-withdrawing amide. As a result the N-terminal –NH₃⁺ is more acidic (pKa ≈ 8) and the C-terminal –COOH is less acidic (pKa ≈ 3 to 3.5) than in the free amino acid.
Remember the direction: a lower pKa means a stronger acid and weaker conjugate base. Stabilizing the protonated form raises the pKa; stabilizing the deprotonated form lowers it.

x1A_045.trap: Lower pKa of an ammonium means a weaker base, not a stronger one; look for what stabilizes or destabilizes the protonated form.

fig.cap: Free glycine (α-NH₃⁺ pKa ≈ 9.6) next to the N-terminus of Gly-Ala (pKa ≈ 8). In the peptide the stabilizing COO⁻ neighbor has been replaced by a neutral amide.
fig.alt: Glycine zwitterion with its carboxylate shaded and pKa about 9.6 beside the dipeptide Gly-Ala with the amide next to the N-terminus shaded and pKa about 8. Tags mark the loss of the adjacent carboxylate as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES; pKa values are typical textbook values.

ox: Incorrect. Hydrophobic describes how a molecule or group interacts with water: a nonpolar group that water excludes. It says nothing about donating or accepting protons. Many amino acids are not hydrophobic at all, yet all of them can act as acids and bases.

Incorrect. Chirality means a molecule is not superimposable on its mirror image, usually because of a carbon with four different groups. It is a geometric property, not an acid–base one. Glycine is not chiral but is still able to donate and accept protons.

Correct. An amphoteric substance can act as either an acid or a base. Amino acids contain a carboxyl group, which can accept a proton (as –COO⁻ → –COOH), and an amino group, which can donate one (as –NH₃⁺ → –NH₂). In acid they pick up a proton and become cations; in base they lose one and become anions. Water and bicarbonate are other amphoteric species. (The term amphiprotic is also used for molecules that can donate and accept protons.)

Incorrect. Aromatic refers to cyclic, planar, conjugated ring systems with 4n + 2 π electrons, as in phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan. It describes electron structure in rings, not proton transfer, and most amino acids are not aromatic.

p: A substance is amphoteric (more precisely, amphiprotic) if it can act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid (proton donor) or base (proton acceptor). Every amino acid has an acidic α-carboxyl and a basic α-amino group, so every amino acid is amphoteric.

In water near neutral pH, an amino acid exists as a zwitterion (⁺H₃N–CHR–COO⁻). Adding acid protonates the carboxylate to give the cation; adding base removes a proton from the ammonium to give the anion. This ability to absorb both added H⁺ and OH⁻ is why amino acids and proteins act as buffers, especially near their pKa values.
Other amphoteric species tested on the MCAT include water (H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ or OH⁻), bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) and dihydrogen phosphate (H₂PO₄⁻).

x1A_046.trap: Amphoteric is about proton transfer in both directions; hydrophobic, chiral and aromatic describe solubility, geometry and electron structure.

fig.cap: Glycine's zwitterion can accept a proton (acting as a base) to become the cation, or donate one (acting as an acid) to become the anion.
fig.alt: Three glycine structures: cation with COOH on the left, zwitterion in the middle, anion with NH2 on the right. Arrows show plus H+ toward the cation (acts as base) and minus H+ toward the anion (acts as acid). Tags mark amphoteric correct and hydrophobic, chiral and aromatic wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.1 Structures of Amino Acids

ox: Incorrect. pH 3.9 lies between histidine's first two pKa values (1.8 and 6.0), about 2 units from each. There the α-carboxyl is about 99% deprotonated and the imidazole about 99% protonated, so neither group exists as a useful acid–base pair. This is close to an equivalence point, where buffering is weak.

Correct. A buffer resists pH change best when both the acid and conjugate base forms of a group are present in equal amounts, which happens at pH = pKa. Histidine's pKa values are 1.8 (α-COOH), 6.0 (imidazole side chain) and 9.2 (α-NH₃⁺). Of the choices, only 6.0 sits exactly on a pKa, where the imidazolium : imidazole ratio is 1 : 1 and buffer capacity is at a maximum. This side-chain buffering near neutral pH is why histidine residues help hemoglobin buffer blood.

Incorrect. 7.6 is histidine's isoelectric point, (6.0 + 9.2)/2 = 7.6, where the neutral form dominates. The pI is an equivalence point between two buffering regions: the imidazole is mostly deprotonated and the α-amino group mostly protonated, so buffering is near a local minimum. Confusing the pI with the best buffering pH is a classic trap.

Incorrect. pH 11.0 is 1.8 units above the highest pKa (9.2), so the α-amino group is about 98% deprotonated. Very little of the acid form remains to neutralize added base, so buffering is poor. Good buffering requires pH within about ±1 of a pKa.

p: A buffer is a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists changes in pH. Its capacity is greatest when [HA] = [A⁻], that is at pH = pKa, and it remains useful roughly from pKa − 1 to pKa + 1.

An amino acid with several ionizable groups has a buffering region around each pKa. On a titration curve these are the flat sections; between them are steep equivalence points, including the pI, where buffering is weakest.

Histidine is special because its side-chain pKa (about 6.0, and closer to 7 in many proteins) lies near physiological pH. That makes histidine-rich proteins, such as hemoglobin, effective physiological buffers and makes His the most common acid–base catalyst in enzymes.

x1A_047.trap: Best buffering is at a pKa (flat region); the pI is an equivalence point where buffering is weakest.

fig.cap: Buffer capacity of free histidine computed from its three pKa values. Capacity peaks at each pKa; pH 6.0 is a peak, while 3.9, 7.6 (the pI) and 11.0 sit in troughs or on the tail.
fig.alt: Curve of relative buffer capacity versus pH with three equal peaks at pH 1.8, 6.0 and 9.2. The peak at 6.0 is marked correct; points at 3.9, 7.6 and 11.0 lie at low values and are marked wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the three pKa values in the question (buffer capacity = ln10 × Σ f(1 − f)).

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. Two fragments would mean only one cut. The peptide has two internal cleavage sites: after Lys2 (the next residue is Gly) and after Arg4 (the next residue is Phe). Missing one usually comes from overlooking that trypsin cuts after arginine as well as lysine.

Correct. Trypsin hydrolyzes the peptide bond on the C-terminal (carboxyl) side of Lys or Arg, unless the next residue is Pro. Scan Ala1-Lys2-Gly3-Arg4-Phe5-Lys6: Lys2 is followed by Gly, so cut; Arg4 is followed by Phe, so cut; Lys6 is the C-terminal residue with no peptide bond after it, so no cut. Two cuts in a linear peptide give 2 + 1 = 3 fragments: Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys. Each fragment ends in Lys or Arg, as expected for a tryptic digest.

Incorrect. Four fragments would require three cuts, which would count the final Lys6. But a protease cuts a bond, and there is no bond after the C-terminal residue. Only internal Lys and Arg residues create new fragments.
