Incorrect. Six fragments would mean every peptide bond (five of them) was cut, releasing all six amino acids. Trypsin is a specific endopeptidase that recognizes the positively charged side chains of Lys and Arg in its S1 pocket (which holds an aspartate); it does not cut after Ala, Gly or Phe.

p: Proteases are enzymes that hydrolyze peptide bonds, often at specific residues. Trypsin cuts on the C-terminal side of the positively charged residues Lys and Arg, because its S1 binding pocket contains a negatively charged aspartate. It does not cut when the next residue is proline. Chymotrypsin cuts after large aromatic residues (Phe, Tyr, Trp); cyanogen bromide (a chemical reagent) cuts after Met.

To count fragments: find each qualifying internal residue, check the residue that follows (not Pro, and not the end of the chain), and count the cuts. A linear peptide cut n times gives n + 1 fragments.
Overlapping fragments from two different cleavage methods are used to reconstruct a protein's sequence, a classic MCAT experimental-reasoning setup.

fx.w: For a linear peptide. A cut requires a peptide bond on the C-terminal side of Lys or Arg that is not followed by Pro.

steps: Lys6 is the C-terminal residue: no bond after it, no cut.
x1A_048.trap: A C-terminal Lys or Arg has no bond after it to cut; count only internal sites not followed by Pro.

fig.cap: The peptide Ala-Lys-Gly-Arg-Phe-Lys with trypsin's two cut sites (after Lys2 and Arg4). The C-terminal Lys6 has no bond after it, so three fragments result.
fig.alt: Six residue boxes Ala, Lys, Gly, Arg, Phe, Lys with Lys and Arg highlighted and dashed red cut lines after positions 2 and 4. Below, three fragments Ala-Lys, Gly-Arg and Phe-Lys and the label 2 cuts give 3 fragments.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Glycine's side chain is a single hydrogen, so its α-carbon carries no Cβ. Most combinations of the backbone torsion angles φ and ψ are forbidden for other residues because the Cβ would collide with backbone atoms; glycine avoids those clashes and can adopt many more φ/ψ combinations, including the left-handed region. That flexibility lets the chain reverse direction sharply, so glycine is common in tight β-turns and flexible loops (and, in collagen, at every third position where the chains pack closely).

Incorrect. Glycine's 'side chain' is just a hydrogen atom bonded to carbon, which cannot form hydrogen bonds. Glycine's preference for turns comes from the absence of a side chain, not from any interactions it makes. Residues that hydrogen-bond through side chains, such as Asn and Ser, are also found in turns, but for a different reason.

Incorrect. Glycine forms normal peptide bonds through its α-amino and α-carboxyl groups on both sides, exactly like every other amino acid. Something unable to form a peptide bond on one side could only sit at a chain end, not inside a turn.

Incorrect. Glycine's side chain is H, which has no acidic or basic group, so it carries no charge at physiological pH. Only the free α-groups ionize, and in a protein those are tied up in peptide bonds. Charge is not why glycine favors turns.

concept.t: Glycine and proline: special backbone residues
p: The backbone conformation of each residue is described by φ (N–Cα) and ψ (Cα–C). A Ramachandran plot shows which φ/ψ pairs are sterically allowed. For most residues, the Cβ atom collides with backbone atoms in large regions of the plot, leaving mainly the α-helix and β-sheet regions.

Glycine has no Cβ, so it can reach many more φ/ψ combinations, including positive φ values that are rare for other residues. That makes it ideal for tight turns and flexible loops, but its flexibility (high conformational entropy) makes it a poor helix former.

Proline is the opposite extreme: its ring fixes φ near −60° and its nitrogen lacks an H, so it breaks helices and favors turns for a different reason. On the MCAT, Gly and Pro are the two 'helix breakers' and the two residues commonly found in turns.

x1A_049.trap: Glycine's special behavior comes from what it lacks (any side chain), not from any interaction it makes.

fig.cap: A glycine residue (side chain H) next to an alanine residue (side chain CH₃) in a short peptide. With no Cβ, glycine avoids steric clashes and can take backbone angles other residues cannot.
fig.alt: Two tripeptides: Ala-Gly-Ala with the glycine residue shaded and labelled side chain H, few clashes, wide phi/psi range; Ala-Ala-Ala with the middle alanine and its methyl shaded, labelled C-beta clashes limit phi/psi. Tags mark tiny side chain flexible backbone correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Incorrect. A charge of −1 means every molecule is the anion H₂N–CH(CH₃)–COO⁻, with the amino group fully deprotonated. That requires a pH well above the amino pKa (about 11.7 or higher for 99%). At pH 9.7 exactly half the amino groups are still –NH₃⁺.

Correct. pH 9.7 equals pKa₂, the pKa of the α-amino group, so by Henderson–Hasselbalch [–NH₂]/[–NH₃⁺] = 10⁰ = 1: half the molecules are zwitterions (net 0) and half are anions (net −1). The carboxyl (pKa 2.3) is fully deprotonated at this pH. The average net charge is (0 + (−1))/2 = −0.5. Any time pH equals a pKa, that group contributes half its full charge.

Incorrect. An average charge of 0 occurs at the isoelectric point, pI = (2.3 + 9.7)/2 = 6.0, where nearly all alanine is the zwitterion. At pH 9.7, 3.7 units higher, half of the amino groups have already lost their proton.

Incorrect. +0.5 is the average charge at pKa₁ = 2.3, where half the molecules are cations (+1) and half zwitterions (0). The sign is wrong for pH 9.7: above the pI an amino acid is negative on average, not positive.

p: In solution, an amino acid exists as a mixture of protonation states, and its average (net) charge is the weighted sum of those states. At a pH equal to a group's pKa, that group is exactly half protonated, so it contributes half of its full charge.

For alanine (pKa₁ 2.3, pKa₂ 9.7): below 2.3 the average approaches +1; at 2.3 it is +0.5; at the pI (6.0) it is 0; at 9.7 it is −0.5; well above 9.7 it approaches −1. The curve of charge against pH is a mirror of the titration curve.

This idea links to electrophoresis (molecules with a fractional average charge still migrate) and to buffering (at a pKa, both forms are present in equal amounts, which gives maximum buffer capacity).

fx.f: average charge of a group = (charge of protonated form) × fraction protonated + (charge of deprotonated form) × fraction deprotonated
fx.w: At pH = pKa each fraction is 0.5. For the α-amino group: (+1)(0.5) + (0)(0.5) = +0.5; with the carboxylate fixed at −1, the total is −0.5.

steps: Carboxyl: pH 9.7 is far above pKa 2.3, so −1.
Amino group: pH = pKa 9.7, so half –NH₃⁺ (+1) and half –NH₂ (0), average +0.5.
x1A_050.trap: At a pKa the group is half charged; the pI (zero charge) is between the two pKa values, not at one of them.

fig.cap: Alanine's average net charge against pH, computed from pKa 2.3 and 9.7. At pH 9.7 the curve passes through −0.5; +0.5, 0 and −1 belong to pH 2.3, 6.0 and well above 9.7.
fig.alt: Net charge of alanine falling from +1 at low pH through +0.5 at pH 2.3, 0 from pH 4 to 8, −0.5 at pH 9.7 (correct, green point), and approaching −1 above pH 12.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the two pKa values in the question.

ref.t: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, 26.2 Amino Acids and the Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation: Isoelectric Points

ox: Incorrect. α-Helices and β-sheets are secondary structure: local, repeating backbone shapes held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N–H groups. They depend on the sequence but are not the sequence itself. A helix can unfold (for example on heating) while the order of residues stays exactly the same, which shows the two levels are different things.

Incorrect. The overall three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide chain is tertiary structure. It comes from how helices, sheets and loops pack together, held mostly by side-chain interactions such as the hydrophobic core, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfide bonds. Tertiary structure is what heat and urea destroy, while the primary structure survives.

Incorrect. How two or more separate polypeptide chains (subunits) fit together is quaternary structure, as in the α₂β₂ tetramer of hemoglobin. Only multi-chain proteins have this level at all. It describes the assembly of finished chains, not the order of residues inside any one chain.

Correct. Primary structure is the linear order of amino acids, read from the N-terminus to the C-terminus, held together by covalent peptide (amide) bonds. It is encoded directly by the gene through the mRNA codons. Because it is covalent, it survives denaturation by heat, urea or pH change; only breaking peptide bonds (hydrolysis or proteolysis) changes it. Every higher level of structure follows from this sequence.

concept.t: The four levels of protein structure
p: Protein structure is described in four levels. Primary is the amino acid sequence joined by peptide bonds. Secondary is local backbone shape (α-helix, β-sheet, turns) held by backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds. Tertiary is the full 3D fold of one chain, held by side-chain interactions: the hydrophobic core, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfide bonds. Quaternary is the arrangement of two or more chains.

The levels differ in the bonds that hold them. Only the primary level is covalent backbone, so denaturants (heat, urea, extreme pH, detergents) remove the higher levels but leave the sequence intact. Disulfide bonds are covalent too, but they are counted as tertiary or quaternary because they link side chains, not the backbone.

On the MCAT, match the description to the level: sequence → primary; helix or sheet → secondary; overall shape of one chain or a domain → tertiary; subunits → quaternary. Remember that the sequence contains the information that determines all the higher levels.

x1A_051.trap: Primary structure is only the sequence; any shape, even a single helix, is a higher level.

fig.cap: The four levels of structure with the bonds that hold each one. Only the primary level (the covalent sequence) survives boiling or urea.
fig.alt: Four panels: primary shown as a chain of lettered beads held by peptide bonds; secondary as a helix and two sheet arrows held by backbone hydrogen bonds; tertiary as a folded chain with a nonpolar core; quaternary as four subunits alpha1, beta1, beta2, alpha2. Tags show primary intact and the other levels lost after boiling or urea.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Incorrect. Ionic bonds (salt bridges) form between oppositely charged side chains, such as the carboxylate of Asp or Glu and the ammonium of Lys or the guanidinium of Arg. They help hold the tertiary fold and subunit contacts together, but they are not what defines a helix or a sheet. A helix made entirely of alanine, which has no charged side chains, is still stable.

Correct. Secondary structure is held by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups: the C=O of one peptide unit accepts a hydrogen bond from the N–H of another. In an α-helix the partners are residue n and n + 4 in the same stretch; in a β-sheet they lie on neighboring strands. Because every residue has the same backbone, these bonds repeat regularly, which is exactly what gives helices and sheets their regular geometry regardless of the side chains.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds are covalent S–S links made by oxidizing two cysteine thiols. They lock together parts of a chain (tertiary) or separate chains (quaternary), especially in secreted proteins. Only cysteine can make them, so they cannot be what stabilizes every helix and sheet in every protein.

Incorrect. Peptide bonds are the covalent amide bonds along the backbone that join residue to residue. They make up primary structure. They are present whether the chain is folded or random, so they do not create the specific helix or sheet shape. They do supply the C=O and N–H groups that form the hydrogen bonds, which is the real answer.

concept.t: Secondary structure and backbone hydrogen bonds
p: Secondary structure is the local, repeating shape of the polypeptide backbone. The two main types are the α-helix and the β-sheet. Both are stabilized by hydrogen bonds between a backbone carbonyl oxygen (C=O, the acceptor) and a backbone amide hydrogen (N–H, the donor). Side chains are not part of these bonds; they point away from them.

What differs is who pairs with whom. In an α-helix each C=O bonds to the N–H four residues later (n → n + 4), so partners are close in sequence. In a β-sheet the bonds link side-by-side strands that may be far apart in sequence or even in different chains.

Keep the bond types straight: peptide bonds = primary; backbone hydrogen bonds = secondary; side-chain interactions (hydrophobic effect, salt bridges, side-chain hydrogen bonds, disulfides) = tertiary and quaternary.

x1A_052.trap: Secondary structure means BACKBONE hydrogen bonds; anything involving side chains is tertiary.

fig.cap: Top: in a helix, hydrogen-bond partners are 4 residues apart; in a sheet, strands far apart in sequence pair up. Bottom: the bond itself is backbone C=O···H–N, with side chains (R) pointing away.
fig.alt: A 30-residue chain drawn as boxes. Residues 2 to 12 form a helix with short arcs linking residue n to n plus 4. Residues 15 to 19 and 25 to 29 form sheet strands linked by long arcs. Below, two backbone chains with carbonyl oxygens of the top chain hydrogen-bonded to amide hydrogens of the bottom chain; R groups point away.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Bonding residue n to n + 2 would require a very tight loop, closing a 7-atom ring. That pattern occurs only in rare, isolated γ-turns, not in a repeating helix. If every residue did this, the backbone could not wind into the regular 3.6-residue spiral of the α-helix.

Correct. In the α-helix the C=O of residue n accepts a hydrogen bond from the N–H of residue n + 4. With 100° of rotation and 0.15 nm of rise per residue, residue n + 4 sits almost directly above residue n, one turn later, so the C=O and N–H line up nearly parallel to the helix axis. This i → i+4 pattern gives 3.6 residues per turn and a pitch of 0.54 nm. (The tighter i → i+3 pattern defines the less common 3₁₀ helix.)

Incorrect. Residue n + 1 is the very next residue. Its N–H is joined to the C=O of residue n through the same planar peptide bond, so the two groups point away from each other and cannot hydrogen-bond. Adjacent residues are covalently linked, not hydrogen-bonded.

Incorrect. Hydrogen bonds to a residue on a neighboring, separate strand define a β-sheet, not an α-helix. In a sheet the partners can be far apart in sequence, while in a helix they are always close: in the same continuous segment, four residues apart.

p: The α-helix is a right-handed coil of the backbone. Each residue adds 100° of rotation and 0.15 nm of rise, so one full turn takes 3.6 residues and spans 0.54 nm (the pitch). Every backbone C=O of residue n hydrogen-bonds to the N–H of residue n + 4, so all the backbone polar groups inside the helix are satisfied.

Because the hydrogen bonds run roughly parallel to the axis, they stitch each turn to the next. The side chains point outward, which is why a helix can have one hydrophobic face and one polar face if the sequence places nonpolar residues every 3 to 4 positions.

Proline breaks helices: its ring nitrogen has no N–H to donate and its rigid ring clashes with the turn before it. Glycine destabilizes helices because its tiny side chain makes the backbone too flexible. Compare the 3₁₀ helix (n → n + 3, 3 residues per turn) and the β-sheet (bonds between strands).

x1A_053.trap: α-helix = n → n + 4 and 3.6 residues per turn; don't mix up 4 (the H-bond spacing) with 3.6 (residues per turn).

fig.cap: An ideal α-helix computed from 100° and 0.15 nm per residue. Dashed green lines join residue n to residue n + 4; one turn is 3.6 residues.
fig.alt: Side view of a helix with residues n to n plus 8 marked; dashed green hydrogen bonds connect n to n plus 4, n plus 1 to n plus 5 and so on. A bar marks one turn as 3.6 residues or 0.54 nanometres. An end-on view shows side chains R pointing outward. Tags: n to n plus 4 alpha-helix correct; n to n plus 3 is a 3-10 helix; n to n plus 1 or n plus 2 too close.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue positions computed from ideal α-helix parameters (100° and 0.15 nm per residue).

ox: Incorrect. The center of an α-helix is already packed tightly with backbone atoms; there is no open channel for side chains. If side chains pointed inward they would collide with each other and with the backbone. Pore-forming proteins create channels by bundling several helices, with side chains lining the gap between helices, not inside one helix.

Incorrect. Side chains lying flat and alternating above and below a plane describes a β-strand in a sheet: each residue flips its side chain to the opposite face of the sheet. A helix has no flat plane; its side chains radiate around the axis like spokes, about 100° apart.

Incorrect. The hydrogen bonds that hold an α-helix are between backbone groups: the C=O of residue n and the N–H of residue n + 4. Side chains are not needed for them, which is why the backbone of almost any sequence can form a helix. Side chains influence how stable the helix is, but they do not form the defining bonds.

Correct. In an α-helix the backbone forms the tightly wound core, and each side chain (R group) projects outward from the axis, rotated 100° from the previous one. This keeps bulky groups out of each other's way and exposes them to the surroundings. It also explains amphipathic helices: if nonpolar residues recur every 3 to 4 positions, they line up on one outer face.

p: Picture an α-helix as a cylinder. The backbone, with its C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds running along the axis, forms the cylinder wall and fills the core. Each side chain points outward from the axis, and successive side chains are rotated 100° around the helix.

This outward arrangement decides how a helix interacts with its surroundings. A helix with nonpolar residues at positions n, n + 3, n + 4, n + 7 has a hydrophobic stripe on one face that can pack into the protein core or against another helix, while the other face is polar and faces water. A transmembrane helix has about 20 nonpolar residues all around.

Contrast the β-strand, where side chains alternate above and below the plane of the sheet (every second residue on the same face). Neither structure uses side chains to form its defining backbone hydrogen bonds.

x1A_054.trap: Helix: side chains point OUT like spokes. Sheet: side chains alternate UP and DOWN.

fig.cap: The end-on view (right) shows side chains (R) radiating outward 100° apart while the backbone fills the core.
fig.alt: End-on view of an alpha-helix: seven backbone alpha-carbons near the center connected by purple lines, each with an orange stick ending in an R circle pointing outward; the helix axis is a dot at the center. A side view on the left shows hydrogen bonds from residue n to n plus 4.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; positions computed from ideal α-helix parameters (100° and 0.15 nm per residue).

ox: Correct. A β-sheet is called antiparallel when neighboring strands run in opposite N-to-C directions, like the two lanes of a road. This lines each C=O directly across from an N–H on the partner strand, so the hydrogen bonds run straight across and are nearly linear, which makes antiparallel sheets slightly more stable. They often form from a hairpin: one strand, a short β-turn, then the returning strand.

Incorrect. Adjacent strands running in the same N-to-C direction define a parallel β-sheet. Parallel strands cannot be joined by a short turn; they need a longer crossover connection, often a helix. Their hydrogen bonds are angled across the strands rather than straight, so parallel sheets are usually a bit less stable and are often buried.

Incorrect. Hydrogen bonds within a single segment describe an α-helix (n to n + 4 along the same stretch). An extended β-strand cannot hydrogen-bond to itself; its C=O and N–H groups point sideways toward neighboring strands. Every β-sheet, parallel or antiparallel, is held by bonds between strands.

Incorrect. Side chains do not lie in the plane of the sheet. Because the backbone is pleated, the side chains alternate above and below the plane. The groups that do lie in the plane are the backbone C=O and N–H, which form the hydrogen bonds between strands. In any case, side-chain position does not distinguish antiparallel from parallel sheets.

p: A β-sheet is built from extended segments (β-strands) lying side by side and hydrogen-bonded through their backbone C=O and N–H groups. Each strand has a direction, from its N-terminus to its C-terminus, so two neighbors can run the same way (parallel) or opposite ways (antiparallel). Mixed sheets contain both.

In antiparallel sheets the hydrogen bonds run straight across between paired residues; in parallel sheets they are angled. Antiparallel strands are often connected by tight β-turns (hairpins), while parallel strands need longer crossover connections.

In both types the side chains alternate above and below the sheet, and the sheet surface is pleated. Silk and amyloid fibers are dominated by β-sheets. On the MCAT, direction is the only thing that separates parallel from antiparallel.

x1A_055.trap: Antiparallel/parallel refers to strand DIRECTION (N→C), not to where side chains point.

fig.cap: Two-stranded sheets seen from above. Arrows run N to C. Antiparallel neighbors point opposite ways with straight hydrogen bonds; parallel neighbors point the same way with angled ones.
fig.alt: Left panel: two strand arrows pointing in opposite directions with vertical dashed hydrogen bonds, tagged antiparallel correct. Right panel: two arrows pointing the same direction with zigzag dashed hydrogen bonds, tagged parallel. A note says hydrogen bonds join different strands and side chains point above and below the sheet.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. If every side chain pointed to the same face, consecutive residues would have to sit at the same height relative to the sheet. In fact the pleated backbone flips each residue relative to the previous one, so residues 1, 3, 5... share one face and residues 2, 4, 6... share the other. Only every second residue points the same way.

Incorrect. Side chains spiraling around with a repeat of 3.6 residues per turn describes an α-helix. A β-strand is nearly fully extended (about 0.33 to 0.35 nm per residue versus 0.15 nm in a helix) and has a two-residue repeat, so its side chains cannot wrap around it.

Correct. A β-strand is extended and pleated, like a folded paper fan. Each α-carbon sits at a pleat, alternately slightly above and below the sheet plane, and its side chain points out of the sheet on that side. So successive side chains alternate faces: residues i, i + 2, i + 4 are on one face and i + 1, i + 3 on the other. This lets a sheet have one hydrophobic face and one polar face when nonpolar and polar residues alternate.

Incorrect. The groups that point toward the neighboring strand are the backbone C=O and N–H, which lie in the plane of the sheet and form the interstrand hydrogen bonds. If side chains pointed sideways into the neighbor strand, they would block those hydrogen bonds. Side chains instead stick out perpendicular to the sheet.

p: A β-strand is an almost fully extended stretch of backbone, about 0.33 to 0.35 nm per residue. The backbone zigzags (pleats) so that each α-carbon is at a fold. The backbone C=O and N–H point sideways, in the plane of the sheet, toward neighboring strands, while side chains point perpendicular to the sheet, alternating above and below.

The repeat is therefore two residues (about 0.7 nm). An alternating pattern of nonpolar and polar residues makes an amphipathic strand, with one face packing into the protein core and the other facing water. Sheets in membrane-spanning β-barrels and in amyloid fibrils use this alternation.

Compare the α-helix: side chains point outward like spokes with a repeat of 3.6 residues, so an amphipathic helix has nonpolar residues every 3 to 4 positions. Spacing of 2 suggests a strand; spacing of 3 to 4 suggests a helix.

x1A_056.trap: Every-2 pattern = β-strand; every-3-to-4 pattern = α-helix.

fig.cap: Edge-on view of one β-strand. Side chains alternate above (nonpolar here) and below (polar here) the sheet plane, with a two-residue repeat.
fig.alt: A zigzag backbone with black alpha-carbons at each pleat. Side chains Val, Ile, Phe, Leu, Val point up above the sheet plane and Ser, Thr, Asn, Gln point down below it. A bar marks a repeat of 2 residues, about 0.7 nanometres. Tags: alternating faces correct; a 3.6-residue spiral is an alpha-helix.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Leucine and isoleucine are large, nonpolar residues. Leucine is one of the strongest helix formers, and β-branched isoleucine favors β-strands; both tend to be buried in the hydrophobic core. Their bulky side chains restrict the backbone angles needed for a tight 180° reversal, so they are uncommon at the corners of β-turns.

Incorrect. Lysine and arginine are long, positively charged residues found mostly on the protein surface. Turns are also usually on the surface, so these residues can appear near turns, but charge does not give them the special backbone geometry a tight turn needs. Lysine is actually a good helix former.

Incorrect. Phenylalanine and tryptophan have large aromatic rings. They prefer β-strands and buried positions, where their rings can stack and pack in the core. Their bulk clashes with the compact backbone conformation of a tight turn, so they are rare at the two central turn positions.

Correct. A β-turn reverses the chain in four residues, held by a hydrogen bond from the C=O of residue i to the N–H of residue i + 3. Proline often sits at position i + 1 because its ring locks the backbone angle φ near −60°, a built-in kink. Glycine often sits at i + 2 because its side chain is only H, so it can adopt backbone angles that other residues cannot. Both are also known as helix breakers.

concept.t: β-turns and the special roles of glycine and proline
p: A β-turn (reverse turn) is a short segment, usually four residues (i to i + 3), that reverses the direction of the chain by about 180°. It is held by a hydrogen bond from the C=O of residue i to the N–H of residue i + 3. Turns connect the strands of antiparallel β-hairpins and are typically on the protein surface.

Glycine has a hydrogen atom as its side chain, so it is the most flexible residue and can take backbone angles forbidden to others. Proline's side chain loops back to bond its own backbone nitrogen, forming a ring that fixes φ near −60° and removes the N–H hydrogen-bond donor. These properties suit tight turns but disrupt α-helices.
So glycine and proline are both turn formers and helix breakers. Bulky residues such as Leu, Ile, Phe and Trp prefer helices, strands and the buried core.

x1A_057.trap: Gly and Pro are opposite in rigidity (most flexible vs most rigid), yet both favor turns and break helices.

fig.cap: A four-residue β-turn with Pro at i + 1 and Gly at i + 2, closed by a C=O(i)···H–N(i + 3) hydrogen bond, plus where each answer pair usually sits in proteins.
fig.alt: A beta-hairpin: two antiparallel strand arrows joined by a turn of residues i, Pro, Gly, i plus 3, with a dashed hydrogen bond between i and i plus 3. Structures of glycine and L-proline drawn with the proline ring highlighted. A table tags Gly and Pro as turn formers (correct) and Leu/Ile, Phe/Trp and Lys/Arg with their usual locations.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Incorrect. The sequence of amino acids is primary structure. It is the covalent backbone order, determined by the gene, and it is the information from which the tertiary fold arises, but it is not the fold itself. A denatured protein keeps its sequence while losing its tertiary structure.

Incorrect. Local helices and sheets on their own are secondary structure. Tertiary structure includes them, but it adds how they are arranged relative to each other in space: which helices pack against which sheets, where the loops go, and which side chains are buried. Describing only the local elements misses the overall fold.

Correct. Tertiary structure is the complete three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide chain: how its helices, sheets and loops fold and pack together. It is stabilized mainly by side-chain interactions: the hydrophobic effect burying nonpolar residues in the core, side-chain hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, metal ions and disulfide bonds. The active site of an enzyme usually comes from residues brought together by the tertiary fold.

Incorrect. How two or more chains assemble is quaternary structure, found only in multi-subunit proteins such as hemoglobin. The same kinds of side-chain interactions hold subunits together, but quaternary structure describes contacts between chains, not the fold within one chain.

p: Tertiary structure is the overall 3D fold of one polypeptide chain. It brings together residues that may be far apart in the sequence, creating binding sites, active sites and the compact globular shape of soluble proteins. Large chains often fold into several domains, each a compact, independently folding unit.

The main driving force is the hydrophobic effect: nonpolar side chains are buried in the core, releasing ordered water. Hydrogen bonds between side chains, salt bridges between opposite charges, coordination of metal ions and covalent disulfide bonds between cysteines add further stability.

Denaturing agents (heat, urea, extreme pH, detergents, organic solvents) destroy tertiary structure by disrupting these noncovalent interactions. Reducing agents such as β-mercaptoethanol are needed to break disulfides. The primary sequence survives all of these, which is why some denatured proteins can refold.

x1A_058.trap: Tertiary = shape of ONE chain; quaternary = arrangement of SEVERAL chains.

fig.cap: Tertiary structure (third panel) is the full fold of one chain, held by side-chain interactions around a nonpolar core.
fig.alt: Four panels for primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure with the bonds that hold each. The tertiary panel shows one folded chain around an orange nonpolar core, held by hydrophobic core, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and disulfides.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Incorrect. Myoglobin is a single polypeptide chain of 153 residues folded around one heme group. It has primary, secondary (mostly α-helix) and tertiary structure, but with only one chain it has no quaternary level. Its single binding site explains its hyperbolic, non-cooperative O₂-binding curve.

Correct. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more separate polypeptide chains. Hemoglobin is a tetramer of two α and two β chains (α₂β₂), each folded much like myoglobin and each carrying a heme. The subunits are held together by noncovalent contacts, and changes at these contacts when O₂ binds produce cooperative, sigmoidal O₂ binding.

Incorrect. Ribonuclease A is a single chain of 124 residues held in shape by four internal disulfide bonds. Disulfides inside one chain are part of tertiary structure. Covalent cross-links create quaternary structure only when they join different chains, as in antibodies or insulin.

Incorrect. By definition a single polypeptide chain cannot have quaternary structure, whatever its length. A 30-residue monomeric peptide may form a helix or a small fold, but quaternary structure requires at least two chains, either identical (a homodimer, for example) or different.

p: Quaternary structure exists only in proteins built from two or more polypeptide chains, called subunits. It describes how the subunits fit together: their number, their arrangement and the contacts between them. Examples include hemoglobin (α₂β₂), antibodies (two heavy and two light chains joined by disulfides) and many enzymes.

Subunits are mostly held together by the same noncovalent forces that stabilize tertiary structure (hydrophobic patches, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges), sometimes reinforced by interchain disulfide bonds. Multiple subunits allow cooperativity and allosteric regulation, as when O₂ binding to one hemoglobin subunit raises the O₂ affinity of the others.
Myoglobin, a single chain, shows a hyperbolic O₂-binding curve; hemoglobin, with quaternary structure, shows a sigmoidal one. Internal disulfides (ribonuclease A) are tertiary, not quaternary.

x1A_059.trap: Count chains, not bonds or residues: one chain means no quaternary structure.

fig.cap: Only hemoglobin, with four separate chains (α₂β₂), has quaternary structure. Myoglobin, ribonuclease A and a monomeric peptide are each a single chain.
fig.alt: Four panels: myoglobin as one blob with a red heme, tagged no quaternary; hemoglobin as four circles alpha1, beta1, beta2, alpha2, tagged quaternary; ribonuclease A as one chain with four dashed disulfides inside, tagged no quaternary; a 30-residue peptide as a single wavy line, tagged no quaternary.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Water cannot hydrogen-bond to nonpolar side chains, so water molecules next to an exposed nonpolar surface become more ordered (a cage-like shell), which lowers water's entropy. When the protein folds and buries those side chains in its core, that water is released into the bulk and its entropy rises. This gain (ΔS of water > 0) makes ΔG = ΔH − TΔS negative. This is the hydrophobic effect, the main driving force for folding.

Incorrect. Nonpolar side chains such as leucine, valine and phenylalanine have no O–H or N–H donors and no strongly electronegative acceptors, so they cannot hydrogen-bond with each other. They do attract weakly through London dispersion forces once packed together, but that is a small contribution compared with the entropy gained by water.

Incorrect. Folding does the opposite to the chain: an unfolded polypeptide can adopt an enormous number of conformations, while the folded one adopts essentially one. So the chain's own conformational entropy decreases on folding (ΔS of chain < 0), which opposes folding. The favorable entropy comes from the surrounding water, not from the protein.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds form only between cysteine residues, which make up a small fraction of most proteins, and they form mainly in oxidizing compartments (ER lumen, extracellular space). Most cytosolic proteins fold with no disulfides at all. Disulfides can lock a fold in place, but they are not what drives nonpolar residues into the core.

p: The hydrophobic effect is the tendency of nonpolar groups to cluster together in water. It is driven mainly by entropy, not by attraction between the nonpolar groups. Water forms an ordered, low-entropy shell around exposed nonpolar surfaces; burying those surfaces frees the water, increasing its entropy and making ΔG negative.

For a folding protein, two entropy terms compete. The chain loses conformational entropy (unfavorable), while water gains entropy as nonpolar side chains are buried (favorable). Hydrogen bonds and salt bridges inside the protein mostly replace bonds the unfolded chain already made with water, so they contribute less than students expect.

The same effect drives membrane bilayer and micelle formation and the binding of nonpolar ligands. Agents that make the solvent less polar (ethanol, detergents) or that solvate nonpolar groups (urea) weaken the hydrophobic effect and denature proteins.

x1A_060.trap: The favorable entropy belongs to the WATER; the protein chain itself loses entropy when it folds.

fig.cap: Unfolded: water forms ordered cages around exposed nonpolar groups. Folded: the groups are buried and the water is released, so water's entropy rises.
fig.alt: Left panel: an unfolded chain with five orange nonpolar groups, each surrounded by a ring of ten blue water molecules, labelled low entropy. Right panel: a folded protein with the orange groups clustered in the core and blue water molecules scattered randomly outside, labelled entropy of water rises. A box gives delta G equals delta H minus T delta S, water entropy positive, chain entropy negative.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Incorrect. If folding had a positive ΔG, proteins would not fold on their own, yet most small proteins refold spontaneously in a test tube with no ATP (Anfinsen showed this with ribonuclease A). ATP is used by some chaperones to bind and release folding chains, but that energy prevents aggregation; it does not pay for the native state itself. The native state is the lowest free-energy state.

Incorrect. Each individual hydrogen bond, van der Waals contact or salt bridge is weak (a few kJ/mol), but a folded protein contains hundreds of them, plus the large hydrophobic effect. Added up, the favorable contributions run to hundreds of kJ/mol. So these interactions contribute a great deal; the puzzle is why the net is so small despite them.

Correct. Folding takes the chain from an enormous number of unfolded conformations to essentially one, so the chain loses a large amount of conformational entropy. In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, that loss makes −TΔS(chain) large and positive, cancelling most of the favorable interaction enthalpy and hydrophobic effect. Net stability is the small difference between large opposing terms, typically only 20 to 60 kJ/mol, which is why one mutation or a modest temperature rise can unfold a protein.

Incorrect. Folded proteins are held mostly by noncovalent forces: the hydrophobic effect, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals contacts and salt bridges. The only common covalent cross-links are disulfide bonds, and many proteins, especially in the cytosol, have none. If folding were held by covalent bonds, simply heating to 60 °C or adding urea could not unfold proteins.

concept.t: Why proteins are only marginally stable
p: The stability of a folded protein is ΔG(unfolding), usually only about 20 to 60 kJ/mol, roughly the energy of a few hydrogen bonds. It is small because two very large terms nearly cancel. Favoring folding: the hydrophobic effect (water entropy gained when nonpolar groups are buried) and many weak interactions (hydrogen bonds, van der Waals packing, salt bridges). Opposing folding: the loss of the chain's conformational entropy.

Marginal stability has consequences. A single point mutation, a temperature rise of a few degrees, or a change in pH can tip the balance toward unfolding. It also lets proteins be flexible and be degraded and recycled. Many proteins are believed to be only as stable as they need to be.
On the MCAT, use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS: folding is spontaneous (ΔG < 0) but barely. Remember which entropy is which: water gains entropy (favorable), the chain loses entropy (unfavorable).

fx.w: ΔG is the free-energy change of folding (kJ/mol; negative means spontaneous), ΔH the enthalpy change from forming interactions, T the absolute temperature (K) and ΔS the entropy change of the system (chain plus water). A large negative ΔH and water entropy term are offset by the large chain entropy loss.

x1A_061.trap: A small net ΔG does not mean small interactions; it means two large terms nearly cancel.

fig.cap: Free-energy contributions to folding (illustrative values, not measurements). Large favorable terms (green) are almost cancelled by the chain's entropy loss (red), leaving a small net ΔG.
fig.alt: Waterfall bar chart: hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and van der Waals minus 250 kilojoules per mole; hydrophobic effect minus 300; chain conformational entropy plus 510; net folding free energy about minus 40.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph; illustrative magnitudes chosen to sum to a typical net stability, consistent with Lehninger's description of protein stability.

ox: Correct. Urea unfolded the enzyme and the reducing agent broke its disulfide bonds, so no structure beyond the sequence remained. When both were removed slowly, the chain refolded, re-formed the correct disulfides and regained full activity with nothing present but its own amino acid sequence and the solvent. So the information needed to reach the native fold is contained in the primary structure. This is Anfinsen's classic experiment with ribonuclease A, which earned the 1972 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Incorrect. No chaperones were present in the test tube, yet the protein refolded fully, so chaperones cannot always be required. In cells, chaperones help many proteins fold efficiently by preventing aggregation in the crowded cytoplasm, but they do not supply the fold, and small proteins like this one fold by themselves.

Incorrect. The direction of information is the reverse. The amino acid sequence is set by the gene during translation, and the sequence then determines which cysteines meet and pair up as the protein folds. Disulfide bonds form after or during folding and cannot specify the sequence.

Incorrect. Neither urea nor a reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol breaks peptide bonds. If the backbone had been cut, the original chain could not be restored simply by removing the reagents, and activity would not return. The full recovery of activity shows that primary structure stayed intact throughout.

p: Christian Anfinsen unfolded ribonuclease A (124 residues, four disulfide bonds) with 8 M urea, which disrupts noncovalent interactions, plus β-mercaptoethanol, which reduces disulfides to free thiols. The enzyme lost all activity. When he removed both reagents slowly and let air oxidize the thiols, the enzyme regained nearly 100% activity.

Conclusion (Anfinsen's thermodynamic hypothesis): the native structure is the lowest free-energy state available to the chain, and the amino acid sequence contains all the information needed to reach it. Higher levels of structure follow from primary structure.

Order matters. If the reduced chain is oxidized while still unfolded in urea, cysteines pair at random and the product is mostly inactive scrambled protein. In cells, chaperones and protein disulfide isomerase speed folding and fix mistakes, but they do not encode the fold.

x1A_062.trap: Chaperones help folding happen efficiently; they never supply the information for the fold.

fig.cap: Anfinsen's experiment. Removing urea and β-mercaptoethanol slowly restores full activity; oxidizing while still unfolded gives scrambled disulfides and about 1% activity.
fig.alt: Flowchart: native RNase A with 4 disulfides and 100% activity, treated with 8 M urea plus beta-mercaptoethanol, becomes unfolded and reduced with 8 free thiols and 0% activity. Path 1, remove urea and reducing agent slowly then oxidize, returns to native with about 100% activity, tagged sequence encodes fold. Path 2, oxidize in 8 M urea, gives scrambled disulfides with about 1% activity. A trace of beta-mercaptoethanol lets scrambled disulfides reshuffle back to native.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content after Anfinsen's ribonuclease A experiments as described in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Incorrect. Urea is a denaturant, not a hydrolytic agent. It disrupts hydrogen bonds and weakens the hydrophobic effect, but it does not cleave the covalent peptide bonds of the backbone, even at 8 M. The same urea treatment in the successful refolding experiment left the enzyme fully recoverable, which proves the backbone was intact.

Incorrect. Oxidizing cysteine thiols (–SH) joins two of them into a disulfide bond (–S–S–). It cannot add carbons or turn cysteine into methionine; that would require building a new side chain (methionine has a thioether, –CH₂–CH₂–S–CH₃). Stronger oxidation can give sulfenic or sulfonic acids, but never methionine.

Incorrect. Primary structure, the sequence of residues joined by peptide bonds, is unchanged by urea and by oxidation. The problem is a covalent mistake beyond the sequence: wrong cysteine pairs. Because the sequence is intact, adding a trace of reducing agent lets the disulfides reshuffle, and the enzyme slowly regains activity, which could not happen if the sequence were lost.

Correct. In 8 M urea the chain is a random coil, so the eight cysteines meet one another at random. Oxidizing at this stage locks in whatever pairs happen to form. There are 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105 ways to pair 8 cysteines into 4 disulfides, and only one is native, so roughly 1% of molecules are correct. When urea is removed, the covalent wrong cross-links trap the chain in non-native shapes it cannot escape, so activity stays very low.

concept.t: Scrambled disulfides and the order of folding
p: Disulfide bonds are covalent cross-links between cysteine thiols. In the native protein they form between cysteines that folding has already brought next to each other. They stabilize the fold but do not direct it: the noncovalent folding process chooses which cysteines meet.

If a reduced protein is oxidized while unfolded (for example in 8 M urea), cysteines pair randomly. For ribonuclease A, with 8 cysteines, there are 105 possible pairings and only one is native, so about 1% of activity returns. The wrong cross-links act like staples in the wrong place, preventing the chain from reaching its native fold even after urea is removed.

Adding a trace of reducing agent allows thiol–disulfide exchange: bonds break and re-form until the most stable (native) set wins. In the ER, protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) catalyzes this reshuffling.

fx.f: Number of ways to pair 2n cysteines = (2n − 1) × (2n − 3) × … × 1
fx.w: For 8 cysteines (n = 4): the first cysteine can pair with any of 7, the next unpaired one with any of 5, then 3, then 1, giving 105 pairings. Only one is native, so random pairing gives about 1/105 ≈ 1% correct.

steps: Reduced ribonuclease A has 8 free cysteines and is unfolded in 8 M urea.
Oxidation now pairs cysteines at random: 7 × 5 × 3 × 1 = 105 possible sets of 4 disulfides.
Only 1 of 105 is native, so about 1% of molecules have the correct bonds.
Removing urea cannot fix the others because their wrong disulfides are covalent, so activity stays near 1%.
x1A_063.trap: Disulfides must form AFTER the chain folds; oxidize first and the wrong pairs get locked in.

fig.cap: Path 2 (lower right) is this experiment: oxidizing in 8 M urea locks in random disulfides, so only about 1 in 105 molecules is native.
fig.alt: Flowchart of Anfinsen's experiment. Unfolded reduced RNase A oxidized while still in 8 M urea gives scrambled disulfides with about 1% activity, tagged disulfides locked before folding. A box explains 7 times 5 times 3 times 1 equals 105 possible pairings, only one native.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content after Anfinsen's ribonuclease A experiments as described in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Incorrect. The information that specifies a protein's native fold is in its own amino acid sequence, as Anfinsen's refolding experiments showed. Chaperones are general helpers that recognize features common to all unfolded chains, such as exposed hydrophobic stretches, so they cannot carry a separate blueprint for each of the thousands of proteins they assist.

Correct. Newly made or stress-damaged chains expose hydrophobic segments that would normally be buried. In the crowded cytoplasm these patches can stick to each other and form aggregates. Chaperones such as Hsp70 bind these exposed hydrophobic regions, and chaperonins such as GroEL/GroES give a chain an enclosed chamber to fold in. ATP hydrolysis drives cycles of binding and release, giving the chain repeated chances to fold correctly. The final fold is still set by the sequence.

Incorrect. Chaperone binding is transient and noncovalent: Hsp70 grips the client through hydrophobic contacts, holding it tightly after it hydrolyzes its bound ATP to ADP, then lets go when the ADP is exchanged for fresh ATP. A permanent covalent bond would leave the client stuck to the chaperone and unable to function, which is the opposite of the chaperone's purpose.

Incorrect. Peptide bonds are formed by the peptidyl transferase center of the ribosome, which is made of rRNA (the ribosome is a ribozyme). Chaperones act on the chain as it emerges or after it is released, helping it fold; they do not add amino acids.

p: Molecular chaperones are proteins that help other proteins fold correctly without becoming part of the final structure. They recognize exposed hydrophobic surfaces typical of unfolded or misfolded chains, bind them noncovalently, and prevent inappropriate interactions and aggregation. Many are heat shock proteins (Hsps), made in greater amounts under stress.

Two main types: Hsp70 family members bind short hydrophobic segments in cycles driven by ATP hydrolysis; chaperonins (GroEL/GroES in bacteria, TRiC in eukaryotes) are barrel-shaped complexes that enclose a chain in a protected chamber. In the ER, BiP (an Hsp70) and protein disulfide isomerase assist secreted proteins.

Key MCAT idea: chaperones affect the efficiency of folding, not the final structure. The sequence still determines the fold. When chaperones fail, misfolded proteins are tagged with ubiquitin and degraded by the proteasome.

x1A_064.trap: Chaperones prevent misfolding; they do not dictate the fold, form covalent bonds or make peptide bonds.

fig.cap: An Hsp70 chaperone binds the exposed hydrophobic patches of a folding chain and releases it (ATP-driven). With protection the chain reaches its native fold; without it, patches stick together into aggregates.
fig.alt: A chain with orange hydrophobic patches is bound by Hsp70, noncovalently, with ATP hydrolysis driving release. The released chain becomes a native fold with buried core, tagged fold set by sequence. Without a chaperone, several chains stick together in an aggregate. Bottom tags: no fold information, not covalent, do not make peptide bonds.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Hydrolyzing peptide bonds requires a protease or prolonged heating in strong acid or base. Urea is a small, neutral organic molecule that cannot cleave the backbone. That is why urea-denatured proteins can often refold once the urea is removed by dialysis: the sequence is still there.

Correct. Urea, (NH₂)₂C=O, has two N–H donors and a C=O acceptor, so at 6 to 8 M it forms hydrogen bonds with backbone C=O and N–H groups and with polar side chains, replacing the protein's internal hydrogen bonds. It also solvates nonpolar side chains better than water does, so burying them in a core gains less free energy, weakening the hydrophobic effect. The unfolded state becomes more favorable while covalent bonds stay intact.

Incorrect. Reducing a disulfide (–S–S–) to two thiols (–SH) requires a reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol or dithiothreitol (DTT), which donates electrons. Urea has no such chemistry. That is why Anfinsen had to add β-mercaptoethanol along with urea to fully unfold ribonuclease A.

Incorrect. Urea acts through reversible, noncovalent interactions, so removing it often allows refolding. Long incubation in old urea solutions can cause a side reaction (carbamylation of lysines by cyanate that forms as urea decomposes), but that is an artifact, not how urea denatures proteins.

p: Urea and guanidinium chloride are chaotropic denaturants used at high concentration (urea 6 to 8 M, guanidinium about 6 M). They unfold proteins without breaking covalent bonds by making the unfolded state more favorable: they hydrogen-bond to the exposed backbone and side chains and they solvate nonpolar groups, weakening the hydrophobic effect.

Because only noncovalent interactions are affected, denaturation by urea is usually reversible. Removing urea slowly by dialysis lets many proteins refold. To break disulfide bonds you must add a reducing agent (β-mercaptoethanol, DTT); to break peptide bonds you need hydrolysis.

Experiments use urea titrations to measure stability: the urea concentration at which half the protein unfolds (the midpoint) is higher for a more stable protein. Compare heat (adds kinetic energy), extreme pH (changes charges), ethanol (lowers solvent polarity) and SDS (coats proteins with negative charge).

x1A_065.trap: Urea alone never breaks disulfides; you need a reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol.

fig.cap: Urea's two denaturing actions, both noncovalent: it competes for backbone hydrogen bonds and solvates nonpolar side chains. Covalent bonds survive.
fig.alt: Structure of urea with two NH2 groups and a C=O. Box 1: competes for hydrogen bonds, backbone C=O to urea H-N and backbone N-H to urea O=C. Box 2: solvates nonpolar side chains, weakening the hydrophobic effect. Green box: peptide bonds and disulfides survive; removing urea allows refolding. Red tags: does not hydrolyze peptide bonds, reduce S-S bonds, or add groups covalently.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; urea structure drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

fig.cap: How common denaturing agents act. Only reducing agents break disulfides, and only hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds.
fig.alt: Table of agents (heat, urea, ethanol, SDS, strong acid or base, high salt, mercury and lead ions, beta-mercaptoethanol or DTT, protease), each with its main action and whether disulfide and peptide bonds survive. All survive except disulfides with reducing agents and peptide bonds with protease.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Secondary structure is held by backbone hydrogen bonds, each worth only a few kJ/mol. Boiling supplies enough thermal energy to break them, so α-helices and β-sheets unravel. Many proteins melt between 40 and 70 °C, well below 100 °C. Some heated proteins later form new, non-native β-sheet aggregates, but the original secondary structure is lost.

Incorrect. Tertiary structure, the specific 3D fold, depends on the hydrophobic effect, side-chain hydrogen bonds and salt bridges, all noncovalent. At 100 °C these interactions are overwhelmed, the protein unfolds and its exposed hydrophobic surfaces usually stick to other molecules, so the enzyme loses its active site and its activity.

Incorrect. Subunits in a multi-chain enzyme are held together by the same noncovalent contacts that hold tertiary structure, so they dissociate or aggregate randomly on boiling. The only quaternary links that would survive are interchain disulfides, and even then the native arrangement of subunits is lost.

Correct. Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids joined by covalent peptide bonds. A peptide bond has partial double-bond character and needs a catalyst (a protease) or harsh chemistry (6 M HCl at about 110 °C for many hours) to hydrolyze at a useful rate. Ten minutes of boiling at neutral pH supplies enough energy to break weak noncovalent interactions but not covalent backbone bonds, so the sequence survives while the higher levels are destroyed.

p: Heating increases molecular motion until the weak noncovalent interactions holding a protein's shape (hydrogen bonds, the hydrophobic effect, salt bridges, van der Waals contacts) can no longer hold it. The protein unfolds: secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure are lost and activity disappears. The melting temperature (Tm) is the temperature at which half the molecules are unfolded.

Covalent bonds are far stronger (hundreds of kJ/mol) and survive brief boiling. Peptide bonds keep the primary structure, and disulfide bonds stay intact too. Hydrolyzing peptide bonds needs a protease or prolonged heating in strong acid.

Heat denaturation is often irreversible in practice, because unfolded chains expose hydrophobic surfaces and aggregate (as in a cooked egg). Small proteins that do not aggregate can refold on cooling, which shows the sequence is intact.

x1A_066.trap: Denaturation removes shape, not sequence: boiling leaves every peptide bond in place.

fig.cap: Each level of structure and what holds it. After boiling only the primary level, held by covalent peptide bonds, remains intact.
fig.alt: Four panels: primary (sequence, peptide bonds) tagged intact after boiling or urea; secondary (backbone hydrogen bonds), tertiary (side-chain interactions) and quaternary (contacts between chains) each tagged lost.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Correct. A protein's fold relies on charged side chains. At very low pH (for example pH 2) carboxylates of Asp and Glu (pKa ≈ 4) gain protons and become neutral –COOH; at very high pH (for example pH 12) Lys amines (pKa ≈ 10.5) lose protons and become neutral –NH₂. Salt bridges then lose one partner's charge, side-chain hydrogen-bond patterns change, and the protein carries a large net charge of one sign, so like charges repel. The fold falls apart even though no covalent bond is broken.

Incorrect. Breaking a disulfide bond is a reduction that requires an electron donor such as β-mercaptoethanol or DTT. Changing the H⁺ concentration does not provide that. (At high pH, disulfides can slowly undergo side reactions, but that is not how acids and bases denature proteins.) Proteins with no disulfides at all are still denatured by extreme pH.

Incorrect. Converting L-amino acids to D-amino acids (racemization) requires removing the α-hydrogen. It does occur slowly in strong base or hot acid, over hours to days, and is used in amino acid dating of fossils. Denaturation by pH happens within seconds to minutes and is often reversible when the pH is restored, which racemization would not be.

Incorrect. Acids and bases do not dehydrate a protein's core. Dehydrating agents and high concentrations of salts or organic solvents change how water interacts with a protein, but extreme pH acts through charge: it alters which groups are protonated. The core is affected only indirectly, after electrostatic repulsion pulls the fold apart.

p: Ionizable side chains change charge when the pH passes their pKa (Henderson–Hasselbalch). Near pH 7, Asp and Glu are −1, Lys and Arg are +1 and His is mostly neutral. Salt bridges (ion pairs) between these groups and many hydrogen bonds depend on these charge states.

At low pH, carboxylates become neutral and the whole protein becomes strongly positive; at high pH, amines become neutral and the protein becomes strongly negative. Salt bridges break and the large net charge produces repulsion that pushes the chain apart, so the protein unfolds. Each protein has a pH range of stability; pepsin, for example, works best near pH 2 in the stomach.

Because only charges change, pH denaturation is often reversible. It does not break disulfides or peptide bonds on the time scale of an experiment. Compare: reducing agents break disulfides; proteases and hot acid break peptide bonds.

x1A_067.trap: pH acts on protonation (charge), not on covalent bonds or stereochemistry.

fig.cap: An Asp–Lys salt bridge at three pH values. Percent charged is computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch (Asp pKa 3.9, Lys pKa 10.5). Only near neutral pH are both partners charged.
fig.alt: Three panels. pH 2: Asp side chain COOH 1% charged, Lys NH3+ 100% charged, no attraction, protein strongly positive, salt bridge lost. pH 7: Asp COO- and Lys NH3+ both 100% charged, attraction, salt bridge holds. pH 12: Asp COO- 100% charged, Lys NH2 3% charged, no attraction, salt bridge lost.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; charge fractions computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation with standard side-chain pKa values.

ox: Incorrect. The isoelectric point is what separates proteins in isoelectric focusing, where each protein migrates through a pH gradient until it reaches the pH at which its net charge is zero, and stops. In SDS-PAGE the bound SDS gives every protein a large negative charge, so all proteins move toward the anode regardless of their pI.

Incorrect. SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate), usually with heat and a reducing agent, unfolds proteins into extended rod-like SDS–protein complexes. This removes differences in native shape, which is the point of the method. Shape does affect migration in native PAGE, where proteins stay folded.

Correct. SDS binds proteins at a nearly constant ratio, about 1.4 g of SDS per gram of protein, so every chain gets roughly the same negative charge per unit mass and the same unfolded shape. The electric force per unit mass is therefore similar for all chains, and the polyacrylamide gel acts as a molecular sieve: smaller chains slip through the pores faster and travel farther. Migration distance is roughly linear in log(mass), so a ladder of known masses lets you estimate an unknown chain's mass.

Incorrect. A protein's own net charge at the running pH is tiny compared with the hundreds of negative sulfate groups contributed by bound SDS. So the intrinsic charge is swamped and plays almost no role. Intrinsic charge does matter in native PAGE and in ion-exchange chromatography.

p: SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) separates polypeptide chains by mass. The anionic detergent SDS denatures proteins and coats them with negative charge in proportion to their length, about 1.4 g SDS per gram protein. Proteins are loaded at the cathode (−) end and all migrate toward the anode (+).

Because charge-to-mass ratio and shape are made uniform, the gel's sieving effect is the only thing that separates them: small chains move farthest. Distance migrated is approximately proportional to −log(mass), so a ladder of known masses gives a calibration. Adding a reducing agent (β-mercaptoethanol or DTT) also breaks disulfide bonds, separating disulfide-linked subunits.

Compare related methods: native PAGE (no SDS; separates by size, shape and charge), isoelectric focusing (by pI), 2D gels (pI in one direction, then SDS-PAGE in the other), and size-exclusion chromatography (by size of the native protein, largest first).

x1A_068.trap: SDS-PAGE gives the mass of each CHAIN, not of the native multi-subunit protein.

fig.cap: An SDS-PAGE gel with a mass ladder. Band positions are computed so that distance is linear in log(mass); smaller chains run farther.
fig.alt: Gel with a ladder lane of 250, 150, 100, 75, 50, 37, 25, 15 and 10 kilodaltons and a sample lane with bands at 120, 60 and 30 kilodaltons. A box explains that SDS unfolds proteins and gives uniform negative charge per mass, so the gel sieves by size. Tags: molecular mass correct; pI belongs to isoelectric focusing; native shape to native PAGE; intrinsic charge is swamped.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; band positions computed from a log-linear mass calibration.

ox: Incorrect. A stabilizing mutation makes the folded state harder to unfold, so more thermal energy is needed and the melting temperature (Tm) rises. Here the Tm drops from 52 °C to 44 °C, which is the opposite. Reading the direction of a Tm change correctly is the whole point of a thermal-melt experiment.

Incorrect. Tm reports thermodynamic stability (the balance between folded and unfolded states), not how fast the enzyme catalyzes a reaction. Catalytic activity must be measured separately, for example from Vmax and Km. A destabilized mutant can be as active as wild type at low temperature, or less active; the melt curve alone cannot say.

Incorrect. A protein that could not fold at any temperature would show no cooperative unfolding transition and no Tm at all. A measurable Tm of 44 °C means the mutant is folded below about 44 °C and unfolds as it is heated past that point, just at a lower temperature than wild type.

Correct. Tm is the temperature at which half the molecules are unfolded, where ΔG(unfolding) = 0. A lower Tm means less heat is needed to tip the balance toward the unfolded state, so the folded state has less free-energy margin. The 8 °C drop shows the mutation destabilizes the fold, for example by removing a buried hydrophobic contact, a hydrogen bond or a salt bridge, or by placing a polar residue in the core.

p: In a thermal-melt experiment, a signal sensitive to folding (circular dichroism, fluorescence or heat uptake) is recorded as temperature rises. For a cooperative, two-state protein the fraction unfolded follows an S-shaped curve. The midpoint, Tm, is where folded and unfolded forms are equal, so K = 1 and ΔG(unfolding) = 0.

A higher Tm means a more stable protein (more heat needed to unfold it); a lower Tm means less stable. Mutations that remove buried hydrophobic contacts, hydrogen bonds or salt bridges, or introduce helix breakers, usually lower Tm. Engineered disulfide bonds and better core packing usually raise it. Proteins from thermophilic organisms have high Tm values.

The same logic applies to chemical denaturation: the urea or guanidinium concentration at the midpoint of unfolding is higher for a more stable protein. Stability (thermodynamics) is separate from activity (catalysis) and from folding rate (kinetics).

x1A_069.trap: Lower Tm = LESS stable. Don't read a lower melting point as tighter binding or higher activity.

fig.cap: Two-state melt curves computed for Tm = 52 °C (wild type) and 44 °C (mutant). The mutant's curve is shifted 8 °C to lower temperature.
fig.alt: Fraction unfolded versus temperature from 25 to 70 degrees Celsius. Blue sigmoid for wild type crosses 0.5 at 52 degrees; red sigmoid for the mutant crosses 0.5 at 44 degrees. An arrow shows delta Tm of minus 8 degrees, less stable. A note says below its Tm the mutant is still mostly folded.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the two-state van 't Hoff model with ΔH = 300 kJ/mol and the Tm values in the question.

ox: Incorrect. Prions contain no nucleic acid at all; that is what made them so surprising. The prion protein (PrP) is encoded by the host's own PRNP gene. Infectious material stays infectious after treatments that destroy DNA and RNA, such as UV irradiation and nucleases, but loses infectivity when proteins are denatured.

Incorrect. In infectious prion disease the amino acid sequence of PrP does not change; what spreads is a conformation. Normal and misfolded PrP have the same sequence and differ only in fold. (Some inherited prion diseases do start with a PRNP mutation, but that mutation is inherited, not passed from cell to cell.)

Correct. Normal cellular PrP (PrPᶜ) is rich in α-helix and soluble. The misfolded form (PrPˢᶜ) is rich in β-sheet. When PrPˢᶜ contacts PrPᶜ, it acts as a template and converts it into the misfolded shape, so each conversion makes another template and the misfolded form spreads. PrPˢᶜ stacks into protease-resistant amyloid aggregates that damage neurons, as in Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease and bovine spongiform encephalopathy.

Incorrect. Prions are notable for resisting breakdown: the β-sheet-rich aggregates are only partly digested by proteases and survive standard heat sterilization. Disease comes from the misfolded protein and its aggregates, not from toxic fragments produced by hydrolysis.

p: A prion is an infectious protein. The prion protein PrP exists in a normal form (PrPᶜ, mostly α-helix) and a misfolded form (PrPˢᶜ, rich in β-sheet). The two have identical amino acid sequences. PrPˢᶜ converts PrPᶜ into more PrPˢᶜ by templated misfolding, a chain reaction that needs no DNA or RNA.

PrPˢᶜ aggregates into amyloid fibrils, stacks of β-sheets that resist proteases, heat and many disinfectants. Accumulation in the brain kills neurons and produces the sponge-like appearance of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, kuru, BSE).

Prions show that one sequence can adopt more than one stable fold, a qualification of Anfinsen's rule. Other amyloid diseases, including Alzheimer's (amyloid-β) and Parkinson's (α-synuclein), also involve β-rich aggregates; these spread between cells in a prion-like way but are not contagious between people in everyday life.

x1A_070.trap: Prions transmit a SHAPE (α → β), not a gene or a mutation.

fig.cap: Templated misfolding. Misfolded PrPˢᶜ (β-rich) converts normal PrPᶜ (α-rich) into another copy of itself, and the cycle repeats.
fig.alt: Normal PrPc drawn as an oval with helices plus misfolded PrPSc drawn as a box with beta-strand arrows, templating to give two PrPSc, which leads to amyloid fibrils and neuron loss; a dashed arrow shows the cycle repeating. Bottom: same amino acid sequence, different fold; no DNA or RNA. Red tags mark wrong mechanisms: DNA or RNA genome, spreading mutations, toxic peptide fragments.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. A subunit is a separate polypeptide chain in a multi-chain protein, such as one α chain of hemoglobin. Subunits belong to quaternary structure. The stem describes a region of a protein, meaning part of one chain, that folds into a compact unit; such a region is connected to the rest of the chain by covalent peptide bonds, not by noncovalent contacts between chains.

Correct. A domain is a segment of a single polypeptide chain, typically 50 to 250 residues, that folds independently into a stable, compact 3D unit and often has its own function, such as binding DNA, ATP or a membrane. Many proteins are built from several domains joined by flexible linkers, like modules. Domains are part of tertiary structure, and the same domain type (for example an SH2 or a zinc-finger domain) can recur in many different proteins.

Incorrect. The primary sequence is simply the order of amino acids along the chain. It encodes the information that makes a domain fold, but it is a one-dimensional list, not a folded, compact three-dimensional unit with its own function.

Incorrect. A β-turn is a short four-residue element that reverses the direction of the chain, held by a hydrogen bond between residues i and i + 3. It is a small piece of secondary structure that connects strands. It is far too small to fold independently or to carry out a function on its own.

p: Large proteins are often organized into domains: compact regions within one polypeptide that fold independently and usually have a distinct function. A domain can often be cut out of its protein and still fold correctly. Multi-domain proteins combine functions, for example a DNA-binding domain plus an activation domain in a transcription factor.

Domains are a feature of tertiary structure. They differ from subunits, which are separate polypeptide chains (quaternary structure). They also differ from motifs (supersecondary structures), small recurring combinations of secondary elements such as the helix-turn-helix or β-hairpin, which may form part of a domain.
Evolution reuses domains: exon shuffling can combine the gene segments that encode domains into new proteins. On the MCAT, independent folding plus its own function within one chain means a domain.

x1A_071.trap: Domain = part of ONE chain; subunit = a SEPARATE chain.

fig.cap: Left: one chain folding into two domains joined by a linker. Right: two separate chains (subunits). A domain is a folded unit within one chain.
fig.alt: Left panel: one teal chain forming two compact blobs labelled domain 1 and domain 2 joined by a linker, tagged domain, tertiary level, correct. Right panel: two separate blobs labelled chain A and chain B, tagged subunits, quaternary. A note says a primary sequence is just the residue order and a beta-turn is a 4-residue reversal too small to fold on its own.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Forming a disulfide bond is an oxidation: 2 Cys–SH → Cys–S–S–Cys + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻. The cytosol is kept strongly reducing by glutathione (GSH:GSSG ratio above about 30:1) and the thioredoxin system, which reduce any disulfides that form, so cytosolic cysteines remain free thiols. The ER lumen is oxidizing (GSH:GSSG about 1:1 to 3:1), and enzymes such as Ero1 and protein disulfide isomerase form and rearrange disulfides in proteins entering the secretory pathway. Outside the cell the environment is oxidizing too, so the bonds stay intact.

Incorrect. Cytosolic proteins contain plenty of cysteines. They are kept as free thiols (–SH), which are important in active sites (cysteine proteases, for example), in metal binding (zinc fingers) and in redox sensing. The difference between compartments is the redox environment, not whether cysteine is present.

Incorrect. Temperature does not decide whether disulfides form. The cytosol and the ER of the same cell are at the same temperature, yet one forms disulfides and the other does not. The controlling factor is the balance of oxidizing and reducing agents in each compartment.

Incorrect. All ribosomes use the same genetic code and translate the cysteine codons UGU and UGC. In fact, secreted proteins are translated by the same kind of ribosome as cytosolic ones; it simply docks on the rough ER and feeds the growing chain into the lumen. Where the protein ends up, not which ribosome made it, decides whether disulfides form.

concept.t: Disulfide bonds and cellular redox compartments
p: A disulfide bond is a covalent S–S link between two cysteine side chains, formed by oxidation of their thiol groups. In proteins it stabilizes tertiary structure (within a chain) or quaternary structure (between chains), as in antibodies and insulin.

Whether disulfides form depends on the local redox environment. The cytosol is reducing: high glutathione (GSH) and thioredoxin keep cysteines as –SH. The ER lumen is oxidizing: the oxidase Ero1 and protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) form disulfides and shuffle incorrect ones into the native pairing. Secreted and cell-surface proteins pass through the ER, so they often carry disulfides that help them survive the harsh extracellular environment.
In the lab, reducing agents such as β-mercaptoethanol and DTT break disulfides; they are added to SDS-PAGE samples to separate disulfide-linked chains.

x1A_072.trap: Disulfide formation is an OXIDATION, so it happens in oxidizing compartments (ER, outside the cell), not the reducing cytosol.

fig.cap: The reducing cytosol keeps cysteines as thiols; the oxidizing ER lumen (with PDI) forms disulfides, which persist after secretion.
fig.alt: Schematic cell. Cytosol labelled reducing, GSH to GSSG above 30 to 1, cysteines as free SH, few disulfides. ER lumen labelled oxidizing, GSH to GSSG about 1 to 1 to 3 to 1, Ero1 and PDI make S-S bonds, tagged secretory pathway. An arrow labelled secretion leads outside, where S-S bonds stay intact. The reaction 2 Cys-SH gives Cys-S-S-Cys plus 2 H+ plus 2 electrons is shown as an oxidation.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; redox ratios from standard cell biology texts (Alberts, Molecular Biology of the Cell).

ox: Incorrect. Peptide bonds are covalent amide bonds in the backbone. Breaking them requires hydrolysis catalyzed by a protease or by prolonged heating in strong acid. Dissolved Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are not catalysts for amide hydrolysis, so 1 M NaCl leaves the primary structure untouched.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds are covalent S–S bonds and can only be broken by a chemical reduction, using a reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol or dithiothreitol. NaCl is neither an oxidant nor a reductant at this concentration, so disulfides are unaffected.

Correct. A salt bridge is an electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged side chains, such as a Lys –NH₃⁺ and a Glu –COO⁻. In 1 M NaCl, mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions cluster around each charge and screen it. The Debye screening length drops from about 3 nm at 0.01 M to about 0.3 nm at 1 M, so at a typical salt-bridge distance of 0.4 nm the attraction is reduced by roughly 70%. That is why high salt weakens salt bridges and is used to elute proteins from ion-exchange columns.

Incorrect. The hydrophobic effect depends on water structure, and many salts (especially sulfate and other kosmotropic ions) actually strengthen it, which is the basis of salting out and hydrophobic-interaction chromatography. So moderate NaCl tends to leave hydrophobic packing intact or slightly stronger, not weaker.

p: A salt bridge (ion pair) is an electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged groups, usually Asp/Glu carboxylates and Lys/Arg/His cations, within or between protein chains. Its strength follows Coulomb's law: it falls with distance and is reduced by the dielectric constant of the surroundings and by dissolved ions.

Dissolved ions form a cloud of opposite charge around each charged group, which screens its field. The screening (Debye) length is about 0.30 nm divided by the square root of ionic strength in M: about 3 nm at 0.01 M, 0.8 nm at physiological 0.15 M and 0.3 nm at 1 M. So high salt specifically weakens electrostatic interactions.

This underlies several lab techniques: increasing salt elutes proteins from ion-exchange columns, low salt increases solubility (salting in) and very high salt precipitates proteins (salting out). Covalent bonds (peptide, disulfide) are unaffected by salt.

fx.w: λD is the Debye screening length in water at 25 °C and I the ionic strength in mol/L (for NaCl, I equals the concentration). U(r) is the screened attraction between opposite charges at distance r; beyond about λD the attraction dies off quickly.

steps: A salt bridge spans about 0.4 nm, so the screening factor is e^(−0.4/0.30) ≈ e^(−1.3) ≈ 0.27.
The attraction is cut to about 27% of its salt-free value, a loss of roughly 73%.
Peptide and disulfide bonds are covalent and unaffected; hydrophobic packing is, if anything, slightly strengthened.
x1A_073.trap: Salt targets ELECTROSTATIC interactions; it cannot break covalent bonds and tends to strengthen hydrophobic ones.

fig.cap: Attraction between a +1 and a −1 charge in water computed with Debye–Hückel screening. At 0.4 nm, 1 M NaCl cuts the attraction from −4.3 to −1.2 kJ/mol.
fig.alt: Attraction energy versus distance from 0.3 to 1.5 nanometres for no salt, 0.01 M, 0.15 M and 1 M NaCl. Higher salt curves are much shallower. An annotation at 0.4 nanometres gives minus 4.3 kilojoules per mole with no salt and minus 1.2 with 1 M NaCl, a 73% reduction.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from Coulomb's law with Debye–Hückel screening (relative permittivity 80, 25 °C).

ox: Correct. The backbone can rotate about two bonds per residue: φ (phi), the N–Cα bond, and ψ (psi), the Cα–C bond; the peptide bond itself is planar and does not rotate. A Ramachandran plot graphs φ against ψ and shades the combinations that avoid steric clashes between backbone atoms and side chains. The allowed regions match the observed secondary structures: right-handed α-helix near (−57°, −47°) and β-sheet near (−120° to −140°, +115° to +135°). Glycine can reach extra regions, and proline is restricted.

Incorrect. A graph of absorbance against wavelength is an absorption spectrum. Proteins absorb at 280 nm because of tryptophan and tyrosine, which is used to measure protein concentration, but such a spectrum says nothing about which backbone angles are allowed.

Incorrect. Reaction rate plotted against substrate concentration is a Michaelis–Menten plot, a hyperbola that levels off at Vmax and reaches half of Vmax at [S] = Km. It describes enzyme kinetics, not the geometry of the polypeptide backbone.
Incorrect. Net charge (or pH) plotted against added base is a titration curve, from which pKa values and the isoelectric point can be read. It describes ionizable groups, not backbone conformation.

concept.t: Backbone torsion angles and the Ramachandran plot
