p: Each residue has three backbone bonds. The peptide bond (C–N) has partial double-bond character, so it is planar and almost always trans. Rotation is possible only about the N–Cα bond (angle φ) and the Cα–C bond (angle ψ). The shape of the whole backbone is set by the list of φ and ψ values.

Many φ/ψ combinations bring atoms too close together. G. N. Ramachandran mapped the allowed combinations; the plot of φ against ψ shows a few allowed regions that match the right-handed α-helix, the β-sheet and, rarely, a left-handed helix. Most residues in real proteins fall in these regions.

Glycine, with only H as its side chain, can occupy regions forbidden to other residues, which is why it appears in tight turns. Proline's ring fixes φ near −60°. Compare the MCAT's other common plots: Michaelis–Menten, Lineweaver–Burk, titration curves and absorption spectra.

x1A_074.trap: φ and ψ rotate; the peptide bond (ω) does not, because it is planar.

fig.cap: Schematic Ramachandran plot. Shaded areas are the sterically allowed φ/ψ regions; dots mark standard α-helix and β-sheet angles.
fig.alt: Plot of psi against phi from minus 180 to plus 180 degrees. Shaded allowed regions in the upper left (beta-sheet, with antiparallel at minus 139, plus 135 and parallel at minus 119, plus 113), the lower left (alpha-helix at minus 57, minus 47) and a small upper-right region (left-handed helix, mostly glycine). White areas are disallowed steric clashes.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic allowed regions and standard angles after Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Incorrect. Salting in occurs at LOW salt concentration: a few ions shield the charged patches on the protein surface, reducing protein–protein electrostatic attraction and increasing solubility. That is the opposite of what the stem describes (the protein comes out of solution at high salt). Salting in and salting out are two ends of the same solubility curve.

Incorrect. Ammonium sulfate does not break peptide bonds, and salting out is not really denaturation. Most proteins precipitated this way keep their native fold and redissolve fully active when the salt is removed by dialysis. That is exactly why salting out is a standard first purification step.

Incorrect. Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) is sulfur in its highest oxidation state (+6); it cannot donate electrons and so it is not a reducing agent. Breaking disulfides requires a thiol reducing agent such as β-mercaptoethanol or DTT. Salting out has nothing to do with disulfide bonds.

Correct. At high concentration the salt ions are strongly hydrated and tie up most of the available water molecules. Too little water is left to hydrate the protein's surface, so exposed hydrophobic patches interact with each other instead, and the proteins aggregate and precipitate. Ammonium sulfate is used because it is very soluble and strongly kosmotropic. Different proteins precipitate at different salt concentrations, which allows fractionation.

p: Protein solubility depends on ionic strength. At low salt (salting in), ions shield surface charges and reduce attractions between protein molecules, so solubility rises. At high salt (salting out), the ions are so heavily hydrated that they compete with the protein for water; the protein's surface is no longer well solvated, hydrophobic patches associate and the protein precipitates.

Ammonium sulfate fractionation exploits this: raising the salt in steps precipitates different proteins at different concentrations. Because the native structure is usually preserved, the precipitate can be redissolved and the salt removed by dialysis.

Related ideas: proteins are also least soluble at their isoelectric point (no net charge, no repulsion), and organic solvents such as ethanol or acetone also precipitate proteins by lowering the dielectric constant of the solvent.

fx.f: log S = log S₀ + A·√I/(1 + √I) − Ks·I
fx.w: S is protein solubility, S₀ solubility in pure water, I ionic strength (M). The positive term (Debye–Hückel) describes salting in at low I; the −Ks·I term (Cohn equation) describes salting out at high I. A and Ks are constants for a given protein and salt.

x1A_075.trap: LOW salt → salting IN (more soluble); HIGH salt → salting OUT (precipitates).

fig.cap: Solubility versus ionic strength computed with illustrative constants: solubility rises slightly at low salt (salting in) and then falls steadily at high salt (salting out).
fig.alt: Graph of log relative solubility against ionic strength from 0 to 8 molar. The curve rises to a maximum near 0.6 molar (salting in, ions shield surface charges) and then falls linearly (salting out, ions bind the water needed to hydrate the protein, so proteins aggregate and precipitate).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Debye–Hückel salting-in term plus the Cohn salting-out equation with illustrative constants (A = 1.2, Ks = 0.25 L/mol).

ox: Incorrect. Two pH units below its pI, a protein has bound extra protons and carries a substantial net positive charge (for the model protein in the figure, about +12). Every molecule is positive, so neighboring molecules repel one another, which keeps them dispersed in solution. Solubility is therefore higher here than at the pI.

Correct. At the isoelectric point the protein's positive and negative charges balance, so its net charge is zero. Without net charge there is no electrostatic repulsion between molecules, and attractive contacts (hydrophobic patches, hydrogen bonds, opposite local charges) let them clump together and precipitate. This is called isoelectric precipitation, and it is how casein curdles when milk is acidified to about pH 4.6, its pI.

Incorrect. Two pH units above the pI the protein has lost protons and carries a net negative charge. All the molecules are negative and repel one another, so they stay in solution. Solubility is higher here than at the pI, just as it is below the pI.

Incorrect. pH 7 is special for water (neutral), not for proteins. Each protein has its own pI set by its composition, from below 2 (pepsin) to above 10 (lysozyme). A protein is least soluble at its own pI, which may be far from 7.

p: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which a molecule's net charge is zero. Below the pI the protein is net positive (more groups protonated); above it, net negative. The further the pH is from the pI, the larger the net charge.

Net charge keeps proteins dissolved because like-charged molecules repel each other and attract a shell of water and counter-ions. At the pI the repulsion disappears and molecules aggregate, so solubility is at a minimum. This principle is used in isoelectric precipitation and isoelectric focusing.

To estimate pI, look at composition: many Lys/Arg give a high pI; many Asp/Glu give a low pI. On the MCAT, use the rules pH < pI → positive, pH = pI → neutral, pH > pI → negative to predict electrophoresis, ion-exchange behavior and solubility.

x1A_076.trap: Least soluble at the pI, not at pH 7; zero NET charge does not mean no charged groups.

fig.cap: Net charge of a model protein computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch for each ionizable group. Net charge crosses zero at the pI (about 6.1), where solubility is lowest.
fig.alt: Curve of net charge against pH from 1 to 13, falling from about plus 25 to minus 29. It crosses zero at pH 6.1, highlighted as the pI where the protein is least soluble. Points mark pI minus 2 with net charge plus 12 and pI plus 2 with net charge minus 3. Below the pI the region is labelled net positive; above it, net negative.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for a model protein (10 Asp, 12 Glu, 4 His, 2 Cys, 6 Tyr, 12 Lys, 8 Arg plus termini) with standard pKa values.

ox: Incorrect. The smallest protein elutes last, not first. Small molecules can enter the pores of the gel beads, so they explore a larger volume of the column (inside and between the beads) and take a longer path. In the computed example a 12 kDa protein elutes at about 20 mL, well after larger proteins.

Correct. Size-exclusion (gel-filtration) chromatography uses porous beads. Proteins too large to enter the pores are confined to the space between beads (the void volume) and are swept straight through, so they elute first. Smaller proteins spend time inside the pores and are delayed. Elution volume decreases roughly linearly with the log of molecular mass, so the column can estimate a protein's native mass, including all its subunits.

Incorrect. Separation by charge is the job of ion-exchange chromatography, where charged beads bind oppositely charged proteins. Size-exclusion beads are uncharged, so a protein's charge has essentially no effect on when it elutes; only its size (hydrodynamic radius) matters.

Incorrect. The pI determines a protein's charge at a given pH, which matters in ion-exchange chromatography and isoelectric focusing. Size-exclusion chromatography does not use charge, so the protein with the lowest pI does not elute in any special order.

p: In size-exclusion chromatography the column is packed with porous beads. Large molecules are excluded from the pores and travel only through the spaces between beads, so they elute early, at the void volume (V₀). Small molecules diffuse into the pores, sample more of the column volume and elute later. Separation is by size (more precisely, hydrodynamic radius), with the largest first.

Because proteins stay folded, the method measures native size and so reveals quaternary structure. Comparing the native mass from gel filtration with the subunit mass from SDS-PAGE gives the number of subunits. It is also used for desalting and buffer exchange.

Do not confuse it with SDS-PAGE, where small chains travel FARTHEST. In gel filtration small molecules come out LAST. Ion-exchange separates by charge; affinity chromatography separates by specific binding.

x1A_077.trap: Gel filtration: big out first. SDS-PAGE: small runs farthest. Both favor small molecules moving through pores, but in opposite visible ways.

fig.cap: A size-exclusion column and its elution profile computed from a log-linear calibration. The 440 kDa protein elutes first (9.5 mL) and the 12 kDa protein last (20.0 mL).
fig.alt: Left: column of porous beads; large purple proteins pass between beads while small orange proteins enter pores. Right: absorbance against elution volume with peaks at 9.5 mL (440 kilodaltons), 12.7 mL (150), 16.2 mL (45) and 20.0 mL (12), after a void volume at 8 mL. Tag: largest elutes first. Note: separation by size only; charge and pI do not matter.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; peaks computed from Ve = V₀ + Kav(Vt − V₀) with an illustrative log-linear Kav calibration.

ox: Incorrect. Separating by mass alone is what SDS-PAGE does: SDS unfolds the proteins and coats them with a uniform negative charge per unit mass, removing differences in shape and native charge. Native PAGE leaves those differences in place, so two proteins of the same mass can run at very different positions.

Incorrect. Separating by pI alone is isoelectric focusing, in which proteins move through a pH gradient until they reach the pH where their net charge is zero. In native PAGE the buffer has a single pH, and proteins keep moving according to their net charge at that pH, as well as their size and shape.

Incorrect. Native PAGE is designed to keep proteins folded, so no SDS or reducing agent is added and samples are not boiled. That is its whole advantage: enzymes can still be active in the gel and protein complexes stay assembled. Denaturing gels are the SDS versions.

Correct. Without SDS, each protein keeps its native fold, its own net charge at the gel's pH and any bound partner subunits. Migration then depends on the charge-to-mass ratio (the driving force) and on size and shape (friction through the gel's pores). A compact, highly charged protein runs far; a large or elongated, weakly charged complex runs a short distance. This makes native PAGE useful for studying intact complexes and active enzymes.

p: Both methods drive proteins through a polyacrylamide gel with an electric field. In SDS-PAGE, SDS (often with heat and a reducing agent) denatures proteins, separates their subunits and gives them uniform charge per mass, so migration depends only on chain mass. In native PAGE no denaturant is used, so proteins keep their native structure, charge and subunit assembly.

In native PAGE, migration reflects charge, size and shape together. A protein whose net charge has the wrong sign for the gel's direction (for example, a positive protein when the anode is at the bottom) moves the other way and never enters the gel. Native gels can be stained for enzyme activity, and complexes appear as single bands.

Compare: isoelectric focusing separates by pI; 2D electrophoresis combines isoelectric focusing with SDS-PAGE; size-exclusion chromatography separates native proteins by size. Running a protein on both native and SDS gels can reveal its subunit composition.

x1A_078.trap: Native PAGE ≠ mass alone. Only SDS-PAGE strips away charge and shape differences.

fig.cap: The same three proteins on a native gel (illustrative positions that depend on charge, size and shape) and on an SDS gel (positions computed from mass). Proteins B and C both run at 30 kDa in SDS.
fig.alt: Two gels. Native PAGE lanes A, B, C: compact very negative 60 kilodalton monomer A runs farthest; weakly charged 60 kilodalton dimer B stays near the top; elongated 30 kilodalton monomer C is in the middle. SDS-PAGE: A at 60 kilodaltons, B and C both at 30 kilodaltons. Tags: native separates by size plus charge plus shape (correct); mass alone is SDS; pI alone is isoelectric focusing.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; SDS band positions computed from a log-linear mass calibration, native positions schematic.

ox: Correct. A protein is positive when the buffer pH is below its pI. At pH 7 the protein with pI 9.5 is 2.5 units below its pI, so it carries a clear net positive charge and binds tightly to the negatively charged cation-exchange beads (for example sulfonate, –SO₃⁻). It stays on the column while the others wash through, and it is eluted later by raising the salt concentration (Na⁺ competes for the bead charges) or raising the pH above 9.5.

Incorrect. With pI 4.5, the buffer pH of 7 is 2.5 units above the pI, so this protein is net negative. It is repelled by the negative beads and flows straight through the column. It would bind well instead to an anion-exchange column, which has positive beads such as diethylaminoethyl (DEAE).

Incorrect. With pI 7.0, this protein has almost no net charge at pH 7, so it has little electrostatic attraction to the beads and binds weakly at best. Local positive patches might give slight retention, but it will elute well before a strongly positive protein.

Incorrect. With pI 5.5, the buffer pH is 1.5 units above the pI, so the protein is net negative and is not retained by the negatively charged beads. It is less negative than the pI 4.5 protein but still the wrong sign to bind a cation exchanger.

p: Ion-exchange chromatography separates proteins by charge. Cation exchangers carry negative groups (carboxymethyl, sulfonate) and bind positively charged proteins; anion exchangers carry positive groups (DEAE, quaternary amines) and bind negatively charged proteins. Bound proteins are released by increasing salt, whose ions compete for the charged sites, or by shifting pH to neutralize the protein.

To predict binding, compare the buffer pH with each protein's pI: pH below pI means net positive; pH above pI means net negative. The further the pH from the pI, the larger the charge and the tighter the binding (the later it elutes in a salt gradient).
Pair it with other methods: size-exclusion separates by size, SDS-PAGE by mass, isoelectric focusing by pI and affinity chromatography by specific binding.

x1A_079.trap: CATion exchanger = negative beads that bind CATions (positive proteins, pH < pI).

fig.cap: Charge at pH 7 for each protein. Only the pI 9.5 protein is positive and sticks to the negative cation-exchange bead.
fig.alt: A pI number line from 3 to 11 with buffer pH 7 marked. Proteins at pI 4.5 and 5.5 are red (net negative), pI 7.0 gray (about zero), pI 9.5 green (net positive). Below, a bead covered in negative charges holds a positive protein (pI 9.5) while negative proteins (pI 4.5 and 5.5) wash through. Elution is by raising salt or pH. Tag: binds most strongly, pI 9.5.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. If the three 50 kDa subunits were joined by disulfide bonds, SDS without reducing agent could not separate them, because SDS breaks only noncovalent interactions. The non-reducing gel would show a 150 kDa band, and only adding a reducing agent would give 50 kDa. Since the 50 kDa band appears either way, there are no interchain disulfides.

Incorrect. A single 150 kDa chain would run at about 150 kDa on SDS-PAGE, with or without reducing agent, because SDS cannot cut peptide bonds. The observed 50 kDa band shows that the 150 kDa native protein must be made of smaller chains.

Correct. Gel filtration measures the native, folded mass: 150 kDa. SDS-PAGE measures the mass of each separate chain: 50 kDa. So 150 ÷ 50 = 3 subunits, and since only one band appears they are the same size (likely identical, a homotrimer). SDS alone, without reducing agent, already separates them, so they are held together only by noncovalent interactions. The protein is a noncovalent trimer of 50 kDa subunits.

Incorrect. A dimer of 75 kDa subunits would have the right native mass (2 × 75 = 150 kDa), but its subunits would run as a 75 kDa band on SDS-PAGE. The observed band is at 50 kDa, so the subunit mass and therefore the number of subunits do not match.

p: Combine methods that measure different things. Size-exclusion chromatography (gel filtration) or native PAGE measures the mass of the intact, folded protein. SDS-PAGE measures the mass of each polypeptide chain after SDS breaks noncovalent contacts. Running SDS-PAGE with and without a reducing agent (β-mercaptoethanol or DTT) shows whether chains are linked by disulfides.

Number of subunits = native mass ÷ subunit mass. If SDS alone gives small bands, the subunits are noncovalently associated. If small bands appear only after reduction, the chains are disulfide-linked. More than one band means different kinds of subunits (for example α₂β₂).
Antibodies are a classic example: about 150 kDa native; non-reducing SDS-PAGE shows about 150 kDa; reducing SDS-PAGE shows 50 kDa heavy and 25 kDa light chains, revealing disulfide links.

steps: Gel filtration gives the native mass: 150 kDa.
SDS-PAGE gives one subunit mass: 50 kDa, so all subunits are the same size.
The 50 kDa band appears even without reducing agent, so SDS alone separates the subunits: no interchain disulfides.
Conclusion: a noncovalent trimer of three 50 kDa subunits.
x1A_080.trap: SDS breaks noncovalent contacts only; a band that changes with reducing agent means disulfides.

fig.cap: Predicted results for each answer compared with the observed data (150 kDa native; 50 kDa on SDS-PAGE with or without reducing agent). Only the noncovalent trimer matches.
fig.alt: Table with columns gel filtration, SDS-PAGE without reducing agent and SDS-PAGE with beta-mercaptoethanol. Observed: 150, 50, 50 kilodaltons. Noncovalent trimer of 3 times 50: 150, 50, 50, check. Disulfide-linked trimer: 150, 150, 50, cross. 150 kilodalton monomer: 150, 150, 150, cross. Noncovalent dimer of 2 times 75: 150, 75, 75, cross.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Hydrogen bonds are among the first interactions lost, not the last survivors. Each is weak (a few kJ/mol), heat supplies enough thermal energy to break them, and urea competes directly for the same C=O and N–H groups. So backbone and side-chain hydrogen bonds of the native protein are disrupted under these conditions.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds do survive, because they are covalent and no reducing agent was added. But salt bridges are noncovalent electrostatic attractions between charged side chains. Once the protein unfolds, the partners are pulled apart and surrounded by solvent, so the native salt bridges are lost. Only half of this pair is right.

Incorrect. Peptide bonds survive, but hydrophobic interactions do not. Urea solvates nonpolar side chains and weakens the hydrophobic effect, and heat further disrupts the packed core, so the buried nonpolar residues become exposed. Pairing a covalent bond with a noncovalent force makes this choice only half right.

Correct. Heat and urea act only on noncovalent interactions: hydrogen bonds, the hydrophobic effect, salt bridges and van der Waals packing. Peptide bonds (the covalent backbone) and disulfide bonds (covalent S–S cross-links) need specific chemistry to break: hydrolysis for peptide bonds and reduction (β-mercaptoethanol, DTT) for disulfides. With no reducing agent present, both covalent bond types remain, so primary structure and any disulfide cross-links are intact.

concept.t: Covalent vs noncovalent bonds in denaturation
p: Proteins are held by two classes of bonds. Covalent bonds, the peptide bonds of the backbone and disulfide bonds between cysteines, have energies of hundreds of kJ/mol and break only through specific reactions. Noncovalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, van der Waals contacts and the hydrophobic effect) are each a few kJ/mol and are disrupted by heat and denaturants.

Match each agent to its target: heat, urea, guanidinium, detergents, organic solvents and extreme pH disrupt noncovalent interactions; reducing agents (β-mercaptoethanol, DTT) break disulfides; proteases or hot concentrated acid hydrolyze peptide bonds.

A useful MCAT habit is to ask whether a bond is covalent or noncovalent and whether the conditions include a reducing or hydrolytic agent. If not, the covalent bonds survive and only the 3D shape is lost.

x1A_081.trap: Urea and heat never break disulfides; you need a reducing agent for that.

fig.cap: Heat and urea (top two rows) disrupt noncovalent forces but leave both disulfide and peptide bonds intact; only reducing agents or proteases break those.
fig.alt: Table of denaturing agents with their main action and whether disulfide and peptide bonds survive. Heat: breaks hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic packing, both covalent bonds survive. Urea: hydrogen-bonds to backbone and solvates nonpolar groups, both survive. Beta-mercaptoethanol or DTT breaks disulfides; protease breaks peptide bonds.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. A transmembrane helix must be nonpolar all the way around, because the whole cylinder sits in the lipid core; it needs about 20 consecutive mostly hydrophobic residues to span the 3 nm bilayer. Charged residues on most of the helix surface would be extremely unfavorable inside the membrane, so this helix cannot be transmembrane.

Incorrect. Leucine is one of the strongest helix-forming residues, and charged residues such as Lys and Glu are also compatible with helices; they can even form i to i + 4 salt bridges that stabilize them. Helix breakers are proline and, to a lesser extent, glycine, neither of which is described here.

Correct. An α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn, so each residue sits 100° around from the one before. Residues spaced 3 or 4 apart (i, i + 3, i + 4, i + 7) are 300° or 400° around, which lands them only 60° or 40° from the starting position. Leucines at that spacing therefore line up as a hydrophobic stripe on one face, while the charged residues fill the opposite face. Such amphipathic helices pack against other helices (as in leucine zippers) or lie on membrane surfaces.

Incorrect. In a β-strand, side chains alternate faces every residue, so the hydrophobic repeat would be every 2 residues (i, i + 2, i + 4). A spacing of 3 to 4 matches the 3.6-residue repeat of an α-helix instead. In addition, the question already tells you the segment is a helix.

concept.t: Amphipathic helices and the helical wheel
p: A helical wheel projects an α-helix down its axis, placing each residue 100° further around than the previous one. It shows which residues end up on the same face. Because 3.6 residues make one turn, residues i, i + 3, i + 4 and i + 7 cluster together.

An amphipathic helix has a hydrophobic face and a polar face. Such helices bury their hydrophobic face against other helices (coiled coils, leucine zippers in which Leu recurs every 7 residues) or against membrane lipids, while the polar face contacts water. Many antimicrobial peptides and apolipoproteins work this way.

Contrast: a transmembrane helix is about 20 residues of mostly nonpolar side chains all around; a β-strand with alternating nonpolar and polar residues (every 2) has one hydrophobic face of a sheet. Spacing patterns are an MCAT clue to structure.

x1A_082.trap: Every 3 to 4 residues = one face of a helix; every 2 residues = one face of a β-strand.

fig.cap: Helical wheel for an 18-residue helix with Leu at positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 11, 12, 15 and 18, each residue placed 100° from the last. All eight leucines cluster on one face.
fig.alt: Helical wheel with 18 residues around a circle. Leucines at positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 11, 12, 15 and 18 occupy one shaded arc labelled hydrophobic face; lysines and glutamates occupy the other side. Tags: amphipathic helix correct; transmembrane helix needs about 20 nonpolar residues; beta-strand repeat is 2.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue angles computed at 100° per residue (3.6 residues per turn).

ox: Incorrect. Disulfide bonds form only between cysteine thiols. Glycine's side chain is a hydrogen atom and alanine's is a methyl group, so neither contains sulfur. Silk fibroin's strength comes from tightly packed β-sheets held by hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts, not covalent cross-links.

Correct. In a β-strand, side chains alternate faces, so in a Gly-Ala repeat every glycine (H) points to one face of the sheet and every alanine (CH₃) to the other. These tiny side chains let sheets stack very closely, Gly face against Gly face (about 0.35 nm) and Ala face against Ala face (about 0.57 nm), with many van der Waals contacts. The dense, interlocking packing makes silk strong and resistant to stretching, since the extended strands cannot be pulled out further.

Incorrect. Glycine and alanine have uncharged, nonpolar side chains (H and CH₃), so they cannot form salt bridges. Salt bridges need charged residues such as Lys, Arg, Asp or Glu. The forces between stacked silk sheets are van der Waals contacts between the small nonpolar side chains.

Incorrect. The stem states that fibroin forms β-sheets, and the sequence suits sheets, not helices. Glycine is actually a helix destabilizer because its flexibility costs too much entropy to hold in a helix. Proteins built on helices, such as α-keratin in hair, have very different sequences with heptad repeats.

p: Fibrous proteins have structures dominated by one repeating secondary structure and sequences to match. Silk fibroin consists largely of repeats such as (Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ser)n that form antiparallel β-sheets. The small side chains allow sheets to stack closely, giving a dense, strong fiber.

Because the β-strands are already almost fully extended, silk resists stretching. It is flexible because the sheets are held together by weak van der Waals forces rather than covalent cross-links. Compare α-keratin (hair, nails): coiled-coil α-helices with heptad repeats, cross-linked by disulfides, which can stretch. Collagen: a Gly-X-Y repeat (X and Y often Pro and hydroxyproline) forming a triple helix, where glycine at every third position fits in the crowded center.
On the MCAT, link sequence to structure: small residues pack densely; glycine every third residue suggests collagen; heptad repeats suggest coiled coils.

x1A_083.trap: Gly and Ala have no sulfur and no charge; their advantage is simply being small.

fig.cap: Edge-on view of stacked silk β-sheets. Glycine H atoms point to one face and alanine CH₃ groups to the other, so sheets interlock closely (about 0.35 nm and 0.57 nm apart).
fig.alt: Five blue zigzag beta-sheets seen edge-on and stacked vertically. In each sheet, small H labels point to one face and orange methyl circles to the other. Gly faces meet about 0.35 nanometres apart and Ala faces about 0.57 nanometres apart. Tags: no sulfur, no charge; beta-sheet not alpha-helix.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; intersheet spacings after Marsh, Corey and Pauling's silk fibroin structure as summarized in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

ox: Correct. Ethanol is less polar than water and has a nonpolar ethyl group, so it can surround nonpolar side chains much better than water can. The hydrophobic effect, the entropy gain from releasing ordered water when nonpolar groups are buried, depends on how poorly the solvent tolerates exposed nonpolar surfaces. In aqueous ethanol, unfolding exposes the core at a smaller free-energy cost, so the folded state is no longer favored and the protein denatures. This is why 70% ethanol works as a disinfectant.

Incorrect. Hydrolyzing a peptide bond requires a protease or prolonged heating in strong acid or base. Ethanol is a neutral alcohol and cannot cleave amide bonds under ordinary conditions. Ethanol-denatured proteins keep their full primary structure, which is why some can refold after the ethanol is removed.

Incorrect. Ethanol is not an oxidizing agent toward cysteine thiols under these conditions; forming disulfides requires an oxidant such as O₂ with a catalyst or oxidized glutathione. Moreover, extra disulfides would tend to stabilize a protein, not unfold it.

Incorrect. Chelators such as EDTA remove metal ions by binding them through several donor atoms at once. Ethanol has a single OH group and is not a chelator. Some metal-dependent proteins are inactivated by chelators, but that is a different mechanism from how ethanol denatures proteins generally.

concept.t: Organic solvents and the hydrophobic effect
p: Folding is driven mainly by the hydrophobic effect: water forms ordered shells around exposed nonpolar groups, and burying those groups in the protein core frees the water and increases its entropy. The size of this driving force depends on the solvent.

Organic solvents such as ethanol, methanol and acetone are less polar than water and contain nonpolar regions. They solvate nonpolar side chains well, so there is less penalty for exposing them, and the folded state loses its advantage. They also lower the dielectric constant, which strengthens electrostatic attraction between protein molecules and can cause precipitation (used in protein purification).

Compare other denaturants: urea solvates nonpolar groups and competes for hydrogen bonds; detergents bind hydrophobic regions; heat adds kinetic energy; extreme pH changes charges; reducing agents break disulfides. None of these breaks peptide bonds; that takes proteases or hot concentrated acid.

x1A_084.trap: Ethanol weakens the hydrophobic effect; it does not cut, oxidize or chelate anything.

fig.cap: Folding releases ordered water from nonpolar surfaces. A less polar solvent such as ethanol solvates those surfaces, so burying them pays less and the fold weakens.
fig.alt: Left: unfolded chain with nonpolar groups each surrounded by an ordered ring of water molecules. Right: folded protein with a buried nonpolar core and free water outside. Text box: delta G equals delta H minus T delta S; water entropy increases on folding; a less polar solvent such as ethanol solvates nonpolar groups so burying them pays less.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

fig.cap: Ethanol's row: it lowers solvent polarity and weakens the hydrophobic effect; disulfide and peptide bonds survive.
fig.alt: Table of denaturing agents with main actions and whether disulfide and peptide bonds survive; the ethanol row reads less polar solvent, weakens hydrophobic effect, both covalent bonds survive.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Heavy-metal ions at toxic concentrations do not catalyze hydrolysis of the peptide backbone. Their damage comes from binding to side chains, mainly cysteine sulfur, and distorting the fold. Cutting peptide bonds requires proteases or harsh acid or base, which metal salts do not provide.

Incorrect. A metal ion cannot rebuild one amino acid's side chain into another's. Converting lysine (an ε-amine) into arginine (a guanidinium group) would require adding carbon and nitrogen atoms through a dedicated biosynthetic reaction. Metals act by binding to existing side chains, not by changing their identity.

Correct. Hg²⁺ and Pb²⁺ are soft Lewis acids, and cysteine's thiol sulfur is a soft Lewis base, so they bind each other very tightly (Hg–S bonds are among the strongest metal–ligand bonds in biology). The metal can bridge two cysteines, block a catalytic –SH group in an active site, or displace Zn²⁺ from zinc fingers and other metal sites. Each of these distorts the fold or blocks function, inactivating the protein. This is why heavy-metal poisoning inhibits many enzymes at once.

Incorrect. Metal salts such as HgCl₂ or Pb(NO₃)₂ are, if anything, slightly acidic in water (hydrated metal ions release H⁺), not strongly basic. Reaching pH 12 would need a strong base such as NaOH. pH effects are not how heavy metals inactivate proteins.

p: Heavy-metal ions such as Hg²⁺, Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺ and Ag⁺ are toxic largely because they bind protein side chains, especially cysteine thiols (–SH), which are soft bases that match these soft metal acids. They also bind histidine imidazoles and carboxylates.

Binding has several effects: it blocks catalytic cysteines (for example in enzymes of glycolysis and in proteins with active-site thiols), forms non-native cross-links between cysteines, and displaces structural or catalytic metals such as Zn²⁺. The protein misfolds or loses function. Lead also inhibits enzymes of heme synthesis, causing anemia.

Treatment uses chelating agents (for example dimercaprol, which itself has two thiol groups, or EDTA) that bind the metal more strongly than the protein does and allow excretion. Compare other denaturants: they disrupt noncovalent forces or break covalent bonds, while metals act by coordination.

x1A_085.trap: Heavy metals target SULFUR (cysteine thiols); think soft acid binding soft base.

fig.cap: Two cysteine thiols bind Hg²⁺ to form a Cys–S–Hg–S–Cys bridge (structures from RDKit, L-cysteine is R), distorting the protein's fold.
fig.alt: Structure of L-cysteine with its SH highlighted, plus mercury(II), losing 2 protons to give two cysteines bridged through S-Hg-S, highlighted. A box explains that soft metal ions bind soft thiol sulfur tightly, bridging cysteines, blocking active sites and displacing zinc. Red tags: peptide bonds cut, lysine turned into arginine, pH pushed above 12; none of these happen.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Correct. Heat unfolds egg-white proteins such as ovalbumin, exposing hydrophobic side chains that were buried in their cores. Exposed patches on neighboring chains stick to each other (and some new disulfides form), building a tangled three-dimensional network. That network scatters light, so the white turns opaque and solid. On cooling, the chains are trapped in the aggregate and cannot reach their native folds, so the change is effectively irreversible even though the sequences are intact.

Incorrect. Cooking does not hydrolyze peptide bonds; that requires proteases (as in digestion) or prolonged boiling in strong acid. And free amino acids are small and water-soluble, so if the proteins really had been broken down to amino acids, the result would be a clear solution, not an opaque solid.

Incorrect. Heating cannot change one class of biomolecule into another. Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; carbohydrates are polymers of sugars joined by glycosidic bonds. Cooking changes the proteins' 3D shape and how they associate, not their chemical class.

Incorrect. Forming new peptide bonds requires activated amino acids and a ribosome (or chemical activation); heat alone does not join protein chains end to end. The aggregates in cooked egg are held mainly by noncovalent hydrophobic contacts, plus some disulfide exchange, not by new peptide bonds.

p: Denaturation is the loss of a protein's native 3D structure without breaking peptide bonds. Whether it is reversible depends on what happens next. A single small protein in dilute solution can refold when conditions return to normal. But unfolded chains expose hydrophobic surfaces, and at high protein concentration (egg white is about 10% protein) they stick to each other faster than they refold.

Aggregation produces tangled networks that are kinetically trapped: refolding would require pulling chains apart, which is extremely slow. Cooked egg, curdled milk and many amyloid diseases are examples. In cells, chaperones and the proteasome exist largely to prevent or clear such aggregates.
Key MCAT point: denaturation leaves primary structure intact; irreversibility usually reflects aggregation, not covalent damage.

x1A_086.trap: Irreversible does not mean the backbone broke; it means the unfolded chains aggregated.

fig.cap: Heat unfolds compact egg-white proteins; their exposed hydrophobic patches stick together into an opaque network that cannot refold on cooling.
fig.alt: Native compact soluble globular proteins, heated, become unfolded chains with orange hydrophobic patches exposed, which stick together into an aggregated network gel that scatters light. A dashed red cooling arrow back to native is blocked because chains are tangled. Red tags: hydrolyzed, made carbohydrate, new peptide bonds; none of these happen.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Phosphorylation by kinases is a reversible regulatory switch: adding a phosphate (usually on Ser, Thr or Tyr) changes a protein's activity, binding partners or location. It is not a general disposal tag and does not export proteins from the cell. (Phosphorylation can sometimes signal that a protein should be ubiquitinated, but the degradation tag is ubiquitin.)

Incorrect. Mannose-6-phosphate is added in the cis-Golgi to N-linked glycans on lysosomal enzymes, and it targets them to lysosomes, not mitochondria. It applies to proteins in the secretory pathway, not to misfolded proteins in the cytosol. Mitochondrial proteins are targeted by N-terminal presequences.

Incorrect. Most glycosylation (N-linked and O-linked oligosaccharides) occurs in the lumen of the ER and Golgi, on proteins in the secretory pathway. A cytosolic protein never enters those compartments. Glycans also mark proteins for folding checks in the ER, but they are not the cytosolic degradation tag.

Correct. Misfolded cytosolic proteins are recognized, often with help from chaperones, by E3 ubiquitin ligases. An enzyme cascade (E1 activates ubiquitin using ATP, E2 carries it, E3 transfers it to a lysine on the target) builds a chain of at least four ubiquitins, typically linked through Lys48. The 26S proteasome recognizes the polyubiquitin chain, unfolds the protein using ATP, and cuts it into short peptides, while ubiquitin is recycled.

p: Ubiquitin is a small, highly conserved 76-residue protein. Cells attach it covalently to lysine side chains of target proteins through a three-enzyme cascade: E1 (activating, uses ATP), E2 (conjugating) and E3 (ligase, which recognizes the substrate and gives specificity). A chain of four or more Lys48-linked ubiquitins is the signal for degradation by the 26S proteasome.

The proteasome is a barrel-shaped protease complex in the cytosol and nucleus. Its regulatory cap binds the ubiquitin chain, unfolds the target and feeds it into the central chamber, where it is cut into short peptides. This system removes misfolded proteins and also controls the levels of regulatory proteins such as cyclins.

Distinguish other tags: phosphorylation (regulation), mannose-6-phosphate (lysosomal targeting in the Golgi), N-glycosylation (ER and Golgi), signal sequences (ER, mitochondria, nucleus). Misfolded proteins in the ER are retrotranslocated to the cytosol and then ubiquitinated (ER-associated degradation).

x1A_087.trap: Ubiquitin = destroy (via proteasome); mannose-6-phosphate = lysosome; phosphate = regulate.

fig.cap: E1, E2 and E3 attach a chain of four or more ubiquitins to a misfolded protein; the 26S proteasome then degrades it into short peptides. Other modifications have different jobs.
fig.alt: Flow: E1 activates ubiquitin using ATP, E2 carries it, E3 ligase recognizes the misfolded protein; the protein gets a chain of at least 4 Lys48-linked ubiquitins and goes to the 26S proteasome, which releases short peptides and recycles ubiquitin. Tag: cytosolic quality control. Box: phosphorylation switches activity, not disposal; mannose-6-phosphate is added in Golgi for lysosomes; glycosylation happens in ER and Golgi.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. About two residues per repeat describes an extended β-strand, where side chains alternate faces and the structure repeats every two residues (about 0.7 nm). An α-helix is far more compact, with each residue rising only 0.15 nm, so many more residues fit in each turn.

Correct. Each residue in an α-helix rotates 100° around the axis and rises 0.15 nm. A full 360° turn therefore takes 360/100 = 3.6 residues, and the rise per turn (pitch) is 3.6 × 0.15 = 0.54 nm. The non-integer value means the pattern of side chains does not repeat exactly each turn, which is why residues i, i + 3, i + 4 and i + 7 line up on one face.

Incorrect. 4.0 is tempting because the hydrogen bonds join residue n to residue n + 4. But the hydrogen-bond spacing and the residues per turn are different numbers: with 3.6 residues per turn, residue n + 4 lies slightly past one full turn (400°), close enough for its N–H to reach back to the C=O of residue n.

Incorrect. Ten is approximately the number of base pairs per turn of B-form DNA (about 10.5), a different double helix with a pitch of about 3.4 nm. A protein α-helix is much tighter, with only 3.6 residues per turn.

p: The α-helix, first proposed by Pauling and Corey, is a right-handed coil with 3.6 residues per turn, a rise of 0.15 nm per residue and a pitch (rise per turn) of 0.54 nm. Each backbone C=O hydrogen-bonds to the N–H four residues ahead (n → n + 4), so the hydrogen bonds run nearly parallel to the axis.

Useful numbers: 100° of rotation per residue; about 1.5 nm of helix for 10 residues; a membrane-spanning helix needs about 20 residues to cross a 3 nm bilayer core. Side chains point outward, and residues 3 to 4 apart share a face.

Do not confuse with the β-strand (about 0.33 to 0.35 nm per residue, 2-residue repeat), B-DNA (about 10.5 bp per turn, 3.4 nm pitch) or collagen (a left-handed polyproline-type helix with about 3 residues per turn, three chains wound together).

fx.f: residues per turn = 360° / (rotation per residue);   pitch = residues per turn × rise per residue
fx.w: For an α-helix, rotation per residue = 100° and rise per residue = 0.15 nm, giving 3.6 residues per turn and a pitch of 0.54 nm.

steps: Rotation per residue in an α-helix = 100°.
x1A_088.trap: 4 is the hydrogen-bond spacing (n → n + 4); 3.6 is residues per turn.

fig.cap: An ideal α-helix computed from 100° and 0.15 nm per residue: one turn spans 3.6 residues and 0.54 nm, while hydrogen bonds link residues n and n + 4.
fig.alt: Side view of a helix with residues n through n plus 8; a bar marks one turn as 3.6 residues equals 0.54 nanometres; dashed hydrogen bonds connect each residue to the one 4 later. End-on view shows side chains pointing outward.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue positions computed from ideal α-helix parameters (100° and 0.15 nm per residue).

ox: Incorrect. Both the α-helix and the β-sheet are held by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups, the C=O of one peptide unit and the N–H of another. Side chains are not involved in either, which is why these structures can form from many different sequences. Side-chain hydrogen bonds belong to tertiary structure.

Correct. In an α-helix every hydrogen bond is local: residue n bonds to residue n + 4 in the same continuous stretch. In a β-sheet the bonds link side-by-side strands, and those strands can be close in sequence (a hairpin joined by a turn), dozens or hundreds of residues apart, or even in different polypeptide chains. So sheet hydrogen bonds can connect distant parts of the sequence, while helix hydrogen bonds always join near neighbors.

Incorrect. Hydrogen bonds are noncovalent in both structures: an attraction between a hydrogen on an electronegative atom (N–H) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom (O=C), worth only a few kJ/mol each. Nothing about a β-sheet makes them covalent, and their weakness is why both helices and sheets unfold on heating.

Incorrect. The fixed n → n + 4 pattern is the defining feature of the α-helix. In a β-sheet the partner residues are set by how the strands line up next to each other, so there is no fixed sequence spacing, and the partners are usually much farther apart than four residues.

concept.t: Local vs nonlocal hydrogen bonding in secondary structure
p: α-Helices and β-sheets both use backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds, but they arrange them differently. In a helix, each C=O bonds to the N–H four residues later (n → n + 4), so all the bonds are local, within one continuous segment, and run roughly parallel to the helix axis.

In a β-sheet, extended strands line up side by side and the bonds run between strands, roughly perpendicular to the strand direction. Strands may be adjacent in sequence (β-hairpin), far apart in sequence, or on different chains (as in some protein–protein interfaces and amyloid fibrils). Strands can be parallel or antiparallel.

Because a helix is self-contained, it can form in a short peptide alone; a sheet needs a partner strand. This difference is a common MCAT comparison, along with side-chain orientation (out from the helix axis vs alternating up and down in a sheet).

x1A_089.trap: Helix bonds are local (n → n + 4); sheet bonds join separate strands that can be far apart.

fig.cap: Along one chain, helix hydrogen bonds join residues 4 apart (short arcs), while sheet hydrogen bonds join strands far apart in sequence (long arcs). Both are backbone C=O···H–N bonds.
fig.alt: A 30-residue chain drawn as boxes. Residues 2 to 12 form a helix with short purple arcs linking each residue to the one 4 later. Residues 15 to 19 and 25 to 29 form two strands linked by long orange arcs. Below, a diagram of two backbone chains joined by C=O to H-N hydrogen bonds, with R groups pointing away, labelled noncovalent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. A pI well below 7 belongs to a protein rich in acidic residues (Asp, Glu), whose carboxylates make the protein negative at neutral pH; you must lower the pH to protonate them before the net charge reaches zero. This protein has the opposite composition, so its pI is high, not low.

Correct. Lys (side-chain pKa ≈ 10.5) and Arg (pKa ≈ 12.5) are positively charged at pH 7, and with few acidic residues to balance them, the protein carries a large net positive charge at neutral pH. To reach net zero you must raise the pH until many of these basic groups lose their protons, which only happens well above 7. In the computed example (32 basic, 6 acidic residues) the pI is about 12. Real basic proteins such as histones and lysozyme (pI ≈ 11) behave this way.

Incorrect. pH 7 is neutral for water, not a default isoelectric point for proteins. A pI of exactly 7 would require the positive and negative charges to balance exactly at pH 7, which a protein with many Lys/Arg and few Asp/Glu does not do. Protein pI values range from below 2 to above 11.

Incorrect. Composition is exactly what lets you estimate the pI: count the groups that are acidic (Asp, Glu, C-terminus) and basic (Lys, Arg, His, N-terminus) and compare. Software predicts pI from sequence this way, and the estimate is usually within about one pH unit.

concept.t: Predicting a protein's pI from its composition
p: A protein's isoelectric point is the pH at which its positive and negative charges balance. Basic residues (Lys, Arg, and partly His) carry positive charge until the pH exceeds their pKa; acidic residues (Asp, Glu) carry negative charge once the pH exceeds their pKa (about 4).

A protein rich in Lys and Arg is strongly positive at pH 7 and has a high pI (above 9); examples are histones, which bind negatively charged DNA, and lysozyme. A protein rich in Asp and Glu is negative at pH 7 and has a low pI; pepsin, which works in stomach acid, has a pI near 1. A balanced composition gives a pI near 5 to 7.

Use this to predict behavior: below its pI a protein is positive (moves toward the cathode, binds cation exchangers); above its pI it is negative (moves toward the anode, binds anion exchangers); at its pI it is least soluble.

x1A_090.trap: More basic residues means a HIGHER pI, because you need a higher pH to strip their protons.

fig.cap: Net charge versus pH computed for two model proteins of similar size. The Lys/Arg-rich protein crosses zero near pH 12; the Asp/Glu-rich one near pH 3.6.
fig.alt: Two net-charge curves against pH from 1 to 14. Blue curve for a Lys/Arg-rich protein (32 basic, 6 acidic) is strongly positive at pH 7 (about plus 26) and crosses zero near pH 12. Red curve for an Asp/Glu-rich protein (6 basic, 34 acidic) is strongly negative at pH 7 and crosses zero near pH 3.6.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation using standard side-chain pKa values for the stated compositions.

ox: Incorrect. A protein is net negative when the buffer pH is ABOVE its pI. Then the solution has fewer H⁺ ions than are needed to keep the protein's groups protonated, so carboxylates are deprotonated (−) and some amines lose their protons, tipping the balance negative. This choice reverses the rule.

Incorrect. A net charge of zero occurs only when the pH equals the pI; that is the definition of the isoelectric point. Note that zero net charge does not mean no charged groups: at the pI the positive and negative groups simply balance. Any pH below the pI gives a nonzero (positive) net charge.

Incorrect. Net charge depends on how many ionizable groups are protonated at a given pH, which is set by each group's pKa relative to the pH, not by molecular mass. Two proteins of the same mass can have opposite charges at pH 7 if one is rich in Lys/Arg and the other in Asp/Glu.

Correct. When the pH is below the pI, the solution has a higher H⁺ concentration than at the pI, so more of the protein's ionizable groups are protonated. Carboxylates pick up H⁺ and become neutral, while amines and imidazoles stay or become protonated and positive. The result is a net positive charge, and the further the pH is below the pI, the more positive the protein. Such a protein moves toward the cathode in electrophoresis and binds cation-exchange resins.

concept.t: Net charge relative to the pI
p: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which a molecule's net charge is zero. A simple rule follows from Henderson–Hasselbalch: if pH < pI, protons are in excess and the molecule is net positive; if pH = pI, net zero; if pH > pI, protons have been removed and the molecule is net negative.

This works for amino acids, peptides and whole proteins. It predicts electrophoresis (positive species move toward the cathode, negative toward the anode), ion-exchange behavior (positive proteins bind cation exchangers), and solubility (lowest at the pI).
A memory aid: low pH means lots of H⁺, and H⁺ is positive, so below the pI the protein is positive. Mass, size and shape do not affect the sign of the charge.

x1A_091.trap: pH below pI → positive (think 'protons pile on'); pH above pI → negative.

fig.cap: Net charge of a model protein versus pH, computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch. Left of the pI (pH < pI) the curve is above zero: net positive.
fig.alt: Net charge against pH from 1 to 13 for a model protein; the curve is positive (shaded red, labelled pH below pI, net positive) at low pH, crosses zero at the pI of about 6.1, and is negative (shaded blue, labelled net negative) above it. pI minus 2 gives net plus 12.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for a model protein with standard pKa values.

ox: Correct. Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are rich in charged and polar residues (Glu, Lys, Arg, Ser, Gln, Pro) and poor in bulky hydrophobic and aromatic residues (Leu, Ile, Val, Phe, Trp). Without enough nonpolar side chains there is no hydrophobic core to bury, so the hydrophobic effect cannot drive collapse, and a high net charge makes the chain repel itself and stay extended. Uversky's charge–hydropathy plot captures this: low mean hydropathy plus high net charge predicts disorder.

Incorrect. Leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine are the bulky hydrophobic residues that form protein cores. A segment rich in them has a strong drive to bury them, so it tends to fold (or, if it cannot fold properly, to aggregate). This is the composition of ordered domains, the opposite of disordered regions.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds are covalent cross-links that reduce the conformational freedom of a chain and stabilize a folded structure. A region full of disulfides would be more constrained and more ordered, not disordered. Many small extracellular proteins (toxins, for example) owe their rigid folds to dense disulfides.

Incorrect. Glycine is common in flexible regions, but real disordered regions have mixed compositions dominated by charged, polar and proline residues, not pure glycine. A pure polyglycine stretch is an unusual, poorly soluble sequence, not the typical composition of intrinsically disordered proteins.

p: Not every functional protein has a single fixed fold. Intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs) exist as dynamic ensembles of conformations under physiological conditions. They are common in signaling, transcription regulation and scaffolding; many eukaryotic proteins contain at least one long disordered segment.

Disorder is encoded in the sequence: low hydrophobicity (few Leu, Ile, Val, Phe, Trp, Tyr), high net charge and many Pro, Glu, Lys, Ser and Gln. With little to bury, the hydrophobic effect cannot drive folding, and like charges repel. Many IDRs fold only when they bind a partner (coupled folding and binding), which lets one region bind several targets.

This fits the same rule as folding: sequence determines structure. Here the sequence specifies 'no stable structure'. Disordered regions are also involved in forming membraneless condensates and, when they misbehave, in aggregation diseases.

fx.w: Uversky's empirical boundary: ⟨R⟩ is the mean net charge per residue and ⟨H⟩ the mean scaled hydropathy (0 to 1). Sequences with hydropathy below the boundary for their charge tend to be disordered.

x1A_092.trap: Disorder comes from FEW hydrophobic residues and MANY charges, not from glycine alone or from cross-links.

fig.cap: Uversky's charge–hydropathy plot. Sequences with low mean hydropathy and high net charge (upper left) are disordered; hydrophobic, weakly charged sequences (lower right) fold.
fig.alt: Plot of mean net charge per residue against mean hydropathy with a straight boundary line H equals (R plus 1.151) divided by 2.785. The upper-left region is labelled intrinsically disordered: low hydropathy, high net charge. The lower-right region is labelled folded: hydrophobic enough to form a core.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph of the boundary equation from Uversky, Gillespie and Fink (2000).

ox: Incorrect. Heat shock proteins are molecular chaperones, not heat-producing enzymes. Body heat comes mainly from metabolism (and in brown fat, from uncoupling protein 1). The name refers to when they are made, after a heat shock, not to what they do.

Incorrect. Proteins are not converted into one another by heat. Each heat shock protein is encoded by its own gene; the rise in their amounts comes from increased transcription and translation of those genes. Heat only partly unfolds existing proteins.

Correct. Higher temperature partly unfolds many proteins and exposes their hydrophobic patches, which risk aggregation. Chaperones such as Hsp70 and Hsp90 bind these exposed regions, which frees the transcription factor HSF1 they normally hold. HSF1 then activates the heat shock genes, so the cell makes more chaperones to refold damaged proteins, prevent aggregation, or hand hopeless ones to the ubiquitin–proteasome system. As refolding catches up, free Hsp70 binds HSF1 again and turns the response off.

Incorrect. Heat shock proteins act on proteins, not on DNA. DNA damage is handled by repair systems such as base-excision, nucleotide-excision and mismatch repair, and DNA is degraded by nucleases. Chaperones recognize the exposed hydrophobic surfaces of partly unfolded polypeptides.

concept.t: Heat shock proteins and the stress response
p: Heat shock proteins (Hsps) are a family of molecular chaperones, many named by size (Hsp70, Hsp90, Hsp60 chaperonins). They are present at all times and help newly made proteins fold, but their synthesis rises sharply under stresses that unfold proteins: heat, oxidative stress, heavy metals and ethanol.

Regulation is a feedback loop. In unstressed cells, Hsp70 and Hsp90 hold the transcription factor HSF1 inactive. Unfolded proteins compete for these chaperones, releasing HSF1, which trimerizes, binds heat shock elements in DNA and boosts transcription of Hsp genes. When enough chaperones exist, they bind HSF1 again.

Chaperones prevent aggregation and promote refolding but do not specify the fold; badly damaged proteins are ubiquitinated and degraded. Since this response protects cells, cancer cells often rely on Hsp90, making it a drug target.

x1A_093.trap: 'Heat shock' describes when they are made, not what they do: they are chaperones for proteins.

fig.cap: Heat partly unfolds proteins, which pull Hsp70/Hsp90 away from HSF1; HSF1 then turns on heat shock genes, making more chaperones, and excess free Hsp70 shuts the response off.
fig.alt: Flowchart: temperature rises; proteins partly unfold exposing hydrophobic patches; Hsp70 and Hsp90 bind them, releasing HSF1; HSF1 trimer enters the nucleus and binds heat shock elements; transcription of HSP genes gives more chaperones; chaperones refold or prevent aggregation, tagged the real job. A dashed feedback loop shows excess free Hsp70 binding HSF1 again. Red tags: heat shock proteins do not make heat, form from other proteins, or repair or digest DNA.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. A more stable folded state resists unfolding, so it would need MORE urea to reach the midpoint, not less. Here the mutant reaches half-unfolded at 2.0 M while wild type needs 4.0 M, which means the mutant is the less stable of the two.

Incorrect. Urea acts through weak, noncovalent interactions: it hydrogen-bonds with the backbone and solvates nonpolar side chains. It does not form covalent bonds with proteins as a denaturing mechanism, and the experiment measures stability of the fold, not any chemical reaction with urea.

Incorrect. A point mutation changes one residue, so the mutant has the same length as wild type. In any case, chain length does not set the unfolding midpoint in a simple way. The midpoint reflects the free-energy difference between folded and unfolded states.

Correct. The midpoint (Cm) is where half the molecules are unfolded and ΔG(unfolding) = 0. In the linear extrapolation model, ΔG(unfolding) = ΔG(H₂O) − m[urea], so ΔG(H₂O) = m × Cm. If both proteins have a similar m value (say 5 kJ/mol per M), wild type has ΔG(H₂O) ≈ 5 × 4.0 = 20 kJ/mol and the mutant ≈ 5 × 2.0 = 10 kJ/mol. The mutation has roughly halved the stability, so less denaturant tips it into the unfolded state.

p: Protein stability can be measured by adding increasing amounts of a denaturant such as urea or guanidinium chloride and monitoring unfolding (for example by fluorescence or circular dichroism). A cooperative protein gives an S-shaped curve. The midpoint, Cm, is the denaturant concentration at which half the molecules are unfolded.

ΔG(unfolding) decreases roughly linearly with denaturant concentration: ΔG = ΔG(H₂O) − m[denaturant]. At the midpoint ΔG = 0, so ΔG(H₂O) = m × Cm. A higher Cm means a more stable protein; a lower Cm means a less stable one, as with destabilizing mutations.
Thermal melts give the same kind of information through the melting temperature, Tm. Neither measurement says anything about catalytic activity, which must be measured separately.

fx.f: ΔG(unfolding) = ΔG(H₂O) − m·[urea];   at the midpoint ΔG = 0, so ΔG(H₂O) = m·Cm
fx.w: ΔG(H₂O) is the stability in water (kJ/mol), m measures how sensitive unfolding is to urea (kJ/mol per M) and Cm is the urea concentration at the midpoint (M).

steps: At the midpoint ΔG(unfolding) = 0, so ΔG(H₂O) = m × Cm.
Assume a typical m ≈ 5 kJ/mol per M, the same for both proteins.
The mutant's folded state is about 10 kJ/mol less stable.
x1A_094.trap: Lower denaturant midpoint = LESS stable, just as lower Tm = less stable.

fig.cap: Unfolding curves computed from ΔG = ΔG(H₂O) − m[urea] with m = 5 kJ/mol per M. Wild type is half unfolded at 4.0 M; the mutant at 2.0 M.
fig.alt: Fraction unfolded against urea concentration from 0 to 8 molar. Red mutant curve crosses 0.5 at 2.0 molar; blue wild-type curve crosses 0.5 at 4.0 molar. An arrow labelled less urea needed, less stable points from the wild-type midpoint to the mutant midpoint. Legend: wild type delta G in water 20 kilojoules per mole, mutant 10.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the linear extrapolation model (two-state, 25 °C) with the midpoints in the question.

ox: Incorrect. Heat disrupts noncovalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, the hydrophobic effect, salt bridges), unfolding secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. Peptide bonds are covalent and do not break during ordinary heating, so the amino acid sequence stays the same even when the protein is fully denatured.

Incorrect. Urea at 6 M unfolds proteins by hydrogen-bonding to the backbone and solvating nonpolar side chains. These are noncovalent effects, so the sequence and its peptide bonds remain intact, which is why urea-denatured proteins can often refold after the urea is removed.

Correct. Primary structure is the covalent sequence of residues joined by peptide bonds, so only a process that breaks (or makes) peptide bonds changes it. Proteolytic cleavage hydrolyzes specific peptide bonds: proinsulin (one chain of 86 residues) is cut to release the C-peptide, leaving insulin's A and B chains (21 and 30 residues) joined by disulfides; zymogens such as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen are activated the same way. The products have different sequences from the precursor.

Incorrect. Lowering the pH from 7 to 3 protonates carboxylate groups, changing charges and breaking salt bridges, which can unfold the protein. But protonation is a reversible acid–base change, not a covalent change to the backbone. The order of amino acids is unchanged.

p: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. It changes only when peptide bonds are broken or formed: by proteolysis (enzymatic hydrolysis), by harsh chemical hydrolysis (6 M HCl at about 110 °C for many hours), or during synthesis on the ribosome. Mutations change it at the gene level.

Proteolytic processing is a normal part of making many active proteins: prohormones (proinsulin → insulin), zymogens (trypsinogen → trypsin, pepsinogen → pepsin), blood-clotting factors and removal of signal peptides. Because hydrolysis is irreversible, these activation steps act as one-way switches.

By contrast, heat, urea, detergents, organic solvents and pH change only the 3D shape (secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure). Reducing agents break disulfides, which changes covalent structure but not the amino acid sequence.

x1A_095.trap: Denaturation changes shape; only cutting or forming peptide bonds changes the sequence.

fig.cap: Proinsulin (86 residues, one chain) is cut at two dibasic sites, releasing the C-peptide and leaving insulin's A and B chains held by disulfides: a change in primary structure.
fig.alt: Bar diagram of proinsulin: B chain 30 residues, Arg-Arg, C-peptide 31 residues, Lys-Arg, A chain 21 residues, with scissors at the two cleavage sites. An arrow labelled hydrolysis of peptide bonds leads to insulin: B chain and A chain joined by two disulfide bonds, and released C-peptide. Tag: primary structure changed. Note: heat, urea and pH change only the fold.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue counts for human proinsulin.

fig.cap: Only the primary level is held by peptide bonds; heat, urea and pH affect the other three levels.
fig.alt: Four panels for primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure with the bonds that hold each; primary tagged intact after boiling or urea, others lost.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; content consistent with OpenStax Biology 2e, 3.4 Proteins.

ox: Incorrect. Motifs are defined by a recurring 3D arrangement of secondary-structure elements, not by an identical sequence. Different helix-turn-helix proteins (such as the λ repressor, Cro and the lac repressor) have quite different sequences that adopt the same structural pattern, and their recognition-helix residues differ so that each binds a different DNA sequence.

Correct. A helix-turn-helix is a supersecondary structure (motif): two α-helices joined by a short turn, roughly 20 residues in all, within one polypeptide. The second, recognition helix fits into the major groove of DNA, where its side chains form hydrogen bonds and van der Waals contacts with the edges of specific base pairs. The first helix helps position it. Many bacterial repressors and eukaryotic homeodomain proteins use this motif.

Incorrect. Quaternary structure is the assembly of separate polypeptide chains. A helix-turn-helix is formed within a single chain from consecutive segments of that chain. Many HTH proteins do bind DNA as dimers, but the motif itself is a feature of one chain's fold.

Incorrect. Transcription factors bind DNA reversibly through noncovalent interactions: hydrogen bonds to bases, salt bridges between Lys/Arg and the phosphate backbone, and van der Waals contacts. A covalent link would make regulation impossible, because the factor could not let go when conditions change.

p: Motifs (supersecondary structures) are small, recurring combinations of secondary-structure elements with a characteristic 3D arrangement. Examples include the β-hairpin, the β-α-β unit, the helix-loop-helix and the helix-turn-helix. A motif may be part of a larger domain.

In the helix-turn-helix, two short α-helices are joined by a tight turn. The recognition helix lies in the major groove of DNA, which is wide enough to expose the distinctive edges of base pairs, so the protein can 'read' a sequence without unwinding the DNA. Binding is noncovalent and reversible.

Other DNA-binding motifs to know: zinc fingers (Zn²⁺-stabilized ββα units), leucine zippers (dimerizing coiled coils with a basic DNA-binding region) and helix-loop-helix proteins. Motifs share structure, not identical sequences.

x1A_096.trap: A motif is a recurring SHAPE within one chain, not a fixed sequence and not a multi-chain assembly.

fig.cap: Helix-turn-helix bound to DNA: helix 1 and the recognition helix (helix 2) are joined by a turn within one chain, and helix 2 sits in the major groove.
fig.alt: DNA double helix drawn as two blue and teal strands with base-pair rungs. An orange helix 1 connects through a short turn to a red helix 2 lying in the major groove. Text: recognition helix sits in the major groove and reads bases through side-chain hydrogen bonds, noncovalent. Bottom tags: one chain, not 4 subunits; sequence varies; no covalent bond to DNA.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Correct. A classic Cys₂His₂ zinc finger is only about 30 residues: a β-hairpin followed by an α-helix. That is too small to bury a real hydrophobic core, so a Zn²⁺ ion takes its place. The zinc is bound tetrahedrally by the sulfur atoms of two cysteines in the hairpin and the nitrogen atoms of two histidines in the helix, tying the two elements together. Removing zinc (for example with EDTA) unfolds the finger. The zinc is structural, not catalytic.

Incorrect. Peptide bonds are formed by the ribosome's peptidyl transferase during translation, between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. Metal ions do not form peptide bonds. Zinc in the finger forms coordinate (dative) bonds with side-chain sulfur and nitrogen atoms.

Incorrect. A disulfide bond is a covalent S–S bond between the sulfur atoms of two cysteine side chains. It cannot form between two metal atoms. In a zinc finger, the cysteines bind the zinc as thiolates (Cys–S⁻···Zn²⁺) rather than pairing with each other, and there is only one zinc per finger.

Incorrect. The zinc in a zinc finger is structural: it holds the fold together and does not catalyze any reaction. Without zinc the finger cannot fold, because its small size gives too little hydrophobic packing. Catalytic zinc is found in other proteins, such as carbonic anhydrase and carboxypeptidase, where it activates water or the substrate.

concept.t: Metal ions as structural elements: zinc fingers
p: Some small protein folds are stabilized by a bound metal ion rather than a large hydrophobic core. In the classic Cys₂His₂ zinc finger (consensus X₂–Cys–X₂₋₄–Cys–X₁₂–His–X₃₋₅–His), Zn²⁺ is coordinated by two cysteines and two histidines, holding a β-hairpin against an α-helix. Zinc is ideal: it is redox-inert and prefers tetrahedral geometry.

Zinc-finger proteins are among the most common DNA-binding transcription factors in humans. Each finger's helix fits into the DNA major groove and contacts about three base pairs; arrays of fingers recognize longer sequences.

Distinguish structural metals (zinc fingers, Ca²⁺ in some proteins) from functional metals such as catalytic Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase or the heme Fe²⁺ that binds O₂ in myoglobin. Heavy metals such as Hg²⁺ and Cd²⁺ can displace zinc and destroy these folds.

x1A_097.trap: Zinc-finger Zn²⁺ is a structural 'staple', not a catalyst and not part of any covalent S–S bond.

fig.cap: A Cys₂His₂ zinc finger: Zn²⁺ is held tetrahedrally by two Cys from the β-hairpin and two His from the α-helix, acting as the core of this tiny fold.
fig.alt: Schematic of a beta-hairpin with two cysteines and an alpha-helix with two histidines, all four bound by dashed lines to a central zinc ion, labelled 4 ligands, tetrahedral, 2 Cys S, 2 His N. Text: about 30 residues, too small for a real hydrophobic core, zinc acts as the core. Tags: structural, not catalytic (correct); zinc makes peptide bonds (wrong); S-S between metals (wrong).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Incorrect. Phosphorylation adds a phosphate to serine's side-chain oxygen (–CH₂–OH → –CH₂–O–PO₃²⁻). No bond to the α-carbon is made or broken, so its configuration stays the same (L-serine, S at the α-carbon, before and after). Changing stereochemistry would require breaking a bond to the α-carbon, which kinases do not do.

Incorrect. Kinases transfer the terminal (γ) phosphate of ATP to the serine hydroxyl. The backbone peptide bonds on either side of the serine are untouched, so the chain stays intact. If phosphorylation cut the chain, it could not be reversed simply by a phosphatase removing the phosphate.

Correct. Phosphorylation adds a phosphate group whose second pKa is about 5.8, so at physiological pH (7.4) it is about 98% in the dianionic form, −2. A neutral hydroxyl becomes a bulky, strongly negative group. It can form new salt bridges with nearby Arg or Lys, repel nearby Asp or Glu, and add hydrogen bonds, which rearranges loops or whole domains. That conformational change switches activity on or off, as in glycogen phosphorylase and many kinase activation loops.

Incorrect. A phosphate group carries a negative charge (−2 at physiological pH, −1 below about pH 5.8). It attracts positively charged groups such as Arg and Lys; it would repel carboxylates. A positive charge would come from protonated amines or guanidinium groups, not phosphate.

p: Protein kinases transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP to the hydroxyl of serine, threonine or tyrosine. Protein phosphatases remove it by hydrolysis. This reversible covalent modification is the most common way cells regulate protein activity.

The phosphate group is large and carries about −2 charge at physiological pH. It changes the local electrostatics: it can pair with Arg and Lys side chains, repel acidic residues and form many hydrogen bonds. These new interactions can shift a loop, a helix or a whole domain into a different conformation, turning activity on or off or creating a binding site (SH2 domains recognize phosphotyrosine, for example).

Phosphorylation does not alter the backbone or stereochemistry. Compare other modifications: acetylation neutralizes lysine's + charge, ubiquitination marks proteins for degradation, glycosylation adds sugars in the ER and Golgi.

x1A_098.trap: Phosphate is NEGATIVE (about −2 at pH 7.4); it pairs with Lys/Arg, not with carboxylates.

fig.cap: A serine residue becomes phosphoserine (structures from RDKit; the α-carbon is S in both). The side chain goes from neutral to about −2 at pH 7.4.
fig.alt: Structure of a serine residue (capped) with its CH2OH side chain highlighted, an arrow labelled kinase plus ATP minus ADP, and phosphoserine with the CH2-O-PO3 2- group highlighted. Note: phosphate pKa2 about 5.8, about 98% minus 2 at pH 7.4; alpha-carbon stays S. Green box: new electrostatic contacts with Arg and Lys rearrange loops and domains; phosphatases reverse it. Red tags: changes alpha-carbon configuration, breaks peptide bond, adds positive charge.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES; dianion fraction computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch.

x1A_098.eli: Serine has an OH 'handle'. A kinase hangs a phosphate on it, like a heavy negatively charged backpack, and the protein reshapes around the new charge.
mem: Polar uncharged (6): S, T, C, N, Q, Y (STC NQY).
Phosphorylation targets S, T and Y (the OH groups).
A phosphate adds a bulky NEGATIVE charge (about −2 at pH 7).
x1A_098.sc: Phosphate = negative = new salt bridges or repulsions.
x1A_098.mn: STC NQY: S=Serine, T=Threonine, C=Cysteine, N=Asparagine, Q=Glutamine, Y=Tyrosine. Say it: 'Stick To Courses; Never Quit Yelling'.

ox: Correct. Stability is the free-energy gap between the unfolded (U) and native (N) states. A disulfide placed between two residues that are already close in the native fold does not strain the native state, but it ties the unfolded chain into a loop, removing many of its possible conformations. Lowering the entropy of U raises its free energy, which widens the gap, so ΔG(unfolding) and the melting temperature rise. This is a common protein-engineering strategy, and the rationale also explains why secreted proteins often carry disulfides.

Incorrect. Leucine buried in the core contributes to the hydrophobic effect. Replacing it with aspartate puts a charged carboxylate in the nonpolar interior, where it cannot be hydrated and has no partner. This costs a large amount of free energy, raising the energy of the native state and making the protein much less stable.

Incorrect. Glycine has no side chain, so it is very flexible. Fixing it in a helix costs more conformational entropy than fixing other residues, and it adds no side-chain packing. Several glycines in the middle of an α-helix therefore weaken the helix and lower overall stability. Glycine is better suited to turns and loops.

Incorrect. A surface salt bridge between, for example, Lys and Glu adds a modest favorable electrostatic interaction to the native state. Mutating both residues to alanine removes it, so the native state loses some stabilization. The effect is usually small (surface salt bridges are partly screened by water and ions), but it lowers stability rather than raising it.

p: Stability is ΔG(unfolding) = G(unfolded) − G(native). It can be raised either by lowering G of the native state (better core packing, more hydrogen bonds or salt bridges, helix-favoring residues) or by raising G of the unfolded state, usually by reducing its conformational entropy.

A disulfide bond does the second: cross-linking two residues that are near each other in the native state constrains the unfolded chain into a loop, reducing the number of conformations it can explore. The longer the loop, the larger the entropy loss of U and the greater the stabilization. Replacing glycine with alanine or adding prolines in loops works by a similar entropy logic.

Destabilizing changes include burying a charged or polar group in the core, placing glycine or proline in the middle of a helix, creating cavities by removing large hydrophobic residues, and removing salt bridges or hydrogen bonds. Stability is measured as Tm or denaturant midpoint (Cm).

x1A_099.trap: A good disulfide stabilizes mainly by destabilizing the UNFOLDED state (lowering its entropy).

fig.cap: Free-energy levels of native (N) and unfolded (U) states for each change (illustrative values, kJ/mol). The engineered disulfide raises U and widens the gap; the other three changes narrow it, drawn here as a less stable native state.
fig.alt: Energy-level diagram with five columns. Wild type: gap 30. Plus engineered S-S bond: U raised, gap 42, tagged more stable. Buried Leu to Asp: N raised, gap 15. Gly in mid-helix: gap 22. Surface salt bridge removed: gap 26. These three tagged less stable.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; illustrative free-energy values.

ox: Incorrect. A cysteine thiolate is the proximal heme ligand in cytochrome P450 enzymes (and in nitric oxide synthase), where its strong electron donation helps activate O₂ for oxidation reactions. In the globins, which must bind O₂ reversibly without oxidizing anything, the proximal ligand is histidine, not cysteine.

Incorrect. Lysine's side chain ends in an amine that is protonated (–NH₃⁺) at physiological pH, so its lone pair is unavailable to coordinate iron. Lysine residues near the heme pocket can interact electrostatically with heme propionates, but they are not iron ligands in globins.

Incorrect. Glutamate's carboxylate can bind some metal ions, for example in non-heme iron or calcium-binding sites, but it is not the heme ligand in globins. Using a hard, negatively charged oxygen ligand would also tend to stabilize Fe³⁺ (methemoglobin), which cannot bind O₂.

Correct. In myoglobin and in each hemoglobin subunit, the heme iron (Fe²⁺) is bound by the four nitrogens of the porphyrin ring in the plane, plus the imidazole nitrogen of the proximal histidine (His F8) below the plane as the fifth ligand. O₂ binds the sixth site on the opposite (distal) side, where the distal histidine (His E7) hydrogen-bonds to it without binding iron.
