When O₂ binds, the iron moves into the porphyrin plane and pulls His F8 and its helix, which triggers hemoglobin's cooperative shift toward the high-affinity R state.

concept.t: The heme pocket of myoglobin and hemoglobin
p: Heme is an iron atom held in a porphyrin ring. In the globins the iron is Fe²⁺ and has six coordination sites: four porphyrin nitrogens in the plane, the proximal histidine (His F8) below, and the O₂-binding site above. The distal histidine (His E7) sits above the plane, hydrogen-bonds to bound O₂ and sterically discourages CO binding.

In deoxyhemoglobin the iron sits slightly out of the porphyrin plane, pulled toward His F8. O₂ binding draws the iron into the plane, moving His F8 and helix F; this shift is transmitted to subunit interfaces and switches the tetramer from the T (tense, low-affinity) to the R (relaxed, high-affinity) state, the structural basis of cooperativity.

The protein environment keeps iron in the Fe²⁺ state; oxidized Fe³⁺ (methemoglobin) cannot bind O₂. Other heme proteins use different ligands for different jobs, such as cysteine in cytochrome P450 and two histidines or His/Met in electron-carrying cytochromes.

x1A_100.trap: Globins: proximal His F8 binds Fe; distal His E7 only hydrogen-bonds to O₂. Cysteine belongs to P450s.

fig.cap: Heme iron's coordination in globins: four porphyrin nitrogens in the plane, the proximal His (F8) imidazole below as the fifth ligand, and O₂ at the sixth site above, hydrogen-bonded by the distal His (E7).
fig.alt: Perspective drawing of a porphyrin plane with Fe2+ at the center bonded to four nitrogens. Below, a histidine imidazole ring binds the iron through its unprotonated nitrogen, labelled proximal His F8, 5th coordination site. Above, O=O binds the 6th site on the distal side; distal His E7 hydrogen-bonds to O2 but is not bonded to iron. Tags: His (globins) correct; Cys (P450s), Lys, Glu wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; schematic, not to scale.

ox: Incorrect. Disulfide bonds form only between the thiol (–SH) groups of two cysteine side chains. Glycine's side chain is a single hydrogen atom, so it has no sulfur and cannot make any covalent cross-link. Mature collagen fibrils are in fact cross-linked through modified lysine side chains (by lysyl oxidase), not through disulfides of glycine.

Correct. The three collagen chains wind around one another in a tight triple helix, and in every Gly-X-Y triplet the first position points straight into the crowded central axis where the chains touch. There is room there only for a hydrogen atom. Glycine is the only amino acid whose side chain is just H, so a substitution with even alanine (CH₃) would clash with the other chains and disrupt the helix. This is why Gly substitutions in collagen cause brittle bones in osteogenesis imperfecta.

Incorrect. Glycine's side chain is a hydrogen atom, which is neither acidic nor basic, so glycine carries no side-chain charge at any physiological pH and cannot form salt bridges. Salt bridges need ionized side chains such as Lys/Arg (+) paired with Asp/Glu (−). The real reason glycine is required is size, not charge.

Incorrect. The residues that get hydroxylated in collagen are proline (to 4-hydroxyproline, usually in the Y position) and lysine (to 5-hydroxylysine). Glycine has no carbon side chain to hydroxylate. Hydroxyproline does stabilize the helix, but that is a separate fact from why every third residue must be glycine.

concept.t: Collagen structure: the Gly-X-Y triple helix
p: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body and the main fibrous protein of the extracellular matrix (skin, tendon, bone, cartilage). Each chain has a repeating Gly-X-Y sequence, where X is often proline and Y is often hydroxyproline. Three such chains, each a left-handed polyproline-type helix, wind around each other into a right-handed triple helix.

Geometry explains the sequence. Every third residue lies at the center of the triple helix, where the chains are packed so closely that only glycine's hydrogen side chain fits. The rigid rings of proline and hydroxyproline in the X and Y positions lock the chain into the extended twist, and hydroxyproline further stabilizes the helix.

On the MCAT, link collagen to: glycine (small size), vitamin C (needed to hydroxylate Pro and Lys), and structural rather than catalytic function. Do not confuse collagen's triple helix with the α-helix (a single chain, secondary structure) or with keratin, the intermediate-filament protein of hair and nails.

x1A_101.trap: Glycine is chosen for its tiny size (side chain = H), not for charge, sulfur or hydroxylation.

fig.cap: In every Gly-X-Y repeat, glycine (G) points into the crowded axis of the triple helix, where only a hydrogen side chain fits; X and Y residues face outward.
fig.alt: Sequence strip Gly-Pro-Hyp-Gly-Pro-Ala-Gly-Lys-Hyp-Gly with glycines highlighted, and a cross-section of three chains with a glycine from each chain touching the central axis. Labels mark the correct reason (only glycine fits) and the three wrong reasons.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Collagen chains are built only from amino acids. Vitamin C (ascorbate) never becomes part of the chain; it acts on the enzymes that modify the chain. A vitamin used as a building block would be a substrate consumed in stoichiometric amounts, but ascorbate is only needed in small, catalytic amounts to keep an enzyme's iron reduced.

Correct. Prolyl 4-hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase add –OH groups to proline and lysine in procollagen in the ER. Both use Fe²⁺, O₂ and α-ketoglutarate, and ascorbate is needed to re-reduce the iron to Fe²⁺ when it becomes oxidized. Without vitamin C, too few hydroxyproline residues form, so the triple helix is unstable at body temperature, and too few hydroxylysines form, so fewer cross-links can be made. The result is fragile vessels, bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

Incorrect. Peptide bonds in collagen, as in every protein, are formed on the ribosome by the peptidyl transferase center of the large-subunit rRNA, using aminoacyl-tRNAs. No vitamin cofactor is required for that step. Scurvy patients make normal collagen chains; they fail at the post-translational modification step.

Incorrect. The covalent cross-links between collagen molecules in a fibril are made by lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme that converts lysine and hydroxylysine side chains to reactive aldehydes. Ascorbate itself does not form cross-links. Vitamin C deficiency reduces cross-linking only indirectly, by reducing the hydroxylysine available for it.

p: Collagen is made as procollagen on rough-ER ribosomes. Before the three chains wind together, specific prolines and lysines are hydroxylated by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. These are Fe²⁺-, O₂- and α-ketoglutarate-dependent enzymes, and ascorbate (vitamin C) keeps their iron in the reduced Fe²⁺ state so they can keep turning over.

Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix, so collagen made without it unfolds at body temperature and is degraded. Hydroxylysine provides attachment points for sugars and for the cross-links later made by lysyl oxidase (a Cu²⁺ enzyme) outside the cell. Scurvy therefore shows up wherever collagen turnover matters: bleeding gums, easy bruising, poor wound healing and weak blood vessels.

This is a classic MCAT example of a vitamin acting as an enzyme cofactor, not as a structural component. Keep the steps distinct: ribosome (peptide bonds), hydroxylases (vitamin C), glycosylation, triple helix assembly in the ER, cleavage of propeptides outside the cell, then lysyl oxidase cross-linking.

x1A_102.trap: Vitamin C is a cofactor for the hydroxylases, not a part of collagen and not the cross-linker itself.

fig.cap: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases add OH groups (shaded) to proline and lysine. Ascorbate keeps their iron as Fe²⁺; without it, collagen lacks Hyp and Hyl.
fig.alt: Proline converted to 4-hydroxyproline by prolyl 4-hydroxylase, and lysine converted to 5-hydroxylysine by lysyl hydroxylase, with a note that ascorbate re-reduces Fe3+ to Fe2+. A red box explains the effects of scurvy, with tags marking the correct and incorrect choices.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Incorrect. Peptide bonds are amide bonds in the protein backbone. They are not broken by the mild reducing agents in a perm lotion (such as thioglycolate); breaking them needs hydrolysis by strong acid, strong base or proteases. If peptide bonds were cut, the keratin chains would fall apart and the hair would be destroyed rather than reshaped.

Incorrect. Hydrogen bonds do help hold hair's shape, but they are weak and are reset just by wetting and drying the hair, which is why a blow-dry style disappears in humid air. A redox treatment (reduce, then oxidize) acts on covalent bonds that can gain and lose electrons, and hydrogen bonds are not redox-active. A perm lasts for weeks because the new shape is locked by covalent bonds.

Incorrect. Glycosidic bonds link sugar units in carbohydrates such as starch, glycogen and cellulose. α-Keratin is a protein, so its chains are held by peptide bonds in the backbone and by disulfide cross-links between chains. Glycosidic bonds are also not broken by reduction.

Correct. α-Keratin is rich in cysteine, and neighboring chains are linked by disulfide (S–S) bonds. A reducing lotion adds hydrogen and breaks each S–S into two –SH groups, so the strands can slide while the hair is held on a curler. An oxidizing lotion (often H₂O₂) then removes the hydrogens, and new disulfide bonds form between cysteines that are now next to each other, locking in the curl.

concept.t: Disulfide bonds: making and breaking them by redox
p: A disulfide bond is a covalent S–S link between the thiol groups of two cysteine residues. Forming it is an oxidation (2 R–SH → R–S–S–R + 2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻), and breaking it is a reduction. The linked pair of cysteines is called cystine. Disulfides stabilize tertiary and quaternary structure, especially in proteins exposed to the oxidizing extracellular environment, such as antibodies, insulin and keratin.

Because they are covalent, disulfides survive conditions that disrupt hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions. That is why hair keeps a perm through washing, and why chemists add reducing agents such as β-mercaptoethanol or dithiothreitol (DTT) before SDS-PAGE to separate disulfide-linked chains.

The MCAT often contrasts bond types by what breaks them: hydrogen bonds (water, heat), salt bridges (pH, salt), disulfides (reducing agents), peptide bonds (hydrolysis by acid, base or proteases). Do not confuse disulfide bonds with peptide bonds; reducing agents leave the primary structure intact.

x1A_103.trap: Reduction breaks S–S bonds, oxidation forms them; peptide bonds need hydrolysis, not reduction.

fig.cap: Top: reducing cystine gives two cysteines, and oxidation re-forms the S–S bond. Bottom: the three steps of a perm, ending with disulfides between new partner cysteines.
fig.alt: Cystine and two cysteine molecules linked by a two-way arrow labeled reduce and oxidize. Below, three panels show two keratin strands with S–S bridges, the bridges broken into SH groups, and new S–S bridges after the strands have slid.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

ox: Correct. Microfilaments (about 7 nm wide, the thinnest cytoskeletal filaments) are built from actin. Globular G-actin monomers bind ATP and polymerize into a two-stranded helical filament called F-actin. Microfilaments form the thin filaments of muscle, drive cell crawling and cytokinesis (the contractile ring), and are the tracks for myosin motors.

Incorrect. Tubulin, as α/β-tubulin heterodimers that bind GTP, polymerizes into microtubules, the widest cytoskeletal filaments (about 25 nm, hollow). Microtubules form the mitotic spindle, the core of cilia and flagella, and the tracks for kinesin and dynein. This choice confuses microtubules with microfilaments.

Incorrect. Keratins are one family of intermediate filament proteins (about 10 nm), found in epithelial cells, hair and nails. Other intermediate filaments include vimentin, neurofilaments and nuclear lamins. Intermediate filaments give tensile strength; they bind no nucleotide and have no motor proteins.

Incorrect. Collagen is not part of the cytoskeleton at all. It is a secreted protein that forms fibrils in the extracellular matrix, outside the cell. It is a fibrous structural protein like the cytoskeletal ones, which is why it is a tempting distractor, but its location and assembly are completely different.

p: The eukaryotic cytoskeleton has three filament systems. Microfilaments (actin, about 7 nm) bind ATP, are polar, and partner with myosin motors for contraction, cytokinesis and cell movement. Microtubules (α/β-tubulin, about 25 nm, hollow) bind GTP, are polar with plus and minus ends, and partner with kinesin and dynein for transport, mitosis and cilia. Intermediate filaments (keratins, vimentin, lamins, neurofilaments, about 10 nm) bind no nucleotide and resist tension.

A quick way to remember: size order is microfilaments < intermediate filaments < microtubules, and nucleotide order is actin-ATP, tubulin-GTP, intermediate filaments-none. Actin and tubulin both show dynamic assembly and disassembly; intermediate filaments are more stable.

MCAT questions often pair each filament with its motor (myosin on actin; kinesin and dynein on microtubules) or a function (spindle = microtubules; contractile ring = actin; nuclear lamina = lamins). Collagen and elastin are extracellular matrix proteins, not cytoskeleton.

x1A_104.trap: Microfilament = actin; microtubule = tubulin; keratin is an intermediate filament; collagen is extracellular.

fig.cap: The three cytoskeletal filaments compared by subunit, size, nucleotide, motors and jobs. Microfilaments are made of actin.
fig.alt: Table comparing microfilaments (G-actin, about 7 nm, ATP, myosins), microtubules (alpha/beta tubulin, about 25 nm, GTP, kinesins and dyneins) and intermediate filaments (keratins, vimentin, lamins, about 10 nm, no nucleotide, no motors). A note says collagen is extracellular, not cytoskeleton.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; values from standard cell biology texts.

ox: Incorrect. ATP is the nucleotide bound by actin, the subunit of microfilaments. ATP-actin adds to the growing filament and is hydrolyzed to ADP-actin afterward, a pattern similar to tubulin's. That parallel makes ATP tempting, but tubulin binds GTP. Remember the pairing: actin–ATP, tubulin–GTP.

Incorrect. Cyclic AMP is a second messenger made by adenylyl cyclase in response to Gs-coupled receptors; it activates protein kinase A. It is a soluble signaling molecule, not a nucleotide bound by cytoskeletal subunits, and plays no direct structural role in microtubule polymerization.

Correct. Each α/β-tubulin dimer binds two GTP molecules: one on α-tubulin that is never hydrolyzed, and one on β-tubulin that is hydrolyzed to GDP soon after the dimer joins the plus end. GTP-bound dimers add readily, so a cap of GTP-tubulin stabilizes a growing end. When hydrolysis catches up and the cap is lost, the GDP lattice curls apart rapidly. This switching between growth and shrinkage is called dynamic instability.

Incorrect. NADH is an electron carrier made in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle; it delivers electrons to the electron transport chain. It is not a nucleotide that binds cytoskeletal proteins, and it does not carry the phosphoanhydride energy that drives polymer dynamics. Choosing it confuses metabolism with cytoskeletal assembly.

p: Microtubules are hollow tubes of 13 protofilaments, each a head-to-tail chain of α/β-tubulin dimers. Because every dimer points the same way, the microtubule has a fast-growing plus end (β-tubulin exposed) and a slower minus end, which in most cells is anchored at the centrosome.

Free tubulin dimers carry GTP. After a dimer joins the plus end, its β-tubulin GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP. As long as new GTP-tubulin adds faster than hydrolysis occurs, a stabilizing GTP cap remains and the microtubule grows. If the cap is lost, the strained GDP lattice peels apart (catastrophe), and the microtubule shrinks quickly until it is rescued. This dynamic instability lets spindle microtubules search for and capture chromosomes.

Drugs such as colchicine and vinblastine block polymerization, and taxol (paclitaxel) blocks disassembly; both arrest mitosis. On the MCAT, pair actin with ATP and tubulin with GTP, and remember that G proteins in signaling also use GTP but are unrelated to the cytoskeleton.

x1A_105.trap: Actin binds ATP; tubulin binds GTP. Do not swap them.

fig.cap: GTP-bound tubulin (green β subunits) adds to the plus end and forms a stabilizing cap. Once the cap is lost, the GDP lattice peels apart (catastrophe).
fig.alt: Side view of a microtubule with GDP-tubulin in gray and a GTP cap in green at the plus end, free GTP-tubulin dimers adding to the tip, and below, a capless microtubule with curling protofilaments and GDP-tubulin falling off. Tags: GTP correct; ATP, cAMP and NADH incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Most kinesins walk toward the plus end of a microtubule. In an axon, all microtubules have their plus ends at the axon terminal, so kinesin carries cargo outward from the cell body to the terminal (anterograde transport), such as new synaptic vesicle components and mitochondria. This choice gets the direction backward.

Incorrect. Myosin II is an actin-based motor; it forms the thick filaments of muscle and the contractile ring in cytokinesis. Long-distance transport along an axon runs on microtubules, not actin, so myosin II is the wrong motor on the wrong track.

Incorrect. Tubulin is the protein that polymerizes into microtubules, so it forms the track, not the motor. Tubulin itself does not bind and walk with cargo. The question asks for the motor protein that moves along the track toward the cell body.

Correct. Axonal microtubules are uniformly oriented with their minus ends toward the cell body and their plus ends toward the terminal. Cytoplasmic dynein moves toward the minus end, so it carries cargo from the terminal back to the soma (retrograde transport), including endosomes, worn-out components and neurotrophin signals. Rabies virus and tetanus toxin exploit this route to reach the central nervous system.

p: Motor proteins convert ATP hydrolysis into directed movement along a polar filament. Two families use microtubules: kinesins (most move toward the plus end) and dyneins (move toward the minus end). Myosins use actin filaments. The direction a motor goes in the cell depends on how its track is oriented.

In axons, microtubules all point the same way: minus ends at the cell body, plus ends at the terminal. So kinesin drives anterograde transport (out to the terminal) and dynein drives retrograde transport (back to the soma). In a typical non-neuronal cell, minus ends are at the centrosome near the nucleus, so kinesin moves cargo toward the periphery and dynein moves it inward.

A useful memory aid: kinesin goes out to the plus end, dynein comes back down. Dynein also powers the beating of cilia and flagella and helps position the mitotic spindle. Do not confuse the motor (kinesin, dynein, myosin) with the track (microtubules made of tubulin; microfilaments made of actin).

x1A_106.trap: Kinesin goes out (+ end, anterograde); dynein comes back (− end, retrograde).

fig.cap: In an axon, microtubule minus ends face the cell body. Kinesin carries cargo out to the terminal; dynein carries it back to the soma.
fig.alt: Neuron with a cell body on the left, an axon with a microtubule marked minus at the soma and plus at the terminal, a green arrow labeled kinesin anterograde pointing right and a red arrow labeled dynein retrograde pointing left. Tags mark dynein as correct and kinesin, myosin II and tubulin as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. The power stroke, the step that pulls the thin filament, happens later in the cycle: after the head with ADP·Pi binds actin, release of Pi triggers the lever arm to swing. ATP binding does the opposite of producing force; it lowers myosin's affinity for actin so the head lets go.

Incorrect. Ca²⁺ binding to troponin and release from it are controlled by Ca²⁺ concentration in the cytosol, which is set by release from and reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). The SR Ca²⁺-ATPase (SERCA) uses ATP to pump Ca²⁺ back, but that is a different protein. ATP binding to the myosin head does not change troponin.

Correct. In the rigor state the myosin head is tightly bound to actin with no nucleotide. When ATP binds the head, myosin's affinity for actin drops sharply and the head detaches. ATP is then hydrolyzed to ADP·Pi, which re-cocks the head for the next cycle. After death, ATP runs out, so heads stay locked to actin in the rigor state, which is why muscles stiffen in rigor mortis.

Incorrect. Thin filaments (F-actin with tropomyosin and troponin) stay polymerized throughout contraction. Muscle shortens because thick and thin filaments slide past each other, not because filaments assemble or disassemble. Actin depolymerization is relevant to cell crawling, not to the cross-bridge cycle.

p: Muscle contracts as myosin heads on the thick filament repeatedly bind, pull and release the actin thin filament. Starting from the rigor state (head bound, no nucleotide): ATP binds and the head detaches; ATP is hydrolyzed to ADP·Pi, which re-cocks the head into its high-energy position; the cocked head binds actin; Pi is released, triggering the power stroke; ADP is released, returning to rigor.

Ca²⁺ is the on switch. When an action potential triggers SR Ca²⁺ release, Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, which moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin. Without Ca²⁺, heads cannot bind actin and the cycle stops at the cocked, detached stage, so the muscle relaxes.

Key MCAT points: ATP is needed for detachment (no ATP → rigor mortis), hydrolysis re-cocks the head, Pi release powers the stroke, and Ca²⁺ regulates access to actin. During contraction the sarcomere, H zone and I band shorten while the A band (thick filament length) stays constant.

x1A_107.trap: ATP is needed to let go of actin, not to pull; no ATP means rigor.

fig.cap: The cross-bridge cycle. The highlighted step is ATP binding, which releases the myosin head from actin.
fig.alt: Four-state cycle: rigor (head bound to actin), ATP bound (head released), ADP and Pi (head re-cocked), and ADP-Pi head bound to actin, with arrows labeled ATP binds and detach, ATP hydrolysis, binds actin, and Pi release power stroke. The ATP-binding arrow is green.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; cycle as taught in standard physiology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 10.3 Muscle Fiber Contraction and Relaxation

ox: Incorrect. ATP binding to the myosin head is the step that releases the head from actin. It ends one cycle of force rather than producing force. This is why a lack of ATP (as after death) leaves heads stuck to actin in rigor rather than producing extra contraction.

Correct. After hydrolysis, the head holds ADP and Pi in a cocked, high-energy conformation. Once Ca²⁺ has exposed the binding sites and the head binds actin, release of Pi from the active site triggers the lever arm to swing, pulling the thin filament toward the center of the sarcomere. ADP is then released and the head ends in the rigor state. The energy of ATP hydrolysis was stored in the cocked head and spent during this Pi-release-linked stroke.

Incorrect. ATP hydrolysis happens while the head is detached from actin. It does not move the filament; it re-cocks the head into its pre-stroke position, storing energy in the head's conformation. A common error is to assume force is produced at the moment ATP is split, but the split and the stroke are separate steps.

Incorrect. Ca²⁺ leaving troponin (when the SR pumps Ca²⁺ back) lets tropomyosin slide back over actin's binding sites, so myosin heads can no longer attach. That ends cross-bridge cycling and leads to relaxation. It is a regulatory switch, not a mechanical step of the head.

p: Myosin is an ATPase whose conformation changes with the nucleotide bound. Each cycle: ATP binding detaches the head; ATP hydrolysis (head detached) re-cocks it, storing energy; the ADP·Pi head binds actin; Pi release triggers the power stroke; ADP release leaves the head in rigor. The chemical energy of ATP is captured in the cocked state and released as mechanical work when Pi leaves.

This sequence lets the head bind actin only when it is ready to pull. Ca²⁺ and the troponin–tropomyosin complex determine whether actin sites are available, so they control whether cycling occurs at all but do not move the head themselves.

MCAT questions test each step's consequence: blocking ATP binding freezes muscle in rigor; blocking hydrolysis keeps heads detached and uncocked; low Ca²⁺ relaxes muscle. Note that 'ATP is used for the power stroke' is loosely true overall, but the step linked to the stroke itself is Pi release.

x1A_108.trap: Hydrolysis cocks the head; Pi release fires it; ATP binding releases it.

fig.cap: The cross-bridge cycle. The highlighted step, Pi release from the actin-bound head, triggers the power stroke.
fig.alt: Four-state cross-bridge cycle with the arrow from the ADP-Pi head bound to actin to the rigor state highlighted green and labeled Pi release, power stroke, then ADP leaves. Tags mark Pi release as correct and ATP binding and hydrolysis as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; cycle as taught in standard physiology texts.

ox: Correct. Hemoglobin is a tetramer (α₂β₂) with four hemes. Binding O₂ at one heme pulls the iron into the porphyrin plane, shifting the subunit interfaces from the low-affinity T (tense) state toward the high-affinity R (relaxed) state, so the remaining hemes bind O₂ more easily. This positive cooperativity makes saturation rise steeply over a narrow PO₂ range, giving a sigmoidal curve. Myoglobin is a single chain with one heme, so it has no partners to cooperate with and its curve is a simple hyperbola.

Incorrect. The opposite is true: myoglobin has the higher O₂ affinity (P50 about 2 to 3 mmHg versus about 26 mmHg for hemoglobin), so its curve lies to the left of hemoglobin's at every PO₂ below saturation. Higher affinity would shift a curve left, but it would not change its shape from hyperbolic to sigmoidal.

Incorrect. Myoglobin does contain heme: one Fe²⁺-protoporphyrin IX per chain, which is where O₂ binds and why muscle is red. A protein with no heme could not bind O₂ at all. The curve shapes differ because of the number of interacting subunits, not because one protein lacks heme.

Incorrect. O₂ binds the Fe²⁺ of heme by a reversible coordinate bond in both proteins; it must come off easily in tissues for either protein to work. Covalent, irreversible binding would give no useful curve at all. The sigmoidal shape comes from cooperativity between subunits.

p: A protein with one binding site, like myoglobin, follows a hyperbolic curve: Y = PO₂/(P50 + PO₂). A protein with several interacting sites, like hemoglobin, can show cooperativity, where binding at one site changes the affinity of the others. Positive cooperativity gives a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve and a Hill coefficient greater than 1 (about 2.8 for hemoglobin).

Hemoglobin switches between the T state (low affinity, favored by H⁺, CO₂ and 2,3-BPG) and the R state (high affinity, favored by O₂ binding). Because its steep region sits between tissue PO₂ (about 40 mmHg, or 20 in exercising muscle) and lung PO₂ (about 100 mmHg), a small drop in PO₂ releases a lot of O₂. Myoglobin, with its much lower P50, stays almost saturated at tissue PO₂ and serves as an O₂ store in muscle.

MCAT questions often ask which protein has the higher affinity (myoglobin), what P50 means (the PO₂ at 50% saturation; lower means tighter binding), and which factors shift hemoglobin's curve. Cooperativity is about interaction among sites, not about the strength of a single bond.

x1A_109.trap: Myoglobin has the HIGHER affinity; hemoglobin's S shape comes from cooperativity, not stronger binding.

fig.cap: Binding curves computed from the Hill equation: myoglobin (n = 1, P50 ≈ 3 mmHg) is hyperbolic; hemoglobin (n ≈ 2.8, P50 ≈ 26 mmHg) is sigmoidal.
fig.alt: Graph of O2 saturation against PO2 from 0 to 100 mmHg. The myoglobin curve rises steeply and hyperbolically, reaching 50 percent near 3 mmHg; the hemoglobin curve is S-shaped, reaching 50 percent at 26 mmHg. Notes explain cooperativity and that myoglobin has the higher affinity.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation, Y = Pⁿ/(P50ⁿ + Pⁿ), with standard textbook P50 and n values.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids

ox: Incorrect. A fall in temperature stabilizes the high-affinity form of hemoglobin and shifts the O₂ curve to the left, so less O₂ is released. Working muscle actually gets warmer, which shifts the curve right. This choice names the right variable but the wrong direction.

Incorrect. Active muscle produces more CO₂, not less. CO₂ lowers hemoglobin's affinity both directly (it forms carbamino groups on the N-termini that stabilize the T state) and indirectly (it generates H⁺ via carbonic anhydrase). A fall in CO₂ would do the opposite, shifting the curve left and holding O₂ more tightly.

Correct. Contracting muscle produces CO₂ and lactic acid, which lower the local pH. H⁺ protonates specific residues of hemoglobin (such as His146 of the β chains), stabilizing the low-affinity T state through extra salt bridges. This is the Bohr effect: the O₂ curve shifts right, so at a given tissue PO₂ more O₂ is released. In the computed example, unloading between 100 and 20 mmHg rises from about 65% to 75% of capacity.

Incorrect. 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate binds the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T state, so less 2,3-BPG means higher affinity and a left shift. 2,3-BPG levels rise, not fall, in chronic hypoxia such as at high altitude, which helps unloading. A fall would make delivery worse.

concept.t: Right and left shifts of the hemoglobin curve
p: Factors that lower hemoglobin's O₂ affinity shift the curve right (higher P50), so more O₂ is released at a given PO₂. The classic list: increased CO₂, increased H⁺ (lower pH, the Bohr effect), increased temperature and increased 2,3-BPG. All of them stabilize the T (tense, deoxy) state. These are exactly the conditions in metabolically active tissue, so O₂ is delivered where it is needed most.

Factors that do the opposite (less CO₂, higher pH, cooler temperature, less 2,3-BPG, plus fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide) shift the curve left (lower P50), so hemoglobin holds O₂ more tightly. A left shift helps loading but hurts unloading.

A common memory aid for a right shift is 'CADET, face right': CO₂, Acid, 2,3-DPG (BPG), Exercise and Temperature. In the lungs the reverse happens: CO₂ is exhaled and pH rises, which raises affinity and helps loading (the Haldane effect describes the mirror image: deoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂ and H⁺).

x1A_110.trap: Every change in active tissue (↑CO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG) shifts the curve right; the 'fall' versions shift it left.

fig.cap: Hill-equation curves for normal blood (P50 26 mmHg) and an illustrative right-shifted curve for active muscle (P50 32 mmHg). At a muscle PO₂ of 20 mmHg the shifted curve releases more O₂.
fig.alt: Two sigmoidal O2 saturation curves; the green active-muscle curve lies to the right of the blue normal curve. At PO2 20 mmHg the green curve is at about 21 percent and the blue at about 32 percent; unloading from 100 to 20 mmHg is 65 percent normally versus 75 percent when shifted.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation (n = 2.8; P50 26 mmHg normal, 32 mmHg illustrative right shift).

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.5 Transport of Gases

ox: Correct. 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) binds in the central cavity between the two β chains of deoxy adult hemoglobin, held by positively charged residues including His143. It stabilizes the low-affinity T state. In fetal hemoglobin the γ chains have a serine at that position, so the cavity is less positive and binds 2,3-BPG weakly. With less of this allosteric inhibitor bound, HbF spends more time in the high-affinity state (P50 about 19 versus 26 mmHg), so O₂ moves from maternal to fetal blood across the placenta.

Incorrect. HbF (α₂γ₂) and HbA (α₂β₂) are both tetramers with one heme per chain, so each has four hemes and binds up to four O₂. Having more hemes would raise O₂-carrying capacity, not affinity; affinity is about how tightly each heme holds O₂ at a given PO₂, shown by P50.

Incorrect. O₂ binds the Fe²⁺ of every heme by a reversible coordinate bond in both HbF and HbA. If fetal hemoglobin bound O₂ covalently, it could never release O₂ to fetal tissues, which would defeat its purpose. Its higher affinity is a modest left shift in a reversible equilibrium.

Incorrect. Fetal hemoglobin is still a cooperative tetramer with a sigmoidal curve; it simply sits to the left of HbA's curve. Loss of cooperativity would turn the curve hyperbolic and would actually make loading in the placenta and unloading in fetal tissues less efficient.

p: The fetus gets O₂ from maternal blood across the placenta, where PO₂ is low (about 30 to 40 mmHg). To pull O₂ from maternal hemoglobin, fetal hemoglobin must bind O₂ more tightly. HbF uses two γ chains in place of β chains (α₂γ₂), and its P50 is about 19 mmHg versus about 26 mmHg for adult HbA.

The difference comes from 2,3-BPG, a glycolytic by-product in red cells that binds one molecule per deoxyhemoglobin tetramer in the central cavity and stabilizes the T state. A key positive residue (β His143) is a serine in γ chains, so HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly and stays more often in the high-affinity form.

On the MCAT, link left-shifted curves to: HbF, carbon monoxide, low 2,3-BPG, low CO₂, high pH and low temperature. Higher affinity means a lower P50. Note that 2,3-BPG rises at high altitude to help unloading in adults.

x1A_111.trap: HbF has the same four hemes; it binds O₂ more tightly because it binds the inhibitor 2,3-BPG weakly.

fig.cap: Hill-equation curves for HbF (P50 ≈ 19 mmHg) and HbA (P50 ≈ 26 mmHg). At a placental PO₂ of 30 mmHg, HbF is about 78% saturated versus 60% for HbA.
fig.alt: Two sigmoidal curves of O2 saturation against PO2; the fetal hemoglobin curve lies to the left of the adult curve. At 30 mmHg the fetal curve reads 78 percent and the adult 60 percent. A note explains that gamma chains bind 2,3-BPG weakly.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation, Y = Pⁿ/(P50ⁿ + Pⁿ), with standard textbook P50 and n values.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.5 Transport of Gases

ox: Incorrect. P50 is the PO₂ at which hemoglobin is half saturated. A lower P50 means half saturation is reached at a lower O₂ pressure, which means tighter binding. Weaker binding would need more O₂ pressure to reach 50%, so it would raise the P50 above 26 mmHg (a right shift), the opposite of this mutant.

Incorrect. P50 measures affinity, not capacity. Each hemoglobin tetramer has four hemes and can carry at most four O₂ molecules no matter what its P50 is. Doubling capacity would require more binding sites, and the P50 value gives no information about that.

Incorrect. P50 is a single point on the curve and tells you where the curve sits, not its shape. Cooperativity is measured by the steepness of the curve (the Hill coefficient). A mutant could have a low P50 with or without cooperativity, so 'lost all cooperativity' cannot be concluded from P50 alone.

Correct. A P50 of 12 mmHg means the mutant is half saturated at less than half the O₂ pressure needed by normal hemoglobin, so its curve is shifted left and it binds O₂ more tightly. It loads fully in the lungs but stays mostly saturated at tissue PO₂. In the computed curves, normal hemoglobin releases about 21% of its O₂ between 100 and 40 mmHg, while the mutant releases only about 3%. High-affinity hemoglobin variants often cause compensatory polycythemia.

concept.t: P50 and what curve shifts mean
p: P50 is the partial pressure of O₂ at which a binding protein is 50% saturated. It is an inverse measure of affinity: low P50 = high affinity = curve shifted left; high P50 = low affinity = curve shifted right. Normal adult hemoglobin has a P50 of about 26 to 27 mmHg; myoglobin's is about 2 to 3 mmHg.

What matters physiologically is how much O₂ is released between lung PO₂ (about 100 mmHg) and tissue PO₂ (about 40 mmHg at rest, lower in exercise). A left-shifted protein loads well but unloads poorly; a right-shifted one unloads more but can load less completely if the shift is extreme. Normal hemoglobin balances the two.

MCAT questions give a P50 and ask about direction of shift, the cause (CO₂, H⁺, temperature, 2,3-BPG, HbF, CO) or the effect on O₂ delivery. Keep three ideas separate: affinity (P50), capacity (number of sites and amount of Hb) and cooperativity (curve steepness, Hill coefficient).

fx.w: Hill equation: Y is fractional saturation, P is PO₂ in mmHg, P50 is the PO₂ at Y = 0.5, and n is the Hill coefficient (about 2.8 for hemoglobin). At P = P50, Y = 0.5 exactly.

steps: Lower P50 (12 versus 26 mmHg) means 50% saturation at a lower PO₂, so affinity is higher (left shift).
Using the Hill equation with n = 2.8: normal Hb is about 98% saturated at 100 mmHg and 77% at 40 mmHg, so it releases about 21% of its O₂.
Mutant Hb is about 99.7% saturated at 100 mmHg and 97% at 40 mmHg, so it releases only about 3%.
Conclusion: tighter binding and much less unloading in tissues.
x1A_112.trap: Low P50 means HIGH affinity. Do not read a smaller number as weaker binding.

fig.cap: Hill-equation curves (n = 2.8) for normal hemoglobin (P50 26 mmHg) and the mutant (P50 12 mmHg). Between 100 and 40 mmHg the mutant releases about 3% of its O₂ versus 21% for normal.
fig.alt: Two sigmoidal O2 saturation curves; the red mutant curve lies left of the blue normal curve, crossing 50 percent at 12 versus 26 mmHg. A dotted line at 40 mmHg shows the mutant still near 97 percent saturated.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation, Y = Pⁿ/(P50ⁿ + Pⁿ), with standard textbook P50 and n values.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids

ox: Incorrect. Positive cooperativity, where binding at one site increases affinity at the others, gives a Hill coefficient greater than 1 and a sigmoidal curve. Hemoglobin is the classic example, with n ≈ 2.8. A value of exactly 1.0 shows no such effect.

Correct. The Hill coefficient (n) measures how strongly binding at one site affects binding at the others. When n = 1, each site binds independently of whether the others are occupied, and the binding curve is a simple hyperbola, like myoglobin's. This is true whether the protein has one site or several independent sites.

Incorrect. Negative cooperativity, where binding at one site lowers the affinity of the remaining sites, gives a Hill coefficient less than 1 and a curve that rises quickly at first and then flattens more than a hyperbola. A coefficient of exactly 1.0 rules it out.

Incorrect. The Hill coefficient is not a count of binding sites. A protein with four independent sites still has n = 1, and hemoglobin has four sites but n ≈ 2.8. The maximum possible n equals the number of sites (perfect cooperativity), but n itself measures interaction, not number.

p: The Hill equation, Y = [L]ⁿ/(K + [L]ⁿ), describes the fraction of sites occupied (Y) as a function of ligand concentration. The exponent n, the Hill coefficient, is read from the slope of a Hill plot and summarizes cooperativity: n > 1 positive, n = 1 none, n < 1 negative.

Positive cooperativity produces a sigmoidal curve, which acts like a switch: a small change in ligand concentration near the midpoint causes a large change in occupancy. That is what lets hemoglobin load O₂ in the lungs and unload it in tissues. With n = 1 the curve is hyperbolic, the same shape as Michaelis–Menten kinetics for a simple enzyme.

Remember that n is bounded by the number of sites but is not equal to it: hemoglobin (4 sites) has n ≈ 2.8. Allosteric enzymes such as aspartate transcarbamoylase show similar sigmoidal kinetics, and the MCAT may ask you to identify cooperativity from a curve's shape.

x1A_113.trap: n = 1 means no cooperativity, not one binding site.

fig.cap: Three binding curves with the same P50 (26) computed from the Hill equation with n = 2.8, 1 and 0.5. Only n = 1 gives a simple hyperbola.
fig.alt: Graph of saturation against PO2 with three curves crossing at 50 percent and 26 mmHg: a sigmoidal blue curve for n = 2.8, a hyperbolic green curve for n = 1, and a flatter orange curve for n = 0.5. A note says n is not the number of sites.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation with P50 = 26 and n = 2.8, 1 and 0.5.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids

ox: Incorrect. CO binds the ferrous (Fe²⁺) iron of heme, the same form that binds O₂; it does not oxidize iron. Oxidation to Fe³⁺ produces methemoglobin, which is caused by agents such as nitrites or certain drugs, not by CO. Methemoglobin also left-shifts the remaining hemes, which is why the two are often confused.

Correct. CO binds heme about 200 to 250 times more tightly than O₂, so it occupies sites and cuts carrying capacity. On top of that, CO-bound hemes push the tetramer toward the high-affinity R state, so the hemes still carrying O₂ hold it more tightly and the curve shifts left. In the computed comparison, blood with half its hemes lost (as in anemia) still releases about 10% of normal capacity between 100 and 40 mmHg, but blood with 50% carboxyhemoglobin releases only about 4%.

Incorrect. CO does not break hemoglobin into subunits; carboxyhemoglobin remains an α₂β₂ tetramer. In fact, the problem depends on the tetramer staying intact, because the cooperative interactions between subunits are what transmit the high-affinity state from the CO-bound hemes to the O₂-bound ones.

Incorrect. Lower affinity at the remaining hemes would shift their curve right and make them release O₂ more easily, which would partly compensate for the lost sites. That is the opposite of what happens: CO increases the affinity of the remaining hemes, which is why CO poisoning is worse than an anemia of the same size.

p: Carbon monoxide binds the Fe²⁺ of heme at the same site as O₂ but with about 200 to 250 times higher affinity, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb). This harms O₂ delivery in two ways. First, each CO-occupied heme cannot carry O₂, reducing capacity. Second, through cooperativity, CO binding stabilizes the R state, raising the O₂ affinity of the remaining hemes and shifting their curve left, so they release less O₂ at tissue PO₂.

This is why a person with 50% COHb is far more impaired than a person with anemia that halves hemoglobin: the anemic person's remaining hemoglobin still unloads normally. Pulse oximeters also misread COHb as oxyhemoglobin, and arterial PO₂ is normal because dissolved O₂ is unaffected. Treatment is 100% or hyperbaric O₂, which competes CO off the heme faster.

Do not confuse CO poisoning with methemoglobinemia (iron oxidized to Fe³⁺, which cannot bind O₂) or with cyanide poisoning (which blocks cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria). The MCAT uses CO as a clear example of how cooperativity affects delivery.

x1A_114.trap: CO does two things: it takes up sites AND left-shifts the remaining hemes, so they unload less.

fig.cap: O₂ content curves: normal blood, blood with half the Hb (normal shape), and blood with 50% COHb, whose remaining hemes are left-shifted (illustrative P50 12 mmHg, n 1.8). From 100 to 40 mmHg they release about 21, 10 and 4 units.
fig.alt: Graph of O2 content as percent of normal capacity against PO2. The normal curve rises to about 98; a dashed anemia curve rises sigmoidally to about 49; the CO curve reaches about 45 already at 40 mmHg and flattens near 49, so it releases very little between 100 and 40 mmHg.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation (normal: P50 26 mmHg, n 2.8; 50% COHb modeled with illustrative P50 12 mmHg, n 1.8 for the remaining hemes).

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 22.5 Transport of Gases

ox: Incorrect. The constant region of the heavy chains, especially the Fc stem, is the same for all antibodies of a class. It does not bind antigen; it determines the antibody's class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD) and binds Fc receptors on phagocytes and the complement protein C1q. It decides what happens after antigen is bound, not what is bound.

Incorrect. The hinge is the flexible stretch of heavy chain between the Fab arms and the Fc stem, held together by interchain disulfide bonds. Its flexibility lets the two arms reach epitopes at different distances, but it contains no antigen-binding surface.

Incorrect. The light-chain constant region (CL) is one of two constant types (κ or λ) and is the same across many different antibodies. A region that does not change from antibody to antibody cannot provide the specificity needed to recognize millions of different antigens. It helps form the Fab arm but does not contact antigen.

Correct. The antigen-binding site sits at the tip of each Fab arm and is built from the variable domains of one heavy chain (VH) and one light chain (VL) together. Each variable domain has three hypervariable loops, the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), so six loops form the binding surface that fits a specific epitope. VDJ recombination and somatic hypermutation create the sequence diversity in these regions.

p: An IgG antibody is a Y-shaped tetramer of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains joined by disulfide bonds. Each arm (Fab, fragment antigen-binding) contains a whole light chain and the first part of a heavy chain. The stem (Fc, fragment crystallizable) is formed by the remaining constant domains of the two heavy chains.

The N-terminal variable domains (VH and VL) at the tips differ among antibodies and together form two identical antigen-binding sites per IgG. Diversity comes from VDJ gene rearrangement in developing B cells, imprecise joining and later somatic hypermutation. The constant regions are shared within a class and determine function: the Fc binds Fc receptors on macrophages, neutrophils and NK cells, and activates complement.

MCAT points: variable = specificity, constant = effector function and class; class switching changes the heavy-chain constant region but keeps the same variable region, so specificity is unchanged. IgM is a pentamer, IgA can be a dimer in secretions, and IgG is the only class that crosses the placenta.

x1A_115.trap: Variable regions of BOTH heavy and light chains form the binding site; constant regions set the effector function.

fig.cap: IgG schematic. The variable domains of the heavy and light chains (green) at each arm tip form the antigen-binding sites; the hinge and Fc are constant heavy-chain regions.
fig.alt: Y-shaped antibody with two heavy chains in blue forming the stem and inner arms, two light chains in orange on the outer arms, green variable regions at all four arm tips with red antigens bound, and black disulfide bonds at the hinge and between heavy and light chains. Labels identify variable regions, constant regions, hinge and Fc.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Opsonization means coating a target to make it easier to eat (from the Greek for preparing food). IgG binds the bacterium by its variable regions, leaving the Fc tails pointing outward. Macrophages and neutrophils carry Fc receptors that grip those tails, which triggers phagocytosis. Complement fragment C3b is the other major opsonin.

Incorrect. Neutralization happens when antibodies bind the parts of a virus or toxin that it uses to attach to host cells, blocking entry or toxic action. It works even without phagocytes. It is an important antibody function, for example against tetanus toxin, but the stem describes enhanced engulfment, which is opsonization.

Incorrect. Agglutination is the clumping of antigen-bearing particles because each antibody (especially the ten-armed IgM pentamer) binds two or more cells at once. Clumping can make clearance easier and is the basis of blood typing, but the defining feature here is phagocytes recognizing bound antibody, not cross-linking.

Incorrect. Class switching (isotype switching) is a genetic change inside an activated B cell that swaps its heavy-chain constant region, for example from IgM to IgG or IgE, while keeping the same variable region and specificity. It changes which antibody is made; it is not something antibodies do to a bacterium.

p: Once an antibody binds antigen, its effect depends on what the Fc region recruits and how many targets it binds. Neutralization: antibodies block a pathogen's or toxin's binding sites. Agglutination: multivalent antibodies cross-link particles into clumps. Opsonization: bound antibodies are recognized by Fc receptors on phagocytes, which engulf the target. Complement activation: IgM and IgG trigger the classical pathway, leading to C3b opsonization and the membrane attack complex.
Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) is related: NK cells bind the Fc of IgG on an infected cell and kill it. IgE bound to mast cells triggers degranulation in allergy.

MCAT questions usually describe a result and ask for the term. Coat to eat = opsonization; block binding = neutralization; clump = agglutination. Class switching and affinity maturation are B-cell processes that change the antibody, not actions of the antibody.

x1A_116.trap: Opsonization means coating for phagocytosis; neutralization means blocking; agglutination means clumping.

fig.cap: Three things bound antibodies do. In opsonization (green), the exposed Fc tails are gripped by macrophage Fc receptors, triggering engulfment.
fig.alt: Three panels: neutralization shows antibodies surrounding a virus so it cannot attach to a host cell membrane; agglutination shows antibodies bridging four bacteria into a clump; opsonization shows a bacterium coated with antibodies whose Fc tails face an engulfing macrophage. A note explains class switching.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. A voltage-gated ion channel opens in response to a change in membrane potential, using charged segments in its transmembrane helices as a voltage sensor. It needs no ligand. The nicotinic receptor opens when acetylcholine binds, regardless of voltage, so it does not fit this class, although its opening causes depolarization that then opens nearby voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.

Incorrect. G protein-coupled receptors are single polypeptides with seven transmembrane helices that activate heterotrimeric G proteins; they contain no ion pore. The muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1 to M5) are GPCRs, which is the source of this distractor, but the nicotinic receptor is a channel. GPCR responses are slower because they go through G proteins and second messengers.

Correct. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a pentamer of subunits arranged around a central pore. When two acetylcholine molecules bind sites on the extracellular domain, the protein changes shape and the pore opens within about a millisecond, letting Na⁺ in (and some K⁺ out). Because the ligand directly gates the channel, it is a ligand-gated ion channel (ionotropic receptor), like GABA-A and NMDA receptors.

Incorrect. Receptor tyrosine kinases, such as the insulin and EGF receptors, are single-pass receptors whose cytoplasmic domains phosphorylate tyrosines after ligand-induced dimerization. They signal through recruited proteins and kinase cascades, not by forming a pore, so they cannot let cations flow directly.

p: Cell-surface receptors fall into a few classes by how they transduce a signal. Ligand-gated ion channels (ionotropic receptors) are both receptor and pore: ligand binding opens the channel directly, giving millisecond responses. G protein-coupled receptors (metabotropic) have seven transmembrane helices and activate G proteins, which regulate enzymes and second messengers. Enzyme-linked receptors, such as receptor tyrosine kinases, have catalytic cytoplasmic domains.

Voltage-gated channels are not receptors for ligands; they open when membrane potential changes. Intracellular receptors (for steroid and thyroid hormones) bind lipid-soluble ligands inside the cell and act as transcription factors.

Acetylcholine is the MCAT's favorite example of one ligand with two receptor types: nicotinic receptors (ligand-gated channels at the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia) and muscarinic receptors (GPCRs at parasympathetic targets such as the heart and glands).

x1A_117.trap: Nicotinic = ion channel; muscarinic = GPCR. Same ligand, different receptor classes.

fig.cap: Four ways membrane proteins respond to signals. Only the ligand-gated channel, such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, is both receptor and pore.
fig.alt: Membrane schematic with four panels: a ligand-gated channel with two acetylcholine molecules bound and ions flowing through its pore; a closed voltage-gated channel; a seven-helix GPCR with a G protein underneath; and a receptor tyrosine kinase dimer with phosphorylated tails. Tags mark the ligand-gated channel as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.1 Signaling Molecules and Cellular Receptors

ox: Incorrect. Integrins are α/β heterodimers that mainly bind extracellular matrix proteins such as fibronectin, laminin and collagen, linking them to the actin cytoskeleton inside the cell. Some integrins bind cell-surface ligands (such as ICAM-1), but they bind a different molecule, not an identical integrin. They depend on divalent cations like Mg²⁺ and Mn²⁺, which can make this choice tempting.

Incorrect. Selectins are lectins: their binding domain recognizes specific carbohydrate groups (such as sialyl-Lewis X) on glycoproteins of another cell. Their binding is Ca²⁺-dependent, which makes this a strong distractor, but they bind sugars, not identical selectin molecules. They mediate the brief rolling contacts of white blood cells on vessel walls.

Incorrect. Aquaporins are channel proteins that let water cross membranes rapidly, for example in kidney collecting ducts under the control of ADH. They do not bind neighboring cells at all, so they are not adhesion molecules of any kind.

Correct. Cadherins (calcium-dependent adherins) bind identical cadherins on the neighboring cell, which is homophilic, like-to-like binding. Ca²⁺ ions bound between their extracellular domains make them rigid enough to bind; removing Ca²⁺ with a chelator such as EDTA makes cells come apart. Inside, cadherins link through catenins to actin in adherens junctions, and desmosomal cadherins link to intermediate filaments. E-cadherin loss helps cancer cells become invasive.

p: Four families of cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) appear on the MCAT. Cadherins: Ca²⁺-dependent, homophilic cell–cell adhesion in adherens junctions and desmosomes. Integrins: α/β heterodimers that bind the extracellular matrix (and some cell ligands) and connect to the actin cytoskeleton, with signaling in both directions. Selectins: Ca²⁺-dependent lectins that bind carbohydrates and mediate transient adhesion of leukocytes to endothelium. Immunoglobulin-superfamily CAMs (such as ICAM-1 and NCAM): Ca²⁺-independent.

A good way to sort them is by partner: same molecule (cadherin), matrix (integrin), sugar (selectin). Junction proteins are a separate topic: tight junctions (claudins, occludins) seal spaces between cells, and gap junctions (connexins) form channels between cytoplasms.
Experimental clue: if cells dissociate when Ca²⁺ is removed and re-aggregate only with cells of their own type, the molecules involved are cadherins.

x1A_118.trap: Selectins also need Ca²⁺, but they bind sugars; only cadherins bind identical cadherins.

fig.cap: Adhesion molecules sorted by partner. Cadherins (green) bind identical cadherins on the neighboring cell and need bound Ca²⁺ (orange dots).
fig.alt: Two cells side by side above an extracellular matrix layer. Between the cells: a gap-junction connexon pair, green cadherin rods from each cell meeting in the middle with calcium ions, and a selectin binding sugar ligands on the second cell. An integrin connects the first cell to the matrix and to actin. Tags mark cadherins as correct and integrins, selectins and aquaporins as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.6 Connections between Cells and Cellular Activities

ox: Incorrect. Cadherins connect cells to other cells by homophilic binding (cadherin to cadherin), and their cytoplasmic tails do link to actin through catenins. But they bind identical molecules on a neighboring cell, not extracellular matrix proteins such as fibronectin.

Incorrect. Selectins bind carbohydrate groups on other cells and mediate brief, low-affinity contacts, such as leukocytes rolling along endothelium. They do not bind fibronectin and are not the main mechanical link between the matrix and the cytoskeleton.

Correct. Integrins are transmembrane heterodimers of an α and a β subunit. Their extracellular heads bind matrix proteins such as fibronectin (often at its RGD sequence), laminin and collagen, and their cytoplasmic tails connect through talin, vinculin and other adaptors to actin filaments at focal adhesions. They signal in both directions: outside-in (matrix binding activates kinases such as FAK) and inside-out (signals inside the cell switch integrins to a high-affinity state).

Incorrect. Connexins assemble into connexons, which pair across two adjacent cells to form gap junction channels. These let ions and small molecules pass directly between cytoplasms, for example to spread electrical excitation through heart muscle. They do not bind the extracellular matrix.

concept.t: Integrins: linking the matrix to the cytoskeleton
p: Integrins are the main receptors cells use to attach to the extracellular matrix (ECM). Each is an α/β heterodimer; different combinations bind fibronectin, laminin, collagen or vitronectin, often recognizing short motifs such as Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD). Inside the cell, adaptor proteins connect integrins to actin at focal adhesions, or to intermediate filaments in hemidesmosomes.

Integrins are also signaling receptors. Binding to the matrix activates intracellular kinases that control survival, growth and migration (outside-in signaling), and signals inside the cell can activate integrins (inside-out signaling), as when leukocyte integrins switch on to bind ICAM-1 on endothelium during inflammation. Platelet integrin αIIbβ3 binds fibrinogen during clotting.
Sort adhesion molecules by partner: cadherins bind cadherins (cell–cell, Ca²⁺), integrins bind matrix, selectins bind sugars, connexins form channels.

fig.cap: Adhesion molecules sorted by partner. Integrins (green) span the membrane, binding matrix proteins outside and actin inside.
fig.alt: Two cells above an extracellular matrix layer. A green integrin pair crosses the bottom membrane of the first cell into the matrix, connected to actin inside. Between the cells are cadherins, a selectin and a gap junction made of connexins. Tags mark integrins as correct and cadherins, selectins and connexins as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.6 Connections between Cells and Cellular Activities

ox: Incorrect. Cadherins hold cells of the same tissue together through homophilic, protein-to-protein binding in adherens junctions and desmosomes. They do not bind carbohydrate ligands, and leukocytes circulating in blood do not use them to tether to endothelium.

Correct. Selectins are carbohydrate-binding proteins (lectins). E- and P-selectin appear on inflamed endothelium, and L-selectin is on leukocytes; they bind sialylated carbohydrate groups such as sialyl-Lewis X on glycoproteins of the other cell. These bonds form and break quickly under the force of blood flow, so the leukocyte tumbles slowly along the wall instead of sticking, giving it time to sense chemokines.

Incorrect. Integrins (such as LFA-1 on leukocytes) mediate the next step, firm arrest. Chemokines activate them by inside-out signaling, and they then bind protein ligands such as ICAM-1 on endothelium tightly enough to stop the cell. They bind proteins, not carbohydrates, so they do not explain rolling.

Incorrect. Collagens are structural proteins of the extracellular matrix, including the basement membrane beneath endothelium. They are not receptors on the surface of leukocytes or endothelial cells and do not mediate the rolling interaction in flowing blood.

p: To reach infected tissue, white blood cells leave the blood in a sequence of steps. Rolling: selectins bind carbohydrate ligands with fast on and off rates, so the cell slows and rolls along the endothelium. Activation: chemokines presented on the endothelium bind leukocyte GPCRs and switch on integrins. Firm arrest: activated integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1) bind ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on endothelium. Transmigration (diapedesis): the leukocyte squeezes between endothelial cells into the tissue.

Each step uses a different adhesion family, matched to its job: weak, reversible lectin–sugar bonds for rolling; strong, regulated integrin–protein bonds for stopping. Inflammatory signals such as histamine, TNF-α and IL-1 make the endothelium express selectins and ICAM-1.

Clinical link: leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I (missing β2 integrin) gives recurrent infections without pus, because leukocytes roll but cannot stop. On the MCAT, the word carbohydrate points to selectins.

x1A_120.trap: Rolling uses selectins binding sugars; stopping uses integrins binding proteins.

fig.cap: Steps of leukocyte extravasation. Rolling (step 1) depends on selectins binding sugar ligands; integrins act later in firm arrest.
fig.alt: A vessel wall with four leukocytes left to right: rolling on selectin tethers, activation by chemokines, flattened firm arrest via integrins and ICAM-1, and transmigration between endothelial cells. A box explains that selectins are lectins binding sialylated carbohydrates.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; steps as described in standard immunology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 21.2 Barrier Defenses and the Innate Immune Response

ox: Correct. Growth factors such as EGF, PDGF and insulin bind the extracellular domains of receptor tyrosine kinases and bring two receptor chains together (insulin's receptor is already a disulfide-linked dimer and is rearranged instead). Close together, each cytoplasmic kinase domain phosphorylates tyrosines on its partner (trans-autophosphorylation). The phosphotyrosines become docking sites for proteins with SH2 domains, such as Grb2, which links to Sos and Ras and then the MAP kinase cascade, or PI3K, which activates Akt.

Incorrect. Exchange of GDP for GTP on a heterotrimeric G protein is how G protein-coupled receptors signal: the ligand-bound seven-helix receptor acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for Gα. Receptor tyrosine kinases do activate a small GTPase, Ras, but indirectly, through Grb2 and Sos after autophosphorylation, and Ras is not a heterotrimeric G protein.

Incorrect. Opening a pore to let Na⁺ into the cell describes a ligand-gated ion channel, such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Receptor tyrosine kinases have a single transmembrane helix per chain and do not form a channel; they signal by enzymatic activity in the cytoplasm.

Incorrect. Receptors that move into the nucleus and act as transcription factors are intracellular receptors for lipid-soluble ligands, such as steroid and thyroid hormones. Receptor tyrosine kinases stay in the plasma membrane (or are internalized into endosomes); they change gene expression only indirectly, through kinase cascades that reach transcription factors.

p: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are single-pass membrane proteins with a ligand-binding extracellular domain and a tyrosine kinase domain inside the cell. Ligand binding causes dimerization (or a rearrangement of a pre-formed dimer). The two kinase domains then phosphorylate each other on tyrosine residues, which both activates the kinases fully and creates phosphotyrosine docking sites.

Proteins with SH2 or PTB domains bind those phosphotyrosines and pass the signal on: Grb2–Sos activates Ras, which starts the Raf → MEK → ERK (MAP kinase) cascade that drives cell division; PI3K makes PIP₃, which activates Akt for growth and survival; insulin receptor substrates (IRS) link the insulin receptor to glucose uptake.

On the MCAT, recognize RTKs by these keywords: growth factor, dimerization, autophosphorylation, tyrosine, Ras, MAP kinase. Mutations that keep an RTK or Ras switched on are classic oncogenes. Compare with GPCRs (seven helices, G proteins, second messengers) and ligand-gated channels (ion flow).

x1A_121.trap: RTKs dimerize and phosphorylate each other; GDP/GTP exchange on a trimeric G protein belongs to GPCRs.

fig.cap: Ligand binding brings two RTK chains together; each kinase domain phosphorylates its partner's tyrosines, and SH2-domain proteins dock on the phosphotyrosines.
fig.alt: Four stages across a membrane: two separate receptor monomers with a ligand above, a ligand-bound dimer, the dimer with phosphate groups on both cytoplasmic tails, and an SH2 protein docking on a phosphotyrosine with the downstream pathways Grb2-Sos-Ras-MAPK and PI3K-Akt listed. Tags mark dimerization and tyrosine phosphorylation as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Incorrect. GPCRs are not kinases for their G proteins. Some GPCRs are themselves phosphorylated by GPCR kinases (GRKs), which leads to desensitization by arrestin, but that is a shut-off mechanism. Tyrosine phosphorylation is the signature of receptor tyrosine kinases, a different receptor class.

Incorrect. GTP hydrolysis turns a G protein off, and it is done by Gα's own intrinsic GTPase activity (often sped up by RGS proteins), not by the receptor. If the receptor hydrolyzed GTP, it would be switching the G protein off rather than on.

Correct. When a ligand binds, the GPCR changes shape and acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF): it opens the Gα nucleotide pocket so that GDP leaves. Because GTP is far more abundant than GDP in the cytosol, GTP fills the pocket. GTP-bound Gα changes conformation, separates from Gβγ, and both can regulate effectors such as adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C until Gα hydrolyzes its GTP.

Incorrect. G protein activation is not proteolytic: the αβγ heterotrimer separates into Gα·GTP and Gβγ by a conformational change, and the parts reassociate after GTP hydrolysis, so the cycle can repeat many times. Proteolytic activation is how zymogens such as trypsinogen and protease-activated receptors work, not how G proteins work.

p: Heterotrimeric G proteins (Gα, Gβ, Gγ) are molecular switches. Off: Gα holds GDP and is bound to Gβγ. On: an activated GPCR acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, Gα releases GDP and binds GTP, then dissociates from Gβγ. Gα·GTP (and in some pathways Gβγ) regulates effectors. Off again: Gα hydrolyzes GTP to GDP with its own GTPase activity and rebinds Gβγ.

Signal duration depends on how long Gα keeps its GTP, so anything that blocks the GTPase (cholera toxin on Gαs) prolongs signaling, and anything that blocks activation (pertussis toxin on Gαi, which prevents coupling to the receptor) prevents it. One activated receptor can activate many G proteins, amplifying the signal.
Remember the vocabulary: GEF = turns on (swaps GDP for GTP); GAP or intrinsic GTPase = turns off. The same logic applies to small GTPases such as Ras, which are activated by GEFs like Sos.

x1A_122.trap: The receptor swaps GDP for GTP (GEF); Gα itself hydrolyzes GTP to turn off.

fig.cap: The G-protein cycle. The highlighted step is the ligand-bound receptor acting as an exchange factor: GDP leaves Gα and GTP enters.
fig.alt: Four boxes in a cycle: inactive Gα-GDP bound to Gβγ; ligand-bound receptor acting as GEF so GDP leaves and GTP enters (highlighted green); active Gα-GTP separated from Gβγ regulating an effector; Gα GTPase hydrolyzing GTP back to GDP. Tags mark GDP to GTP exchange as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.1 Signaling Molecules and Cellular Receptors

ox: Correct. Gαq·GTP activates phospholipase C-β, which cleaves the membrane lipid PIP₂ (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate) into two second messengers. IP₃ is water-soluble, diffuses to the ER and opens IP₃-gated Ca²⁺ channels, raising cytosolic Ca²⁺. DAG stays in the membrane and, together with Ca²⁺, activates protein kinase C. Examples include α₁-adrenergic and M1/M3 muscarinic receptors.

Incorrect. Activation of adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and activating protein kinase A, is the Gs pathway, used by β-adrenergic, glucagon and many other receptors. Gq does not act on adenylyl cyclase.

Incorrect. Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP, is the Gi pathway, used by α₂-adrenergic and M2 muscarinic receptors (Gi's βγ subunits also open K⁺ channels in the heart). It is the opposite of Gs, but it is still not the Gq pathway.

Incorrect. A ligand-gated Na⁺ channel is itself the receptor and opens directly when its ligand binds; no G protein is involved. Gq signals through an enzyme, phospholipase C, and its effects on ion channels are indirect, via Ca²⁺ and PKC.

p: The Gα subunit determines which effector a GPCR controls. Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase (ATP → cAMP → PKA). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (less cAMP). Gq stimulates phospholipase C-β, which cleaves PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER, and DAG plus Ca²⁺ activates PKC.

These second messengers amplify the signal and spread it through the cell. Ca²⁺ acts further through calmodulin, and cAMP is degraded by phosphodiesterase (which caffeine inhibits). Adrenergic receptors show all three: β (Gs), α₂ (Gi), α₁ (Gq). A popular memory aid is 'QISS and QIQ' for α₁ Gq, α₂ Gi, β₁ Gs, β₂ Gs; M1 Gq, M2 Gi, M3 Gq.
On the MCAT, a question naming IP₃, DAG, PIP₂, phospholipase C or Ca²⁺ release from the ER points to Gq; cAMP points to Gs or Gi.

x1A_123.trap: IP₃ and DAG come only from the Gq → phospholipase C branch; cAMP is the Gs/Gi branch.

fig.cap: The three classic Gα pathways. Gq (green) activates phospholipase C, which makes IP₃ (Ca²⁺ release) and DAG (PKC activation).
fig.alt: Three columns of flowchart boxes: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and PKA; Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP; Gq activates phospholipase C-beta, PIP2 is cleaved to IP3 and DAG, IP3 releases ER calcium, DAG and calcium activate PKC. Example receptors are listed under each.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Incorrect. Gαs stimulates adenylyl cyclase; it is Gαi that inhibits it. Cholera toxin locks Gαs in its active form, so the cyclase is stimulated more, not less, and cAMP rises. This choice confuses Gs with Gi; pertussis toxin is the toxin that affects Gi signaling.

Incorrect. Phospholipase C and IP₃ belong to the Gq pathway. Cholera toxin acts on Gαs, whose effector is adenylyl cyclase, so the second messenger that stays high is cAMP, not IP₃. IP₃ would matter for a toxin or drug acting on Gq-coupled receptors, such as α₁-adrenergic receptors.

Incorrect. The toxin does not touch the receptor at all. Its A subunit enters the cell and ADP-ribosylates Gαs itself. The receptor can still bind its ligand normally; the problem is that Gαs stays switched on even when no ligand is present.

Correct. Cholera toxin transfers an ADP-ribose group onto an arginine of Gαs, which disables its GTPase. Gαs therefore stays in the GTP-bound, active form and keeps stimulating adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP stays high. In intestinal epithelial cells, cAMP activates protein kinase A, which opens CFTR Cl⁻ channels; Cl⁻, Na⁺ and water flow into the gut lumen, causing the massive watery diarrhea of cholera.

p: Because a G protein's signal lasts as long as Gα holds GTP, blocking the GTPase is a way to lock the switch on. Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαs, preventing GTP hydrolysis, so adenylyl cyclase is continuously stimulated and cAMP stays high. In the small intestine, PKA phosphorylates and opens the CFTR chloride channel, and secretion of Cl⁻ followed by Na⁺ and water causes severe dehydration. Treatment is oral rehydration with glucose and salt, which uses the intact Na⁺-glucose cotransporter.

Pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαi so it cannot couple to its receptor; Gi can no longer inhibit adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP also rises, by a different route. Both toxins are examples of how blocking the off switch or blocking an inhibitor gives the same downstream result.
MCAT approach: identify which Gα is affected, which effector it controls, and whether the toxin locks it on or off; then predict the second messenger level.

x1A_124.trap: Blocking Gαs's GTPase keeps it ON, so cAMP rises; it does not shut the pathway down.

fig.cap: Cholera toxin blocks step 4 (Gα's GTPase), so Gαs·GTP stays active and cAMP stays high, driving CFTR Cl⁻ secretion.
fig.alt: G-protein cycle with the off-switch step crossed out in red and dashed. A box beneath traces the consequences: toxin ADP-ribosylates Gαs, no GTPase, adenylyl cyclase stays on, cAMP high, PKA opens CFTR, chloride, sodium and water enter the gut lumen. Tags mark cAMP staying high as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Incorrect. Myosin pulling on actin drives muscle contraction, cytokinesis and cell crawling, but the core of a cilium or flagellum, the axoneme, is built from microtubules, not actin. Actomyosin plays no role in axoneme bending.

Correct. The axoneme has nine outer microtubule doublets around a central pair (the 9 + 2 arrangement). Axonemal dynein arms anchored on one doublet walk along the neighboring doublet toward its minus end, using ATP. Because the doublets are tied together by nexin links and radial spokes, they cannot simply slide apart, so the sliding force is converted into bending. Alternating activity on opposite sides makes the cilium beat.

Incorrect. A rotary motor powered by a proton gradient describes the bacterial flagellum, which is a rigid helical filament of flagellin turned by a motor in the cell envelope. Eukaryotic cilia and flagella are completely different structures covered by the plasma membrane and powered by ATP hydrolysis by dynein.

Incorrect. Most kinesins walk toward microtubule plus ends, not minus ends, and kinesins move cargo rather than bend the axoneme. (Some kinesins in cilia carry material along the axoneme in intraflagellar transport, but they do not produce the bending.) The bending motor is axonemal dynein.

p: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella share a core called the axoneme: nine microtubule doublets around two central single microtubules (9 + 2), all covered by plasma membrane and anchored by a basal body (with 9 triplets, like a centriole). Dynein arms on each doublet use ATP to walk on the adjacent doublet; nexin links and radial spokes convert this sliding into bending.

Motile cilia move fluid across surfaces (mucus in the airway, the egg in the oviduct), and a flagellum propels a sperm cell. Defects in dynein arms cause primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome): chronic respiratory infections, male infertility, and in about half of patients situs inversus.

Contrast with prokaryotes: the bacterial flagellum is made of flagellin, sits outside the membrane, and rotates like a propeller driven by H⁺ flow. Also remember the motor-track pairs: dynein and kinesin on microtubules, myosin on actin.

x1A_125.trap: Eukaryotic flagella bend by dynein sliding microtubule doublets; only bacterial flagella rotate.

fig.cap: Left: the 9 + 2 axoneme with dynein arms (red) on each doublet. Right: dynein makes doublets slide, and because nexin links tie them together, sliding becomes bending.
fig.alt: Cross-section of an axoneme showing nine microtubule doublets in a ring, each with red dynein arms and gray radial spokes, and a central pair. On the right, two parallel doublets connected by dynein arms with an arrow for sliding, and below them a bent pair of doublets. A box notes that bacterial flagella are rotary motors.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Hemoglobin is the main protein inside red blood cells, not a dissolved plasma protein; free hemoglobin in plasma is normally almost zero, and when red cells break open the free hemoglobin is quickly bound by haptoglobin and cleared. It carries O₂ and CO₂, not fatty acids and drugs.

Correct. Albumin, made by the liver, is the most abundant plasma protein (about 3.5 to 5 g/dL, roughly 55 to 60% of plasma protein by mass). Because oncotic pressure depends on the number of dissolved particles that cannot cross the capillary wall, this abundant, relatively small protein supplies most (about 75 to 80%) of plasma oncotic pressure. It also has binding sites, many of them hydrophobic pockets, that carry fatty acids, bilirubin, thyroid hormone and many drugs, and it binds much of the protein-bound Ca²⁺. Low albumin (liver disease, malnutrition, kidney loss) causes edema.

Incorrect. Fibrinogen is a clotting protein that thrombin converts into fibrin. It is present at only about 0.2 to 0.4 g/dL, far less than albumin, so it contributes little to oncotic pressure. Serum is plasma with fibrinogen and other clotting factors removed.

Incorrect. Immunoglobulin G is the most abundant antibody (about 1 g/dL) and part of the globulin fraction. It provides immunity, crosses the placenta and opsonizes pathogens, but it is present at a few times lower concentration than albumin and is not a general carrier of fatty acids and drugs.

p: Plasma contains about 6 to 8 g/dL of protein: albumin (the largest share), globulins (α, β and γ; the γ-globulins are antibodies) and fibrinogen. Most are made by the liver, except immunoglobulins, which are made by plasma cells.

Oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure is the osmotic pressure due to proteins that cannot easily cross capillary walls. It pulls fluid back into capillaries and opposes hydrostatic pressure in the Starling balance. Because osmotic pressure depends on the number of particles, the most abundant plasma protein, albumin, provides most of it. When albumin falls, fluid leaks into tissues and edema results.

Albumin is also the main plasma carrier for hydrophobic and charged substances: free fatty acids, unconjugated bilirubin, some hormones, Ca²⁺ and many drugs. Drug binding to albumin matters in pharmacology because only the unbound fraction is active.

x1A_126.trap: Oncotic pressure tracks particle number, so the most abundant plasma protein, albumin, dominates.

fig.cap: Typical plasma concentrations: albumin about 4.2 g/dL, IgG about 1.1, fibrinogen about 0.3, and free hemoglobin near zero.
