fig.alt: Horizontal bar chart of typical plasma protein concentrations: albumin 4.2 g/dL in green with a note that it supplies 75 to 80 percent of oncotic pressure and is a carrier; immunoglobulin G 1.1, fibrinogen 0.3 and free hemoglobin about zero in red with notes on their roles.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest chart; mid-range adult reference values from standard physiology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 18.1 An Overview of Blood

ox: Incorrect. Ca²⁺ is removed from the cytosol by separate transporters: the plasma-membrane Ca²⁺-ATPase (PMCA), the SERCA pump into the ER or SR, and the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger. Calmodulin is a small soluble protein with no transmembrane segments and cannot pump ions, although Ca²⁺-calmodulin does activate PMCA.

Incorrect. Calmodulin has no catalytic activity of its own. It activates kinases such as CaM kinase II and myosin light-chain kinase, which then do the phosphorylating. Treating the adaptor as the enzyme is the error here.

Incorrect. Using GTP hydrolysis as a timer is the mechanism of G proteins (heterotrimeric Gα and small GTPases like Ras). Calmodulin binds no nucleotide; its on and off states are set simply by whether Ca²⁺ is bound, which tracks the cytosolic Ca²⁺ concentration.

Correct. Calmodulin has four EF-hand Ca²⁺-binding sites. When cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises from about 0.1 μM to about 1 μM, the sites fill and calmodulin changes shape, exposing hydrophobic surfaces that wrap around target proteins. Ca²⁺-calmodulin then activates enzymes such as CaM kinase II, myosin light-chain kinase in smooth muscle, calcineurin and phosphodiesterase. When Ca²⁺ is pumped away, calmodulin releases Ca²⁺ and lets go of its targets.

p: Ca²⁺ is a second messenger: cytosolic levels are kept very low (about 10⁻⁷ M) by pumps, and signals open channels in the plasma membrane or ER (for example via IP₃) to raise it briefly. Cells read this signal with Ca²⁺-binding proteins, the most widespread being calmodulin, a small protein with four EF-hand motifs.

Binding Ca²⁺ changes calmodulin's conformation so it can bind and activate dozens of targets. This is a general mechanism of allosteric regulation by a regulatory protein. In smooth muscle, Ca²⁺-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase to start contraction. In neurons, CaM kinase II contributes to synaptic plasticity. Troponin C, which triggers skeletal muscle contraction, is a close structural relative.
Keep the parts of the system straight: channels and IP₃ raise Ca²⁺; calmodulin senses it; kinases and phosphatases act; pumps remove Ca²⁺ and end the signal.

x1A_127.trap: Calmodulin is a Ca²⁺-activated adaptor that switches on enzymes; it is not itself a pump, kinase or GTPase.

fig.cap: A Ca²⁺ rise fills calmodulin's four EF hands; the shape change lets it bind and activate target enzymes. Pumps lower Ca²⁺ to switch it off.
fig.alt: Flowchart: a signal raises cytosolic calcium from about 0.1 to 1 micromolar; apo-calmodulin binds four calcium ions and changes shape; calcium-calmodulin activates targets such as CaM kinase II, myosin light-chain kinase, calcineurin and phosphodiesterase. A side box describes pumps switching it off. Tags mark the adaptor role as correct and pump, kinase and GTP roles as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.2 Propagation of the Signal

ox: Correct. The rate of a reaction depends on the fraction of molecules with enough energy to reach the transition state, which falls off exponentially with the activation energy (Ea). An enzyme's active site binds the transition state more tightly than the substrate, using H-bonds, ionic contacts, acid–base groups and proximity, so the transition state's energy drops. With a lower barrier, many more molecules react per second, often 10⁶ to 10¹⁷ times more.

Incorrect. ΔG is the difference in free energy between products and reactants, a state function that depends only on the starting and ending states. An enzyme does not change either state, so it cannot make ΔG more negative and cannot make an unfavorable reaction favorable; it can only couple it to a favorable one, such as ATP hydrolysis.

Incorrect. Enzymes are catalysts, not heat sources; they work at the constant temperature of the cell. Raising temperature would speed reactions, but it is not how enzymes act, and high temperature would denature most enzymes.

Incorrect. A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so the equilibrium constant and the equilibrium position stay the same. Enzymes only help a reaction reach equilibrium sooner. Shifting the equilibrium would require changing ΔG°, which catalysts do not do.

p: Every reaction must pass through a high-energy transition state, and the height of that barrier above the reactants is the activation energy (Ea). By the Arrhenius relation, rate ∝ e^(−Ea/RT), so even a modest drop in Ea gives a huge increase in rate. Enzymes provide an alternative pathway with a lower barrier, chiefly by binding and stabilizing the transition state.

Strategies include proximity and orientation of substrates, general acid–base catalysis, covalent catalysis (as with the serine of serine proteases), metal ion catalysis and strain or induced fit that favors the transition state geometry.

What enzymes do not change: ΔG, ΔH, Keq, the equilibrium position and the final amounts of products. They are not consumed. The MCAT often pairs this with a reaction-coordinate diagram: the catalyzed curve has a lower peak but the same start and end heights.

x1A_128.trap: Enzymes change the height of the hill (Ea), never the difference between the valleys (ΔG).

fig.cap: Reaction-coordinate diagram (illustrative values). The enzyme lowers Ea from 100 to 60 kJ/mol, while reactants and products, and so ΔG (−30 kJ/mol), stay the same.
fig.alt: Free energy against reaction progress: a red uncatalyzed curve peaking at 100 and a lower green enzyme-catalyzed curve peaking at 60, both starting at 0 and ending at −30. Arrows mark each activation energy and the unchanged ΔG.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; curves drawn to scale from the stated illustrative energies.

ox: Incorrect. Forming more product would mean a new equilibrium ratio [B]/[A], which requires a different equilibrium constant. Keq depends only on ΔG° (ΔG° = −RT ln Keq) and temperature, and a catalyst changes neither. The enzyme speeds product formation and product breakdown equally, so there is no net change.

Incorrect. Forming more reactant would also mean a new equilibrium ratio, just shifted the other way. Catalysts favor neither direction. This distractor tempts students who think the enzyme might drive the reverse reaction at equilibrium, but it accelerates both directions by the same factor.

Correct. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are already equal. An enzyme lowers the activation energy for both directions by the same amount, because both pass through the same transition state, so both rates increase by the same factor and remain equal. The concentrations of reactants and products therefore stay the same. All the enzyme can do is make a system that is not yet at equilibrium get there faster.

Incorrect. Equilibrium is dynamic: molecules keep converting in both directions at equal rates, so the reaction never stops, it only shows no net change. Adding an enzyme makes the forward and reverse conversions faster, not slower, but the concentrations still do not change.

p: The equilibrium constant is set by thermodynamics: ΔG° = −RT ln Keq. A catalyst changes the pathway (kinetics) but not the energies of the reactants and products (thermodynamics), so Keq and the equilibrium concentrations are unchanged. Because the forward and reverse reactions share a transition state, lowering its energy speeds both by the same factor, keeping kforward/kreverse = Keq.

In a reaction mixture that starts away from equilibrium, an enzyme simply shortens the time needed to reach the same final ratio. In a mixture already at equilibrium, adding an enzyme produces no change in concentrations.

In cells, many reactions are kept away from equilibrium by constant supply and removal of metabolites, so enzymes appear to drive them in one direction. That directionality comes from concentrations and coupling (ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q), not from the enzyme.

x1A_129.trap: A catalyst can never push a system past equilibrium; at equilibrium it changes nothing.

fig.cap: A ⇌ B with Keq = 3, computed from first-order rate laws. With or without enzyme (rates ×100), the product fraction settles at 0.75; adding enzyme at equilibrium changes nothing.
fig.alt: Graph of fraction as product B against time from 0 to 400 minutes. The green curve with enzyme jumps to 0.75 almost immediately; the red uncatalyzed curve rises gradually to the same 0.75 plateau. An arrow at 300 minutes marks enzyme being added at equilibrium with no change.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from reversible first-order kinetics with kf = 0.02 per min and kr = 0.0067 per min (enzyme: both ×100).

ox: Incorrect. Active sites evolved to be most complementary to the transition state, not to the substrate, so a molecule that mimics the transition state fits better, not worse. Weaker binding would be expected for a molecule that resembled neither substrate nor transition state.

Incorrect. If the enzyme bound the transition state no more tightly than the substrate, it would lower the energy of both equally and the activation barrier would not change, so there would be no catalysis. Preferential binding of the transition state is exactly what makes catalysis possible.

Incorrect. A transition-state analog mimics the species that forms in the active site during the reaction, so it binds the active site and acts as a competitive inhibitor. Allosteric sites bind regulators that are generally unrelated in structure to the substrate or the transition state.

Correct. An enzyme lowers the activation energy because its active site binds the transition state far more tightly than the substrate (Pauling's principle). A stable compound shaped like the transition state can make all those favorable contacts without reacting, so it binds much more tightly than the substrate, often by many orders of magnitude. That is why transition-state analogs are potent competitive inhibitors and useful drugs, such as oseltamivir and many HIV protease inhibitors.

p: Enzymes catalyze reactions by binding the transition state more strongly than the substrate. If an enzyme bound the substrate too tightly, the substrate would sink into a deep energy well and the barrier from there would be higher. Instead, active sites are shaped and charged to complement the transition state, for example an oxyanion hole that stabilizes the negative charge of a tetrahedral intermediate in proteases.

Transition states exist for only about the time of one bond vibration (around 10⁻¹³ s) and cannot be isolated. Chemists design stable mimics, such as phosphonates that copy a tetrahedral carbon. These transition-state analogs bind tightly to the active site and act as competitive inhibitors. Catalytic antibodies (abzymes) raised against such analogs can even catalyze the corresponding reaction.
On the MCAT, connect three ideas: lowered Ea, tighter transition-state binding, and competitive inhibition by analogs (which raise apparent Km but leave Vmax unchanged).

x1A_130.trap: Enzymes bind the transition state best, so its stable mimic binds more tightly than the substrate.

fig.cap: Cartoon of shape complementarity. The active site fits the transition state best; a stable analog of that shape makes the same contacts and binds more tightly than the substrate.
fig.alt: Three panels with the same V-shaped enzyme pocket: a flat substrate bar touching only the pocket edges, an orange V-shaped transition state filling the pocket with four contact dots, and a green V-shaped stable analog filling the pocket with the same contacts. Tags mark tighter binding as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Emil Fischer's lock-and-key model (1894) pictures a rigid active site whose shape already matches the substrate exactly, like a key fitting a lock. It explains specificity but predicts no change in the enzyme's shape on binding, so crystal structures showing the active site reshaping contradict it rather than support it.

Incorrect. The concerted (MWC, symmetry) model describes allosteric proteins with several subunits, such as hemoglobin or aspartate transcarbamoylase, in which all subunits switch together between T and R states. It concerns cooperativity between sites, not how a single active site changes shape to fit its substrate.

Correct. Daniel Koshland's induced-fit model (1958) proposes that the active site is flexible and that substrate binding causes a conformational change that brings catalytic groups into position and wraps the site around the substrate. Crystal structures with and without substrate, such as hexokinase closing its two lobes around glucose, show exactly this. The closed form also excludes water and helps stabilize the transition state.

Incorrect. The fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972) describes biological membranes as a fluid lipid bilayer with proteins floating in it. It is a membrane model, not a model of enzyme–substrate binding, and says nothing about active-site shape.

concept.t: Lock and key versus induced fit
p: Two classic models describe how substrates bind enzymes. Lock and key: the active site is rigid and pre-shaped to fit the substrate. Induced fit: the active site is flexible, and binding of the correct substrate induces a conformational change that creates the best fit and positions catalytic residues. Modern structural data strongly support induced fit (and the related idea of conformational selection) for most enzymes.

Induced fit helps explain specificity: a molecule that binds but does not trigger the right shape change is not converted. Hexokinase is the textbook example; its cleft closes around glucose, which shields the reaction from water so ATP's phosphate goes to glucose and is not simply hydrolyzed.

Do not confuse these binding models with the concerted (MWC) and sequential (KNF) models of allostery, which explain cooperativity among subunits. Koshland also proposed the sequential model, which is a frequent source of mix-ups.

x1A_131.trap: A shape change on substrate binding means induced fit; lock and key assumes a rigid, pre-formed site.

fig.cap: Lock and key (top): a rigid site already matches. Induced fit (bottom): binding reshapes the site, which closes around the substrate.
fig.alt: Two rows of cartoons. Top: a rectangular pocket in a blue enzyme accepts an orange substrate with no change in shape. Bottom: a wide green pocket narrows and its rim closes around the substrate after binding. Tags mark induced fit as correct and the lock and key, concerted and fluid mosaic models as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Lyases (EC 4) break or form bonds without hydrolysis, redox chemistry or ATP, often forming or adding to a double bond or ring. Examples include aldolase and decarboxylases. Some lyases join molecules in reverse (synthases), but they do not couple the joining to ATP hydrolysis; the similar-sounding name is the trap.

Correct. Ligases (EC 6) join two molecules into one by forming a new bond (C–O, C–S, C–N, C–C or a phosphodiester) and pay for it by hydrolyzing ATP or another nucleoside triphosphate. DNA ligase seals nicks in DNA, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach amino acids to tRNAs, and pyruvate carboxylase joins CO₂ to pyruvate. Many ligases are named synthetases, which signals that a nucleoside triphosphate is used.

Incorrect. Hydrolases (EC 3) do the opposite kind of chemistry: they split one molecule into two by adding water across a bond. Proteases, lipases, nucleases and phosphatases are hydrolases. They do not join molecules or need ATP.

Incorrect. Isomerases (EC 5) rearrange atoms within a single molecule to form an isomer, as triose phosphate isomerase converts DHAP to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. They take one substrate and give one product with the same formula, so they cannot join two molecules.

p: Enzymes are classified by the reaction they catalyze. 1 Oxidoreductases transfer electrons (dehydrogenases, oxidases, reductases). 2 Transferases move a functional group from one molecule to another (kinases move phosphate, transaminases move amino groups). 3 Hydrolases split bonds by adding water. 4 Lyases break or form bonds without hydrolysis or redox, often making or adding across a double bond. 5 Isomerases rearrange a molecule. 6 Ligases join two molecules using energy from ATP. (A seventh class, translocases, which move ions or molecules across membranes, was added in 2018.)

Watch the names: synthetase (uses a nucleoside triphosphate) usually means ligase, while synthase (no NTP needed) often means lyase. Kinase means transferase, even though it uses ATP, because ATP is the group donor, not an energy source for joining.

On the MCAT, classify by asking: Is water added (hydrolase)? Do electrons move (oxidoreductase)? Does a group move between molecules (transferase)? Are two molecules joined with ATP (ligase)? Is one molecule rearranged (isomerase)? Otherwise, a non-hydrolytic split or addition is a lyase.

x1A_132.trap: Joining two molecules with ATP = ligase; using ATP as a phosphate donor = transferase (kinase).

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes by reaction type. Ligases (green) join two molecules using ATP; the three distractor classes are shown in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes with their reaction types and examples. Ligases are highlighted green with the description join two molecules using ATP; hydrolases, lyases and isomerases are highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Correct. Hexokinase moves the terminal (γ) phosphate group from ATP to the 6-OH of glucose, making glucose-6-phosphate and ADP. Moving a functional group from a donor molecule to an acceptor molecule is the definition of a transferase (EC 2). All kinases are transferases (subclass EC 2.7, phosphotransferases), even though they consume ATP.

Incorrect. Ligases join two molecules into one and use ATP hydrolysis as the energy source for the new bond, as DNA ligase does. Hexokinase does not join glucose to ATP; it takes a phosphate group from ATP and transfers it to glucose. Using ATP is not enough to make an enzyme a ligase.

Incorrect. Hydrolases add water across a bond to split it. If ATP were simply hydrolyzed, the phosphate would go to water and give ADP + Pi; hexokinase's closed active site actually excludes water so the phosphate goes to glucose instead. No bond is split by water here.

Incorrect. Oxidoreductases move electrons, often as a hydride to or from NAD⁺ or FAD. In the hexokinase reaction the oxidation states of the carbons in glucose do not change, and no electron carrier is involved; only a phosphoryl group is moved.

p: A transferase moves a functional group (phosphate, amino, methyl, acyl or glycosyl) from one molecule to another. Kinases are the most common example: they transfer the γ-phosphate of ATP to an acceptor such as glucose (hexokinase), fructose-6-phosphate (phosphofructokinase-1) or a protein's serine, threonine or tyrosine (protein kinases).

The opposite reaction, removing a phosphate by hydrolysis, is done by phosphatases, which are hydrolases. Phosphorylases add inorganic phosphate (not water) across a bond, as glycogen phosphorylase does, and are also transferases.

The trap on the MCAT is the word ATP. Ask what happens to the atoms: if a group moves from ATP to another molecule, it is a transferase; if ATP hydrolysis powers the joining of two separate molecules, it is a ligase.

x1A_133.trap: Kinases use ATP but are transferases: they move a phosphate group, they do not join two molecules.

fig.cap: Hexokinase moves the γ-phosphate of ATP onto glucose's 6-OH, giving glucose-6-phosphate (phosphate shaded) and ADP: a group transfer.
fig.alt: Glucose plus ATP converted by hexokinase to glucose-6-phosphate plus ADP, with the phosphate group of the product highlighted. A green box explains that a group moves from one molecule to another, defining a transferase. Tags mark transferase as correct and ligase, hydrolase and oxidoreductase as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes, with transferases highlighted as correct and the three distractor classes in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes; transferases highlighted green with examples kinases and transaminases; oxidoreductases, hydrolases and ligases highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Incorrect. Hydrolases split bonds by adding water, with the –H going to one fragment and the –OH to the other. Aldolase adds no water: fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (C₆H₁₄O₁₂P₂) splits into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (each C₃H₇O₆P), and the two products add up to exactly the original formula.

Incorrect. Oxidoreductases move electrons between substrates, usually with NAD⁺, NADP⁺ or FAD. In the aldolase reaction no electron carrier is used and the products together are at the same overall oxidation level as the substrate; it is a retro-aldol cleavage, not a redox step.

Correct. Lyases (EC 4) break (or form) bonds by means other than hydrolysis or oxidation, often creating a double bond or a new carbonyl. Aldolase cleaves the C3–C4 bond of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate by a retro-aldol reaction, giving two three-carbon sugars. Like many lyases, it is reversible: in gluconeogenesis the same enzyme joins the two trioses, still without ATP.

Incorrect. Ligases join two molecules and use ATP to do it. Aldolase splits one molecule into two, and even when it runs in reverse to join trioses it uses no ATP, so it is not a ligase. A ligase example is pyruvate carboxylase, which joins CO₂ to pyruvate while hydrolyzing ATP.

p: A lyase breaks a bond without hydrolysis and without oxidation, or forms one by adding a group to a double bond. Typical lyase reactions are aldol cleavage (aldolase), decarboxylation (pyruvate decarboxylase), dehydration (fumarase and enolase run as hydratases or dehydratases) and adding groups to double bonds. Enzymes called synthases (no ATP needed) are often lyases running in the synthetic direction, though the name alone does not settle the class.

Aldolase in glycolysis: fructose-1,6-bisphosphate → dihydroxyacetone phosphate + glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Mass balance is the quickest check: the two products together have the same formula as the substrate, so no water was added (not a hydrolase) and no hydrogens moved to a carrier (not an oxidoreductase).
MCAT strategy: compare formulas. Added H₂O → hydrolase. Gain or loss of H₂ equivalents with NAD(P)H or FADH₂ → oxidoreductase. Same atoms, one molecule → two (or reverse) without ATP → lyase.

x1A_134.trap: Splitting a molecule does not mean hydrolysis; check whether water is actually added.

fig.cap: Aldolase cleaves the C3–C4 bond (shaded) of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate with no water, redox or ATP: a lyase reaction.
fig.alt: Open-chain fructose-1,6-bisphosphate with carbons 3 and 4 highlighted, converted by aldolase into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. A green box states no water added, no electrons transferred, no ATP used. Tags mark lyase as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes, with lyases highlighted as correct and the three distractor classes in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes; lyases highlighted green with examples aldolase and decarboxylases; oxidoreductases, hydrolases and ligases highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Correct. Lactate dehydrogenase transfers a hydride ion (H⁻, carrying two electrons) from NADH to the ketone carbon of pyruvate, and a proton from solution goes to the oxygen. Pyruvate is reduced to lactate, and NADH is oxidized to NAD⁺. Any enzyme that catalyzes electron transfer between substrates is an oxidoreductase (EC 1), and every dehydrogenase belongs to this class.

Incorrect. A transferase moves a functional group such as phosphate, amino, methyl or acyl from one molecule to another. Although NADH donates a hydride, that is a transfer of electrons, which defines an oxidoreductase. No functional group of the kind transferases move is passed between pyruvate and another molecule.

Incorrect. Isomerases interconvert isomers, molecules with the same formula. Pyruvate (C₃H₃O₃⁻) and lactate (C₃H₅O₃⁻) differ by two hydrogens, so they are not isomers, and the change in hydrogen count is itself a sign of reduction.

Incorrect. Lyases break bonds without water or redox, often forming a double bond, or add groups across double bonds. In the LDH reaction no carbon skeleton bond is broken; the C=O of pyruvate is reduced to an alcohol, C–OH, by adding hydrogen with electrons from NADH.

p: Oxidoreductases catalyze oxidation–reduction reactions, in which electrons move from one molecule to another, often as a hydride (H⁻) or as hydrogen atoms. They use electron-carrier coenzymes: NAD⁺/NADH and NADP⁺/NADPH (from niacin) and FAD/FADH₂ and FMN (from riboflavin). Subtypes include dehydrogenases, oxidases (using O₂), reductases, peroxidases and oxygenases.

Lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH in anaerobic conditions so glycolysis (which needs NAD⁺ at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step) can keep making ATP. In exercising muscle this produces lactate, which the liver can turn back into glucose (the Cori cycle).

Quick redox check: a carbon gaining H or losing O is reduced; a carbon losing H or gaining O is oxidized. Look for NAD⁺, NADH, FAD or 'dehydrogenase' in a question: these all point to oxidoreductases.

x1A_135.trap: Moving electrons (hydride) is oxidoreduction, not a group transfer; all dehydrogenases are oxidoreductases.

fig.cap: LDH: NADH gives a hydride to pyruvate's ketone carbon (shaded), reducing it to L-lactate (shaded C–OH) and oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺.
fig.alt: Pyruvate plus NADH and H+ converted by lactate dehydrogenase into L-lactate plus NAD+, with the ketone of pyruvate and the alcohol carbon of lactate highlighted. A green box explains the hydride transfer and that lactate has two more hydrogens than pyruvate. Tags mark oxidoreductase as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; structures drawn with RDKit from SMILES.

fig.cap: The six enzyme classes, with oxidoreductases highlighted as correct and the three distractor classes in red.
fig.alt: Table of six enzyme classes; oxidoreductases highlighted green with examples dehydrogenases and oxidases; transferases, lyases and isomerases highlighted red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; enzyme classes per the IUBMB Enzyme Commission scheme.

ox: Incorrect. Coenzymes are the organic subset of cofactors: small carbon-based molecules, often made from vitamins, such as NAD⁺, FAD, coenzyme A and PLP. Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are inorganic ions, so they are cofactors but not coenzymes. Many students use the two words interchangeably; the MCAT does not.

Incorrect. Substrates are the molecules an enzyme converts into products, and they are consumed in the reaction. Metal ions such as Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase or Mg²⁺ bound to ATP in kinases are regenerated unchanged at the end of each cycle, so they are helpers, not substrates.

Incorrect. Zymogens (proenzymes) are inactive precursor forms of enzymes, such as pepsinogen, trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen, that are activated by cleavage of part of the chain. They are whole proteins, not small ions that enzymes need for activity.

Correct. A cofactor is any non-protein chemical component an enzyme needs for activity. Cofactors are either inorganic (metal ions such as Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺ and Mn²⁺) or organic (coenzymes). Mg²⁺ commonly binds ATP and helps orient and shield its phosphates; Zn²⁺ acts as a Lewis acid in carbonic anhydrase and in many proteases.

p: Many enzymes need a non-protein helper for activity, called a cofactor. Cofactors split into two chemical groups: inorganic metal ions (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu⁺/Cu²⁺, Mn²⁺, Mo, Se) and organic molecules called coenzymes, most of which come from water-soluble vitamins (NAD⁺ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, TPP from thiamine, PLP from B₆, CoA from pantothenate).

Metal ions help catalysis by binding and orienting substrates, stabilizing negative charges, acting as Lewis acids to make water a better nucleophile, and carrying electrons (iron and copper in redox enzymes). Coenzymes usually carry groups or electrons, such as hydride (NADH), acyl groups (CoA) or carboxyl groups (biotin).

Vocabulary to keep separate: apoenzyme (protein without its cofactor, inactive) + cofactor = holoenzyme (active). Prosthetic group = a tightly or covalently bound cofactor. Cosubstrate = a loosely bound coenzyme that leaves after each reaction. Zymogen = inactive precursor activated by cleavage.

x1A_136.trap: All coenzymes are cofactors, but metal ions are cofactors that are NOT coenzymes.

fig.cap: Cofactors sorted by chemistry and by binding. Metal ions such as Mg²⁺ and Zn²⁺ are inorganic cofactors; coenzymes are the organic ones.
fig.alt: Diagram: apoenzyme plus cofactor gives holoenzyme. Cofactors are sorted by chemistry into inorganic metal ions (highlighted) and organic coenzymes, and by binding into cosubstrates and prosthetic groups. A glossary defines substrate, zymogen and coenzyme. Tags mark cofactors as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Riboflavin (vitamin B₂) is the precursor of FAD and FMN, the flavin coenzymes used by enzymes such as succinate dehydrogenase and in the electron transport chain. FAD and NAD⁺ are both electron carriers, which makes this a tempting mix-up, but riboflavin does not supply NAD⁺.

Correct. Niacin (vitamin B₃, nicotinic acid or nicotinamide) provides the nicotinamide ring of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺; the name NAD itself stands for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide. That ring is the part that accepts a hydride ion when NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH. Niacin can also be made in small amounts from tryptophan. Severe deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia).

Incorrect. Thiamine (vitamin B₁) is made into thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), the coenzyme for decarboxylating α-keto acids in pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and for transketolase. Thiamine-dependent enzymes often work alongside NAD⁺, but thiamine is not part of it. Deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome.

Incorrect. Vitamin C (ascorbate) is not a precursor of any coenzyme in the usual sense; it acts directly as a reducing agent, for example keeping the iron of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in the Fe²⁺ state during collagen synthesis. It is not part of NAD⁺.

p: Most water-soluble B vitamins are converted into coenzymes: B₁ thiamine → TPP (decarboxylations); B₂ riboflavin → FAD and FMN (redox); B₃ niacin → NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ (redox, hydride transfer); B₅ pantothenate → coenzyme A (acyl carrier); B₆ pyridoxine → PLP (amino acid metabolism, transamination); B₇ biotin → carboxylase cofactor; B₉ folate → tetrahydrofolate (one-carbon units); B₁₂ cobalamin → methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin.

This is why vitamins are needed only in small amounts: coenzymes are recycled, not consumed. NAD⁺ picks up a hydride to become NADH in catabolic reactions and is regenerated by the electron transport chain or by fermentation.
MCAT tip: the name often reveals the source. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide → niacin. Flavin adenine dinucleotide → riboflavin. Thiamine pyrophosphate → thiamine. Pyridoxal phosphate → pyridoxine.

x1A_137.trap: NAD⁺ = nicotinamide = niacin (B₃); FAD comes from riboflavin (B₂). Both carry electrons, so they are easy to swap.

fig.cap: Water-soluble vitamins and their coenzymes. Niacin (B₃) is the source of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺; the three distractor vitamins are shown in red.
fig.alt: Table listing vitamins B1 thiamine to TPP, B2 riboflavin to FAD and FMN, B3 niacin to NAD+ and NADP+ (highlighted green), B5 pantothenate to coenzyme A, B6 pyridoxine to PLP, B7 biotin, B9 folate to THF, and vitamin C used directly; thiamine, riboflavin and ascorbate rows are red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; vitamin-coenzyme pairs from standard biochemistry texts.

ox: Incorrect. A cosubstrate is a coenzyme that binds loosely, is chemically changed during the reaction and then leaves, to be regenerated by another enzyme. NAD⁺ in most dehydrogenases and coenzyme A are typical. The stem describes the opposite: a cofactor that stays bound throughout.

Correct. A prosthetic group is a cofactor that is tightly bound, often covalently, and remains attached to the enzyme throughout the catalytic cycle, being restored to its original state before the next round. Examples include heme in cytochromes and catalase, FAD covalently attached in succinate dehydrogenase, biotin linked to a lysine in carboxylases, and PLP held as a Schiff base in transaminases.

Incorrect. An apoenzyme is the protein part of an enzyme without its required cofactor, and it is inactive. It is the enzyme that lacks the helper, not the helper itself. Apoenzyme plus cofactor (or prosthetic group) gives the active holoenzyme.

Incorrect. Allosteric effectors are molecules that bind a regulatory site distinct from the active site and raise or lower enzyme activity, such as ATP and AMP on phosphofructokinase-1. They regulate the enzyme and come and go with their concentration; they are not groups that the catalytic chemistry depends on.

p: Cofactors can be grouped by how they bind. Prosthetic groups are tightly or covalently bound and stay with the enzyme; any chemical change they undergo is reversed within the same catalytic cycle. Cosubstrates (sometimes called loosely bound coenzymes) bind like substrates, are changed, and dissociate, so they are regenerated elsewhere, for example NADH being reoxidized by the electron transport chain.

Prosthetic groups can be organic (heme, FAD in some flavoproteins, biotin, lipoate, PLP) or inorganic (tightly bound metal ions such as Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase). Proteins that carry prosthetic groups include hemoglobin and myoglobin (heme), which shows that the term also applies to non-enzyme proteins.

Vocabulary chain: apoenzyme (inactive protein) + cofactor → holoenzyme (active). Cofactor (any non-protein helper) includes metal ions and coenzymes (organic); by binding strength, a cofactor is either a prosthetic group (tight) or a cosubstrate (loose).

x1A_138.trap: Tight or covalent and stays = prosthetic group; loose and leaves each cycle = cosubstrate.

fig.cap: Cofactors sorted by chemistry and by binding. A prosthetic group (green) is tightly or covalently bound and stays; a cosubstrate binds loosely and leaves.
fig.alt: Diagram: apoenzyme plus cofactor gives holoenzyme; cofactors sorted into metal ions and coenzymes by chemistry and into cosubstrates and prosthetic groups by binding, with the prosthetic group box highlighted. A glossary defines apoenzyme and allosteric effector. Tags mark prosthetic group as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. A holoenzyme is the complete, active enzyme: the protein together with all of its required cofactors. It is the opposite of the form described in the stem. A useful memory hook is holo = whole.

Incorrect. A ribozyme is a catalytic RNA molecule, such as the peptidyl transferase center of the large ribosomal subunit, RNase P or self-splicing introns. Ribozymes are defined by being made of RNA, not by lacking a cofactor (many ribozymes in fact need Mg²⁺).

Incorrect. Isozymes (isoenzymes) are different protein forms, often encoded by different genes, that catalyze the same reaction but differ in kinetics, regulation or tissue location, such as the LDH isozymes or hexokinase versus glucokinase. They are active enzymes, not cofactor-free ones.

Correct. An apoenzyme is the protein portion of an enzyme that lacks a required cofactor (a metal ion or coenzyme), so it is catalytically inactive. When the cofactor binds, the complete, active form is called the holoenzyme: apoenzyme + cofactor → holoenzyme. For example, removing Zn²⁺ from carbonic anhydrase with a chelator leaves the inactive apoenzyme.

p: Enzymes that need a cofactor exist in two forms. The apoenzyme is the protein alone, without its cofactor, and is inactive. The holoenzyme is the apoenzyme plus its bound cofactor, and is active. The cofactor can be a metal ion or an organic coenzyme, and if it is tightly bound it is called a prosthetic group.

Other commonly confused terms: zymogen (proenzyme), an inactive precursor activated by cleavage, such as trypsinogen; ribozyme, a catalytic RNA; isozymes, different proteins catalyzing the same reaction; allosteric enzyme, one whose activity is regulated by effectors binding a separate site. In molecular biology, holoenzyme also describes complete multi-subunit enzymes such as RNA polymerase holoenzyme (core plus σ factor).
Apoenzymes appear on the MCAT in experiments: dialysis or a chelator removes a cofactor and activity drops; adding the cofactor back restores it, showing the cofactor is required.

x1A_139.trap: Apo = protein alone (inactive); holo = whole enzyme with cofactor (active).

fig.cap: Apoenzyme (green) + cofactor → holoenzyme. The glossary defines holoenzyme, ribozyme and isozyme, the three distractors.
fig.alt: Diagram showing apoenzyme (protein only, inactive, highlighted) plus cofactor gives holoenzyme (complete and active), with cofactor categories below and a glossary of holoenzyme, ribozyme and isozyme. Tags mark apoenzyme as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Correct. Thiamine (vitamin B₁) is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP). In the E1 subunit of pyruvate dehydrogenase, TPP's thiazolium ring forms a carbanion that attacks pyruvate's carbonyl carbon, allowing CO₂ to be removed. Without enough thiamine, pyruvate cannot be converted to acetyl-CoA efficiently, so pyruvate and lactate build up and energy production from glucose falls, which especially harms the brain (Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome) and heart (wet beriberi).

Incorrect. Biotin (B₇) is the prosthetic group of carboxylases, enzymes that add CO₂, such as pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → oxaloacetate) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase. It is used to attach CO₂, the opposite of the decarboxylation performed by pyruvate dehydrogenase, and is not needed by that complex.

Incorrect. Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), from vitamin B₆, is the coenzyme of transaminases, many amino acid decarboxylases and glycogen phosphorylase. It forms Schiff bases with amino groups. It is not a coenzyme of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

Incorrect. Tetrahydrofolate (THF), from folate (B₉), carries one-carbon units (methyl, methylene, formyl) for nucleotide synthesis and amino acid metabolism. Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects, not a block of pyruvate dehydrogenase.

concept.t: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its coenzymes
p: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle: pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH. It is a large complex of three enzymes using five coenzymes: TPP (from thiamine, B₁), lipoic acid, coenzyme A (from pantothenate, B₅), FAD (from riboflavin, B₂) and NAD⁺ (from niacin, B₃). A common memory aid is 'Tender Loving Care For Nancy'.

TPP performs the decarboxylation step. The same TPP-dependent chemistry is used by α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase in the citric acid cycle and by transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway, which is why thiamine deficiency affects many pathways and why red-cell transketolase activity is used to test thiamine status.

Thiamine deficiency (common with chronic alcohol use and malnutrition) causes beriberi and Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome. Clinically, thiamine is given before glucose in such patients, because a glucose load increases demand on these thiamine-dependent enzymes.

x1A_140.trap: Decarboxylation of α-keto acids needs TPP (B₁); carboxylation needs biotin (B₇).

fig.cap: Water-soluble vitamins and their coenzymes. Thiamine (B₁) → TPP, used by pyruvate dehydrogenase; the three distractor coenzymes come from B₆, B₇ and B₉.
fig.alt: Table listing vitamins and coenzymes with the B1 thiamine to TPP row highlighted green and used by pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase; the B6 pyridoxine to PLP, B7 biotin and B9 folate to THF rows are red.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest table; vitamin-coenzyme pairs from standard biochemistry texts.

ox: Incorrect. The covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate is formed by serine 195: its side-chain oxygen attacks the substrate's carbonyl carbon and becomes ester-linked to the acyl part of the substrate. Histidine makes this possible by activating serine, but histidine itself never forms the covalent bond with substrate.

Incorrect. Substrate specificity comes from the S1 pocket, a cleft next to the active site that holds the side chain of the residue just before the bond to be cut. Its shape and charge differ among trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase, while the catalytic His is the same in all three, so His cannot be what selects the side chain.

Correct. Histidine 57 acts as a general base: its imidazole nitrogen pulls the proton off serine 195's hydroxyl as serine attacks, turning the weakly nucleophilic –OH into a strongly nucleophilic alkoxide-like oxygen. Aspartate 102 hydrogen-bonds to the other ring nitrogen, holding His in the right orientation and stabilizing its positive charge. Later in the cycle, protonated His acts as a general acid, giving the proton to the departing amine.

Incorrect. Serine proteases hydrolyze peptide bonds; they do not perform redox chemistry. Reducing disulfides requires a reducing agent or a thiol-disulfide oxidoreductase such as thioredoxin or protein disulfide isomerase. The catalytic triad contains no cysteine to swap disulfides.

p: Serine proteases (chymotrypsin, trypsin, elastase, thrombin) use three active-site residues, Ser195, His57 and Asp102, that lie far apart in sequence but meet in the folded enzyme. Asp positions His; His acts as a general base to remove the Ser hydroxyl proton; the activated Ser oxygen attacks the substrate's carbonyl carbon (covalent catalysis), forming a tetrahedral intermediate whose negative oxygen is stabilized in the oxyanion hole by backbone N–H groups.

The intermediate collapses, the amine half of the substrate leaves (protonated by His acting as a general acid) and an acyl-enzyme remains. Water, activated by His in the same way, then hydrolyzes the acyl-enzyme to release the carboxylic acid half and regenerate free Ser.

This one mechanism illustrates several catalytic strategies the MCAT names: general acid–base catalysis (His), covalent catalysis (Ser), transition-state stabilization (oxyanion hole) and specificity through binding pockets (S1). Organophosphates such as DIFP and sarin block the reactive serine irreversibly.

x1A_141.trap: Serine makes the covalent bond; histidine is the general base that activates it.

fig.cap: Asp102 positions His57, which pulls the proton from Ser195 so its oxygen can attack the substrate's C=O. The table lists each part's job.
fig.alt: Schematic of aspartate 102 hydrogen-bonded to the imidazole ring of histidine 57, which is hydrogen-bonded to the hydroxyl of serine 195, with curved arrows showing histidine taking serine's proton and serine's oxygen attacking the substrate carbonyl. A table lists the roles of histidine, serine, aspartate, oxyanion hole and S1 pocket, with histidine highlighted as the general base.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; mechanism as in standard biochemistry texts (chymotrypsin numbering).

x1A_141.eli: Histidine is the proton handler: it pulls the proton off serine so serine can attack the substrate.
mem: Histidine pKa ≈ 6.0: the only side chain near physiological pH, so it can pick up or give protons.
Serine protease triad: Ser (nucleophile), His (general base), Asp (orients His).
Order: S-H-D.
x1A_141.sc: 'General base taking a proton' + histidine = the triad's His.
x1A_141.mn: Ser-His-Asp: 'SHeD the proton': Serine attacks, Histidine moves the proton, aspartate holds it steady.

ox: Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes hydration, CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺, in which carbon stays at the +4 oxidation state. Reducing CO₂ to formate (HCOO⁻, carbon +2) would require an electron donor and is done by entirely different enzymes, such as formate dehydrogenase run in reverse.

Incorrect. A catalyst must be regenerated at the end of each cycle. After Zn–OH⁻ attacks CO₂, the bicarbonate formed is displaced by a new water molecule and released. A permanent covalent bond to product would leave the enzyme stuck after one turnover, which is the behavior of an irreversible inhibitor, not a catalyst.

Incorrect. No catalyst changes the equilibrium constant. Keq depends only on ΔG° for CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺, which the enzyme does not alter. Carbonic anhydrase speeds both directions equally, which is why it can both make bicarbonate in tissues and release CO₂ in the lungs.

Correct. Zn²⁺, held by three histidines, is a Lewis acid. It withdraws electron density from the bound water, lowering that water's pKa from about 14 to 16 for free water to about 7. At physiological pH a large fraction is therefore zinc-bound hydroxide, a much stronger nucleophile than water, ready to attack the carbon of CO₂ to make HCO₃⁻. The released proton is shuttled out by His64. This is metal ion catalysis, and it makes carbonic anhydrase one of the fastest enzymes known.

concept.t: Metal ion catalysis in carbonic anhydrase
p: Metal ions help catalysis in several ways: as Lewis acids that polarize bonds or activate water, by shielding or stabilizing negative charges, by holding substrates in position, and by carrying electrons in redox enzymes. Zinc is a classic example because it is a strong Lewis acid that does not undergo redox reactions in cells.

In carbonic anhydrase, Zn²⁺ lowers the pKa of its bound water to about 7, generating Zn–OH⁻ at neutral pH. The hydroxide attacks CO₂ to form bicarbonate, water displaces bicarbonate, and a histidine shuttle removes the proton to regenerate Zn–OH⁻. The enzyme converts up to about 10⁶ CO₂ molecules per second.

Physiology link: in red blood cells, carbonic anhydrase converts CO₂ to HCO₃⁻ for transport in plasma (the chloride shift) and reverses it in the lungs. It also acidifies gastric juice and renal fluid. Inhibitors such as acetazolamide are used for glaucoma and altitude sickness.

x1A_142.trap: The metal makes water a better nucleophile; it never changes Keq or the product.

fig.cap: Zn²⁺ (held by three histidines) binds water, lowers its pKa to about 7 so it loses H⁺, and the resulting Zn–OH⁻ attacks CO₂ to give HCO₃⁻, which is then released.
fig.alt: Three panels of a zinc ion coordinated by three histidines: with bound water, with bound hydroxide (highlighted), and with bound bicarbonate. A box explains that zinc is a Lewis acid that turns water into a hydroxide nucleophile. Tags mark the zinc-hydroxide nucleophile as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; mechanism as in standard biochemistry texts.

ox: Incorrect. How exergonic a reaction is (ΔG) depends only on the free energies of reactants and products, and an enzyme changes neither. Holding substrates together lowers the activation barrier for the reaction step, not the overall ΔG.

Incorrect. Enzymes do not supply heat; they work at the cell's temperature. Any heat released by binding spreads into the solvent and does not drive the reaction. The rate increase comes from changing the pathway (the transition-state free energy), not from adding thermal energy.

Correct. For two free molecules to react, they must meet in solution and line up their reactive groups in exactly the right orientation, which means losing a great deal of translational and rotational freedom. That large loss of entropy makes the uncatalyzed transition state costly. When an enzyme binds both substrates side by side in the right pose, binding energy pays that entropy cost in advance, so the remaining barrier is much lower. The effect is like raising the effective concentration of each reactant enormously.

Incorrect. A catalyst is regenerated unchanged at the end of the reaction. If the substrates were permanently fused to the enzyme, it could act only once, which describes an irreversible inhibitor or suicide substrate. In proximity catalysis the products are released and the enzyme binds the next substrates.

p: The activation free energy has enthalpy and entropy parts: ΔG‡ = ΔH‡ − TΔS‡. For a reaction between two molecules, a big part of the barrier is entropic: two independently moving molecules must come together and adopt one precise orientation. Enzymes bind substrates next to each other, correctly oriented, and use favorable binding interactions to pay that entropy cost.

This proximity and orientation effect can speed reactions enormously, which is often described as raising the effective molarity of the reacting groups. It works alongside other strategies: general acid–base catalysis, covalent catalysis, metal ion catalysis and preferential binding of the transition state.

As with every catalytic strategy, ΔG, ΔH of the overall reaction and Keq are not changed. MCAT questions may ask you to name a catalytic strategy from a description: holding two substrates together = proximity and orientation (an entropy effect).

x1A_143.trap: Proximity lowers the activation barrier by reducing entropy loss; it does not change ΔG.

fig.cap: In solution, reactants A and B rarely meet in the right orientation. In the active site, they are held side by side with their reactive groups (red) aligned, so the entropy cost is paid by binding.
fig.alt: Left panel: scattered A and B molecules with red reactive bars pointing in random directions. Right panel: an enzyme pocket holding A and B together with their reactive bars touching. A box explains ΔG‡ = ΔH‡ − TΔS‡ and the entropy cost. Tags mark lower entropy cost as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

ox: Incorrect. Trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase share the same catalytic triad (Ser195, His57, Asp102) and the same nucleophile, serine. That shared machinery is exactly why their different specificities must come from somewhere else: the binding pocket next to the active site.

Correct. The residue on the N-terminal side of the bond to be cut (P1) slots into the enzyme's S1 pocket. In chymotrypsin that pocket is deep and lined with nonpolar groups, with a serine (Ser189) at the bottom, so large hydrophobic aromatic side chains such as Phe, Tyr and Trp fit best. Trypsin's pocket has a negatively charged Asp189 at the bottom and selects Lys and Arg; elastase's pocket is partly blocked by Val and Thr side chains and accepts only small residues such as Ala and Gly.

Incorrect. Phenylalanine's side chain is a benzyl group, which is nonpolar and uncharged at every pH. A positively charged side chain (Lys or Arg) is what trypsin selects, through ionic attraction to Asp189. Chymotrypsin prefers Phe precisely because it is large and hydrophobic.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds in a substrate protein are not what chymotrypsin recognizes. Specificity depends on the side chain of the residue just before the scissile bond fitting the S1 pocket. Disulfides in chymotrypsin itself help hold its structure, but they play no part in choosing where it cuts.

concept.t: Protease specificity and the S1 pocket
p: Proteases cut specific peptide bonds. In the serine protease family, the catalytic machinery is identical, but each enzyme has a different S1 pocket that binds the side chain of the residue on the N-terminal side of the bond to be cleaved. Chymotrypsin: deep, hydrophobic, prefers aromatic residues (Phe, Tyr, Trp). Trypsin: deep with Asp189 at the bottom, prefers Lys and Arg. Elastase: shallow, prefers small neutral residues (Ala, Gly, Val).

This is a clear example of how binding interactions (hydrophobic, ionic, steric) produce specificity, while catalytic residues produce rate. Swapping a few pocket residues can change a protease's preference without touching its triad.

On the MCAT this appears in protein sequencing and peptide-mapping questions: trypsin cuts on the C-terminal side of Lys and Arg, chymotrypsin on the C-terminal side of Phe, Tyr and Trp (and less so Leu), and cyanogen bromide (a chemical, not an enzyme) cuts after Met.

x1A_144.trap: Catalysis comes from the shared triad; specificity comes from the S1 pocket's shape and charge.

fig.cap: Three serine proteases with the same triad but different S1 pockets. Chymotrypsin's deep hydrophobic pocket fits an aromatic side chain such as Phe.
fig.alt: Three panels: chymotrypsin with a deep pocket holding a phenylalanine ring (highlighted), trypsin with a deep pocket holding a lysine with Asp189 at the bottom, and elastase with a shallow pocket holding alanine. Tags mark the hydrophobic S1 pocket as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; pocket features from standard biochemistry texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.7 Chemical Digestion and Absorption: A Closer Look

ox: Correct. The stomach lumen is strongly acidic (about pH 1.5 to 3.5) because parietal cells secrete HCl. Enzymes that work there, such as pepsin, have evolved charge and structure that are stable and active at low pH; pepsin is activated from pepsinogen by acid and has its optimum near pH 2. Its two catalytic aspartates need one protonated and one deprotonated form, which happens near this pH.

Incorrect. pH 7.4 is the pH of blood and most extracellular fluid, the environment of enzymes such as plasma clotting factors. A stomach enzyme at pH 7.4 would be largely inactive; pepsin is in fact irreversibly denatured near neutral pH, which is one way its action stops when food moves into the duodenum.

Incorrect. A pH near 8 is the optimum for pancreatic enzymes such as trypsin, chymotrypsin and pancreatic lipase, which work in the small intestine after bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes stomach acid. It is the right answer for an intestinal enzyme, not a gastric one.

Incorrect. No digestive compartment is as basic as pH 11. At that pH most proteins would denature, and side chains such as lysine and tyrosine would begin to lose protons, disrupting structure. Enzyme pH optima generally match the compartment where they function.

p: Every enzyme has an optimal pH where it is most active. pH affects activity by changing the ionization of catalytic residues (for example, a His that must be neutral to act as a base) and of residues that hold the structure together through salt bridges. Far from the optimum, activity falls, and extreme pH can denature the enzyme.

pH optima usually match the compartment: pepsin about 2 (stomach), salivary amylase about 7, trypsin and pancreatic lipase about 8 (small intestine), lysosomal acid hydrolases about 4.5 to 5, most cytosolic enzymes about 7.2. Lysosomal enzymes being acid-dependent protects the cytosol if a lysosome leaks.

MCAT questions often show a bell-shaped activity versus pH curve and ask where an enzyme works, or which residue's pKa explains an edge of the curve. The model curves here are computed from two ionizable groups per enzyme.

x1A_145.trap: Match the enzyme to its compartment: stomach ≈ 2, blood ≈ 7.4, small intestine ≈ 8.

fig.cap: Model pH–activity curves for a pepsin-like stomach enzyme (peak near 2) and a trypsin-like intestinal enzyme (peak near 8), with the four answer pH values marked.
fig.alt: Graph of relative activity against pH from 0 to 12. A green curve peaks at pH 2 and a blue curve peaks at pH 8. Dotted lines mark pH 2 (stomach, correct), 7.4 (blood), 8 (small intestine) and 11 (no such compartment).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from a two-pKa ionization model (illustrative pKa 1.0 and 3.0 for the stomach enzyme, 6.5 and 9.5 for the intestinal enzyme).

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.7 Chemical Digestion and Absorption: A Closer Look

ox: Correct. Two effects compete. As temperature rises, molecules move faster and a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy to cross the activation barrier, so the rate rises, roughly doubling per 10 °C for many enzymes. But the enzyme's folded shape is held by weak interactions; above a certain temperature it unfolds (denatures) cooperatively, and the active site is lost. The optimum is where these effects balance, and the drop after it is steep because unfolding is cooperative. In the model shown, the optimum falls near 41 °C.

Incorrect. Substrate breakdown would lower the amount of substrate available, but most substrates are small, stable molecules that are not destroyed at moderately high temperatures. The sharp drop just above the optimum is explained by loss of the enzyme's structure, which is why it is often irreversible on cooling.

Incorrect. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS does vary with temperature, but a change in ΔG shifts the equilibrium; it does not explain a sudden loss of catalytic rate. Even if a reaction became less favorable, a still-folded enzyme would speed whichever direction is favored. The pattern described is a kinetic and structural one.

Incorrect. Enzymes do not need cold to bind substrate; binding generally works across the normal temperature range. Activity rises from low to moderate temperatures because reactions speed up, not because binding requires cooling. This choice gets the low-temperature side of the curve backward.

p: Reaction rate rises with temperature because more molecules have energy above the activation energy (Arrhenius equation, k = A·e^(−Ea/RT)). For enzymes, this rising trend continues only while the protein stays folded. Proteins are held together by many weak interactions (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic effects, salt bridges), and heating eventually disrupts them cooperatively, so the enzyme unfolds over a narrow temperature range.

Observed activity is therefore the product of a rising rate and a falling fraction of folded enzyme, giving an asymmetric curve: a gradual rise, a peak (the temperature optimum, near 37 to 40 °C for many human enzymes) and a steep fall. Enzymes from thermophiles, such as Taq polymerase used in PCR, are stable at much higher temperatures.

Distinguish denaturation (loss of secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, primary sequence intact) from hydrolysis of the backbone. Low temperature slows enzymes reversibly without denaturing them, which is why cooling preserves biological samples.

x1A_146.trap: The rise is kinetics; the sharp fall is denaturation of the enzyme, not of the substrate.

fig.cap: Model: Arrhenius rate (Ea = 50 kJ/mol) times the fraction of folded enzyme (two-state unfolding, Tm = 45 °C). Their product rises, peaks near 41 °C and falls steeply.
fig.alt: Graph of relative value against temperature from 0 to 70 °C. A dashed blue Arrhenius curve keeps rising, a dashed purple folded-fraction curve stays at 1 then drops sharply near 45 °C, and the green observed activity curve rises, peaks near 41 °C and falls to zero by about 52 °C.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Arrhenius equation (Ea 50 kJ/mol) and a two-state unfolding model (Tm 45 °C, ΔH 500 kJ/mol); illustrative parameters.

ox: Incorrect. A lysine side chain (typical pKa about 10.5, sometimes lower in a protein) loses its proton at high pH, so a lysine that must be positive explains the drop on the high-pH side of the curve, above pH 9. Below pH 6 that lysine would be even more fully protonated and still positive, so it cannot explain the low-pH drop.

Incorrect. Hydrolyzing peptide bonds with acid requires very harsh conditions, such as 6 M HCl at about 110 °C for many hours. Mildly acidic conditions like pH 5 leave the backbone intact. The loss of activity below pH 6 reflects a change in the ionization of a side chain, which is reversible.

Correct. The histidine imidazole side chain has a pKa near 6. Above pH 6 it is mostly neutral, with a free lone pair that can accept a proton as a general base. Below pH 6 it becomes mostly protonated (positively charged) and can no longer accept a proton. Using Henderson–Hasselbalch, at pH 5 only about 9% of the histidine is neutral, so activity falls about tenfold, matching the low-pH edge of the bell.

Incorrect. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held by covalent peptide bonds. A change of a few pH units does not alter the sequence. It can alter ionization of side chains and, at extremes, disrupt tertiary structure, but the primary structure stays the same.

p: When an enzyme's activity is bell-shaped against pH, each edge often reflects one ionizable group whose state matters for catalysis. The low-pH edge is set by a group that must be deprotonated (it loses activity when protonated); the high-pH edge is set by a group that must be protonated. The pH at each half-maximum is roughly that group's pKa.

Typical side-chain pKa values to match to edges: Asp/Glu about 4, His about 6, Cys about 8, Tyr about 10, Lys about 10.5, Arg about 12.5. Because histidine's pKa is close to physiological pH, it is uniquely suited to act as both a general acid and a general base in active sites, such as in serine proteases and RNase A.

The protein environment can shift pKa values by a few units (a buried lysine may have a lower pKa), so an edge at pH 9 can still be a lysine. MCAT questions often combine this with Henderson–Hasselbalch reasoning.

fx.w: From Henderson–Hasselbalch for a group with acid dissociation constant Ka. At pH = pKa half the groups are deprotonated; each pH unit below the pKa makes the deprotonated (neutral His) form ten times rarer.

steps: Activity falls below pH 6, so a group with pKa ≈ 6 must be deprotonated for catalysis.
His imidazole pKa ≈ 6: neutral above 6, protonated (+) below 6. Neutral His can accept a proton, so it is the general base.
At pH 5: fraction neutral = 1/(1 + 10^(6 − 5)) = 1/11 ≈ 0.09, so activity drops to about 9% of the maximum contribution from this group.
The high-pH edge (above 9) fits a group that must stay protonated, such as Lys, but that explains the other side of the curve.
x1A_147.trap: Low-pH edge = a group that must be deprotonated (His, pKa ≈ 6); high-pH edge = a group that must stay protonated.

fig.cap: Activity modeled as (fraction His neutral, pKa 6) × (fraction Lys protonated, pKa 9). His protonation sets the low-pH edge; Lys deprotonation sets the high-pH edge.
fig.alt: Graph from pH 2 to 12 with a dashed blue curve for fraction of histidine neutral rising around pH 6, a dashed purple curve for fraction of lysine protonated falling around pH 9, and a green bell-shaped activity curve that is their product, half-maximal near pH 6 and 9.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from Henderson–Hasselbalch fractions with pKa 6 (His) and 9 (Lys).

ox: Correct. The active site is a three-dimensional pocket formed when the polypeptide folds into its tertiary structure. Hydrophobic collapse, hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and sometimes disulfides fold the chain so that residues far apart in sequence end up next to each other. In chymotrypsin, His57, Asp102 and Ser195 are spread across a 245-residue chain, yet they sit within a few ångströms of one another in the folded enzyme. This is why denaturation destroys activity even though the sequence is unchanged.

Incorrect. Peptide bonds link each residue only to the residues immediately before and after it in the chain, forming the backbone during translation. No additional peptide bonds form between distant residues after translation; doing so would create branched or cyclic backbones, which normal proteins do not have.

Incorrect. Substrate binding can cause small conformational changes (induced fit), but it does not create covalent links between enzyme residues. The catalytic residues must already be close together in the folded enzyme before substrate arrives, or the enzyme could not bind and act on the substrate in the first place.

Incorrect. Disulfide bonds stabilize the fold of many secreted proteins, but many enzymes, especially those inside the reducing environment of the cytosol, have no disulfides at all. Even where present, disulfides do not join the catalytic residues to each other. The universal mechanism is folding into tertiary structure.

concept.t: Tertiary structure creates the active site
p: Protein structure is described at four levels: primary (sequence), secondary (local α-helices and β-sheets held by backbone hydrogen bonds), tertiary (the overall 3D fold of one chain, held by side-chain interactions, the hydrophobic effect and sometimes disulfides) and quaternary (assembly of several chains). An active site is a feature of tertiary (and sometimes quaternary) structure.

Because the fold is determined by the sequence (Anfinsen's experiments with ribonuclease), the right sequence folds so that residues distant in the chain come together in a precise arrangement. Denaturing agents such as heat, urea, extreme pH or detergents unfold the protein, separating these residues and abolishing activity without breaking peptide bonds.

MCAT questions may give residue numbers far apart in sequence and ask how they cooperate, or ask what level of structure a mutation or denaturant affects. Mutations that disturb folding, even far from the active site, can abolish catalysis.

x1A_148.trap: Residues far apart in sequence meet through folding (tertiary structure), not through new covalent bonds.

fig.cap: In chymotrypsin's sequence, His57, Asp102 and Ser195 are far apart; folding brings them together into one active site.
fig.alt: Top: a horizontal bar for the 245-residue chain with His57, Asp102 and Ser195 marked at separate positions. Bottom: a folded gray chain whose loops bring the three colored residues together inside an orange active-site circle. Tags mark the 3D fold as correct and new peptide bonds, substrate links and disulfides as incorrect.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; residue numbers from chymotrypsin (chymotrypsinogen numbering).

ox: Incorrect. If only the forward rate increased while the reverse rate stayed the same, the ratio kforward/kreverse would rise by 10⁶, and since that ratio equals Keq, the enzyme would have changed the equilibrium constant. Catalysts cannot do this, because Keq is set by ΔG°, which depends only on the reactants and products.

Incorrect. A catalyst never slows either direction. Slowing the reverse reaction while speeding the forward one would change Keq by a factor of 10¹², an even bigger violation of thermodynamics. Both rates must change by the same factor.

Incorrect. The rate enhancement is a property of the lowered activation barrier and applies at every moment the enzyme is present. The reverse rate does depend on how much B is present (more B means faster conversion back to A), but the rate constant, and so the speed-up factor, is 10⁶ from the start.

Correct. The forward and reverse reactions pass through the same transition state. An enzyme that lowers that transition state's free energy by ΔΔG‡ lowers both barriers by the same amount, so both rate constants increase by the same factor. A 10⁶-fold increase corresponds to ΔΔG‡ = RT ln 10⁶ ≈ 35.6 kJ/mol at 37 °C. Since kforward/kreverse = Keq, the ratio, and so the equilibrium, is unchanged.

concept.t: Catalysis is symmetric: the principle of microscopic reversibility
p: A reaction A ⇌ B has a forward rate constant kf and a reverse rate constant kr, and at equilibrium Keq = kf/kr. Both directions go over the same energy barrier, just from opposite sides: the forward barrier is G‡ − G of A and the reverse barrier is G‡ − G of B.

A catalyst provides a lower transition state. It lowers both barriers by exactly the same amount, so kf and kr increase by the same factor and their ratio, Keq, stays the same. This is why enzymes speed the approach to equilibrium from either side but never change its position, and why the same enzyme can work in both directions depending on conditions (for example, carbonic anhydrase in tissues versus lungs).

Rate constants depend exponentially on barrier height: each 5.7 kJ/mol of barrier lowering at 25 °C (or about 5.9 at 37 °C) speeds a reaction about tenfold. A millionfold speed-up therefore needs about 34 to 36 kJ/mol of transition-state stabilization.

fx.f: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT);   kcat/kuncat = e^(ΔΔG‡/RT);   Keq = kforward / kreverse
fx.w: k is a rate constant, A the pre-exponential factor, Ea (or ΔG‡) the activation barrier, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T the absolute temperature, and ΔΔG‡ the amount by which the enzyme lowers the barrier. The same ΔΔG‡ applies to both directions.

steps: Forward speed-up of 10⁶ means ΔΔG‡ = RT ln 10⁶ = (8.314 × 10⁻³ kJ/(mol·K))(310 K)(13.8) ≈ 35.6 kJ/mol.
The reverse reaction crosses the same transition state, so its barrier also drops by 35.6 kJ/mol (in the figure, from 110 to 74.4 kJ/mol while the forward drops from 90 to 54.4).
Same ΔΔG‡ → same factor: the reverse rate constant also increases 10⁶-fold.
x1A_149.trap: Lowering the transition state lowers BOTH barriers equally, so both directions speed up by the same factor.

fig.cap: One transition state serves both directions. Lowering it by RT ln 10⁶ ≈ 35.6 kJ/mol drops the forward barrier from 90 to 54.4 and the reverse barrier from 110 to 74.4 kJ/mol (illustrative energies).
fig.alt: Reaction-coordinate diagram for A to B with a red uncatalyzed curve peaking at 90 kJ/mol and a green catalyzed curve peaking at 54.4, both starting at 0 and ending at −20. A purple arrow shows the 35.6 kJ/mol lowering, with forward and reverse barrier values listed on each side.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; curves drawn to scale, with the barrier change computed as RT ln 10⁶ at 310 K.

ox: Incorrect. The discovery of ribozymes showed that some catalysts are RNA, not that all are. The great majority of enzymes, including those of glycolysis, DNA replication and digestion, are proteins. Overgeneralizing from one example is the error here.

Correct. The high-resolution structure of the large ribosomal subunit (2000) showed that the peptidyl transferase center, where each new peptide bond is made, is formed entirely of ribosomal RNA (23S rRNA in bacteria, 28S in eukaryotes), and no ribosomal protein side chain is positioned to carry out the chemistry. That makes the ribosome a ribozyme, an RNA catalyst. Other ribozymes include RNase P and self-splicing introns, and the existence of catalytic RNA supports the RNA world hypothesis for early life.

Incorrect. Ribosomal proteins are needed for translation in practice: they help the rRNA fold correctly, assemble the subunits, and bind factors and tRNAs. The finding is that they are not the catalysts of peptide bond formation, not that they can be removed. Saying they are unneeded goes well beyond the evidence.

Incorrect. Ribozymes are true catalysts, and no catalyst, whether RNA or protein, changes the equilibrium constant of a reaction. They lower the activation energy and speed the approach to equilibrium. Peptide bond formation on the ribosome is driven forward by the energy stored in the aminoacyl-tRNA ester bond, not by the catalyst.

p: Enzymes are biological catalysts, and while most are proteins, some are RNA molecules called ribozymes. RNA can fold into complex 3D shapes with pockets that bind substrates and metal ions, and its 2′-OH groups and bases can take part in acid–base catalysis. Known ribozymes include the ribosome's peptidyl transferase center, RNase P (which trims tRNA precursors), group I and II self-splicing introns, and the snRNAs at the catalytic core of the spliceosome.

Cech and Altman shared the 1989 Nobel Prize for discovering catalytic RNA, and the ribosome structures (Nobel Prize 2009) confirmed that the ribosome's catalytic core is RNA. These findings support the RNA world hypothesis: early life may have used RNA both to store information and to catalyze reactions.
Like protein enzymes, ribozymes lower activation energy, are regenerated after each cycle, and leave Keq unchanged. On the MCAT, remember 'enzyme' does not automatically mean protein.

x1A_150.trap: Some catalysts are RNA; that does not make all enzymes RNA or make ribosomal proteins unnecessary.

fig.cap: The ribosome's peptidyl transferase center (PTC) is made of rRNA, with ribosomal proteins mostly on the surface. Most biological catalysts are proteins, but ribozymes are RNA.
fig.alt: Schematic ribosome with a large and small subunit; a green circle labeled PTC, all rRNA, sits in the large subunit away from orange protein circles. A box lists protein enzymes as the great majority and ribozymes including peptidyl transferase, RNase P, self-splicing introns and spliceosome snRNAs. Tags mark some catalysts are RNA as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; facts from standard molecular biology texts.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 15.5 Ribosomes and Protein Synthesis

ox: Incorrect. The maximum rate is Vmax, the plateau that the v versus [S] curve approaches when every active site is occupied. Vmax is a rate (for example μmol/min), not a concentration, so it sits on the y-axis of the plot, while Km is read on the x-axis. Vmax is used to define Km (Km is where v reaches half of it), which is why the two are easy to mix up.

Correct. Substitute [S] = Km into v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]): v = Vmax·Km/(2Km) = Vmax/2. So experimentally you measure initial rates over a range of [S], estimate Vmax from the plateau, and read Km as the substrate concentration where the rate is half of that. Km has units of concentration and, for many enzymes, roughly reflects how much substrate is needed to occupy half the active sites.

Incorrect. The number of substrate molecules converted per second by one active site is the turnover number, kcat, found as Vmax/[E]T. It has units of s⁻¹ and describes catalytic speed once substrate is bound. Km and kcat are separate parameters: one enzyme can have a low Km and a low kcat, another a high Km and a high kcat.

Incorrect. The Michaelis–Menten curve is a rectangular hyperbola: v approaches Vmax asymptotically but never equals it at any finite [S]. Even at [S] = 10 Km the rate is 10/11 ≈ 91% of Vmax, and at 100 Km it is still only 99%. A parameter defined at the point v = Vmax could never be measured, which is exactly why the half-maximal point is used instead.

p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. Setting [S] = Km gives v = Vmax/2, which is the working definition you read off a graph.

Km has units of concentration. A low Km means the enzyme reaches half its maximal rate at low [S], which usually (not always) means high apparent affinity for the substrate. Vmax depends on how much enzyme is present: Vmax = kcat[E]T, where kcat (the turnover number, s⁻¹) is the number of substrate molecules one active site converts per second.

On the MCAT, keep the three parameters separate: Vmax is a rate (y-axis), Km is a concentration (x-axis), and kcat is a first-order rate constant. Because the curve only approaches Vmax, Km is defined at the half-maximal point, never at the maximum.

fig.cap: A Michaelis–Menten curve. Km is the [S] at which v = Vmax/2; the curve only approaches Vmax, and kcat is not a point on this graph at all.
fig.alt: Hyperbolic curve of initial rate versus substrate concentration rising toward a dashed Vmax line at 100; dashed lines mark v = 50 at [S] = Km = 2; a point at [S] = 20 shows the rate is still only 91 percent of Vmax.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with illustrative Vmax = 100 and Km = 2.

x1A_151.trap: Km is a substrate concentration measured at HALF of Vmax; the curve never actually reaches Vmax.

ox: Incorrect. 33 μmol/min comes from computing Vmax × Km/[S] = 100 × 2/6, which inverts the substrate term and drops the sum in the denominator. That expression even predicts that rate falls as [S] rises, the opposite of real enzyme behavior. The correct ratio is [S]/(Km + [S]), the fraction of active sites occupied.

Incorrect. 50 μmol/min is Vmax/2, the rate at [S] = Km = 2 mM. Here [S] is 6 mM, three times Km, so the enzyme is more saturated and the rate must be higher than 50. Choosing 50 usually means recognizing the half-Vmax rule but not checking whether [S] actually equals Km.

Correct. Use v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with the values in the stem: v = 100 × 6/(2 + 6) = 600/8 = 75 μmol/min. A shortcut: [S] = 3 Km gives v/Vmax = 3/(1 + 3) = 3/4. The answer must lie between Vmax/2 (because [S] > Km) and Vmax (because the curve only approaches it), and 75 does.

Incorrect. 300 μmol/min would come from multiplying Vmax by [S]/Km = 3, as if rate kept rising linearly with substrate. No enzyme can exceed Vmax: when every active site is occupied, adding more substrate cannot make the reaction faster. Any calculated rate above Vmax signals a setup error.

p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax.

The ratio [S]/(Km + [S]) is the fraction of the maximum rate, and it is also the fraction of active sites occupied. It is handy to express [S] as a multiple of Km: at [S] = Km the enzyme runs at 1/2 Vmax, at 3 Km at 3/4, at 9 Km at 9/10, and at Km/3 at 1/4.

Sanity checks catch most mistakes: v must rise with [S], must be below Vmax, and must be above Vmax/2 when [S] > Km. If your answer violates any of these, recheck which quantity sits in the numerator and denominator.

fx.w: v = initial rate (same units as Vmax, here μmol/min); [S] = substrate concentration; Km = Michaelis constant (same units as [S], here mM). Applies to initial rates of a single-substrate enzyme without cooperativity.

steps: Check: [S] = 3 Km, so v/Vmax = 3/4 = 0.75, between 0.5 and 1 as expected.

fig.cap: The curve for Km = 2 mM and Vmax = 100 μmol/min. At 6 mM the rate is 75; 50 is the rate at Km, 33 lies well below the curve, and 300 is above the Vmax ceiling.
fig.alt: Michaelis–Menten curve rising toward a dashed line at 100; a green point at 6 mM and 75; a gray point at 2 mM and 50; a red tick at 33 near 6 mM.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with Km and Vmax from the question.

x1A_152.trap: Check that your rate is below Vmax and above Vmax/2 whenever [S] is greater than Km.
x1A_152.eli: Km is the 'half-full' point of the enzyme. At [S] = 3 × Km the enzyme is three-quarters full, so it runs at three-quarters of top speed.
mem: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).
[S] = Km → v = Vmax/2.
Rate can never exceed Vmax.

fm.f: v = Vmax·[S] / (Km + [S]), where v = initial rate, Vmax = top speed, [S] = substrate concentration, Km = [S] at half of Vmax
