fm.why: We use Michaelis–Menten because it links how much substrate there is to how fast the enzyme works.

x1A_152.sc: Write [S] as a multiple of Km: 6 = 3 × 2, so v/Vmax = 3/(1 + 3) = 3/4 and v = 75.
x1A_152.mn: Km = 'Keep half': the [S] where the enzyme runs at half speed.

ox: Incorrect. 0.9 × Km is the number you get by reading 90% straight onto the [S] axis, as if rate were proportional to [S]. At [S] = 0.9 Km the fraction of Vmax is 0.9/(1 + 0.9) = 0.9/1.9 ≈ 0.47, so the enzyme is still below half-maximal. Rate is only proportional to [S] when [S] is far below Km.

Correct. Set v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]) = 0.9. Then [S] = 0.9Km + 0.9[S], so 0.1[S] = 0.9Km and [S] = 9Km. Check: 9/(1 + 9) = 9/10. The general rule is that to reach a fraction f of Vmax you need [S] = Km·f/(1 − f), so the last few percent of Vmax cost a lot of extra substrate.

Incorrect. 10 × Km is a rounded guess (90% sounds like ten times). At [S] = 10 Km, v/Vmax = 10/11 ≈ 0.91, which is slightly more than 90%. The question asks for the concentration that gives exactly 90%, and algebra gives 9 Km, not 10 Km.

Incorrect. 90 × Km treats the percentage as a multiplier. At [S] = 90 Km the enzyme reaches 90/91 ≈ 99% of Vmax, nearly saturated. Using ten times more substrate than needed is a big overshoot; it illustrates how slowly the hyperbola creeps toward its plateau.

concept.t: Fraction of Vmax and substrate needed
p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. The fraction v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]) equals the fraction of active sites that are occupied.

Solving for [S] gives [S] = Km·f/(1 − f), where f is the target fraction of Vmax. So 50% needs 1 Km, 75% needs 3 Km, 90% needs 9 Km, and 99% needs 99 Km. The approach to Vmax is slow because each extra bit of saturation requires the remaining free enzyme to find substrate.

This is why Vmax is estimated by extrapolation (for example from a Lineweaver–Burk plot) rather than measured directly, and why physiological substrate levels near Km let a cell's flux respond sensitively to changes in [S].

fx.w: Rearranged Michaelis–Menten equation. f = v/Vmax, the desired fraction of Vmax (a number between 0 and 1); [S] comes out in the same units as Km.

fig.cap: Percent of Vmax against [S]/Km on a log axis. The 90% line is crossed at 9 Km; 0.9 Km gives only 47%, 10 Km gives 91% and 90 Km gives 99%.
fig.alt: S-shaped curve on a logarithmic x-axis from 0.1 to over 100 Km; points at 0.9 Km (47 percent), 9 Km (90 percent, green), 10 Km (91 percent) and 90 Km (99 percent).
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), written as v/Vmax = x/(1 + x) with x = [S]/Km.

x1A_153.trap: Rate is not proportional to [S] near or above Km; solve f = [S]/(Km + [S]) instead of scaling.
x1A_153.eli: To fill 90% of the seats you need nine times as much substrate as the half-full point.
mem: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]).
90% of Vmax needs [S] = 9 Km; 99% needs 99 Km.
Reaching Vmax needs infinite substrate.

fm.f: v / Vmax = [S] / (Km + [S]), where v/Vmax = fraction of top speed, [S] = substrate, Km = Michaelis constant
fm.why: We solve the Michaelis–Menten ratio backward to find the substrate needed for a target speed.

x1A_153.sc: For a fraction f, [S] = f/(1 − f) × Km: f = 0.9 → 0.9/0.1 = 9.

ox: Correct. Write [S] = Km/3 and substitute into v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]): (Km/3)/(Km + Km/3) = (1/3)/(4/3) = 1/4 = 0.25. Km cancels, so the answer holds for any enzyme obeying Michaelis–Menten kinetics. Only a quarter of the active sites are occupied at this substrate level.

Incorrect. 0.33 comes from treating the rate as directly proportional to [S]/Km, that is, using v/Vmax = [S]/Km and dropping [S] from the denominator. That linear approximation is only good when [S] is much smaller than Km (say below Km/10); at Km/3, [S] is a third of Km and cannot be ignored, so it overestimates the rate.

Incorrect. 0.5 is the fraction at [S] = Km, the definition of Km. Here [S] is only one-third of Km, so fewer active sites are filled and the rate must be below half of Vmax. Picking 0.5 means applying the half-Vmax rule without checking the actual [S].

Incorrect. 0.75 is the fraction when [S] = 3 Km, because 3/(1 + 3) = 3/4. It comes from inverting the ratio, using Km/[S] = 3 instead of [S]/Km = 1/3. Below Km the enzyme must be under half-saturated, so any answer above 0.5 is impossible here.

p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. Dividing top and bottom by Km gives v/Vmax = x/(1 + x), where x = [S]/Km, so the fraction depends only on how [S] compares with Km.
Useful benchmarks: x = 1/3 gives 1/4, x = 1 gives 1/2, x = 3 gives 3/4, x = 9 gives 9/10. Notice the symmetry: going from Km/3 to 3 Km takes the enzyme from 25% to 75% of Vmax.
When x is very small, 1 + x ≈ 1 and v/Vmax ≈ x, the first-order regime. Students often apply that shortcut where it no longer holds; it is fine at x = 0.01 but is off by a third at x = 1/3.

fx.w: Michaelis–Menten equation in dimensionless form. x is substrate concentration in units of Km; v/Vmax is the fraction of maximal rate and of active sites occupied.

fig.cap: v/Vmax against [S]/Km. At one-third of Km the true curve gives 0.25; the dashed straight line (ignoring Km in the denominator) gives 0.33. 0.5 and 0.75 need [S] = Km and 3 Km.
fig.alt: Hyperbolic curve of v over Vmax against x from 0 to 4 with points at x = 1/3 (0.25, green), x = 1 (0.5) and x = 3 (0.75); a red dashed straight line y = x passes 0.33 at x = 1/3.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), written as v/Vmax = x/(1 + x).

x1A_154.trap: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]), not [S]/Km; the linear shortcut only works when [S] is far below Km.
x1A_154.eli: At one-third of the half-full point the enzyme is only one-quarter full.
mem: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]).
[S] = Km/3 → v/Vmax = 1/4.
Low [S] (≪ Km): rate rises almost linearly with [S].

fm.f: v / Vmax = [S] / (Km + [S]), where v/Vmax = fraction of top speed, [S] = substrate, Km = Michaelis constant
fm.why: We put [S] in units of Km so the Km cancels and only fractions remain.

ox: Incorrect. First-order kinetics (rate proportional to [S]) is the low-substrate limit. When [S] ≪ Km, the denominator Km + [S] ≈ Km and v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S], so doubling [S] doubles the rate. That is the opposite end of the curve from the condition in the question.

Incorrect. Second order in substrate would mean v ∝ [S]², so the rate would quadruple when [S] doubles. A single-substrate enzyme obeying Michaelis–Menten kinetics never shows that; its order in [S] moves from 1 at low [S] toward 0 at high [S]. Apparent orders above 1 hint at cooperative (allosteric) binding instead.

Incorrect. Negative order would mean adding substrate slows the reaction. That happens in substrate inhibition, a special case where excess substrate binds unproductively, but it is not part of the Michaelis–Menten model, whose curve rises steadily toward Vmax. Nothing in the stem suggests substrate inhibition.

Correct. When [S] ≫ Km, Km + [S] ≈ [S], so v ≈ Vmax[S]/[S] = Vmax, a constant. Every active site is occupied (the enzyme is saturated), so extra substrate has no free enzyme to bind and the rate no longer depends on [S]. A rate that does not depend on a reactant's concentration is zero order in that reactant.

concept.t: Reaction order in the two limits of Michaelis–Menten
p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax.

Two limits matter. When [S] ≪ Km, most enzyme is free, v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S], and the reaction is first order in substrate: rate rises in proportion to [S]. When [S] ≫ Km, nearly all enzyme is bound as ES, v ≈ Vmax, and the reaction is zero order in substrate: it runs at a constant maximum rate set by enzyme amount and kcat.

Between these limits the apparent order slides continuously from 1 to 0. The MCAT likes to ask what happens when [S] is doubled: near-proportional increase at low [S], almost no change at saturation. Alcohol dehydrogenase saturated by ethanol is a familiar example of zero-order (constant-rate) elimination.

fig.cap: The two limits of the Michaelis–Menten curve: a straight-line (first-order) region at low [S] and a flat (zero-order) region once [S] is far above Km.
fig.alt: Curve of v over Vmax against [S] over Km from 0 to 20; a dashed tangent line through the origin marks the first-order low-substrate region; a dashed horizontal line at 1 and a shaded region from 10 to 20 Km mark the zero-order saturated region.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).

x1A_155.trap: Saturated enzyme means zero order in substrate; first order is the low-[S] end of the curve.

ox: Correct. When [S] ≪ Km, the [S] term in the denominator is negligible, so Km + [S] ≈ Km and v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S]. The rate is then directly proportional to substrate concentration, a first-order reaction with apparent rate constant Vmax/Km = (kcat/Km)[E]T. This is why kcat/Km is the key measure of efficiency at low substrate levels.

Incorrect. v ≈ Vmax is the opposite limit, reached when [S] ≫ Km and the enzyme is saturated. At very low [S], most enzyme molecules are free and waiting for substrate, so the rate is far below Vmax. This choice comes from swapping the two limiting cases.

Incorrect. v = Vmax/2 holds at exactly one point, [S] = Km, which is the definition of Km. It is not a limiting form of the equation, and when [S] is far below Km the enzyme runs at only a small fraction of Vmax, well under half.

Incorrect. v ≈ Km/[S] would make the rate grow as substrate decreases and become infinite as [S] → 0, which is physically impossible. It also has the wrong units: Km/[S] is dimensionless, not a rate. This expression usually comes from inverting a fraction while simplifying.

p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax.

When [S] ≪ Km, almost all enzyme is free, and the rate is v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S] = (kcat/Km)[E]T[S]. The reaction is first order in substrate, so the curve starts as a straight line through the origin with slope Vmax/Km. When [S] ≫ Km, the enzyme is saturated and v ≈ Vmax (zero order).

The low-[S] slope involves kcat/Km, the specificity constant, which measures how efficiently an enzyme captures and converts substrate when substrate is scarce. Many cellular substrates are present below or near their Km, so this regime is physiologically common. Be careful: the linear approximation fails as [S] approaches Km.

fig.cap: At low [S] the curve follows the dashed line v = (Vmax/Km)[S] (first order); at high [S] it flattens toward Vmax (zero order). Vmax/2 occurs only at [S] = Km.
fig.alt: Curve of v over Vmax against [S] over Km; a dashed tangent through the origin labelled v ≈ (Vmax/Km)[S]; a dashed plateau at Vmax labelled zero order; a point at Km marks Vmax/2.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).

x1A_156.trap: Drop the SMALLER term from Km + [S]: at low [S] drop [S] (v ∝ [S]); at high [S] drop Km (v ≈ Vmax).

ox: Incorrect. 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ comes from dividing [E]T by Vmax: (2 × 10⁻⁸)/(2 × 10⁻⁴) = 10⁻⁴. Besides the wrong value, the units come out as s (M divided by M/s), not s⁻¹. A turnover number of 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ would mean one reaction per site every few hours, absurdly slow given the measured Vmax.

Incorrect. 4 × 10⁻¹² comes from multiplying the two values: 2 × 2 = 4 and 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻⁸ = 10⁻¹². Multiplying gives units of M²/s, which is not a rate constant at all. The relationship is Vmax = kcat[E]T, so kcat is found by dividing Vmax by [E]T.

Correct. At saturation every active site turns over at its maximum rate, so Vmax = kcat[E]T. Rearranging, kcat = Vmax/[E]T = (2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s)/(2 × 10⁻⁸ M) = 1 × 10⁴ s⁻¹. The molar units cancel, leaving s⁻¹. Each active site converts about 10,000 substrate molecules into product per second.

Incorrect. 10¹² comes from an exponent error, such as adding the magnitudes (4 + 8 = 12) instead of subtracting the exponents. When dividing powers of ten you subtract: 10⁻⁴/10⁻⁸ = 10⁻⁴⁻⁽⁻⁸⁾ = 10⁴. A kcat of 10¹² s⁻¹ would also be far faster than any known enzyme, whose turnover numbers top out near 10⁶ to 10⁷ s⁻¹.

p: The turnover number kcat is the maximum number of substrate molecules one active site converts to product per second. It is defined by Vmax = kcat[E]T, where [E]T is the total concentration of active sites. kcat has units of s⁻¹ and is a property of the enzyme, while Vmax also depends on how much enzyme is in the tube.

Typical kcat values range from below 1 s⁻¹ to about 10⁶ to 10⁷ s⁻¹ (carbonic anhydrase, about 10⁶ s⁻¹, and catalase, about 4 × 10⁷ s⁻¹, are among the fastest). Dividing by kcat gives the time for one catalytic cycle: kcat = 10⁴ s⁻¹ means one cycle every 100 μs.

On the MCAT, kcat calculations are scientific-notation practice: divide coefficients, subtract exponents, and confirm the units cancel to s⁻¹. Remember that doubling the enzyme doubles Vmax but leaves kcat and Km unchanged.

fx.w: kcat = turnover number (s⁻¹); Vmax = maximal rate (M/s); [E]T = total concentration of active sites (M). Valid when the enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics and every site is counted.

steps: Start from Vmax = kcat[E]T, so kcat = Vmax/[E]T.

fig.cap: kcat is Vmax divided by the active-site concentration. The three wrong values come from dividing upside down, multiplying, and an exponent slip.
fig.alt: Three boxes reading Vmax 2 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, divided by [E]T 2 × 10⁻⁸ M, equals kcat 10⁴ per second, with red pills for the wrong values and a green pill for the correct one.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram using the values in the question.

x1A_157.trap: kcat = Vmax ÷ [E]T; when dividing powers of ten, subtract the exponents and check the units are s⁻¹.

ox: Incorrect. This enzyme's efficiency is kcat/Km = 100/10⁻⁵ = 10⁷ M⁻¹s⁻¹. That is high, and it is the second best of the four, but it is ten times lower than the enzyme with kcat = 10 s⁻¹ and Km = 10⁻⁷ M. It is a trap for anyone who stops after finding a good value instead of comparing all four.

Incorrect. kcat/Km = 1000/10⁻³ = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹. The kcat of 1000 s⁻¹ looks impressive, but a Km of 1 mM means the enzyme needs a lot of substrate to work near its maximum. Efficiency combines speed and substrate capture, and here the weaker capture pulls the ratio down.

Incorrect. kcat/Km = 10⁴/10⁻² = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹. This enzyme has the highest turnover number of the four, which tempts students who equate efficiency with kcat alone. Its very high Km (10 mM) means it rarely meets substrate at low concentration, so its efficiency is only 10⁶.

Correct. Catalytic efficiency is kcat/Km, the apparent second-order rate constant for free enzyme meeting free substrate. Here kcat/Km = 10/10⁻⁷ = 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹, the largest of the four (the others give 10⁷, 10⁶ and 10⁶). Despite the slowest turnover, its very low Km means it binds and converts scarce substrate extremely well, approaching the diffusion limit of about 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹.

p: kcat/Km (the specificity constant) measures how effectively an enzyme turns substrate into product when substrate is scarce. From the low-[S] form of Michaelis–Menten, v = (kcat/Km)[E][S], so kcat/Km is a second-order rate constant with units M⁻¹s⁻¹.

A high kcat means fast turnover once substrate is bound; a low Km means substrate is captured at low concentration. Efficiency needs both, so compare the ratio, not either number alone. An upper limit is set by how fast enzyme and substrate can diffuse together, about 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹.

MCAT questions often bury the most efficient enzyme behind a modest kcat. Divide kcat by Km for each choice (subtract the exponents) and pick the largest ratio. kcat/Km also tells you which of two substrates an enzyme prefers when they compete.

fx.w: kcat in s⁻¹ divided by Km in M gives M⁻¹s⁻¹. It is the rate constant for E + S → product when [S] ≪ Km.

steps: kcat = 10 s⁻¹, Km = 10⁻⁷ M: 10¹/10⁻⁷ = 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹, the largest.

fig.cap: Left: turnover number of each enzyme in the question. Right: kcat/Km. The enzyme with the slowest turnover (kcat 10¹, Km 10⁻⁷) has the highest efficiency, 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹.
fig.alt: Two bar charts. Left, log kcat values 2, 3, 4 and 1. Right, log kcat over Km values 7, 6, 6 and 8, with the last bar green.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the kcat and Km values in the question.

x1A_158.trap: Efficiency is kcat/Km, not kcat; a slow but very tight-binding enzyme can win.

ox: Correct. Apply v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]) to enzyme Y: 5/(10 + 5) = 5/15 = 1/3 ≈ 33%. Because [S] is half of Y's Km, the enzyme is less than half-saturated. Enzyme X's Km is irrelevant here; it is a distractor that tests whether you plug in the right enzyme's constant.

Incorrect. 50% of Vmax is reached only when [S] equals Km. For enzyme Y that would require 10 mM substrate, twice the 5 mM given. Since [S] < Km, Y must be below half of its Vmax. Choosing 50% means applying the half-Vmax rule without checking how [S] compares with this enzyme's Km.

Incorrect. 67% comes from Km/(Km + [S]) = 10/15, which is the fraction of enzyme that is free (unbound), not the fraction working. Swapping numerator terms flips the answer around 50%. Check the direction: below Km, the bound fraction must be under one-half.

Incorrect. 98% is enzyme X's fraction: 5/(0.1 + 5) = 5/5.1 ≈ 0.98. With a Km of only 0.1 mM, X is nearly saturated at 5 mM. The question asks about Y, whose much higher Km means it is far from saturation at the same substrate level.

p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. What matters is [S] relative to each enzyme's own Km: v/Vmax = [S]/(Km + [S]).

An enzyme with a low Km is nearly saturated at modest [S], so its rate barely changes when [S] fluctuates. An enzyme with a high Km works in the sensitive part of the curve, so its rate tracks [S]. This is the logic behind isozymes such as hexokinase (low Km, about 0.1 mM glucose) and glucokinase in liver and pancreas (half-saturated near 8 to 10 mM), which responds to rises in blood glucose.
Do not confuse Km with Vmax: a lower Km does not mean a faster maximum rate; it means saturation is reached at lower substrate concentration.

fx.w: Fraction of maximal rate for one enzyme; use that enzyme's own Km. Units of [S] and Km must match (here mM).

fig.cap: Rate as a percent of Vmax for enzyme X (Km 0.1 mM) and enzyme Y (Km 10 mM). At 5 mM, X is at 98% but Y is at only 33%.
fig.alt: Two hyperbolic curves against substrate concentration from 0 to 30 mM; the purple X curve rises almost immediately to near 100 percent, the blue Y curve rises gradually; a dotted line at 5 mM meets X at 98 percent and Y at 33 percent.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with the Km values in the question.

x1A_159.trap: Use the Km of the enzyme being asked about, and [S] over (Km + [S]), not Km over (Km + [S]).

ox: Incorrect. 1/Vmax is the y-intercept, found by setting 1/[S] = 0 (infinite substrate, so v = Vmax). It sits on the vertical axis, not the horizontal one. A larger y-intercept means a smaller Vmax, which is how noncompetitive inhibition shows up on this plot.

Incorrect. Km/Vmax is the slope of the Lineweaver–Burk line, the coefficient of 1/[S] in 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. Slope is a ratio of rise over run, not an intercept. It increases with competitive, mixed and pure noncompetitive inhibitors, but not with uncompetitive ones, which lower Km and Vmax by the same factor and leave the slope unchanged.

Correct. Taking the reciprocal of the Michaelis–Menten equation gives 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. On the x-axis 1/v = 0, so (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) = −1/Vmax, which gives 1/[S] = −1/Km. The x-intercept lies to the left of the origin, and a point closer to zero means a larger Km.

Incorrect. Neither intercept gives Vmax directly; both are reciprocals. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km, so −Vmax mixes up which parameter belongs on which axis and forgets the reciprocal. To get Vmax you take 1 divided by the y-intercept.

p: Taking the reciprocal of v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) gives 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, the equation of a straight line when 1/v is plotted against 1/[S]. This double-reciprocal (Lineweaver–Burk) plot turns the hyperbola into a line, so Vmax and Km can be read from intercepts rather than estimated from a curve that never flattens completely.
Three features to memorize: y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax. A higher line (larger y-intercept) means lower Vmax; an x-intercept closer to zero means higher Km.

The plot is most useful for diagnosing inhibitors: competitive lines cross on the y-axis (same Vmax), pure noncompetitive lines cross on the x-axis (same Km), and uncompetitive lines are parallel (same slope).

fx.w: Lineweaver–Burk form of the Michaelis–Menten equation: y = 1/v, x = 1/[S], slope Km/Vmax, y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km.

fig.cap: A Lineweaver–Burk line. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the slope is Km/Vmax, and extrapolating the line back to the x-axis gives −1/Km.
fig.alt: Straight line of 1 over v against 1 over [S]; data points at positive 1 over [S]; a dashed extension crosses the y-axis at 1 over Vmax and the x-axis at minus 1 over Km, marked in green.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Lineweaver–Burk equation with illustrative Km = 2 and Vmax = 100.

x1A_160.trap: Both intercepts are reciprocals: y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km.
x1A_160.eli: The Lineweaver–Burk plot flips the Michaelis–Menten curve into a straight line so you can read Km and Vmax from where it crosses the axes.
mem: LB plot: x = 1/[S] (independent), y = 1/v (dependent).
y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = −1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax.
Lines meeting on the y-axis = competitive; on the x-axis = noncompetitive; parallel = uncompetitive.

fm.f: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)·(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, where v = rate, [S] = substrate, Km = half-Vmax substrate level, Vmax = top speed
fm.why: We set 1/v to zero because the x-intercept is where the line crosses y = 0.

x1A_160.sc: x-intercept = −1/Km, y-intercept = 1/Vmax. Remember: x ↔ Km (negative), y ↔ Vmax (positive).
x1A_160.mn: X = −1/Km, Y = 1/Vmax: 'X marks the Km, Y marks the Vmax'.

ox: Incorrect. These are the raw intercept values copied without inverting them. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the axes are reciprocals (1/v and 1/[S]), so the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km. Reading 0.02 as Vmax and 0.25 as Km also gives units of min/μM and μM⁻¹, not μM/min and μM, which is a giveaway.

Correct. The y-intercept equals 1/Vmax, so Vmax = 1/(0.02 min/μM) = 50 μM/min. The x-intercept equals −1/Km, so −1/Km = −0.25 μM⁻¹ and Km = 1/0.25 = 4 μM. As a check, the slope Km/Vmax should be 4/50 = 0.08 min, consistent with a line passing through both intercepts (0.02/0.25 = 0.08).

Incorrect. Vmax is right (1/0.02 = 50 μM/min), but Km was not inverted. The x-intercept is −1/Km, so a value of −0.25 μM⁻¹ means Km = 4 μM, not 0.25 μM. Treating one intercept as a reciprocal and not the other is a common half-finished calculation.

Incorrect. This swaps the two parameters: it puts the x-axis information into Vmax and the y-axis information into Km. The y-intercept (at infinite substrate) is about the maximal rate, and the x-intercept is about substrate concentration, so the y-axis gives Vmax and the x-axis gives Km. With the reciprocals done correctly, Vmax = 50 μM/min and Km = 4 μM.

concept.t: Extracting Km and Vmax from a Lineweaver–Burk plot
p: The Lineweaver–Burk equation, 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, is a straight line with y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km and slope Km/Vmax. To get the parameters, take the reciprocal of each intercept (and drop the minus sign for Km).

Units help: the y-axis has units of 1/rate (for example min/μM), so its reciprocal is a rate; the x-axis has units of 1/concentration, so its reciprocal is a concentration. If your Vmax is not in rate units, you forgot to invert.

You can check consistency with the slope: slope = Km/Vmax = (y-intercept)/(|x-intercept|). The MCAT often asks how an inhibitor moves these intercepts, so being fluent with which intercept is which saves time.

fx.w: From 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The y-intercept is in min/μM here, so Vmax comes out in μM/min; the x-intercept is in μM⁻¹, so Km comes out in μM.

steps: Check: slope = Km/Vmax = 4/50 = 0.08 min, and 0.02/0.25 = 0.08. Consistent.

fig.cap: The line from the question: y-intercept 0.02 min/μM and x-intercept −0.25 μM⁻¹. Inverting gives Vmax = 50 μM/min and Km = 4 μM.
fig.alt: Double-reciprocal plot with a straight line crossing the y-axis at 0.02 and, when extended, the x-axis at −0.25; both intercepts marked in green with their inverted values.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Lineweaver–Burk equation with the intercepts in the question.

x1A_161.eli: Read the two crossing points and flip them: take 1 over the y-intercept for Vmax, and 1 over the x-intercept (without the minus) for Km.
mem: Vmax = 1 / (y-intercept).
Km = −1 / (x-intercept).
Units: Vmax in μM/min, Km in μM.

fm.f: Vmax = 1 / (y-intercept) and Km = −1 / (x-intercept), where y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km
fm.why: The intercepts are reciprocals, so we flip them to get the real values.

x1A_161.mn: Flip it: intercept → reciprocal → real value.

ox: Correct. Lines that share an x-intercept share −1/Km, so the inhibitor leaves Km unchanged; the inhibited line is higher on the y-axis, so 1/Vmax is larger and Vmax is lower. Unchanged Km with lower Vmax is the signature of pure noncompetitive inhibition, in which the inhibitor binds E and ES with equal affinity at a site other than the active site.

Incorrect. A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, because enough substrate can always outcompete it. On a Lineweaver–Burk plot the lines therefore share the y-intercept (1/Vmax) and cross on the y-axis, with the inhibited line steeper. A crossing on the x-axis is the opposite pattern.

Incorrect. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only ES and lowers Km and Vmax by the same factor, so Km/Vmax (the slope) does not change. The lines are parallel and never cross. Lines meeting on the x-axis must have different slopes and the same Km, which rules this out.

Incorrect. A mixed inhibitor that binds free enzyme more tightly than ES raises Km and lowers Vmax, so its lines cross to the left of the y-axis and above the x-axis, not on it. The x-axis crossing happens only in the special case where the inhibitor binds E and ES equally, which is pure noncompetitive inhibition.

p: Reversible inhibitors are classified by which enzyme forms they bind. Competitive inhibitors bind only free enzyme (E), usually at the active site, so they raise apparent Km but can be outcompeted by substrate, leaving Vmax unchanged. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both Km and Vmax by the same factor. Mixed inhibitors bind both E and ES; when they bind both equally the special case is called pure noncompetitive, which lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged.

On a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v against 1/[S]), the y-intercept is 1/Vmax and the x-intercept is −1/Km. So the shared point tells you which parameter is unchanged: lines meeting on the y-axis share Vmax (competitive), lines meeting on the x-axis share Km (pure noncompetitive), and parallel lines share the slope Km/Vmax (uncompetitive). Mixed inhibitors give lines meeting off both axes.

Memory aid: competitive inhibitors compete for the substrate's spot, so substrate can win (Vmax recovers); noncompetitive inhibitors do not care whether substrate is bound, so Km is untouched but fewer enzymes work.

fig.cap: Lineweaver–Burk patterns: competitive lines meet on the y-axis, uncompetitive lines are parallel, pure noncompetitive lines meet on the x-axis, and mixed lines meet off both axes.
fig.alt: Four small double-reciprocal plots, each with a blue no-inhibitor line and a red inhibitor line: crossing on the y-axis, parallel, crossing on the x-axis, and crossing left of the y-axis above the x-axis.

x1A_162.trap: The shared intercept is the unchanged parameter: y-axis cross means same Vmax, x-axis cross means same Km.
x1A_162.eli: Different inhibitors change the line differently. Same x-axis meeting point means Km did not move, only Vmax dropped.
mem: Competitive: Vmax SAME, Km UP; lines cross on the y-axis.
Noncompetitive: Vmax DOWN, Km SAME; lines cross on the x-axis.
Uncompetitive: Vmax DOWN, Km DOWN; parallel lines.
x1A_162.sc: Where do the lines meet? y-axis → competitive; x-axis → noncompetitive; they never meet → uncompetitive.
x1A_162.mn: C-y, N-x, U-parallel: Competitive crosses Y; Noncompetitive crosses X; Uncompetitive runs Unmet (parallel).

ox: Incorrect. An inhibitor that occupies the active site and blocks substrate is competitive. Because it binds only free enzyme, high [S] can push it out, so Vmax is unchanged while apparent Km rises. That is the reverse of the pattern in the question.

Incorrect. An inhibitor that binds only the ES complex is uncompetitive. By pulling ES into a dead-end ESI complex it shifts the E + S ⇌ ES equilibrium toward ES (Le Châtelier), so apparent Km falls along with Vmax. Pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged, so this cannot be the explanation.

Correct. When the inhibitor binds E and ES with the same dissociation constant (Ki = Ki′), it removes the same fraction of each form. Whether or not substrate is bound makes no difference to the inhibitor, so the substrate concentration needed for half-saturation of the remaining active enzyme is unchanged (Km constant). But the inhibitor-bound fraction cannot make product, and adding substrate cannot displace an inhibitor that does not compete with it, so Vmax falls.

Incorrect. Reversible inhibitors act on the enzyme, not by chemically destroying substrate. If substrate were being destroyed, the measured rate would fall because [S] was lower, but Km and Vmax are properties of the enzyme measured at defined [S], and they would not shift in this specific way.

concept.t: Why pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged
p: Reversible inhibitors are classified by which enzyme forms they bind. Competitive inhibitors bind only free enzyme (E), usually at the active site, so they raise apparent Km but can be outcompeted by substrate, leaving Vmax unchanged. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both Km and Vmax by the same factor. Mixed inhibitors bind both E and ES; when they bind both equally the special case is called pure noncompetitive, which lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged.

In the general model, an inhibitor at concentration [I] multiplies free enzyme by α = 1 + [I]/Ki and ES by α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′. The apparent constants are Vmax,app = Vmax/α′ and Km,app = Km·α/α′. If Ki = Ki′, then α = α′, so Km,app = Km while Vmax drops by α′. Effectively the inhibitor just lowers the amount of working enzyme.

That is why pure noncompetitive inhibition looks like having less enzyme: the Lineweaver–Burk lines meet on the x-axis. Many textbooks use noncompetitive loosely for any inhibitor binding outside the active site; the MCAT usually means the pure, equal-affinity case.

x1A_163.trap: Noncompetitive means the inhibitor binds E and ES equally, so Km stays put; binding only ES is uncompetitive.
x1A_163.eli: A noncompetitive inhibitor is like jamming the machine itself, not blocking the door. Fewer working enzymes means lower Vmax; the ones that still work like substrate just as much.
mem: Noncompetitive: binds E and ES equally; Vmax DOWN, Km SAME.
Competitive inhibitors can be overcome with more substrate; noncompetitive cannot.
It does not bind at the active site.

ox: Correct. An inhibitor that binds only ES is uncompetitive. It traps ES as an inactive ESI complex, so Vmax falls. At the same time, removing ES pulls the E + S ⇌ ES equilibrium toward ES, so the enzyme looks as if it binds substrate more tightly and apparent Km falls. Both are divided by the same factor α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′, so Km/Vmax is unchanged and the Lineweaver–Burk lines are parallel.

Incorrect. Km rising with Vmax unchanged is competitive inhibition, in which the inhibitor binds only free enzyme. Substrate and inhibitor compete for E, so extra substrate restores the full rate. An inhibitor that requires substrate to be bound first cannot be overcome that way.

Incorrect. Unchanged Km with lower Vmax is pure noncompetitive inhibition, where the inhibitor binds E and ES with equal affinity. When the inhibitor binds only ES, the binding is not symmetrical, so Km changes too, decreasing rather than staying constant.

Incorrect. Km up and Vmax down is mixed inhibition in which the inhibitor prefers free enzyme (Ki < Ki′). Binding E would make substrate binding look weaker. An inhibitor that binds only ES has the opposite effect on Km, which is why uncompetitive inhibitors lower Km.

p: Reversible inhibitors are classified by which enzyme forms they bind. Competitive inhibitors bind only free enzyme (E), usually at the active site, so they raise apparent Km but can be outcompeted by substrate, leaving Vmax unchanged. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both Km and Vmax by the same factor. Mixed inhibitors bind both E and ES; when they bind both equally the special case is called pure noncompetitive, which lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged.

Uncompetitive inhibitors need substrate bound first, often because the inhibitor's site forms only after substrate binds. Since they bind ES, both apparent constants are divided by α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′: Km,app = Km/α′ and Vmax,app = Vmax/α′. The ratio Km/Vmax, the slope of the Lineweaver–Burk line, is unchanged, so the lines are parallel.

The counterintuitive part is that an inhibitor makes Km smaller. Explain it with Le Châtelier's principle: draining ES into ESI pulls more E and S together. Uncompetitive inhibitors are most effective at high [S], the opposite of competitive inhibitors.

x1A_164.trap: Binding only ES LOWERS Km (Le Châtelier), even though the substance is an inhibitor.

ox: Incorrect. Km and Vmax both decreasing is what a mixed inhibitor does when it prefers the ES complex (Ki′ < Ki), or what an uncompetitive inhibitor does. Preferential binding to ES drains ES and makes substrate binding look tighter. Here the inhibitor prefers free enzyme, which pushes Km the other way.

Incorrect. Km rising with Vmax unchanged is the purely competitive pattern, which requires that the inhibitor cannot bind ES at all. A mixed inhibitor binds ES too, even if weakly, and an inhibitor bound to ES cannot be displaced by more substrate. So Vmax must fall at least somewhat.

Incorrect. If neither parameter changed, the compound would not be acting as an inhibitor. Any inhibitor that can bind the ES complex lowers Vmax, because no amount of substrate removes it from ESI. Only an inhibitor that binds neither form, or a very low [I], would leave both unchanged.

Correct. In mixed inhibition Km,app = Km·α/α′ and Vmax,app = Vmax/α′, where α = 1 + [I]/Ki (binding to E) and α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′ (binding to ES). Binding E much more tightly means Ki is small, so α > α′ and Km rises. Because the inhibitor can also bind ES, α′ > 1 and Vmax falls. The Lineweaver–Burk lines cross to the left of the y-axis, above the x-axis.

p: Reversible inhibitors are classified by which enzyme forms they bind. Competitive inhibitors bind only free enzyme (E), usually at the active site, so they raise apparent Km but can be outcompeted by substrate, leaving Vmax unchanged. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both Km and Vmax by the same factor. Mixed inhibitors bind both E and ES; when they bind both equally the special case is called pure noncompetitive, which lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged.

Mixed inhibitors bind a site away from the active site and can attach to both E and ES, but with different affinities. Every mixed inhibitor lowers Vmax (Vmax/α′). Its effect on Km depends on which form it prefers: Km,app = Km·α/α′. Preferring E (α > α′) raises Km; preferring ES (α′ > α) lowers Km; equal preference leaves Km unchanged (pure noncompetitive).

On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, mixed inhibitor lines cross left of the y-axis: above the x-axis if E is preferred, below if ES is preferred. A quick rule: an inhibitor that likes free enzyme behaves partly like a competitive one (Km up); one that likes ES behaves partly like an uncompetitive one (Km down).

fx.w: α = 1 + [I]/Ki (inhibitor binding free enzyme) and α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′ (inhibitor binding ES). Both factors are ≥ 1; the larger one decides whether Km rises or falls.

x1A_165.trap: Every inhibitor that can bind ES lowers Vmax; which form it prefers decides whether Km goes up or down.

ox: Incorrect. Ethanol is an ordinary substrate of alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH): it binds reversibly, is oxidized to acetaldehyde, and leaves. Nothing in this treatment destroys the enzyme, and destroying ADH would not be needed. Covalent, irreversible inactivation is what suicide inhibitors do, and it is not how ethanol works.

Correct. Methanol itself is relatively harmless; the danger comes from ADH converting it to formaldehyde, which is then oxidized to formic acid, causing acidosis and optic nerve damage. Ethanol binds the same active site, and with a much lower Km for ADH, at high levels it occupies most of the enzyme. For methanol this acts like competitive inhibition: methanol's apparent Km rises, toxic products form slowly, and unchanged methanol is excreted or removed by dialysis.

Incorrect. No human enzyme converts methanol into glucose. Methanol is a one-carbon alcohol; its metabolism runs through formaldehyde to formic acid, not toward sugars. Gluconeogenesis builds glucose from pyruvate, lactate, glycerol and some amino acids, not from methanol.

Incorrect. Ethanol binds the active site, since it is a substrate, not an allosteric site. And raising Vmax would speed up formation of formaldehyde and formic acid, making poisoning worse. The goal of treatment is to slow methanol's metabolism, not accelerate it.

concept.t: Competing substrates act as competitive inhibitors
p: A competitive inhibitor binds the free enzyme at the active site and prevents substrate binding. A second substrate of the same enzyme does exactly that for the first substrate: while the active site holds ethanol, it cannot hold methanol. The effect on methanol's kinetics is a rise in apparent Km with no change in Vmax, so a large excess of ethanol strongly slows methanol oxidation.

In methanol (and ethylene glycol) poisoning, the parent alcohol is not very toxic; its oxidation products are (formate for methanol, glycolate and oxalate for ethylene glycol). Blocking ADH buys time to remove the alcohol. Today fomepizole, a direct competitive inhibitor of ADH, is preferred over ethanol, but the kinetic principle is the same.
On the MCAT, recognize that competitive inhibition is overcome by high substrate: here the roles are reversed, and the high concentration of the competing substrate wins the active site.

fig.cap: Methanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) to formaldehyde and then to toxic formic acid. A high ethanol level occupies the ADH active site, slowing the methanol step.
fig.alt: Pathway methanol to formaldehyde to formic acid with ADH and ALDH arrows; below, ethanol binding the ADH active site and being converted to acetaldehyde; a note explains that ethanol acts as a competitive inhibitor for methanol.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; pathway facts from standard pharmacology and biochemistry texts.

x1A_166.trap: A second substrate competing for the same active site behaves exactly like a competitive inhibitor.

ox: Incorrect. Km doubling with Vmax unchanged is the competitive pattern, in which an inhibitor reversibly competes with substrate for the active site and can be outcompeted by high [S]. An irreversibly inactivated enzyme is simply gone from the pool; it does not compete with anything, so substrate affinity of the remaining enzymes is unaffected.

Correct. Vmax = kcat[E]T, so if half of the enzyme molecules are permanently inactivated, the working [E]T and therefore Vmax are halved. The remaining molecules are completely normal, with the same substrate affinity and turnover, so they still reach half of their (new) maximum at the same [S]: Km is unchanged. Kinetically it looks like simply using half as much enzyme.

Incorrect. Halving both Km and Vmax is the uncompetitive pattern, produced by a reversible inhibitor that binds only the ES complex and shifts the binding equilibrium. Permanently removing enzyme molecules does not change how the remaining ones bind substrate, so Km has no reason to fall.

Incorrect. If half the enzyme no longer works, the sample cannot reach the same maximal rate: Vmax depends directly on the concentration of active enzyme. Only Km, an intrinsic property of each active molecule, stays the same.

p: Irreversible inhibitors form covalent bonds with (or otherwise permanently destroy) enzyme molecules. Examples include aspirin acetylating cyclooxygenase, organophosphate nerve agents phosphorylating acetylcholinesterase, and penicillin acylating bacterial transpeptidases. Each inactivated molecule is removed from the working pool.

Because Vmax = kcat[E]T, losing active enzyme lowers Vmax in proportion. Km and kcat are properties of each individual active site, so they do not change. On a graph this mimics pure noncompetitive inhibition (lower plateau, same half-saturation point), but unlike a reversible inhibitor, dialysis or dilution will not restore activity; only making new enzyme does.
The same logic answers questions about adding enzyme: doubling [E]T doubles Vmax and leaves Km unchanged.

fx.w: kcat = turnover number per active site (s⁻¹); [E]T = concentration of active enzyme. Km does not depend on [E]T.

fig.cap: Inactivating half of the enzyme halves Vmax (100 → 50), but both curves reach half of their own maximum at the same [S], so Km is unchanged.
fig.alt: Two hyperbolic curves: blue rising toward 100 and red rising toward 50; dashed lines show both reach half of their maximum at [S] = 2.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with illustrative Km = 2 and Vmax = 100 or 50.

x1A_167.trap: Less active enzyme lowers Vmax only; Km is a per-molecule property and does not depend on enzyme amount.

ox: Incorrect. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged, so it reduces the rate by the same fraction at every [S]. Here the inhibited rate is 52% of control at 1 μM, 81% at 10 μM and 97% at 100 μM, so the fractional inhibition shrinks as [S] rises. That rules out noncompetitive inhibition.

Incorrect. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds the ES complex and lowers Vmax, so its effect does not disappear at high [S]; in fact its fractional effect is largest at high [S], where most enzyme is in the ES form. In these data the inhibitor barely matters at 100 μM, the opposite pattern.

Incorrect. An irreversible inhibitor removes active enzyme, which lowers Vmax. The rate at saturating substrate would then stay well below the control, no matter how much substrate is added. At 100 μM the inhibited rate (95) almost matches the control (98), so the full catalytic capacity is still there.

Correct. The inhibitor cuts the rate roughly in half at low [S] (33 → 17) but has almost no effect at high [S] (98 → 95), so high substrate overcomes it and Vmax is unchanged. The data fit Vmax = 100 μM/s with Km = 2 μM without inhibitor and an apparent Km = 5 μM with it. A rise in Km with no change in Vmax is competitive inhibition.

concept.t: Recognizing competitive inhibition from rate data
p: Reversible inhibitors are classified by which enzyme forms they bind. Competitive inhibitors bind only free enzyme (E), usually at the active site, so they raise apparent Km but can be outcompeted by substrate, leaving Vmax unchanged. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both Km and Vmax by the same factor. Mixed inhibitors bind both E and ES; when they bind both equally the special case is called pure noncompetitive, which lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged.

With rate data, compare the inhibited rate to the control at low and high [S]. If the inhibitor's effect vanishes at high [S], Vmax is unchanged: competitive. If the rate drops by the same fraction at every [S]: pure noncompetitive. If the effect is largest at high [S]: uncompetitive. If the plateau is permanently lowered and not restored by dilution: irreversible.

You can also check by fitting: 100 × 1/(2 + 1) = 33, 100 × 10/12 = 83, 100 × 100/102 = 98 without inhibitor; 100 × 1/(5 + 1) = 17, 100 × 10/15 = 67, 100 × 100/105 = 95 with inhibitor. Only Km changed.

steps: Ratio inhibited/control: 17/33 ≈ 0.52 at 1 μM; 67/83 ≈ 0.81 at 10 μM; 95/98 ≈ 0.97 at 100 μM.
The inhibition fades as [S] rises, so it is overcome by substrate and Vmax is unchanged.
Fit check: control data match Vmax = 100, Km = 2 μM; inhibited data match Vmax = 100, Km,app = 5 μM.
Same Vmax, higher Km: competitive inhibition.

fig.cap: The data in the question plotted on a log [S] axis. The inhibited rate is 52% of control at 1 μM but 97% at 100 μM; both curves approach the same Vmax.
fig.alt: Two sigmoid-looking curves on a log x-axis, blue control and red inhibited, with data points at 1, 10 and 100 μM labelled 33 vs 17, 83 vs 67 and 98 vs 95; both approach 100.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); points are the data in the question, curves fit with Vmax = 100 μM/s and Km = 2 or 5 μM.

x1A_168.trap: If the inhibitor's effect disappears at high [S], Vmax is unchanged: competitive.

ox: Correct. Both parameters changed: Vmax fell (100 → 60 μM/s), so the inhibitor can bind the ES complex, and Km rose (2 → 5 μM), so it also binds free enzyme, and more tightly. Using Vmax,app = Vmax/α′ gives α′ = 100/60 ≈ 1.7, and Km,app = Km·α/α′ gives α = 5 × 1.7/2 ≈ 4.2. Since α > α′, the inhibitor prefers free E: mixed inhibition.

Incorrect. A competitive inhibitor raises Km but leaves Vmax unchanged, because high substrate can always displace it from the active site. Here Vmax dropped by 40%, which means some inhibitor is bound to ES where substrate cannot displace it. The rise in Km alone would fit competitive, but the Vmax drop does not.

Incorrect. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only ES and lowers both Km and Vmax by the same factor. Here Km went up, not down, so this cannot be uncompetitive. A rising Km requires the inhibitor to bind free enzyme.

Incorrect. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds E and ES with equal affinity, so Vmax falls while Km stays the same. Here Km changed from 2 to 5 μM, so binding is not equal. Pure noncompetitive inhibition is the special case of mixed inhibition with Ki = Ki′.

concept.t: Identifying mixed inhibition from parameter changes
p: Reversible inhibitors are classified by which enzyme forms they bind. Competitive inhibitors bind only free enzyme (E), usually at the active site, so they raise apparent Km but can be outcompeted by substrate, leaving Vmax unchanged. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both Km and Vmax by the same factor. Mixed inhibitors bind both E and ES; when they bind both equally the special case is called pure noncompetitive, which lowers Vmax but leaves Km unchanged.

Use a two-question check. Did Vmax change? If yes, the inhibitor binds ES (uncompetitive, mixed or noncompetitive). Did Km change, and which way? Unchanged means pure noncompetitive, down means the inhibitor favors ES (uncompetitive or mixed favoring ES), up means it favors E (competitive if Vmax is unchanged, mixed if Vmax fell).
Formally, Vmax,app = Vmax/α′ and Km,app = Km·α/α′, with α = 1 + [I]/Ki and α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′. Computing α and α′ from data tells you which form the inhibitor prefers.

fx.w: α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′ reflects binding to ES; α = 1 + [I]/Ki reflects binding to free E. If α > α′ the inhibitor prefers free enzyme and Km rises.

steps: Vmax fell (100 → 60), so the inhibitor binds ES: α′ = 100/60 ≈ 1.67.
α (4.2) > α′ (1.67): the inhibitor binds free E more tightly than ES.
Both parameters changed, Km upward: mixed inhibition.

fig.cap: The parameters from the question: without inhibitor Km = 2 μM and Vmax = 100 μM/s; with inhibitor Km = 5 μM and Vmax = 60 μM/s. Both change, the mark of mixed inhibition.
fig.alt: Two hyperbolic curves, blue approaching 100 and red approaching 60; dashed lines mark half-maximal points at 2 μM and 5 μM.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with the Km and Vmax values in the question.

fig.cap: The inhibitor can bind free enzyme (EI, constant Ki), the enzyme–substrate complex (ESI, constant Ki′), or both. Which forms it binds sets how apparent Km and Vmax change.
fig.alt: Reaction scheme E plus S to ES to E plus P, with E binding inhibitor to form EI and ES binding inhibitor to form ESI; below, a table listing five binding patterns with their effects on apparent Km, apparent Vmax and Lineweaver–Burk lines.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; relationships from the standard general (mixed) inhibition model as presented in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

x1A_169.trap: If BOTH Km and Vmax change and Km goes up, think mixed (favoring E), not competitive.

ox: Incorrect. 1 μM comes from dividing Km by 3 instead of multiplying. That would mean the enzyme appears to bind substrate more tightly in the presence of a competitive inhibitor, which is backwards: the inhibitor occupies some free enzyme, so more substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax.

Incorrect. 3 μM is the uninhibited Km, which assumes the inhibitor has no effect on Km. That would be true for pure noncompetitive inhibition (Km unchanged, Vmax lower), but a competitive inhibitor always raises apparent Km while leaving Vmax unchanged.

Incorrect. 6 μM uses a factor of [I]/Ki = 2 instead of 1 + [I]/Ki = 3. The 1 in the factor accounts for the free enzyme that is not inhibitor-bound; without it, the formula would wrongly predict Km,app = 0 when [I] = 0. Always check that the factor equals 1 when no inhibitor is present.

Correct. For a competitive inhibitor, Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). With [I] = 2Ki, the factor α = 1 + 2 = 3, so Km,app = 3 μM × 3 = 9 μM. Vmax is unchanged, so the enzyme still reaches the same maximum rate, but it needs three times as much substrate to reach half of it.

concept.t: Apparent Km with a competitive inhibitor
p: A competitive inhibitor binds free enzyme at the active site, setting up a competition between substrate and inhibitor. The free enzyme is split between E and EI, which multiplies the substrate needed for half-saturation by α = 1 + [I]/Ki, where Ki is the inhibitor's dissociation constant. So Km,app = αKm, and Vmax stays the same because at very high [S] the substrate wins.
Benchmarks: [I] = Ki doubles Km (α = 2); [I] = 2Ki triples it; [I] = 9Ki multiplies it by 10. Ki has units of concentration, and a smaller Ki means a more potent inhibitor.
The common mistake is to drop the 1 and use [I]/Ki alone. Always check: with no inhibitor, α must be 1 and Km,app must equal Km.

fx.w: Applies to competitive inhibition. [I] = inhibitor concentration; Ki = dissociation constant of the EI complex (same units as [I]). Vmax is unchanged.

fig.cap: With the competitive inhibitor at 2 Ki, the curve reaches Vmax/2 at 9 μM instead of 3 μM, while the plateau (Vmax) stays the same.
fig.alt: Two hyperbolic curves of v over Vmax, blue reaching one-half at 3 μM and red reaching one-half at 9 μM; a red tick at 6 μM marks the wrong factor of 2.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with Km = 3 μM and Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki).

x1A_170.trap: The factor is 1 + [I]/Ki, not [I]/Ki: at [I] = 2Ki, Km triples.
x1A_170.eli: A competitive inhibitor makes the enzyme look 'pickier', so you need more substrate to reach half speed. Km goes up, Vmax stays the same.
mem: Competitive: apparent Km = Km(1 + [I]/Ki).
Vmax is unchanged.
[I] = 2·Ki multiplies Km by 3.

fm.f: Km(app) = Km × (1 + [I]/Ki), where Km = normal Km (3 μM), [I] = inhibitor concentration, Ki = inhibitor binding constant
fm.why: We multiply Km by (1 + [I]/Ki) because the inhibitor competes with substrate for the same site.

ox: Incorrect. A straight line through the origin would mean the rate keeps rising in proportion to [S] forever, so the enzyme would never saturate. Every enzyme has a finite number of active sites and a maximum turnover, so both Michaelis–Menten and allosteric enzymes level off at Vmax. A line is only the low-[S] approximation of a Michaelis–Menten curve.

Incorrect. Cooperative enzymes still speed up as substrate rises; cooperativity actually makes the rise steeper in the middle range. A rate that falls with more substrate would indicate substrate inhibition, an unusual special case unrelated to cooperative subunits.

Correct. In positive cooperativity, substrate binding to one subunit shifts the other subunits toward the high-affinity R state. At low [S], few sites are filled and affinity is low, so the curve starts flat; once binding begins, affinity rises and the rate climbs steeply; finally it saturates at Vmax. The result is an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve, described by the Hill equation with n > 1, rather than the hyperbola of Michaelis–Menten kinetics.

Incorrect. If the plot were identical to a hyperbola, the subunits would be binding independently (Hill coefficient n = 1) and there would be no cooperativity. Cooperative interaction between active sites is exactly what changes the shape from hyperbolic to sigmoidal, so the two plots cannot be the same.

p: Allosteric enzymes are usually multi-subunit proteins whose activity is changed by molecules binding at sites other than the active site (allosteric sites). Many switch between a low-affinity, less active T (tense) state and a high-affinity, more active R (relaxed) state. In positive cooperativity, binding of substrate to one subunit makes the other subunits bind more easily.

Cooperativity gives a sigmoidal v versus [S] curve, flat at low [S], steep around the half-maximal point (called K0.5 rather than Km), and saturating at Vmax. The steep middle acts like a switch: a small change in [S] causes a large change in activity. The Hill coefficient n measures cooperativity: n = 1 none (hyperbolic), n > 1 positive, n < 1 negative.

Hemoglobin is the classic cooperative protein (O₂ saturation curve, n ≈ 2.8), and aspartate transcarbamoylase and phosphofructokinase-1 are classic cooperative enzymes. Michaelis–Menten equations and Lineweaver–Burk lines do not strictly apply to them.

fig.cap: A Michaelis–Menten enzyme gives a hyperbola; a cooperative allosteric enzyme with the same half-maximal [S] gives a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve that is flat at low [S] and steep in the middle.
fig.alt: Blue hyperbolic curve and purple S-shaped curve of v over Vmax against substrate concentration, crossing at the half-maximal point at [S] = 5.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation v/Vmax = [S]ⁿ/(K0.5ⁿ + [S]ⁿ) with n = 1 and n = 2.8 and K0.5 = 5 (illustrative).

x1A_171.trap: Cooperative enzymes give an S-shaped curve but still saturate; they are not described by a simple hyperbola.

ox: Incorrect. A molecule that binds the active site and is converted into product is a substrate, not an allosteric activator. Allosteric activators bind a separate regulatory site and are not chemically changed by the enzyme; they leave and can act again.

Incorrect. Shifting the T ⇌ R equilibrium toward T (the low-affinity state) moves the curve to the right, so more substrate is needed for the same rate. That is what an allosteric inhibitor does, for example ATP on phosphofructokinase-1 or CTP on aspartate transcarbamoylase. An activator does the opposite.

Incorrect. ΔG is fixed by the free energies of reactants and products, not by the enzyme. Activators, inhibitors and enzymes themselves change only the rate (by changing the activation energy or substrate binding), never the equilibrium constant or the reaction's ΔG.

Correct. An allosteric activator binds preferentially to the R (relaxed, high-affinity) state and stabilizes it. That shifts the T ⇌ R equilibrium toward R, so substrate binds more readily and the sigmoidal v versus [S] curve moves left: K0.5 falls and less substrate is needed to reach half of Vmax. Vmax itself often stays the same in this type of regulation; the enzyme simply responds at lower [S].

p: Allosteric enzymes are usually multi-subunit proteins whose activity is changed by molecules binding at sites other than the active site (allosteric sites). Many switch between a low-affinity, less active T (tense) state and a high-affinity, more active R (relaxed) state. Substrate and activators bind the R state better; inhibitors bind the T state better.

By mass action, any molecule that binds one state preferentially shifts the T ⇌ R equilibrium toward that state. Activators favor R and shift the sigmoidal curve left (lower K0.5, often less sigmoidal); inhibitors favor T and shift it right (higher K0.5, more sigmoidal). In K-type regulation Vmax is unchanged; some enzymes instead show V-type effects on Vmax.

Examples: AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate phosphofructokinase-1 while ATP and citrate inhibit it; ATP activates and CTP inhibits aspartate transcarbamoylase. Remember that regulators never change ΔG or Keq.

fig.cap: A sigmoidal enzyme with no effector (black), with an activator that favors R (green, shifted left) and with an inhibitor that favors T (red, shifted right). Vmax is the same in all three.
fig.alt: Three S-shaped curves of v over Vmax against [S]; green half-maximal at 2.5, black at 5, red at 10; arrows show the activator shifting the curve left and the inhibitor shifting it right.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation v/Vmax = [S]ⁿ/(K0.5ⁿ + [S]ⁿ) with n = 2.5 and K0.5 = 2.5, 5 and 10 (illustrative).

x1A_172.trap: Activator → R state → curve shifts LEFT; inhibitor → T state → curve shifts RIGHT. ΔG never changes.

ox: Incorrect. Feedforward activation is when an early metabolite in a pathway activates an enzyme further down the pathway, preparing it for incoming flux. The classic example is fructose-1,6-bisphosphate activating pyruvate kinase in glycolysis. In the question, the regulating molecule is the final product acting on the first enzyme, which is the opposite direction and the opposite sign.

Incorrect. Zymogen activation is the conversion of an inactive precursor protein (a zymogen or proenzyme) into an active enzyme by cutting specific peptide bonds, as with trypsinogen to trypsin. It switches an enzyme on, irreversibly, and does not involve a pathway product inhibiting an earlier step.

Correct. Feedback inhibition (negative feedback) occurs when the end product of a pathway binds an allosteric site on the enzyme of the first committed step and slows it. When the product accumulates, the whole pathway slows at its entry point, saving material and energy and preventing intermediates from piling up; when the product is used up, inhibition is relieved. Examples: isoleucine inhibiting threonine deaminase and CTP inhibiting aspartate transcarbamoylase.

Incorrect. Substrate-level phosphorylation is a way of making ATP, by transferring a phosphate directly from a high-energy substrate to ADP, as by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase in glycolysis or succinyl-CoA synthetase in the citric acid cycle. It is an energy-producing reaction, not a regulatory mechanism.

p: In feedback inhibition, the end product of a metabolic pathway inhibits an enzyme near the start of that pathway, usually the first committed step (the first irreversible reaction unique to the pathway). The product typically acts as an allosteric inhibitor, binding a regulatory site distinct from the active site.

Controlling the first committed step is efficient: it stops the whole pathway before any intermediates are made, and it does not starve other pathways that share earlier metabolites. In branched pathways, each end product often inhibits the first step of its own branch.

Distinguish feedback inhibition (late product → early enzyme, inhibitory) from feedforward activation (early metabolite → later enzyme, activating). Both are fast, reversible allosteric controls, unlike slower changes in gene expression.

fig.cap: A linear pathway A → B → C → D → end product. The end product binds the first enzyme (E1, the committed step) and inhibits it.
fig.alt: Five boxes A, B, C, D and end product connected by arrows labelled E1 to E4; a red dashed arc runs from the end product back to the E1 arrow ending in a blocking bar.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

x1A_173.trap: End product inhibiting the FIRST committed step is feedback inhibition; feedforward goes the other way and activates.

ox: Incorrect. Subunits changing one at a time as each binds ligand is the sequential (Koshland–Némethy–Filmer, KNF) model. It allows hybrid molecules with some subunits in T and some in R, and binding to one subunit induces neighbors to change. The concerted model forbids such mixed states.

Correct. In the concerted (Monod–Wyman–Changeux, MWC) model, the whole oligomer exists in either an all-T or an all-R conformation, preserving symmetry. The R state binds ligand more tightly, so each binding event shifts the T ⇌ R equilibrium toward R for the whole molecule, raising the affinity of the remaining empty sites. That produces cooperativity without any mixed T/R molecules.

Incorrect. Both models rely on conformational change: cooperativity arises precisely because subunits switch between low-affinity T and high-affinity R conformations. A protein whose subunits never changed shape would show independent binding and a hyperbolic curve.

Incorrect. The concerted model does not distinguish catalytic and regulatory subunits; it treats all subunits as switching together. Enzymes such as aspartate transcarbamoylase do have separate catalytic and regulatory subunits, and in them both kinds change conformation during the T to R transition.

concept.t: Concerted vs sequential models of cooperativity
p: Allosteric enzymes are usually multi-subunit proteins whose activity is changed by molecules binding at sites other than the active site (allosteric sites). Many switch between a low-affinity, less active T (tense) state and a high-affinity, more active R (relaxed) state. Two classic models explain how binding at one site raises affinity at others.

Concerted (MWC): all subunits are in the same state at once, either all T or all R. The equilibrium between the two whole-molecule states shifts toward R as more ligand binds, because R binds ligand better. Symmetry is conserved, and mixed T/R molecules are not allowed. This model explains positive cooperativity and heterotropic effects well.

Sequential (KNF): each subunit changes conformation when it binds ligand, and that change alters the affinity of its neighbors. Hybrid states exist. This model can also explain negative cooperativity, which the simple concerted model cannot. Real proteins such as hemoglobin show features of both.

fig.cap: Concerted model: a tetramer is either all T (squares) or all R (circles); binding shifts the balance. Sequential model: subunits switch from T to R one by one as they bind ligand, so mixed molecules exist.
fig.alt: Top panel shows pairs of tetramers with zero to four bound ligands, each an all-square T form in equilibrium with an all-circle R form. Bottom panel shows a series of tetramers in which one more subunit becomes a circle with each ligand bound.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic of the Monod–Wyman–Changeux and Koshland–Némethy–Filmer models.

x1A_174.trap: Concerted = all subunits switch together (no hybrids); sequential = one at a time (hybrids allowed).

ox: Correct. An allosteric effect is homotropic when the effector molecule is the same as the substrate (or ligand) of the protein. Here substrate binding at one active site raises the affinity of the other active sites, which is positive homotropic cooperativity. It produces a sigmoidal v versus [S] curve; O₂ binding to hemoglobin is the classic example.

Incorrect. A heterotropic effect is caused by a molecule different from the substrate, binding at a separate regulatory site. Examples include 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, H⁺ and CO₂ lowering hemoglobin's O₂ affinity, or AMP and ATP acting on phosphofructokinase-1. In the question the effector is the substrate itself, so the effect is homotropic.

Incorrect. Competitive inhibition is when a molecule (usually a substrate analog) occupies the active site and blocks substrate from binding, raising apparent Km. In the question, substrate binding at one site helps other sites bind substrate, which is cooperativity, the opposite of inhibition.

Incorrect. Covalent modification means attaching or removing a chemical group by forming or breaking a covalent bond, for example phosphorylation by a kinase or removal by a phosphatase. Substrate binding at an active site is noncovalent and reversible, so it is not covalent modification.

p: Allosteric enzymes are usually multi-subunit proteins whose activity is changed by molecules binding at sites other than the active site (allosteric sites). Many switch between a low-affinity, less active T (tense) state and a high-affinity, more active R (relaxed) state. Effects are named by what the effector is.

Homotropic effects: the effector is the protein's own substrate or ligand, so binding at one active site changes binding at the others (cooperativity). Positive homotropic effects make the binding curve sigmoidal. Heterotropic effects: the effector is a different molecule binding a different (regulatory) site, and it can activate or inhibit.

Hemoglobin shows both: O₂ is a homotropic effector (cooperative binding), while 2,3-BPG, H⁺ and CO₂ are heterotropic effectors that shift the curve right (Bohr effect). The prefixes help: homo = same molecule, hetero = different molecule.

fig.cap: Homotropic: substrate bound at one active site raises affinity at another active site. Heterotropic: a different molecule binds a regulatory site and changes substrate binding.
fig.alt: Left panel: a two-subunit enzyme with substrate bound in site 1 and an arrow to site 2 labelled affinity up. Right panel: an enzyme with a substrate at the active site and a triangle effector at a separate regulatory site, with an arrow between them.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic.

x1A_175.trap: Homo = the substrate itself is the effector; hetero = a different molecule.

ox: Incorrect. Zymogens are inactive precursors: their active sites are blocked or not yet properly formed, so they digest essentially nothing until a specific peptide bond is cut. Making a protease as a zymogen deliberately slows it down until it reaches the right place, the opposite of digesting faster.

Incorrect. Pancreatic juice drains through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum, not the stomach, and it is alkaline (rich in HCO₃⁻) to neutralize stomach acid. The zymogen form is not acid protection. Pepsinogen, the stomach's zymogen, is actually activated by acid, which shows the logic runs the other way.

Correct. Active proteases would hydrolyze the proteins of the acinar cells that make them, and the ducts that carry them. Secreting them as inactive zymogens (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) means activation happens only in the duodenum, where enteropeptidase on the brush border cuts trypsinogen to trypsin. Premature activation inside the pancreas is a cause of acute pancreatitis.

Incorrect. Zymogens are activated by proteolysis, the cleavage of specific peptide bonds that rearranges the protein into its active shape, not by binding a coenzyme. Pancreatic serine proteases need no coenzyme at all. Requiring a cofactor is how some other enzymes (apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme) are controlled.

p: A zymogen (proenzyme) is an inactive enzyme precursor that becomes active when specific peptide bonds are cleaved. Cleavage changes the protein's conformation, typically forming the substrate-binding pocket or the oxyanion hole of the active site. Names often end in -ogen or begin with pro-.

Digestive proteases are made as zymogens to protect the cells and ducts that produce them. Pancreatic zymogens are activated in the duodenum, starting with enteropeptidase (enterokinase) converting trypsinogen to trypsin; pepsinogen in the stomach is activated by HCl and then by pepsin. Blood clotting factors and caspases (apoptosis) are other zymogen cascades.

Zymogen activation is irreversible, so these enzymes are switched off by protein inhibitors (such as pancreatic trypsin inhibitor) or by degradation. Premature activation inside the pancreas causes pancreatitis.

fig.cap: The pancreas makes inactive zymogens. In the duodenum, enteropeptidase on the brush border cuts trypsinogen to trypsin, and trypsin then cleaves trypsinogen and the other zymogens.
fig.alt: Left box, pancreas, with trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase. Right box, duodenum: enteropeptidase cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin; trypsin arrows lead back to trypsinogen and on to chymotrypsin, elastase and carboxypeptidase.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; facts from standard physiology and biochemistry texts (e.g. OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, chemical digestion).

x1A_176.trap: Zymogens prevent self-digestion of the gland; they are activated by cleavage, not by cofactors or acid (except pepsinogen).

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.7 Chemical Digestion and Absorption: A Closer Look

ox: Correct. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase), anchored on the duodenal brush border, has one main target: it cuts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin is itself a protease, and it cleaves and activates more trypsinogen (autoactivation) and the other pancreatic zymogens: chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase. One initial step therefore sets off an amplifying cascade.

Incorrect. Enteropeptidase is highly specific for a sequence in trypsinogen and does not efficiently activate the other zymogens. If it activated each one separately, trypsin would not be the master switch, and loss of trypsin activity would not block the others, yet it does. The design relies on trypsin to amplify the signal.

Incorrect. Zymogen activation happens by cleavage of specific peptide bonds, which permanently changes the protein's structure. Trypsin does not bind to an allosteric site on the other proteases; it cuts their precursor forms. Allosteric activation is reversible and noncovalent, while zymogen activation is covalent and irreversible.

Incorrect. Activation by low pH describes pepsinogen in the stomach, which partially unfolds in HCl and cleaves itself to pepsin. The duodenum is close to neutral because pancreatic juice is rich in bicarbonate, and the pancreatic zymogens require trypsin rather than acid to become active.

p: Pancreatic proteases are secreted as zymogens and must be activated in the small intestine. The trigger is enteropeptidase, a brush-border enzyme of the duodenum, which converts trypsinogen to trypsin by removing a short N-terminal peptide.

Trypsin then acts as the common activator: it cleaves trypsinogen (positive feedback), chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase, and activates prophospholipase A₂ (a lipase precursor). Because one enzyme molecule activates many others, the response is amplified, the same logic as the blood-clotting cascade.

Contrast the stomach: pepsinogen is activated by acid and by pepsin itself. On the MCAT, link enteropeptidase → trypsin → everything else, and remember that zymogen activation is irreversible cleavage, not allosteric binding.

fig.cap: The pancreas makes inactive zymogens. In the duodenum, enteropeptidase on the brush border cuts trypsinogen to trypsin, and trypsin then cleaves trypsinogen and the other zymogens.
fig.alt: Left box, pancreas, with trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase and procarboxypeptidase. Right box, duodenum: enteropeptidase cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin; trypsin arrows lead back to trypsinogen and on to chymotrypsin, elastase and carboxypeptidase.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; facts from standard physiology and biochemistry texts (e.g. OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, chemical digestion).

x1A_177.trap: Enteropeptidase activates only trypsinogen; trypsin then activates all the others.

ref.t: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e, 23.7 Chemical Digestion and Absorption: A Closer Look

ox: Incorrect. Phosphorylation is covalent, but it is readily reversible: kinases add phosphate groups to serine, threonine or tyrosine residues using ATP, and phosphatases remove them by hydrolysis. That on/off pairing is what makes phosphorylation such a useful signaling switch, for example in glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase control.

Incorrect. Allosteric inhibitors bind noncovalently through hydrogen bonds, ionic and hydrophobic interactions, and they dissociate when their concentration falls. Activity returns as soon as the inhibitor leaves, which lets the cell adjust enzyme activity within milliseconds to changing metabolite levels.

Incorrect. A competitive inhibitor such as a substrate analog binds the active site noncovalently and reversibly. It can be outcompeted by raising [S] or removed by dilution or dialysis, which is why Vmax is unchanged in competitive inhibition. Only irreversible (covalent) inhibitors behave differently, and the choice does not describe one.

Correct. Zymogen activation works by cleaving one or more peptide bonds, which rearranges the protein into its active conformation. The cell has no mechanism to re-form those bonds and restore the zymogen, so the activation is irreversible. The active enzyme is turned off only by binding protein inhibitors or by being degraded.

p: Cells regulate enzymes in several ways. Allosteric regulation and reversible inhibition are noncovalent and act within milliseconds. Covalent modification (phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation) is covalent but reversible because separate enzymes add and remove the group. Proteolytic activation of zymogens is covalent and irreversible.

Because zymogen activation cannot be undone, these enzymes need separate off switches: protein inhibitors such as pancreatic trypsin inhibitor or antithrombin, and degradation. Irreversible activation suits processes that should run to completion once started, such as digestion, blood clotting and apoptosis (caspases).
Do not confuse irreversible regulation with irreversible inhibitors (such as aspirin or organophosphates), which covalently inactivate enzymes rather than activate them.

fig.cap: Phosphorylation, allosteric inhibition and competitive inhibition all run both ways. Zymogen activation is a one-way cut.
fig.alt: Four rows. Phosphorylation, allosteric inhibitor and competitive inhibitor each show double arrows between two states; zymogen activation shows a single red arrow from zymogen to active enzyme plus peptide.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

x1A_178.trap: Covalent does not mean irreversible: phosphorylation is undone by phosphatases; only proteolysis cannot be undone.

ox: Incorrect. By definition, isozymes (isoenzymes) catalyze the same chemical reaction. Two enzymes that catalyze different reactions are simply different enzymes, even if they are related in structure or evolution.

Correct. Isozymes are distinct proteins, usually encoded by different genes, that catalyze the same reaction. Their different amino acid sequences give them different Km, Vmax, regulation and tissue distribution. Example: hexokinase I in most tissues has a Km for glucose of about 0.1 mM and is inhibited by its product, while glucokinase in liver and pancreatic β-cells has a much higher half-saturation (about 8 mM) and is not product-inhibited, so it responds to rising blood glucose. Lactate dehydrogenase and creatine kinase isozymes are also used clinically as tissue markers.

Incorrect. No enzyme changes the equilibrium constant of a reaction; Keq depends only on the free-energy difference between reactants and products. Enzymes, including isozymes, speed up both forward and reverse reactions equally, so all isozymes reach the same equilibrium, only at different rates.

Incorrect. Molecules that are identical are the same enzyme, not isozymes. Isozymes differ in primary structure (and therefore in properties), which is why they can be separated by electrophoresis and why measuring a particular isozyme in blood can point to damage in a particular tissue.

p: Isozymes are different forms of an enzyme that catalyze the same reaction but differ in amino acid sequence, and therefore in kinetic properties (Km, Vmax), regulation and tissue location. They let each tissue tune a shared reaction to its own needs.

Hexokinase vs glucokinase is the classic MCAT example. Hexokinase (low Km, product-inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate) keeps most tissues phosphorylating glucose even when blood glucose is low. Glucokinase (high half-saturation, about 8 mM, and cooperative) works mainly after meals, letting the liver store glucose and β-cells sense glucose for insulin release. Lactate dehydrogenase has heart-type and muscle-type subunits that combine into five isozymes.
Isozymes do not change ΔG or Keq; they change how fast equilibrium is approached under each tissue's conditions.

fig.cap: Hexokinase I (Km ≈ 0.1 mM) is saturated at all normal blood glucose levels, while glucokinase (half-saturated near 8 mM) speeds up as blood glucose rises after a meal.
fig.alt: Two curves of rate as a fraction of each enzyme's Vmax against glucose from 0 to 20 mM; hexokinase rises almost immediately to near 1; glucokinase rises gradually in an S shape; a shaded band marks blood glucose from 4 to 10 mM.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation (hexokinase, Km 0.1 mM) and the Hill equation (glucokinase, S0.5 8 mM, n 1.7), typical textbook values.

x1A_179.trap: Isozymes catalyze the SAME reaction with different kinetics; no enzyme changes Keq.
