ox: Incorrect. The standard derivation assumes the opposite: substrate is in large excess over enzyme ([S] ≫ [E]T). That keeps [S] nearly equal to its starting value while ES forms, and it allows a steady state to be established quickly. When enzyme exceeds substrate, ES would consume much of the substrate and the steady-state approximation breaks down.

Correct. Briggs and Haldane's steady-state assumption is that, after a very brief pre-steady-state period (milliseconds), ES is formed as fast as it breaks down, so d[ES]/dt ≈ 0. Setting k₁[E][S] = (k₋₁ + kcat)[ES] and using [E]T = [E] + [ES] gives [ES] = [E]T[S]/(Km + [S]) with Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁, and v = kcat[ES] gives the Michaelis–Menten equation.

Incorrect. At chemical equilibrium the net rate is zero, so there would be no rate to measure. Michaelis–Menten kinetics describes initial rates, measured when the reaction is far from equilibrium and little product exists. The equilibrium that is sometimes assumed is only the rapid binding step E + S ⇌ ES (the original Michaelis–Menten rapid-equilibrium assumption), not the overall reaction.

Incorrect. The derivation assumes the reverse reaction from product is negligible, which is why initial rates are measured before product accumulates. Allowing P to convert back to ES would add a k₋₂[E][P] term and give a more complex, reversible rate law.

p: The Michaelis–Menten model is E + S ⇌ ES → E + P, with rate constants k₁ (binding), k₋₁ (unbinding) and kcat (catalysis). The steady-state assumption (Briggs–Haldane) says that during the initial-rate period the concentration of ES is approximately constant: d[ES]/dt ≈ 0, because ES forms and breaks down at equal rates.

Combining this with conservation of enzyme ([E]T = [E] + [ES]) and v = kcat[ES] gives v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), with Vmax = kcat[E]T and Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁. Other assumptions: [S] ≫ [E]T so free [S] ≈ initial [S], and negligible product so the reverse reaction can be ignored.
The steady state is not equilibrium: substrate keeps flowing to product. [ES] stays nearly constant only until substrate starts running out, which is why rates are measured early.

fx.w: Steady-state condition. Combined with [E]T = [E] + [ES], it gives [ES] = [E]T[S]/(Km + [S]), with Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁.

fig.cap: A simulated reaction. [ES] rises within milliseconds (pre-steady state), then stays nearly constant for seconds while [S] is still close to its starting value (steady state, the initial-rate window), and falls only when substrate runs out.
fig.alt: Two stacked graphs on a logarithmic time axis. Top: substrate stays near 100 μM then falls while product rises. Bottom: [ES] rises over about 30 ms to a plateau near 0.9 μM, stays flat until about 10 s, then drops.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph from a numerical (Runge–Kutta) solution of the mass-action equations with k₁ = 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹, k₋₁ = 5 s⁻¹, kcat = 5 s⁻¹, [E]T = 1 μM, [S]₀ = 100 μM.

x1A_180.trap: Steady state means [ES] is constant, not that the reaction is at equilibrium; and [S] ≫ [E], not the reverse.

ox: Incorrect. If kcat ≫ k₋₁, most ES complexes go on to product rather than falling apart, so Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁ ≈ kcat/k₁, which is much larger than Kd = k₋₁/k₁. In that case Km overstates Kd and makes the enzyme look as if it binds substrate more weakly than it really does. This is the opposite of the condition needed.

Incorrect. k₁ is the rate constant for E and S combining. If k₁ were zero, no ES complex would form, there would be no catalysis, and both Km and Kd (each divided by k₁) would be undefined, effectively infinite. The question needs a condition in which binding happens normally but catalysis is slow.

Incorrect. Km and Kd are defined differently. Kd = k₋₁/k₁ is a true equilibrium dissociation constant, while Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁ includes the catalytic step, so Km = Kd + kcat/k₁. They match only when kcat is negligible compared with k₋₁, which is not guaranteed for every enzyme.

Correct. Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁. If kcat ≪ k₋₁, then k₋₁ + kcat ≈ k₋₁, so Km ≈ k₋₁/k₁ = Kd. Physically, ES falls apart back to E + S many times before it reacts, so the binding step reaches near-equilibrium (the original Michaelis–Menten rapid-equilibrium assumption). Only then does a low Km reliably mean tight binding.

concept.t: Km versus the dissociation constant Kd
p: In E + S ⇌ ES → E + P, the dissociation constant of the ES complex is Kd = k₋₁/k₁, a pure measure of binding affinity (smaller Kd, tighter binding). The Michaelis constant from the steady-state derivation is Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁ = Kd + kcat/k₁, so Km is always at least as large as Kd.

When catalysis is slow compared with substrate release (kcat ≪ k₋₁), Km ≈ Kd, and Km can be read as affinity. When catalysis is fast (kcat comparable to or greater than k₋₁), Km is larger than Kd and underestimates affinity, because ES is being drained by the forward reaction as well as by dissociation.
That is why textbooks say a low Km means high affinity only approximately. On the MCAT, treat Km as an inverse measure of apparent affinity unless a question gives rate constants that let you check.

fx.w: k₁ = association rate constant (M⁻¹s⁻¹); k₋₁ = dissociation rate constant of ES (s⁻¹); kcat = catalytic rate constant (s⁻¹); Kd = k₋₁/k₁ (M). Km ≈ Kd when kcat ≪ k₋₁.

fig.cap: Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁. With slow catalysis (kcat ≪ k₋₁) Km is almost exactly Kd; with fast catalysis Km is many times larger than Kd.
fig.alt: Reaction scheme with rate constants k₁, k₋₁ and kcat, the formulas for Km and Kd, and two example boxes: with kcat 1 per second Km equals 1.01 times 10⁻⁵ M, close to Kd; with kcat 1000 per second Km is 1.1 times 10⁻⁴ M, eleven times Kd.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram with illustrative rate constants; Km computed from (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁.

x1A_181.trap: Km equals Kd only when catalysis is much slower than substrate release (kcat ≪ k₋₁).

ox: Correct. Early in the reaction [S] is still essentially at the concentration you added, so you know exactly what [S] the rate belongs to, and almost no product exists. That avoids three complications that grow with time: substrate depletion (which lowers the rate), the reverse reaction P → S, and product inhibition. These are the conditions assumed in deriving the Michaelis–Menten equation.

Incorrect. Enzymes are catalysts: they are not used up, and most keep turning over for minutes to hours under assay conditions. The rate falls over time because the concentrations change (less substrate, more product), not because the enzyme stops working after a few seconds.

Incorrect. Vmax is not measured at time zero of one reaction. It is estimated by measuring initial rates at many different substrate concentrations and fitting the curve (or a Lineweaver–Burk line). Each initial rate is a single point; Vmax is a property extracted from the whole set.

Incorrect. Substrate binds within milliseconds of mixing; after this short pre-steady-state burst, [ES] is at steady state. The initial rate is measured after binding has occurred, during the steady-state period, so the idea that no substrate is bound yet describes a time window far too short for ordinary assays.

p: An enzyme assay follows product formation over time (a progress curve). The curve starts as a straight line and then bends over as substrate is consumed and product accumulates, finally flattening at equilibrium. The initial rate v₀ is the slope of the early, nearly straight part.

Initial rates are used because then [S] ≈ [S]₀ (known), [P] ≈ 0 (no reverse reaction or product inhibition), and [ES] is at steady state. These are exactly the assumptions of the Michaelis–Menten derivation, so v₀ values at several [S] can be fitted to find Km and Vmax.
A common confusion: the reaction slowing down over time is not enzyme failure. It is mass action: less substrate and more product.

fig.cap: A simulated progress curve. The initial slope (dashed) is measured while [S] is still near its starting value; later the curve bends as substrate is used up.
fig.alt: Product concentration against time rising steeply at first then leveling off at 100 μM; a dashed tangent line through the origin shows the initial rate of 8.3 μM per minute; the first two minutes are shaded as the initial-rate window.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph from numerical integration of d[S]/dt = −Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with Vmax = 10 μM/min, Km = 20 μM, [S]₀ = 100 μM (illustrative).

x1A_182.trap: Rates fall over time because [S] drops and [P] builds, not because the enzyme wears out.

ox: Incorrect. A denatured enzyme has lost its folded active site and would show little or no activity at any [S]. Here the enzyme gives a steady, presumably substantial, rate at both 10 and 20 mM, which means it is working; it just cannot go any faster. Saturation is not denaturation.

Incorrect. When [S] is well below Km, the rate is nearly proportional to [S] (first order), so doubling [S] from 10 to 20 mM would nearly double the rate. An unchanged rate is the opposite signature: it shows that substrate is no longer the limiting factor at all.

Correct. If doubling [S] does not raise the rate, the rate no longer depends on [S]: the reaction is zero order in substrate. That happens when [S] ≫ Km and nearly every active site is already occupied, so v ≈ Vmax. For example, if Km were 1 mM, v would be 10/11 ≈ 91% of Vmax at 10 mM and 20/21 ≈ 95% at 20 mM, a change too small to notice.

Incorrect. A competitive inhibitor would be overcome by raising [S], so the rate would increase when substrate is doubled. An unchanged rate means substrate is no longer limiting, which is a statement about saturation, not about an inhibitor. Nothing in the data requires an inhibitor to be present.

p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax.

The fraction of active sites occupied is [S]/(Km + [S]). At [S] = 10 Km about 91% of sites are full; at 20 Km about 95%. Once nearly all sites are busy, adding substrate cannot increase the rate, because there is almost no free enzyme left to bind it. The rate is then set by enzyme amount and kcat (v ≈ Vmax = kcat[E]T).

Experimentally: if doubling [S] doubles the rate, [S] ≪ Km (first order); if it barely changes the rate, [S] ≫ Km (zero order). To raise the rate of a saturated enzyme you must add more enzyme or raise kcat (for example by an activator or a temperature change within the stable range).

fig.cap: Active-site occupancy at four substrate levels, computed from [S]/(Km + [S]). Doubling [S] from 10 Km to 20 Km only raises occupancy from 91% to 95%.
fig.alt: Four panels of 20 enzyme circles each; filled circles show bound substrate: 2 of 20 at 0.1 Km, 10 at Km, 18 at 10 Km and 19 at 20 Km, with captions 9, 50, 91 and 95 percent occupied.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; occupancy computed from the Michaelis–Menten fraction [S]/(Km + [S]).

fig.cap: At [S] far above Km the Michaelis–Menten curve is flat: the rate is near Vmax and no longer depends on [S] (zero order).
fig.alt: Curve of v over Vmax against [S] over Km from 0 to 20, with a dashed tangent at low [S] marking first order and a shaded region above 10 Km marking the zero-order saturated plateau.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).

x1A_183.trap: Constant rate despite more substrate = saturation (zero order), not denaturation or inhibition.

ox: Incorrect. The substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax is Km, the Michaelis constant. It has units of concentration and reflects how much substrate the enzyme needs, not how fast it converts substrate once bound. Km and kcat are independent: two enzymes can share a Km yet differ a thousand-fold in kcat.

Incorrect. The total amount of enzyme is [E]T, which is part of Vmax = kcat[E]T but is set by the experimenter (or by gene expression in a cell). kcat is what you get after dividing Vmax by [E]T, precisely to remove the dependence on how much enzyme is present.

Incorrect. How tightly an inhibitor binds is described by the inhibition constant Ki, the dissociation constant of the enzyme–inhibitor complex. A small Ki means a potent inhibitor. Ki is a concentration, whereas kcat is a rate constant in s⁻¹.

Correct. kcat, the turnover number, is the maximum number of substrate molecules each active site converts to product per second when the enzyme is saturated. It equals Vmax/[E]T and has units of s⁻¹; it is the first-order rate constant for the ES → E + P step (or the slowest step after binding). Values range from under 1 s⁻¹ to about 10⁶ s⁻¹ for carbonic anhydrase and about 4 × 10⁷ s⁻¹ for catalase.

concept.t: The kinetic parameters and what they mean
p: Each Michaelis–Menten parameter answers a different question. Vmax (rate units): how fast the whole sample can go at saturation. [E]T (concentration): how much enzyme is present. kcat = Vmax/[E]T (s⁻¹): how many catalytic cycles one active site completes per second. Km (concentration): how much substrate gives half of Vmax. Ki (concentration): how tightly an inhibitor binds.
kcat measures catalytic speed per site and does not change when you add more enzyme. kcat/Km (M⁻¹s⁻¹) combines speed and substrate capture into catalytic efficiency.
The reciprocal of kcat is the time for one cycle: kcat = 100 s⁻¹ means one product every 10 ms per site. MCAT questions often test whether you can match a parameter to its definition and units.

fx.w: kcat = turnover number (s⁻¹); Vmax = maximal rate (M/s); [E]T = total active-site concentration (M).

fig.cap: kcat counts how many times per second one active site completes the cycle E → ES → E + P at saturation. Km, [E]T and Ki describe other things.
fig.alt: Cycle of three circles labelled E, ES and E plus P with arrows for binding, catalysis by kcat, and return to free enzyme; below, the formula kcat = Vmax/[E]T and pills: Km, [E]T and Ki in red, kcat in green.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram.

x1A_184.trap: kcat is per active site per second; Km is a concentration, [E]T is enzyme amount, Ki is inhibitor binding.

ox: Incorrect. Weak substrate binding means a high Km, which would make kcat/Km small, not large. A kcat/Km near 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ means the enzyme captures and converts substrate almost every time the two meet, the opposite of weak binding. (The question says nothing about Km alone, but the ratio rules out poor capture.)

Incorrect. kcat/Km is a kinetic quantity: it says how fast the reaction goes at low [S], not whether it is favorable. ΔG depends only on reactants and products and is unaffected by the enzyme. An enzyme with any kcat/Km can catalyze a reaction with negative or positive ΔG; it simply speeds the approach to equilibrium.

Correct. kcat/Km is the second-order rate constant for free enzyme meeting free substrate. Its ceiling is the rate at which molecules diffuse together in water, about 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹. An enzyme near 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ converts substrate on nearly every encounter, so its rate is limited by diffusion, not by chemistry. Such enzymes, including triose phosphate isomerase, fumarase and acetylcholinesterase, are called catalytically perfect.

Incorrect. Catalytic efficiency and regulation are separate properties. Some diffusion-limited enzymes, such as triose phosphate isomerase and carbonic anhydrase, are not allosterically regulated at all, while many regulated enzymes are far from the diffusion limit. A kcat/Km value alone cannot tell you whether an enzyme has allosteric sites.

concept.t: The diffusion limit and catalytic perfection
p: At low [S], v = (kcat/Km)[E][S], so kcat/Km is the rate constant for the encounter of free enzyme and free substrate followed by catalysis. It cannot exceed the rate at which two molecules diffuse together in solution, roughly 10⁸ to 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹.

Enzymes with kcat/Km in that range are diffusion-controlled: nearly every collision leads to product, so making the chemistry faster would not help. Examples (approximate): acetylcholinesterase 1.6 × 10⁸, triose phosphate isomerase 2.4 × 10⁸, carbonic anhydrase 8 × 10⁷ M⁻¹s⁻¹. Some enzymes in complexes channel substrates between active sites to beat the limit.
Do not mix up kinetics and thermodynamics: a large kcat/Km means a fast approach to equilibrium, not a different equilibrium or ΔG.

fig.cap: kcat/Km values of well-known fast enzymes cluster near 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹. The enzyme in the question, at 10⁹, sits at the top of the diffusion-limited band.
fig.alt: Horizontal bar chart on a logarithmic axis of kcat over Km for catalase, carbonic anhydrase, β-lactamase, acetylcholinesterase, fumarase, triose phosphate isomerase and crotonase, all between 4 times 10⁷ and 3 times 10⁸, plus a green bar for the question's enzyme at 10⁹; a shaded band marks 10⁸ to 10⁹.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph; kcat/Km values as tabulated in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

x1A_185.trap: kcat/Km ≈ 10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ means diffusion-limited (catalytically perfect); it says nothing about ΔG or regulation.

ox: Incorrect. cAMP is a cyclic nucleotide second messenger, not a phosphate donor. The phosphate that protein kinase A (PKA) transfers to its targets comes from ATP. PKA's catalytic subunits are activated by being released, not by being phosphorylated by cAMP.

Correct. In the inactive R₂C₂ holoenzyme, each regulatory (R) subunit has a pseudosubstrate segment that sits in the active site of a catalytic subunit (a C subunit) and blocks it. cAMP binds the R subunits (two per R), changing their conformation so they release the C subunits. The freed C subunits phosphorylate serine and threonine residues on target proteins. When phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP, R rebinds C and the kinase switches off.

Incorrect. Activation of PKA is reversible and noncovalent: cAMP binds and later dissociates. Cleaving the regulatory subunits would be proteolytic activation, like a zymogen, which is irreversible and would leave the cell unable to switch PKA off when the hormone signal ends.

Incorrect. cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, not the catalytic active site, and it is not converted to product. The substrates of PKA are ATP and target proteins with serine or threonine residues. cAMP acts as an allosteric effector, binding a regulatory site and changing the protein's conformation.

concept.t: Regulation by regulatory subunits: protein kinase A
p: Some enzymes are held inactive by separate regulatory subunits. Protein kinase A is a tetramer of two regulatory (R) and two catalytic subunits, called C. Each R subunit contains a pseudosubstrate sequence that occupies a C subunit's active site.

When a hormone such as glucagon or epinephrine activates a Gs-coupled receptor, adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP from ATP. cAMP binds the R subunits (two molecules each, four per holoenzyme), causing them to release active C subunits, which phosphorylate target enzymes, for example activating glycogen phosphorylase kinase. Phosphodiesterase degrades cAMP, R reassociates with C, and the signal ends.
This is reversible, noncovalent allosteric control by dissociation, which is different from covalent modification (phosphorylation of the targets) and from zymogen activation (irreversible cleavage).

fig.cap: Inactive PKA is an R₂C₂ tetramer. Four cAMP molecules bind the two regulatory subunits, which then release two active catalytic subunits.
fig.alt: Left: two R boxes paired with two C boxes. Arrow labelled plus 4 cAMP. Right: two R boxes each carrying two cAMP circles, plus two separate green C boxes labelled active.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; mechanism as described in standard biochemistry texts (e.g. Lehninger, Alberts).

x1A_186.trap: cAMP binds the REGULATORY subunits and releases C; it does not donate phosphate or cleave anything.

ref.t: OpenStax Biology 2e, 9.3 Response to the Signal

ox: Correct. An unchanged y-intercept means 1/Vmax, and so Vmax, is the same: enough substrate fully overcomes the inhibitor. A steeper slope (Km/Vmax) with the same Vmax means apparent Km has risen. Same Vmax and higher Km is competitive inhibition, typically by a molecule that resembles the substrate and occupies the active site of free enzyme.

Incorrect. An inhibitor that binds only the ES complex is uncompetitive: it lowers Km and Vmax by the same factor, leaving the slope Km/Vmax unchanged and raising the y-intercept. That gives parallel lines, which is the opposite of what is described (slope changed, intercept unchanged).

Incorrect. Destroying enzyme molecules covalently lowers the amount of active enzyme and therefore Vmax. A lower Vmax raises the y-intercept (1/Vmax). Since the y-intercept here is unchanged, Vmax has not fallen, ruling out irreversible inactivation.

Incorrect. An inhibitor that binds an allosteric site on E and ES with equal affinity is pure noncompetitive. It lowers Vmax (raising the y-intercept) while leaving Km unchanged, so the lines meet on the x-axis. The description requires an unchanged y-intercept, which noncompetitive inhibition cannot produce.

concept.t: Competitive inhibition on a Lineweaver–Burk plot
p: A competitive inhibitor binds the free enzyme, usually at the active site, because it resembles the substrate (a substrate analog). Substrate and inhibitor cannot bind at the same time, so a high enough [S] outcompetes the inhibitor: Vmax is unchanged, but apparent Km rises to Km(1 + [I]/Ki).

On a Lineweaver–Burk plot (1/v against 1/[S]) the y-intercept 1/Vmax is unchanged while the slope Km/Vmax increases, so the lines pivot around the same y-intercept and cross on the y-axis. The x-intercept −1/Km moves toward zero.
Classic examples: methotrexate (a folate analog) on dihydrofolate reductase, statins on HMG-CoA reductase, and malonate on succinate dehydrogenase.

fig.cap: Lineweaver–Burk patterns: competitive lines meet on the y-axis (steeper slope, same 1/Vmax), uncompetitive lines are parallel, pure noncompetitive lines meet on the x-axis, and mixed lines meet off both axes.
fig.alt: Four small double-reciprocal plots, each with a blue no-inhibitor line and a red inhibitor line: crossing on the y-axis, parallel, crossing on the x-axis, and crossing left of the y-axis above the x-axis.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from 1/v = (αKm/Vmax)(1/[S]) + α′/Vmax with illustrative α and α′ values.

fig.cap: Where a reversible inhibitor binds (free E, ES, or both) determines how apparent Km and Vmax change and how the Lineweaver–Burk lines look.
fig.alt: Reaction scheme E plus S to ES to E plus P with inhibitor binding E to form EI and ES to form ESI; below, a table of five binding patterns with their effects on apparent Km, apparent Vmax and Lineweaver–Burk lines.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; relationships from the standard general (mixed) inhibition model as presented in Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry.

x1A_187.trap: Same y-intercept = same Vmax = competitive; changes in slope alone mean Km changed.

ox: Incorrect. Reversible binding at an allosteric site describes an allosteric inhibitor, which changes the enzyme's conformation and comes off again when its concentration falls. A suicide inhibitor acts at the active site and ends up permanently attached; nothing about it is reversible.

Incorrect. A molecule that competes with substrate for the active site and is easily displaced is a reversible competitive inhibitor. A suicide inhibitor does start by binding the active site like a substrate, but it is not displaced: it becomes covalently bonded to the enzyme, so raising [S] cannot restore activity.

Correct. A mechanism-based (suicide) inhibitor is an unreactive substrate look-alike. The enzyme binds it and begins its normal catalytic mechanism, which converts the inhibitor into a highly reactive intermediate inside the active site; that intermediate forms a covalent bond with an active-site residue or cofactor, permanently inactivating the enzyme. Because only the target enzyme can activate it, it is very specific; examples are clavulanic acid on β-lactamase and eflornithine on ornithine decarboxylase.

Incorrect. Raising the temperature can denature enzymes, but that is a physical condition, not an inhibitor mechanism, and it affects all proteins non-specifically. Inhibitors act through chemical binding to the enzyme. Suicide inhibitors are prized precisely because they are highly selective.

p: Irreversible inhibitors permanently inactivate enzymes, usually by forming a covalent bond to an active-site residue. A mechanism-based or suicide inhibitor is a special type: it is chemically unreactive until the target enzyme processes it. During the enzyme's normal catalytic steps, the inhibitor is converted into a reactive species that attacks the active site, so the enzyme in effect commits suicide.

Because activation requires the target enzyme's own mechanism, these drugs have few off-target effects. Examples: clavulanic acid (inactivates bacterial β-lactamase, protecting amoxicillin), eflornithine/DFMO (ornithine decarboxylase; African sleeping sickness), and 5-fluorouracil, whose metabolite FdUMP traps thymidylate synthase.
Kinetically, irreversible inactivation reduces active [E]T and Vmax; the surviving enzyme molecules keep their normal Km. Activity returns only when new enzyme is made.

fig.cap: A suicide inhibitor resembles the substrate, binds the active site, is activated by the enzyme's own catalysis, and then bonds covalently to the active site.
fig.alt: Five boxes in a row: inhibitor looks like substrate, binds the active site, enzyme starts normal catalysis, reactive group unmasked, covalent bond to active site. Below, three drug examples and pills marking allosteric, competitive and heat as wrong and suicide as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; drug examples from standard pharmacology texts.

x1A_188.trap: Suicide inhibitors need the enzyme's own catalysis to become reactive; then they bind covalently and permanently.

ox: Correct. Changing gene transcription requires making new mRNA, processing and exporting it (in eukaryotes), translating it into protein, and folding the protein, which takes hours. Likewise, lowering expression only takes effect as existing enzyme is degraded. This makes transcriptional control slow but long-lasting, suited to adapting to diet or hormones over hours to days, such as insulin inducing glucokinase in liver.

Incorrect. Allosteric inhibitors such as ATP on phosphofructokinase-1 bind and unbind noncovalently within milliseconds or less, so activity tracks metabolite levels almost instantly. That makes allosteric control the fastest kind of regulation, not the slowest.

Incorrect. Phosphorylation by a kinase that already exists modifies enzyme molecules that are already present. It typically takes seconds to minutes, for example when glucagon or epinephrine signaling through PKA rapidly activates glycogen breakdown. It is slower than allosteric binding but far faster than making new protein.

Incorrect. A competitive inhibitor that is already present binds the active site in milliseconds, as fast as substrate binding. Its effect appears essentially at once and disappears as soon as its concentration falls, so it is among the fastest controls.

p: Cells regulate enzymes on very different timescales. Fastest: substrate availability, allosteric effectors and reversible inhibitors, which bind noncovalently in milliseconds. Next: covalent modification of existing enzyme (phosphorylation, dephosphorylation), in seconds to minutes, typically driven by hormone signaling cascades. Also fast: proteolytic activation of zymogens.

Slowest: changing the amount of enzyme by altering gene expression (induction or repression) or degradation rate. Making new enzyme requires transcription, RNA processing and translation, so effects appear over hours and persist for hours to days. Examples include induction of lipogenic enzymes by insulin and of gluconeogenic enzymes during fasting.
A useful rule: the more steps needed to make a change, the slower but more durable it is.

fig.cap: Approximate time to take effect: allosteric and competitive binding act in milliseconds, phosphorylation in seconds to minutes, and making new enzyme through transcription in hours.
fig.alt: Horizontal bars on a logarithmic time axis from milliseconds to days: allosteric binding and competitive inhibitor binding near 1 to 100 ms, phosphorylation from 1 s to 10 min, new enzyme via transcription from 1 hour to 1 day, marked slowest.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph; ranges are approximate order-of-magnitude textbook values.

x1A_189.trap: Anything needing new protein synthesis is slowest (hours); binding and modifying existing enzyme is fast.

ox: Incorrect. 30 μM/s is what you get by treating the inhibitor as pure noncompetitive: halving Vmax to 45 and keeping Km = 2 μM gives 45 × 4/(2 + 4) = 30. A competitive inhibitor does not lower Vmax; it raises apparent Km, so the factor of 2 belongs on Km.

Correct. For competitive inhibition, Km,app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). With [I] = Ki, the factor is 2, so Km,app = 4 μM and Vmax stays 90 μM/s. Then v = 90 × 4/(4 + 4) = 45 μM/s. Notice [S] now equals Km,app, so the enzyme runs at exactly half of Vmax.

Incorrect. 60 μM/s is the uninhibited rate: 90 × 4/(2 + 4) = 60. It ignores the inhibitor entirely. Any inhibitor present at [I] = Ki must lower the rate at a non-saturating [S], so the answer must be below 60.

Incorrect. 90 μM/s is Vmax, the rate only approached when [S] is far above Km,app. At [S] = 4 μM the enzyme is far from saturated, and v can never equal Vmax at any finite [S]. A competitive inhibitor leaves Vmax unchanged, but that does not mean every rate equals Vmax.

concept.t: Calculating rates with a competitive inhibitor
p: A competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km by the factor α = 1 + [I]/Ki and leaves Vmax unchanged. The rate is v = Vmax[S]/(αKm + [S]). At [I] = Ki, α = 2, so Km doubles.

Compare with pure noncompetitive inhibition at the same [I] = Ki: Km is unchanged and Vmax is halved. The two types give different numbers at low [S], which is how MCAT distractors are built. At very high [S], competitive inhibition disappears, while noncompetitive inhibition remains.

Strategy: identify the inhibition type, adjust the right parameter (Km for competitive, Vmax for noncompetitive, both for uncompetitive), then plug into Michaelis–Menten. A quick check: when [S] equals the apparent Km, v is half of the apparent Vmax.

fx.w: Michaelis–Menten equation with a competitive inhibitor. [I] = inhibitor concentration; Ki = dissociation constant of EI. Vmax is unchanged.

steps: Km,app = 2 × 2 μM = 4 μM; Vmax stays 90 μM/s.
Check: without inhibitor, v = 90 × 4/6 = 60 μM/s, so the inhibitor lowered the rate by 25%.

fig.cap: At [S] = 4 μM: 60 μM/s without inhibitor, 45 μM/s with the competitive inhibitor (Km,app = 4 μM), and 30 μM/s if the inhibitor had instead halved Vmax.
fig.alt: Three curves: blue uninhibited, green competitive with the same plateau of 90, red dashed noncompetitive with plateau 45; a dotted vertical line at 4 μM meets them at 60, 45 and 30.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with Km = 2 μM, Vmax = 90 μM/s and Km,app = 4 μM.

x1A_190.trap: Competitive inhibition changes Km, not Vmax: double Km at [I] = Ki, then use the equation.
x1A_190.eli: First find the new Km (inhibitor makes it larger), then use Michaelis–Menten as usual.
mem: Competitive: Km(app) = Km(1 + [I]/Ki), Vmax same.
Then v = Vmax·[S]/(Km(app) + [S]).
[I] = Ki doubles Km.

fm.f: v = Vmax·[S] / (Km(app) + [S]) with Km(app) = Km(1 + [I]/Ki), where Vmax = 90 μM/s, [S] = 4 μM, Km = 2 μM, [I] = Ki
fm.why: We first correct Km for the inhibitor and then apply Michaelis–Menten to get the rate.

ox: Correct. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor lowers Vmax by the factor α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki and leaves Km unchanged. At [I] = Ki the factor is 2, so Vmax,app = 120/2 = 60 μM/s. Because Km is unchanged, [S] = Km still gives half of the (new) maximum: v = 60 × Km/(Km + Km) = 30 μM/s.

Incorrect. 40 μM/s is what a competitive inhibitor at [I] = Ki would give: Km doubles, Vmax stays 120, and v = 120 × Km/(2Km + Km) = 120/3 = 40. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor does not change Km, so this applies the wrong inhibition model.

Incorrect. 60 μM/s is reached by applying only one of the two effects: either it is the new Vmax,app (forgetting that [S] = Km gives only half of it) or it is the uninhibited rate at [S] = Km (120/2, forgetting the inhibitor). The correct answer needs both halvings: 120 → 60 for the inhibitor, then 60 → 30 for [S] = Km.

Incorrect. 120 μM/s is the original Vmax. It ignores both the inhibitor and the fact that [S] = Km gives only half-maximal rate. Even without any inhibitor, the rate at [S] = Km would be 60, not 120, because Km is by definition the point of half-maximal rate.

concept.t: Calculating rates with a pure noncompetitive inhibitor
p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax.

A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds free enzyme and ES equally, so it removes a fixed fraction of working enzyme no matter how much substrate is present. Vmax,app = Vmax/(1 + [I]/Ki) and Km is unchanged. At [I] = Ki, Vmax is halved.

Combine the two pieces step by step: first adjust the parameter the inhibitor changes, then apply Michaelis–Menten at the given [S]. Compare with competitive inhibition at [I] = Ki, which doubles Km and leaves Vmax alone; at [S] = Km that gives v = Vmax/3 instead of Vmax/4.

fx.w: Pure noncompetitive inhibition: Vmax divided by α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki; Km unchanged. At [S] = Km the second factor is 1/2.

steps: Km is unchanged, so at [S] = Km the fraction [S]/(Km + [S]) = 1/2.

fig.cap: At [S] = Km: 60 μM/s without inhibitor, 30 μM/s with the pure noncompetitive inhibitor (Vmax halved, Km unchanged), and 40 μM/s if it had acted competitively.
fig.alt: Three curves against [S]/Km: blue uninhibited rising toward 120, green noncompetitive rising toward 60, red dashed competitive rising toward 120 more slowly; a dotted line at [S] = Km meets them at 60, 30 and 40.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) with Vmax = 120 μM/s and [I] = Ki.

x1A_191.trap: Noncompetitive: halve Vmax at [I] = Ki, keep Km, then remember [S] = Km gives half of the new Vmax.

ox: Incorrect. A shift in the x-intercept with a fixed y-intercept means Km changed while Vmax stayed the same, the competitive-inhibitor pattern. Adding enzyme does the opposite: it raises Vmax and leaves Km (a per-molecule property) untouched, so the x-intercept cannot move.

Incorrect. A parallel shift keeps the slope Km/Vmax constant while changing the y-intercept, which happens when Km and Vmax change by the same factor, the uncompetitive pattern. With more enzyme, Vmax rises but Km does not, so the slope Km/Vmax decreases and the new line is not parallel.

Incorrect. Vmax = kcat[E]T, so it is directly proportional to enzyme concentration. Adding enzyme raises Vmax and therefore lowers 1/Vmax, the y-intercept. The line must change; only Km stays the same.

Correct. Doubling [E]T doubles Vmax (Vmax = kcat[E]T), so the y-intercept 1/Vmax halves. Km depends on the rate constants of each enzyme molecule, not on how many molecules there are, so the x-intercept −1/Km stays put. The line pivots down around the fixed x-intercept, with its slope Km/Vmax also halved.

concept.t: How enzyme concentration affects Km and Vmax
p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. Vmax = kcat[E]T, so Vmax is proportional to the amount of enzyme.

Km and kcat are intrinsic properties of each enzyme molecule and do not depend on how much enzyme is in the tube. So adding more enzyme raises Vmax but leaves Km unchanged; removing active enzyme (for example with an irreversible inhibitor) lowers Vmax with Km unchanged.

On a Lineweaver–Burk plot, changing [E]T moves the y-intercept (1/Vmax) while the x-intercept (−1/Km) stays fixed, so lines for different enzyme amounts meet on the x-axis, the same pattern as pure noncompetitive inhibition. That resemblance is not a coincidence: a noncompetitive inhibitor acts like having less enzyme.

fig.cap: Doubling the enzyme halves the y-intercept (1/Vmax from 0.02 to 0.01) while the x-intercept (−1/Km) stays fixed.
fig.alt: Two double-reciprocal lines meeting at the same point on the negative x-axis; the green line for twice the enzyme crosses the y-axis at 0.01, the blue line at 0.02.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Lineweaver–Burk equation with Km = 2 and Vmax = 50 or 100 (illustrative).

x1A_192.trap: More enzyme raises Vmax only; Km never depends on enzyme concentration.

ox: Incorrect. Equal concentrations would give equal rates only if the enzyme handled both substrates equally well. At low [S], each rate is (kcat/Km)[E][S], so with the same [E] and [S], the rates differ by exactly the ratio of kcat/Km values, here 100-fold.

Correct. When two substrates compete for the same enzyme, they share the same pool of free enzyme, and at low concentrations each rate is v = (kcat/Km)[E][S]. Dividing, vA/vB = (kcat/Km)A[A]/((kcat/Km)B[B]). With [A] = [B], the ratio is 10⁶/10⁴ = 10² = 100, so A : B = 100 : 1. This is why kcat/Km is called the specificity constant.

Incorrect. 2 : 1 comes from comparing the exponents themselves (6 − 4 = 2) instead of the numbers they represent. 10⁶ and 10⁴ differ by a factor of 10², which is 100, not 2. On a log scale, a difference of 2 units means a 100-fold difference.

Incorrect. 10⁴ : 1 comes from a powers-of-ten slip, for example taking substrate B's value alone or treating the exponents incorrectly. When dividing powers of ten, subtract the exponents: 10⁶/10⁴ = 10⁶⁻⁴ = 10².

p: kcat/Km measures how efficiently an enzyme captures and converts a particular substrate. At low [S], v = (kcat/Km)[E][S]. When two substrates are present together, they compete for the same free enzyme, so the ratio of their rates is vA/vB = (kcat/Km)A[A] / (kcat/Km)B[B].

This holds at any substrate concentration for competing substrates, not just low ones, because the free enzyme term cancels. It explains enzyme specificity: the substrate with the larger kcat/Km is processed preferentially, which is why kcat/Km, not Km or kcat alone, is the best single measure of preference.
Work powers of ten carefully: a difference of 2 in the exponent is a factor of 100.

fx.w: Rates of two substrates competing for one enzyme; free enzyme cancels. kcat/Km in M⁻¹s⁻¹; concentrations in the same units.

fig.cap: Two substrates at equal concentration compete for one enzyme. The ratio of rates equals the ratio of their kcat/Km values: 10⁶/10⁴ = 100.
fig.alt: Two boxes for substrate A with kcat/Km 10⁶ and substrate B with kcat/Km 10⁴; the calculation vA/vB = 10⁶⁻⁴ = 100; a green pill for 100 to 1 and red pills for 1 to 1, 2 to 1 and 10⁴ to 1.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram using the values in the question.

x1A_193.trap: Compare the actual values (10⁶/10⁴ = 100), not the exponents (6 vs 4).

ox: Incorrect. Na⁺ is the main extracellular cation and is important for membrane potential and transport, but it is monovalent and binds ATP only weakly. It cannot bridge two phosphate groups the way a divalent ion does, and it is not the partner ion kinases use.

Correct. Inside cells most ATP exists as a Mg²⁺·ATP complex. Mg²⁺ (divalent) binds between the β and γ phosphates, partially neutralizing ATP's negative charges and holding the phosphates in a defined geometry. This makes the γ-phosphorus easier for a nucleophile to attack and lets the enzyme bind ATP in the right orientation. Kinases and most other ATP-using enzymes need Mg²⁺ for activity.

Incorrect. Cl⁻ is an anion. ATP's phosphate groups are themselves negatively charged, so a chloride ion would be repelled rather than bound. Charge shielding requires a cation that can sit between the negative phosphate oxygens.

Incorrect. Iron is a common cofactor, but its role is redox chemistry: it cycles between Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ in heme groups (cytochromes, hemoglobin) and iron–sulfur clusters. It is not the ion that complexes ATP for phosphoryl transfer, and free Fe³⁺ is kept at very low levels in cells because it is toxic and insoluble.

p: Many enzymes need a cofactor, a non-protein helper: either a metal ion (inorganic cofactor) or an organic molecule (coenzyme, often derived from a vitamin, such as NAD⁺ or coenzyme A). The protein without its cofactor is the apoenzyme; with it, the holoenzyme.

ATP carries four negative charges at physiological pH. Mg²⁺ binds the β and γ phosphates, shielding charge and fixing their geometry, so the true substrate of kinases, ATPases and synthetases is usually Mg²⁺·ATP. Low Mg²⁺ therefore impairs many ATP-dependent reactions.
Other metal cofactors have different jobs: Zn²⁺ (carbonic anhydrase, a Lewis acid), Fe and Cu (redox, electron transport), and Mn²⁺. Recognize which ion fits which role.

fig.cap: ATP⁴⁻ with its β and γ phosphates shaded. Mg²⁺ binds between them, neutralizing charge and positioning the γ-phosphate for transfer.
fig.alt: Chemical structure of ATP with four negative charges on the triphosphate, the β and γ phosphates highlighted; a side box explains Mg²⁺ bridging; pills mark Mg²⁺ as correct and Na⁺, Cl⁻ and Fe³⁺ as wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; ATP structure drawn with RDKit from SMILES (stereocentres checked: C1′ R, C2′ R, C3′ S, C4′ R).

x1A_194.trap: Kinases use Mg²⁺·ATP; iron is a redox cofactor, not the ATP partner.

ox: Incorrect. The site where substrate binds and is converted to product is the active site. It contains the catalytic residues and is shaped to stabilize the transition state. An allosteric site is defined by being somewhere else on the enzyme.

Incorrect. A cleavage site is the specific peptide bond that a protease cuts, for example when trypsin or enteropeptidase activates a zymogen. Cleavage permanently changes the enzyme's covalent structure, whereas allosteric sites bind regulators reversibly.

Incorrect. The DNA sequence that controls a gene's expression is a promoter (or an enhancer or other regulatory element). It is part of the gene, not of the enzyme protein, and it regulates how much enzyme is made rather than how active existing enzyme molecules are.

Correct. An allosteric site (from Greek allos, other, and stereos, shape or site) is a binding site distinct from the active site. An effector binding there changes the enzyme's conformation, which is transmitted to the active site and raises or lowers its activity or substrate affinity. Allosteric activators and inhibitors, such as AMP and ATP on phosphofructokinase-1, act this way, reversibly and noncovalently.

p: Allosteric enzymes are usually multi-subunit proteins whose activity is changed by molecules binding at sites other than the active site (allosteric sites). Many switch between a low-affinity, less active T (tense) state and a high-affinity, more active R (relaxed) state. An allosteric site is any regulatory binding site separate from the active site.

Effectors that bind allosteric sites change the enzyme's shape, which is transmitted through the protein to the active site. Activators stabilize the active (R) form and inhibitors the inactive (T) form. Because binding is noncovalent, allosteric control is fast (milliseconds) and reversible, which suits feedback inhibition by pathway end products.

Distinguish: active site (catalysis), allosteric site (regulation by binding), cleavage site (irreversible zymogen activation), phosphorylation site (covalent modification), and promoter (gene-level control of enzyme amount).

fig.cap: An enzyme with an active site holding substrate and a separate allosteric site where an effector binds; binding there changes the enzyme's shape and the active site's activity.
fig.alt: Schematic enzyme with a pocket at the top holding substrate S, labelled active site, and a triangular pocket at the bottom with an effector, labelled allosteric site; a dashed arrow labelled conformational change links them; pills mark allosteric site correct and active site, cleavage site and promoter wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest schematic.

x1A_195.trap: Allosteric = 'other site': a regulatory binding site that is NOT the active site.

ox: Correct. When the cell uses ATP faster than it makes it, ADP accumulates and adenylate kinase (2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP) converts some of it to AMP. Because [ATP] is high and [AMP] low normally, a small drop in ATP causes a large relative rise in AMP, making AMP a sensitive low-energy signal. AMP binds PFK-1 allosterically, relieves ATP inhibition, and speeds glycolysis to make more ATP.

Incorrect. Plenty of energy is signaled by high ATP (and citrate), which binds an allosteric inhibitory site on PFK-1 and slows glycolysis. High AMP means the opposite: ATP has been spent and the cell needs to make more. This choice reverses the meaning of the signal.

Incorrect. PFK-1's substrates are fructose-6-phosphate and ATP; it transfers a phosphate from ATP to make fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. AMP is not a substrate; it binds a separate allosteric site and acts as an activator. Confusing effector and substrate is a common error.

Incorrect. Gluconeogenesis consumes ATP (and GTP) to build glucose, so it is the opposite of what an energy-poor cell needs. High AMP actually inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, the gluconeogenic enzyme opposing PFK-1, so the two pathways are regulated reciprocally: AMP turns glycolysis on and gluconeogenesis off.

p: Phosphofructokinase-1 catalyzes the first committed step of glycolysis (fructose-6-phosphate + ATP → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate + ADP) and is its main control point. It is an allosteric enzyme with sigmoidal kinetics.

ATP is both a substrate and, at high levels, an allosteric inhibitor that favors the low-affinity T state; citrate adds to this inhibition. AMP, and in liver fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, are activators that relieve ATP inhibition and shift the curve left. AMP is the key low-energy signal because adenylate kinase amplifies small ATP drops into large AMP rises.
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (gluconeogenesis) is regulated oppositely, so the cell avoids running both pathways at once (a futile cycle).

fig.cap: PFK-1 activity against fructose-6-phosphate. With high ATP alone the curve is shifted right; adding AMP shifts it left, so at the same [F6P] the enzyme is far more active.
fig.alt: Two sigmoidal curves: a green curve shifted left labelled high ATP plus high AMP and a red curve shifted right labelled high ATP alone; at the same fructose-6-phosphate level marked by a dotted line, the green point is near 0.85 and the red point near 0.15.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Hill equation with n = 2.5 and illustrative K0.5 values; regulatory facts from standard biochemistry texts.

x1A_196.trap: High AMP = low energy = speed up glycolysis; high ATP = plenty of energy = slow it down.

ox: Incorrect. Substrate inhibition, in which excess substrate binds unproductively and lowers the rate, does occur for a few enzymes, but it would make the rate fall at high [S], not level off. Typical Michaelis–Menten enzymes plateau because they run out of free active sites, not because substrate inhibits them.

Incorrect. The equilibrium constant depends only on the free energies of reactants and products (ΔG° = −RT ln Keq) and on temperature; it does not change with [S] or with the enzyme. Also, initial rates are measured far from equilibrium, so Keq is not what limits them.

Correct. The fraction of active sites holding substrate is [S]/(Km + [S]). As [S] rises far above Km this fraction approaches 1: at 10 Km about 91% of sites are full and at 100 Km about 99%. Once nearly every site is busy, extra substrate has no free enzyme to bind, so the rate approaches the maximum set by enzyme amount and turnover, Vmax = kcat[E]T.

Incorrect. Denaturation is the loss of a protein's three-dimensional structure, caused by heat, extreme pH, detergents or chaotropic agents, and it destroys activity. Saturated enzymes are fully folded and working at top speed. Confusing the plateau (saturation) with loss of structure (denaturation) is a classic mistake.

p: The Michaelis–Menten equation, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]), describes how the initial rate v of a simple enzyme depends on substrate concentration [S]. Vmax is the rate when every active site is busy, and Km is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax.

The plateau arises because enzymes have a limited number of active sites. At low [S] most sites are empty, so adding substrate fills more of them and the rate climbs nearly in proportion. At high [S] almost all sites are occupied; each enzyme is already working as fast as kcat allows, so the rate levels off at Vmax and becomes independent of [S] (zero order).
To raise a saturated rate you must add enzyme or increase kcat. Do not confuse saturation with denaturation (structure lost, activity drops) or with equilibrium (net rate zero).

fig.cap: Fraction of active sites holding substrate, computed from [S]/(Km + [S]). Above about 10 Km nearly every site is busy, so extra substrate cannot raise the rate.
fig.alt: Four panels of 20 enzyme circles each; filled circles show bound substrate: 2 of 20 at 0.1 Km, 10 at Km, 18 at 10 Km and 19 at 20 Km.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; occupancy computed from the Michaelis–Menten fraction [S]/(Km + [S]).

fig.cap: The Michaelis–Menten curve levels off at Vmax once [S] is far above Km.
fig.alt: Curve of v over Vmax against [S] over Km flattening toward 1, with the saturated zero-order region shaded.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the Michaelis–Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).

x1A_197.trap: The plateau is saturation of active sites, not denaturation, equilibrium or substrate inhibition.

ox: Incorrect. No reversible inhibitor makes an enzyme more efficient. Every type divides apparent kcat/Km by α = 1 + [I]/Ki (the factor for binding free enzyme), which is 1 or more, so kcat/Km can stay the same (uncompetitive) or fall, but never rise. An increase would point to an activator, not an inhibitor.

Incorrect. An unchanged kcat/Km is the uncompetitive case: an inhibitor that binds only ES lowers apparent kcat and apparent Km by the same factor, so their ratio is unchanged. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor lowers kcat but leaves Km alone, so the ratio cannot stay the same.

Incorrect. Reversible inhibition is partial and concentration-dependent: at any finite [I], some enzyme is free and active. kcat/Km is divided by (1 + [I]/Ki), which approaches zero only as [I] becomes very large. It does not drop to zero at ordinary inhibitor levels.

Correct. A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds E and ES equally, so it divides the apparent kcat (and Vmax) by α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki while leaving Km unchanged. The apparent kcat/Km = (kcat/α′)/Km therefore falls by the same factor, for example to half at [I] = Ki. In effect fewer active enzyme molecules are available.

p: kcat/Km governs the rate at low [S]: v = (kcat/Km)[E]T[S]. How each reversible inhibitor changes it follows from what it does to kcat and Km.

Competitive (binds E): kcat same, Km × α, so kcat/Km ÷ α. Uncompetitive (binds ES): kcat ÷ α′ and Km ÷ α′, so kcat/Km is unchanged; uncompetitive inhibitors have little effect at low [S]. Pure noncompetitive (binds E and ES equally): kcat ÷ α′, Km same, so kcat/Km ÷ α′. Mixed: kcat/Km ÷ α.

A neat consequence: kcat/Km (the low-[S] rate constant) reflects only binding to free enzyme, while kcat (the high-[S] rate) reflects binding to ES. Inhibitors that bind free enzyme hurt most at low [S].

fig.cap: Apparent kcat, Km and kcat/Km relative to control when α or α′ = 2. kcat/Km falls for competitive and pure noncompetitive inhibitors but is unchanged for an uncompetitive one.
fig.alt: Grouped bar chart for no inhibitor, competitive, uncompetitive and pure noncompetitive inhibition showing apparent kcat, Km and kcat over Km; kcat over Km is 1, 0.5, 1 and 0.5, with the last highlighted green.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest graph computed from the general inhibition model with α = 1 + [I]/Ki and α′ = 1 + [I]/Ki′ set to 2.

x1A_198.trap: Uncompetitive leaves kcat/Km unchanged; pure noncompetitive lowers it because Km stays put while kcat falls.

ox: Incorrect. Halving is the change in total activity (1000 → 500 units), which is the yield: 50% of the enzyme was recovered. Specific activity divides activity by total protein, and because protein dropped far more than activity, specific activity rises.

Incorrect. A 100-fold change is the drop in total protein alone (500 → 5 mg). If no enzyme had been lost, specific activity would indeed rise 100-fold, but half of the activity was lost, so the actual rise is 100/2 = 50-fold.

Correct. Specific activity = total activity ÷ total protein. Before: 1000 units/500 mg = 2 units/mg. After: 500 units/5 mg = 100 units/mg. The ratio 100/2 = 50 is the purification fold. Specific activity rises because the steps removed mostly contaminating proteins, so the enzyme is a much larger share of the remaining protein, even though half of it was lost.

Incorrect. Specific activity stays the same only if activity and protein fall in proportion, meaning the steps removed enzyme and contaminants equally and achieved no purification. Here protein fell 100-fold and activity only 2-fold, so the enzyme has been enriched.

p: Total activity (units) measures how much enzyme is present by what it does; total protein (mg) measures everything in the sample. Specific activity = total activity / total protein (units/mg) and measures purity: it rises as contaminating proteins are removed.

A purification table tracks yield (total activity now ÷ starting total activity, here 50%) and fold purification (specific activity now ÷ starting specific activity, here 50-fold). Good steps raise specific activity a lot while losing little activity. A pure enzyme reaches a maximum, constant specific activity.
Common errors: mixing up yield with purification, and using only the protein change. Always compute both specific activities and take their ratio.

fx.f: specific activity = total activity / total protein
fx.w: Units per mg of protein. Fold purification = specific activity (step) ÷ specific activity (start); yield = total activity (step) ÷ total activity (start).

fig.cap: Purification table from the question: protein fell 100-fold and activity 2-fold, so specific activity rose 50-fold, from 2 to 100 units/mg.
fig.alt: Table with rows start (500 mg, 1000 units, 2 units per mg) and final (5 mg, 500 units, 100 units per mg); a change row shows divide by 100, divide by 2 and times 50; pills mark times 50 correct and times 100, divide by 2 and unchanged wrong.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram using the values in the question.

x1A_199.trap: Specific activity = activity ÷ protein; compute both values, do not use the protein change alone.

ox: Incorrect. If the active site were destroyed, the enzyme would no longer catalyze the reaction. The stem says it still catalyzes and now gives a normal hyperbolic curve, so the catalytic machinery is intact. What has been lost is regulation and cooperativity, not catalysis.

Correct. Allosteric enzymes such as aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase) are built from catalytic subunits (two c₃ trimers) and regulatory subunits (three r₂ dimers). Mercurials such as p-hydroxymercuribenzoate react with cysteine thiols in the regulatory chains and cause the complex to fall apart without breaking peptide bonds. The free catalytic trimers still make product, but without the regulatory subunits and the inter-subunit contacts that drive the T ⇌ R transition, they lose cooperativity (sigmoidal → hyperbolic) and no longer respond to the inhibitor CTP.

Incorrect. Hydrolyzing the primary structure means cutting peptide bonds, which would require a protease or harsh acid or base, not mild mercurial treatment. Breaking the chains would also likely destroy catalysis. The observations fit a reversible separation of subunits held together by noncovalent forces.

Incorrect. If the inhibitor were covalently attached in the active site, the enzyme would be blocked and would stop catalyzing. Instead the enzyme keeps working, and simply ignores the inhibitor. That points to the loss of the inhibitor's binding site (on the regulatory subunits), not to an inhibitor stuck in the active site.

p: Allosteric enzymes are usually multi-subunit proteins whose activity is changed by molecules binding at sites other than the active site (allosteric sites). Many switch between a low-affinity, less active T (tense) state and a high-affinity, more active R (relaxed) state. In some, catalysis and regulation sit on different subunits.

Aspartate transcarbamoylase (ATCase), the first committed step of pyrimidine synthesis, is the classic example: c₆r₆, two catalytic trimers and three regulatory dimers. CTP (the pathway end product) inhibits it by binding the regulatory subunits (feedback inhibition), and ATP activates it. Mercurial treatment separates the subunits: the catalytic trimers remain active but show hyperbolic kinetics and no regulation, while the regulatory dimers bind effectors but cannot catalyze.

This experiment shows that cooperativity and allosteric control arise from subunit interactions in the quaternary structure, not from the active site itself. Protein kinase A (R₂C₂) is another enzyme with separate regulatory subunits.

fig.cap: Mild mercurial treatment separates ATCase (c₆r₆) into two catalytic trimers and three regulatory dimers. The free catalytic trimers still work but give a hyperbolic curve and ignore allosteric effectors.
fig.alt: Left: native enzyme with two catalytic trimers and three regulatory dimers. Arrow labelled mild mercurial. Right: separated catalytic trimers labelled still catalytic and regulatory dimers labelled bind CTP and ATP, no catalysis. Below: a small graph with a sigmoidal native curve and a hyperbolic curve for free catalytic trimers, and pills marking subunits separated as correct.
fig.credit: Original 520 Quest diagram; small curves computed from the Hill equation (n = 2 and n = 1). Facts after the classic Gerhart and Schachman ATCase experiments as described in Lehninger and Berg biochemistry texts.

x1A_200.trap: Loss of cooperativity and regulation with catalysis intact means the catalytic and regulatory subunits were separated.

ox: Wrong. +1 counts only the amino group. The side-chain and the alpha carboxyl are both negative at pH 7.4, so they outweigh it. Trap: forgetting the side chain.
Wrong. 0 is what you get if you leave the side-chain carboxyl neutral. Its pKa is about 3.9, far below 7.4, so it has lost its H and is negative.
Correct. Alpha-NH3+ is +1, alpha-COO- is -1, and the side-chain COO- is -1. Total: +1 -1 -1 = -1.
Wrong. -2 would need the amino group to be neutral. Its pKa is about 9.6, well above 7.4, so it still holds its H and stays +1.

p: A pKa is the pH at which a group is half protonated (holds an H) and half deprotonated (has lost it). If the pH is BELOW the pKa, the group mostly keeps its H. If the pH is ABOVE the pKa, it mostly loses its H.
Acids (COOH) are neutral with H and -1 without. Amines (NH3+) are +1 with H and neutral without. Add up every group to get the net charge.

q1.eli: Think of each group as a kid holding a balloon. In a weak 'acid crowd' (low pH) they hold on. In a strong 'base crowd' (high pH) they let go.
mem: Alpha-COOH pKa about 2, alpha-NH3+ pKa about 9-10
Aspartate and glutamate side chains are acidic (pKa about 4) and negative at pH 7.4
pH below pKa means protonated; pH above pKa means deprotonated

fm.f: Net charge = sum of group charges, where each group's charge depends on whether pH is above or below its pKa
fm.why: Charges of separate groups simply add together.
fm.nc: Only compare pH to each pKa and add three small integers.

q1.sc: Acidic side chain (Asp, Glu) at body pH means one extra negative charge on top of the neutral zwitterion backbone.
q1.trap: Forgetting the side chain. The backbone alone is neutral (+1 and -1), so the side chain sets the net charge.
q1.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biochemistry texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. The inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site. Extra substrate can outcompete it, so Vmax stays the same (100). More substrate is needed to reach half Vmax, so apparent Km rises (2.0 to 5.0).
Wrong. Same Km and lower Vmax is the pattern of noncompetitive inhibition, where the inhibitor removes working enzyme. Trap: mixing up the two types.
Wrong. Both falling is uncompetitive inhibition (Vmax 50, Km 1.0). The inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex. This is not competition for the active site.
Wrong. A lower Km means higher apparent affinity. An inhibitor that fights the substrate makes binding look weaker, not stronger.

p: Km is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. A higher Km means the enzyme looks like it grabs substrate less well. Vmax is the top speed when every enzyme is busy.

A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate and sits in the active site. If you flood the system with substrate, the substrate wins, so top speed is unchanged. But you need more substrate to get halfway, so Km goes up.

q2.eli: Two kids want the same swing. If a huge crowd of kids lines up for it, eventually the swing is always full (same top speed), but each kid has to push harder to get a turn (higher Km).
mem: Competitive: Vmax same, Km up
Noncompetitive: Vmax down, Km same
Uncompetitive: Vmax down, Km down
Competitive inhibition can be overcome by adding more substrate
q2.trap: Mixing up which constant moves. Competitive keeps Vmax because substrate can win the fight.
q2.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biochemistry texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Competitive lines share the same y-intercept (1/Vmax) and cross on the y-axis, with different slopes. They are not parallel.
Wrong. Noncompetitive lines share the same x-intercept (-1/Km) and cross on the x-axis. They have different slopes, so they are not parallel.
Correct. Uncompetitive: Vmax falls 100 to 50 and Km falls 2.0 to 1.0, both by the same factor. Slope = Km/Vmax = 2/100 = 1/50 and 1/50 again. The slope is unchanged, so the lines are parallel.
Wrong. Mixed inhibition changes both Km and Vmax by different amounts, so the lines cross somewhere off both axes. They are not parallel.

p: A Lineweaver-Burk plot graphs 1/rate (y) against 1/[substrate] (x). It gives a straight line. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the x-intercept is -1/Km, and the slope is Km/Vmax.

Inhibitors change these numbers. If Km and Vmax both drop by the same factor, the slope Km/Vmax does not change. Lines with the same slope are parallel. That is the signature of uncompetitive inhibition.

q3.eli: Two ramps with the same steepness but starting at different heights never meet. Parallel lines means the same slope.
mem: Parallel lines: uncompetitive
Lines cross on the y-axis: competitive
Lines cross on the x-axis: noncompetitive
x-intercept = -1/Km, y-intercept = 1/Vmax, slope = Km/Vmax

fm.f: Slope = Km / Vmax, where Km = substrate level at half Vmax, Vmax = top speed
fm.v: No inhibitor: Km = 2.0, Vmax = 100. Uncompetitive: Km = 1.0, Vmax = 50
fm.why: Equal slopes mean parallel lines on the plot.
fm.nc: Both ratios reduce to 1/50 by simple division.

q3.trap: Remembering only the crossing points and forgetting that parallel is the odd one out.
q3.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biochemistry texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Proline's side chain loops back and bonds to its own backbone nitrogen, forming a rigid ring. That fixes the backbone angle so it cannot fit a helix. Its nitrogen also has no H, so it cannot donate the H-bond that holds helix turns together.
Wrong. Disulfide bonds come from cysteine, and they link distant parts of the protein. They are not what disrupts helices. Trap: mixing up proline and cysteine.
Wrong. Proline's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged. A full positive charge describes lysine or arginine.
Wrong. Proline is not limited to beta-sheets. It breaks beta-sheets too and is common in turns and loops.

p: An alpha-helix is a spiral held together by hydrogen bonds. Each backbone N-H donates its H to a backbone C=O four residues away. The backbone must also twist at specific angles.
Proline is special. Its side chain bonds to its own nitrogen, making a ring. The ring locks the angle, and the nitrogen has no H to donate. So proline kinks the helix and is often found at turns.

q4.eli: A helix is like a spring held in shape by tiny hooks. Proline is a stiff metal bar with no hook, so the spring bends.
mem: Proline: rigid ring, no backbone N-H, helix breaker and turn former
Glycine is also a helix breaker (too flexible)
Cysteine forms disulfides
q4.trap: Picking a charged or disulfide answer. The reason is shape plus a missing H-bond donor.
q4.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biochemistry texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Methionine has sulfur, but it is a thioether (S bonded to two carbons) with no H to lose. It cannot link to another residue by oxidation. Trap: sulfur does not equal disulfide.
Correct. Cysteine has a thiol (-SH). When two thiols are oxidized, they lose their H atoms and form an S-S disulfide bond. This covalent bridge stabilizes tertiary and quaternary structure.
Wrong. Serine has a hydroxyl (-OH). Oxygen does not form this kind of covalent cross-link. It is a site for phosphorylation instead.
Wrong. Tyrosine has an aromatic ring with an -OH (phenol). It can be phosphorylated but does not form disulfides.

p: A thiol is an -SH group. Oxidation removes H atoms. When two cysteine thiols are oxidized, their sulfur atoms join to make an S-S bond called a disulfide bridge.

This is a covalent bond, much stronger than hydrogen bonds or ionic interactions. It holds parts of a protein together, which is common in secreted proteins like antibodies and insulin. Reduction breaks the bridge.

q5.eli: Two Velcro strips that get permanently glued together is a disulfide bridge. Glue is stronger than Velcro.
mem: Only cysteine makes disulfide bonds
Oxidation forms S-S; reduction breaks it
Two cysteines joined are called cystine
q5.trap: Choosing methionine because it also has sulfur. Only cysteine has a free -SH.
q5.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biochemistry texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Vmax = kcat x [E]total. Double the enzyme and you double the number of active sites, so Vmax doubles (100 to 200). Km is a property of how the enzyme binds the substrate, so it stays the same.
Wrong. Km depends on the enzyme-substrate pair, not on the amount of enzyme. Trap: thinking more enzyme means better affinity.
Wrong. Vmax does double, but Km does not. Km is intrinsic.
Wrong. More enzyme means more catalytic sites working at once. Maximum rate rises.

p: Vmax is the top speed when every enzyme is busy. More enzyme molecules means more workers, so a higher top speed. Km is how much substrate it takes to reach half of Vmax. It tells you how tightly one enzyme grabs the substrate.
Adding more of the same enzyme does not change how well each one grabs substrate. So Vmax changes with enzyme amount; Km does not.

q6.eli: More cashiers means more customers served per minute (higher Vmax). Each cashier picks up a customer just as readily as before, so how well each one grabs a customer (Km) stays the same.
mem: Vmax = kcat x [E]total
Km is intrinsic to the enzyme and substrate
Changing enzyme amount changes Vmax only

fm.f: Vmax = kcat x [E]total, where kcat = turnover number (reactions per enzyme per second), [E]total = total enzyme concentration, Vmax = top speed
fm.v: Original Vmax = kcat x [E] = 100 (example). New enzyme = 2 x [E]
fm.why: Each enzyme works at the same rate, so twice as many gives twice the top speed.

q6.sc: Ask: does the change affect the enzyme's shape or its amount? Amount changes Vmax only. Shape or inhibitors can change Km.
q6.trap: Assuming Km changes too. Km never changes with enzyme amount.
